PREFACE 

It has been my purpose, in the preparation of this work, to present a review of all of the Florida decisions involving questions of chancery pleading and practice. With this in mind, every decision of the Supreme Court of Florida bearing upon the subject has been carefully examined and digested. The material so obtained was both competent and abundant. While the 1931 Chancery Act completely revised Florida chancery procedure, it did not change the fundamental principles of equity pleading and practice and, with the exception of a few cases based upon statutes or rules which are now obsolete, all decisions examined are still pertinent and have been cited in this volume. 

In addition to the Florida decisions, I have also cited a number of decisions of the Federal courts construing former Federal equity rules which are identical with provisions of the 1931 Chancery Act. 

Under well settled principles of law, these decisions, except where they are not in harmony with the spirit and policy of the 1931 Chancery Act, may be considered as controlling in determining the construction of that Act.

In each instance where a provision of the 1931 Chancery Act has been cited, I have, for convenience, given a reference to both the Compiled General Laws of Florida, 1927, Permanent Supplement, and to the Florida Chancery Act, Annotated, 2nd edition, by Mr. Edward McCarthy, Jr. There is also included, as an appendix, a copy of the 1931 Chancery Act. 

In the preparation of this volume, I am deeply indebted to my wife, Neeta B. Kooman. Without her constant labor in copying annotations and quotations from the many decisions examined, in typing and re-typing the drafts of the various chapters as they were revised and amended, and in the vast amount of other detail work involved in the preparation of the final manuscript, this work would have been impossible. I also gratefully acknowledge the assistance and co-operation of Messrs. John M. Elliott and J. T. Doonan, of 

The Harrison Company. 

St. Petersburg, Florida

February 13, 1939 HAROLD A. KOOMAN

CHAPTER I ORIGIN OF EQUITY COURTS § 1. Historical Development of English Equity Courts. 

2. Equity Courts in the United States. 

3. Equity Courts in Florida. 

§ 1. Historical Development of English Equity Courts.-Prior to the colonization of America, English jurisprudence had developed into two divisions generally known as "law" and "equity." Equity was the more recent development. 

Originally all judicial authority in England was considered to be vested in the king. But the physical impossibility of its exercise by him led to its delegation to agencies known as courts of common law. These courts exercised their jurisdiction in accordance with arbitrary and rigid forms and principles supposed to have been established from time immemorial. The failure of the common law courts to do justice and to meet the needs of a developing social and economic life was directly responsible for the growth of equity and equity courts.

One of the principal causes of the inadequacy of the common law courts to meet the needs of the times was their inability to enforce justice where the offending party was rich and powerful and the complaining party poor and weak. Throughout the Middle Ages the attempts of the feudal barons to extend their influence and to prevent the extension of royal power created a condition of turbulence and partial anarchy which enabled the powerful to frequently frustrate the remedies of the common law courts. nature arose even as late as the sixteenth century. was considered to be the source of all judicial authority, the practice grew up of petitioning him to do justice and to relieve his 

Cases of this 

Since the king

[Ch. 1 subjects from oppression of this kind, and the king's authority was often exercised for that purpose.' 

Another and perhaps the principal cause of the inadequacy of the common law courts to meet the needs of the times was their rigid adherence to certain "forms of action." It was required that every remedial right be enforced through one of these forms. 

Every action was begun by the issuance, in the name of the king, of a document called a "writ" which contained a statement of the facts upon which the action was based and indicated what form of action was brought and what remedy demanded. If these writs could have been altered and increased to meet the requirements of changing social relationships and an expanding commercial life, the common law courts would no doubt have eventually been the sole agency for the exercise of judicial authority. But the clerks issuing these writs could not draw up new ones or alter the old ones in any material respect. If there was no existing writ containing facts substantially the same as those presented by the complaining party, or no existing form of action appropriate to the relief sought, he was denied a remedy. Furthermore, even the issuance of a writ by the clerks in a particular case did not insure a remedy. The common law judges constantly exercised the power of determining the sufficiency of the writ and, if it did not conform to the rigid requirements of the form of action for which it was issued, the case was dismissed.

In general, the forms of action employed by the common law courts gave but three kinds of judgments. These were judgments for the recovery of real property, judgments for the recovery of chattels, and judgments for the recovery of money. In addition to denying even these remedies except in cases conforming to rigid and arbitrary rules, such as the rule that no contract could be enforced unless it created a debt in a fixed amount, or was evidenced by an instrument under seal, the remedies themselves were obviously inadequate to meet the needs of a social organization rapidly becoming more complex. Legislation enacted late in the thirteenth century and designed to remedy this condition met with only partial success due to the strict and narrow construction placed upon it by the common law judges. It was but natural, therefore, that a king

ORIGIN OF EQUITY COURTS 

who had been called upon to remedy the wrongs committed upon his subjects by those too powerful to be within reach of the law should also be called upon to mitigate the harshness and to remedy the defects of the common law itself.2 

Petitions of this nature were originally passed upon by the king or by the king and his council. But the ever increasing number of such petitions, and the growing demands of matters of state upon the time of the king and his council, gradually compelled a reference of most of the petitions to the chancellor. This official was a member of the king's council and was an adviser and personal representative of the king. His clerks issued the writs with which common law actions were commenced and he himself exercised judicial powers in a limited class of common law cases. Because of his familiarity with the laws of the realm he was the natural official to whom to refer petitions for the exercise of the royal prerogative in judicial matters. By the middle of the fourteenth century it was required by royal decree that all such petitions be addressed directly to the chancellor. The effect of this decree was to recog-. nize and establish a separate court, under the chancellor, for granting relief in all matters requiring the exercise of the royal prerogative.3

This court of chancery grew rapidly in importance and in the volume of business which it handled. There were numerous reasons for this growth. The chancellor, when no common law remedy was applicable, could and would summon the parties to litigation before him and examine them under oath. This practice, known as "probing the conscience," gave to the court of chancery an advantage in discovering truth and doing justice not possessed by common law courts. Furthermore, the chancellor could grant the remedy of injunction which was unknown to the common law courts. The judicial recognition of uses, the predecessor of the modern trust, by the court of chancery in the latter part of the fourteenth century also served to enlarge its sphere of activity.4 

After some controversy between the common law and chancery courts as to the line of demarcation between their respective juris-

dictions, the courts of chancery, by the latter part of the fifteenth century, had emerged with a distinct jurisdiction and procedure. 

Their jurisdiction was based mainly on fraud, accident, and trust. 

Suits were commenced by the filing of a bill of complaint and a subpoena was thereupon issued to the defendant. By the seventeenth century the principles of equity jurisprudence were beginning to be clearly defined and, as indicating the growing importance of precedents, the decisions of the court of chancery were being reported. Most of the reports of English equity cases date from 

1660. But the passing of the royal prerogative and the appointment as chancellor of men schooled in the common law soon gave to equity jurisprudence and procedure a substantial measure of the fixity of principle and technicality of procedure of the common law. With some modifications and changes the English courts of equity, as thus constituted, existed until 1873. In that year they were combined with the courts of common law and the principles of law and equity were required to be administered by the same court and the same judge and legal and equitable relief was permitted to be granted in the same action. § 2. Equity Courts in the United States.-English equity, like the common law, was a part of the system of jurisprudence brought to America by the colonists. However, pioneer conditions did not require the rapid development of equity courts. It was not until after the Revolution that equity courts and equity jurisprudence became firmly established in most of the United States.5 In many states the distinction between law and equity has now been abolished and, as in England, both are administered by the same court and judge in the same action. In other states, and in the Federal courts until very recent years, the distinction between law and equity has been preserved, although both have been administered in the same court and by the same judge. In a few states, law and equity are still administered in different courts and by distinct sets of judges. § 3. Equity Courts in Florida. Florida is among those states which preserve the distinction between law and equity but administer both in the same courts.6

ORIGIN OF EQUITY COURTS 

The territory of Florida was ceded by Spain to the United States by a treaty ratified in 1821. From that date until 1845, Florida. was governed as a Federal territory and her courts were Federal courts. In 1838, in preparation for the state's admission to the 

Union, a Constitution was drafted and in 1839 this Constitution was ratified by a vote of the territorial electorate. The admission of the state to the Union was deferred, however, until 1845 and the Constitution of 1838 did not go into effect until March 3, 1845. 

It was provided in this Constitution that the judicial power of the state should be vested in a supreme court, courts of chancery, and circuit courts.7 It was further provided, however, that the circuit courts should exercise original equity jurisdiction unless the general assembly should establish a separate court or courts having such jurisdiction. The separate courts of chancery contemplated by the Constitution were to be presided over by chancellors distinct from the judges of the circuit courts. However, the general assembly never established these separate chancery courts. Appellate jurisdiction in equity was vested in the supreme court.9 Substantially the same provisions in regard to equity courts were contained in the Constitution of 1861,10 which was adopted when Florida seceded from the Union, and in the Constitution of 1865,11 which was adopted when Florida again became one of the United States. But separate courts of chancery were never created under either of these constitutions. 

The Constitution of 1868 unconditionally conferred equity jurisdiction upon the circuit courts. It provided that those courts should have "original jurisdiction in all cases of equity,"12 and that the supreme court should have "appellate jurisdiction in all cases in equity."13 The circuit judges were appointed by the governor and confirmed by the senate and held office for eight years.14

The present Constitution of Florida, known as the Constitution of 1885, contains provisions regarding equity courts similar to those contained in the Constitution of 1868. It provides that "the circuit courts shall have exclusive original jurisdiction in all cases in equity."15 The circuit courts are presided over by judges appointed by the governor and confirmed by the senate and hold office for six years.16 In practice, however, it is customary for the governor to appoint the candidate receiving a majority vote of the electors participating in the Democratic party primary for the circuit in which the judge is to serve. The supreme court has appellate jurisdiction in all cases in equity originating in the circuit courts.17 

The Constitution of Florida thus recognizes the powers and functions of courts of equity18 and strictly preserves the distinction between courts of equity and courts of law and their respective fields of operation.19

§ 4.-Definition of Equity Jurisdiction.-There is a clear distinction between the term "jurisdiction," in its strict meaning, and as generally used in equity jurisprudence.' "Jurisdiction," in the strict meaning of the term, and as applied to judicial officers and tribunals, is the power or authority to hear and determine a cause.2 It is the power lawfully conferred to deal with a general abstract question, to hear the facts in any case relating to that question, and to determine whether those facts are sufficient to invoke the exercise of the power. Jurisdiction includes the power to inquire into facts, to apply the law, to make a decision, and to render a judgment.4 The test of jurisdiction is whether the tribunal had the power to enter upon the inquiry in question, 1. Malone v. Meres, 91 Fla. 709, 109 

So. 677. 

2. Bucky v. Willard, 16 Fla. 330; 

Hays v. McNealy, 16 Fla. 409; Johnson v. McKinnon, 54 Fla. 221, 45 So. 

23, 127 Am. St. Rep. 135, 13 L. R. A. (N. S.) 874, 14 Ann. Cas. 180; Malone v. Meres, 91 Fla. 709, 109 So. 677; 

Lovett v. Lovett, 93 Fla. 611, 112 So. 768. 

3. Lovett v. Lovett, 93 Fla. 611, 112

4. McGowin v. McGowin, 122 Fla. 

394, 165 So. 274.

[Ch. 2 

and not whether its method was regular, its findings right, or its conclusions in accordance with law. Jurisdiction means no more than the power to adjudge concerning a general question, and it is not dependent upon the state of facts which may appear in a particular case or the ultimate existence of a good cause of action in the plaintiff therein.5

Want of jurisdiction of the subject matter is to be distinguished from an erroneous exercise of jurisdiction. Want of jurisdiction renders a judgment void and open to collateral attack, whereas an erroneous exercise of jurisdiction merely renders a judgment open to reversal on appeal. "Equity jurisdiction," as distinguished on the one side from the general power to decide matters at all, and on the other from jurisdiction "at law," is the power to hear certain kinds and classes of civil cases according to the method and procedure adopted by courts of chancery and to decide those cases in accordance with the doctrines and rules of equity jurisprudence. Such decisions may involve either the determination of equitable rights or the granting of equitable remedies. In order that a case may come within the scope of equity jurisdiction one of two alternatives is essential. 

Either the primary right, estate, or interest to be maintained, or the violation of which furnishes the cause of action, must be in its nature purely equitable, or, if a remedy is sought which may also be given by a court of law, it must be one which, under the facts and circumstances of the case, can only be made complete and adequate through equitable modes of procedure.7 

At the same time, however, if a court having general jurisdiction of all actions at law and suits in equity should hear and decide, according to equitable methods, a case which did not fall within the scope of equity jurisdiction because both the primary right and the remedy granted were wholly legal and properly within the domain of the common law, the judgment, though subject to reversal, would not necessarily be null and void. Whether the relief sought in a particular case should properly be through an action at law or a

suit in equity does not ordinarily involve the power of the court to enter a judgment in the matter. The question is one of procedure unless the right to a jury trial is unlawfully denied. If a suit in equity is brought when an action at law is the proper remedy, and the defendant is duly served with process or appears and does not challenge the plaintiff's right to proceed in equity, and the court does not sua sponte raise the question and dismiss the cause, and a final decree is rendered, whether upon a decree pro confesso or a contest made, the decree, if erroneous, is not void. And after the time for taking an appeal has expired the defendant is not entitled to have the decree vacated or set aside on collateral attack. On the contrary, the objection that the case does not come within the equity jurisdiction of the court must ordinarily be raised by the defendant at the commencement of the proceeding or it will be regarded as waived and the judgment will not even be erroneous. 

Where the court has jurisdiction to adjudicate the rights involved in a case, the enforcement of those rights at law or in equity depends upon the action of the parties and the acquiescence of the court.

Thus, where a bill in equity is brought in a court of general equity and common law powers for the purpose of enforcing a mortgage or other lien predicated upon a written instrument which, taken alone or in connection with the allegations of the bill, is not a mortgage but a conditional sales contract with no lien features, and the defendant appears and suffers a decree pro confesso to be entered against him, or contests the merits, and a final decree is rendered enforcing a lien under the written instrument, the decree, though erroneous, is not void for want of jurisdiction over the subject matter. The defendant, having appeared and failed to challenge the right to proceed in equity, and having failed to seek relief by appropriate procedure such as a bill of review or appeal from the final decree within the time allowed by law, is not entitled to have the decree vacated on the ground that it is void.

In some instances, however, where the facts show very clearly that the rights involved in the controversy and the remedies demanded are purely legal and completely within the scope of ordinary legal proceedings, the equity court will itself raise the objection at any stage of the cause even though the question was not in any way raised by the parties.10 

§ 5.-Equity Jurisdiction as Affected by Adequacy of Remedy at 

Law. As previously stated, equity jurisdiction cannot be invoked unless the right sought to be protected or enforced is purely equitable and not recognized by courts of common law, or unless the right, though legal in its nature, is one which cannot be adequately enforced or protected by a common law remedy.¹¹ In the first case, of course, the common law gives no remedy whatsoever; in the second case, the common law remedy, though existing, is inadequate. Equity jurisdiction may therefore be said to depend upon the existence and adequacy of a remedy at law. 

This rule has been expressed in various ways. It is often said that, where there is a plain and adequate remedy at law, resort to a court of equity is unnecessary and improper. 12 In some cases it is stated that equity will not take jurisdiction where the remedy at law is full, adequate, and complete.13 In other cases it is said that, where the remedy at law is adequate, there is no jurisdiction in a court of equity to hear and determine the controversy. 14 

In any event, no principle of law is better settled, 15 and it has been repeatedly held that a bill of complaint which shows on its face that the plaintiff has an adequate remedy at law cannot be main-

Where the existence of an adequate remedy at law is in doubt, a court of equity will not, of its own motion, refuse to proceed with the cause.

Nor will the objection be regarded with favor if first raised by the defendant in the appellate court. By its very nature, the objection is of that class which ought to be taken at the earliest stage of the suit, before costs have accumulated, in order that the lapse of time may not cause irreparable injury. The well established rule of practice on this question is that, if the subject matter of the suit is not without the jurisdiction of a court of equity, the objection that there is an effectual and complete remedy at law must be taken by motion to dismiss and comes too late at the hearing or on appeal.19

In order to preclude the exercise of equity jurisdiction it is not sufficient to merely show that there is a comparable remedy at law. 

The legal remedy must be as complete and beneficial and as practical and efficient to the ends of justice and its prompt administration as the remedy in equity.21 Stated in another way, the jurisdiction in equity attaches unless the legal remedy, both as regards the final relief and the mode of obtaining it, is as efficient as the remedy which equity would confer under the same circumstances.22 

If the remedy at law would afford only partial relief, it is incomplete and inadequate and the jurisdiction of equity may be invoked.23 

And in cases where it is doubtful whether the legal remedy is complete and adequate, and where a more ample and appropriate remedy is thereby afforded, courts of equity will take cognizance and give relief if that can be done in accordance with recognized principles of chancery jurisprudence.24 In this connection it has been. stated that an aggrieved party resorting to the courts to settle a controversy has a right to select the forum through which he can secure full, adequate, and complete relief. He is not required to invoke the aid of a forum which will give inadequate relief and at the same time afford his adversary the best means to "back

The right to equitable relief is not dependent upon whether the computation of damages is simple or complex, but merely upon whether the legal remedy is adequate.26 And the inadequacy of a remedy at law to produce money has no bearing upon equity jurisdiction. All remedies, whether legal or equitable, frequently fail to do that, and to make that the test of equity jurisdiction would be substituting the result of a proceeding for the proceeding which is invoked to produce the result. The true test in cases of this character is whether a judgment could be obtained in a proceeding at law, and not whether the judgment would procure pecuniary compensation.27

Although the adequacy of a remedy at law is most frequently spoken of as a test of the jurisdiction of equity to hear and determine a cause, it is strictly inaccurate to call it so. The objection that the plaintiff has an adequate remedy at law is no more than a rule of practice in courts of chancery upon which an action will be dismissed or transferred to a law court if the objection is raised at the proper time and in the proper manner. And, even if a court of equity should erroneously proceed after the question is properly raised, its decree would not be void. It might be erroneous and subject to reversal in a direct proceeding, but it could not be collaterally impeached or disregarded.28 Such a result does not violate the rule that jurisdiction of the subject matter, that is, power to adjudicate the class of cases to which the particular case belongs, cannot be conferred by consent or acquiescence of the parties.29

Where no special circumstances are alleged in a bill of complaint bringing the case under some recognized head of equity jurisdiction, the issuance of a writ of prohibition to stop further proceedings in the cause is authorized even though there is not a complete absence of jurisdiction over the class of suits involved. One class of cases in which the question of the adequacy of the legal remedy has been frequently raised is that involving the legal title to land. In such cases courts of equity have consistently held that they will not take jurisdiction to try a mere question of legal title or the right to possession.31 A plaintiff, if entitled to the possession of land, may establish his legal title in an action of ejectment and recover possession and mesne profits in the same action.32

Where there is some supervening equity, however, which a court of common law cannot take notice of or protect, a court of equity may take jurisdiction to try a question of legal title to land.33 One supervening equity of this nature is a confusion of boundaries. 

But even this ground of equity jurisdiction is not favored unless special facts are shown to sustain it. Between independent proprietors such cases are left to the proper remedy at law. The general rule is not to entertain jurisdiction upon the ground that boundaries are in controversy unless there is also shown some act of fraud, negligence, omission, or misconduct on the part of persons whose special duty it is to preserve or perpetuate the boundaries.34 Thus, where the true boundaries of land are matters of fact equally accessible to both parties, and are capable of definite ascertainment by available evidence in a court of law where a jury trial is an organic right, equity will not take jurisdiction.35 

The fact that land was sold under a Federal court decree alleged to be invalid for want of jurisdiction is not such a supervening equity as will enable a plaintiff to resort to a state court of equity to settle the question of title between himself and the purchaser at the judicial sale.36 And, even though a plaintiff may be entitled

As in the case of real property, courts of equity will not, except in peculiar cases, take jurisdiction of controversies respecting the title to or possession of personal property.40 Thus equity will not take jurisdiction of a controversy involving the title to and possession of a plant for making abstracts of title to land.41 The remedy at law is adequate. Either trespass or an action for conversion may be resorted to for recovering the value of the property, or the property itself, with damages for its wrongful detention, may be recovered in replevin.42

The principle that equity will not take jurisdiction where legal remedies are adequate is also frequently applied to actions for breach of contract. Where the legal remedies for the breach of a contract are ample, the basis for equitable relief must be otherwise shown.43 Some substantial ground of equitable jurisdiction must be both alleged and proved before a mere money decree will be granted.44

Thus, if a party brings a suit merely to recover the purchase money which he has paid on an executory contract for the purchase of land, without seeking a rescission of the contract, he has no standing in a court of equity. His proper remedy is an action of general assumpsit.45 In fact, actions on money counts are often

In any case where fraud is not alleged or a trust is not sought to be impressed upon specific property, a suit in equity on an alleged obligation not essentially equitable in its nature cannot be maintained.48 For example, a bill to establish a lost conditional contract for the sale of personal property, and for a personal decree against the defendant party for the amount of money due thereunder, or a return of the property sold, is without equity. The bare allegation that the contract was lost affords no ground of equitable relief. And a judgment for the purchase price or a return of the property is relief obtainable in an action at law in which the contents of the lost contract can be established by secondary evidence.49

 § 6. Nature of Cases Cognizable in Equity.-The Constitution of 

Florida gives to the circuit courts "exclusive original jurisdiction in all cases in equity."51 The "cases in equity" referred to in the organic provision include all cases which are inherently cognizable in equity as distinguished from common law cases.52 

A complete analysis of the numerous grounds of equity jurisdiction and an analysis of the requirements for invoking jurisdiction under each of those grounds is the function of a treatise on equity jurisprudence and cannot be adequately dealt with in a work on equity pleading and practice. Therefore, the various heads of equity jurisdiction will be no more than mentioned, although the following summary is not intended to be exclusive:

Fraud, including the rescission and cancellation of contracts; mistake, including the reformation of contracts; the specific perlands caused by the operation of a railway on a street in front of the injured property cannot be recovered in equity. The remedy at law is adequate. Tampa R. Co. v. Mulhern, 

73 Fla. 146, 74 So. 297. 

A landlord has no standing in a court of equity to compel the payment of his rent out of any particular property unless he has a specific lien by mortgage or otherwise so as to render resort to chancery necessary to foreclose it. Without a specific lien, the remedy at law is simple and ample. 

The landlord may distrain or levy upon the property of his tenant for the rent. The question of any exemption from levy may be tried by an action of replevin or in case or trespass for the wrongful seizure. Haynes v. Mc- 

Gehee, 17 Fla. 159. 

A husband imprisoned in the penitentiary for life cannot maintain a suit in equity against his wife and another, to whom she has sold his property, for the purpose of adjusting the respective rights of the three, by charging that the sale is void and admitting that the wife has an interest in the property which should be determined. The wife has no interest in the property which can become the subject of a suit between them under the circumstances and the husband has his remedy at law against the purchaser if the sale is void. Willingham v. King, 23 Fla. 478, 2 So. 851.

A bill filed by a creditor for the purpose of subjecting lands to levy and sale under execution alleging that the debtor has a good legal title by deed and adverse possession, but that the title deed has been lost and the record thereof destroyed by fire, which bill is brought against a grantee of the heirs of a former owner who claims title, shows no ground of equity jurisdiction. The whole matter is cognizable in a court of law. Coogler v. 

Mayo, 21. Fla. 126. 

Resort to a court of equity to stay an execution at law is unnecessary since there is statutory authority in the law courts to stay executions issued by and returnable to them. C. 

G. L. 4516; Barnett v. Hickson, 52 

Fla. 457, 41 So. 606. The same is true of an illegal levy of execution. Bryan v. Long, 14 Fla. 366, McCall v. Matheson, 66 Fla. 157, 63 So. 701. 

51. Constitution of Florida, Article V, Section 11. 

52. State v. Atkinson, 102 Fla. 112, 135 So. 866.

[Ch. 2 

formance of contracts to convey land or contracts to sell chattels of peculiar value; trusts, including express, resulting, and constructive trusts, and other fiduciary relationships; accounting, where the accounts are so complicated as to render the remedy at law inadequate; the granting of injunctive relief in numerous cases; the foreclosure of liens such as mortgages and vendors' and vendees' liens; subrogation; the marshalling of assets; the protection of creditors. through the setting aside of fraudulent conveyances and the appointment of receivers; and the quieting of title to real estate. 

Many other instances of equity jurisdiction, both inherent and of subjects conferred by statute, could be enumerated. It will be noted that in practically all of the cases of equity jurisdiction above listed the remedy usually sought in equity is not a judgment for money or for the recovery of possession of real or personal property, these being the only remedies known to the courts of common law.53 This, of course, is one reason for the exclusive jurisdiction of equity over the matters mentioned. 

§ 7.-Equity Having Jurisdiction for One Purpose Will Settle En tire Controversy.— In order to avoid a multiplicity of suits, and in order that a complete, effectual, and final decree adjusting the rights. and equities of all parties in interest may be entered and enforced, a court of equity, having assumed jurisdiction of a cause on any equitable ground, will at the same time take jurisdiction of all other matters arising out of the subject matter of the suit and germane and necessary to the attainment of justice between the parties.54

In the accomplishment of this object, the court will enjoin actions at law55 and bring before it all parties having an interest in the subject matter of the cause.56 The jurisdiction so acquired will be retained until all matters involved in the litigation between the parties or growing out of or connected with the subject matter of the suit are finally determined.

Thus, on granting an injunction to restrain waste, to compel the abatement of a dam, or for any other cause, a court of equity may, in order to do complete justice, decree that an accounting be taken and also ascertain and award damages as incidental to the main relief sought.57 Similarly, when a court of equity has assumed jurisdiction for the purpose of reforming a written contract, it may retain jurisdiction and proceed to enforce the contract after its reformation so that full and complete justice may be administered.58 Where a trustee under an indenture of trust in the nature of a mortgage files suit to foreclose the lien of the deed, a court of equity, on petition of the first trustee, will also take jurisdiction to appoint a successor trustee.59

In cases where it is sought to rescind and cancel a contract for the sale of real estate, the court may, in addition to such relief, adjudicate and enforce a lien against the property described in the contract for the amount of the purchase money paid thereunder.60 

So also, where a court of equity assumes jurisdiction for the purpose of re-establishing a lost deed, and all the parties in interest are before the court, and the only question at issue is the amount and description of the land conveyed by the lost deed, which issue is found against the grantors, the court will, upon a proper prayer, retain jurisdiction of the case and make a final decree enjoining the grantors from further prosecuting a suit in ejectment against a party in possession of the land claiming under the grantee in the lost

Within the spirit of the rule that when the equity powers of the court have once been brought into action its active jurisdiction will be continued until full justice has been done between the parties come also all of those cases in which the defendant in a case demands equitable relief in consequence of equitable aid having been given to the plaintiff. Accordingly, a court of equity will, on assuming jurisdiction of a case, render to the defendant all relief' against the plaintiff or against co-defendants to which he may be equitably entitled.63 Thus, where a second mortgagee files a bill to foreclose his mortgage and to redeem the land from a first mortgage, an assignee of the latter mortgage may, by cross-bill or counterclaim, obtain a decree against the assignor for any moneys received by the assignor on account of the first mortgage which were not credited thereon and which were not disclosed to the assignee at the time of the transfer.64

When a court of equity has original jurisdiction of a case for one purpose, it will proceed to a complete adjudication of the entire case, including the settlement of purely legal rights and the granting of legal remedies which would otherwise be beyond the scope of its authority.65 In explanation of this principle it has been frequently stated that, when a court of equity can determine a matter, it will not be a handmaid to other courts, nor beget a suit to be ended elsewhere.66 Thus, where a court of equity has acquired jurisdiction to enjoin a trespass in digging and taking phosphate from the soil of land, it also has authority to decree an account of the phosphate

A common case in which courts of equity, having acquired jurisdiction because of some matter of equitable cognizance, will proceed to determine legal rights in order that the entire controversy may be terminated in one suit is one in which the court, having jurisdiction for purposes of discovery, will proceed to adjust the relative rights of the parties in order to avoid the multiplicity of suits which might result from sending them back to a court of law. 

Jurisdiction to determine legal rights in such cases will be entertained in most cases of fraud, account, accident, mistake, agency, waste, partnership, and similar matters. 68 Thus, where a plaintiff who had recovered in ejectment brought a bill in equity for the discovery of a map by which lots on the land had been sold, and sought relief against its fraudulent alteration and use, it was held that he was entitled to an account of mesne profits in the same action even though the latter relief was also obtainable through an action of trespass at law.69 

While it is true that a court of equity, having once obtained jurisdiction of a cause, will retain it for all purposes and administer complete relief, it is generally conceded that, in order to authorize relief which can be obtained in a suit at law, there must be some substantial ground of equitable jurisdiction. If there is no equitable ground of jurisdiction, and the relief sought can be as well obtained in an action at law, a court of equity cannot retain jurisdiction and grant a purely legal remedy. Mere statements in a bill on which the chancery jurisdiction might be maintained, but which are not proved, will not suffice to authorize a decree on such parts of the bill as, standing alone, would not give the court jurisdiction. To justify the retention of the cause for the granting of a purely legal remedy, not only must some substantial ground of equitable jurisdiction be alleged, but it must also be proved on the hearing.70

In order to authorize an equity court to grant legal relief under the foregoing rule, the legal demand must constitute some part of and be incidental to the equitable demand. Thus, a court of chancery cannot enter a personal decree for the payment of money claimed as a broker's commission when the claim, although embraced in a bill stating a proper cause of action for equitable relief, is an entirely different cause of action interjected into the suit by the plaintiff as a ground for relief additional to the equitable relief sought.73

As previously stated, the doctrine of retaining jurisdiction to completely adjust a controversy extends to the granting of relief to the defendant. In accordance with this rule, a defendant also may be granted relief of a legal character if his claim grows out of or is connected with the equities of the original bill. In order to afford complete relief between the parties, the court may consider and decree upon matters alleged in a counterclaim or cross-bill which are cognizable at law if they are germane to the original bill.74 

The doctrine that a court of equity, in order to completely and finally settle a controversy, will pass upon purely legal rights and grant legal remedies does not violate the constitutional guaranty75 of a trial by jury. § 8. Power of Legislature to Enlarge Equity Jurisdiction.-The 

Constitution of Florida gives to the circuit courts "exclusive original jurisdiction in all cases in equity" and "original jurisdiction ** of such other matters as the legislature may provide."77

The powers and functions of equity courts are thus recognized by the Constitution of Florida78 and the "cases in equity" referred to in the constitutional provision include all cases which are inherently cognizable in equity as distinguished from common law cases.79 

These cases have already been discussed.80 In ac- In addition, however, to the "cases in equity" which are peculiar to an equity forum, the legislature may by statute confer upon courts of equity jurisdiction of other matters which are not inappropriate to an equity forum, even though such cases are not embraced within the inherent jurisdiction of equity courts.81 cordance with this power, the legislature has authorized the foreclosure of tax liens in equity.82 The administration of the assets of a bank that is insolvent or being liquidated is not inherently an equity function, but it may by statute be conferred upon persons to be appointed by and to act under the direction of a court of equity.83

Courts of equity are also clothed by statute with full and complete jurisdiction over the matter of the homestead and exemptions allowed by the Constitution, not only to adjudicate as to the rights of parties thereto, but to control and direct the setting apart and allotment thereof, to restrain interference therewith or sale thereof under any inhibited process of law, and to pass upon and adjudicate the propriety of any exemption set apart by any officer, and to rectify it if improper.84

The legislature may not, however, enlarge the powers and jurisdiction of courts of equity so as to infringe upon the constitutional right to a trial by jury.85 It is well settled that the constitutional guaranty applies only to causes of action which were entitled to be tried by a jury according to the course of the common law of England as it existed at the time of the adoption of the first constitution of Florida. Courts of chancery, strictly speaking, are not courts of common law. Their jurisdiction and practice was derived principally from the civil law, where no jury was employed.86 

Consequently, the right to a trial by jury has no reference to equity courts, and is confined to legal claims and demands.87 But in the latter class of cases, the right exists in all its vigor, and it cannot be violated by conferring upon an equity court jurisdiction of a cause of action originally cognizable at law. 

Thus, actions for the recovery of real property have always been at law and, while statutes providing for the quieting of titles in equity will be sustained if this can be done without impairing constitutional rights, such statutes are invalid where their effect is to deprive parties of their right to a trial by jury as known and recognized when the first state constitution was framed.88 And, while the legislature may authorize the issuance of injunctions in cases of trespass to land where that right did not exist before the adoption of the constitutional guaranty, it cannot at the same time authorize an equity court to assess damages for the trespass under circumstances which would not have authorized the assessment of such damages prior to the adoption of the first constitution.89 

Of course, the statutory enlargements upon the equity jurisdiction of the circuit courts may be curtailed by the legislature as it wishes, but the inherent equity powers which those courts derive from the Constitution cannot be impaired by the legislature.90

 § 9.-Effect of Statutes Authorizing Law Courts to Grant the Same 

Relief as Equity Courts.-It frequently happens that statutes are enacted authorizing law courts to grant the same relief as equity courts or relief substantially similar to that granted by equity courts. The rule applicable under such circumstances is that the grant of jurisdiction to one court, without words of exclusion as to other courts having like powers, simply constitutes these tri bunals courts of concurrent jurisdiction. A grant of jurisdiction is not like a grant of property, which cannot have several owners at the same time. When a remedy in equity exists, and a remedy at law is subsequently created, the equity jurisdiction is not destroyed unless by an express provision of the law.91

Accordingly, it has been held that a statute creating a method of enforcing materialmen's liens by an action at law does not deprive equity of jurisdiction to foreclose such liens.92 Where a statute provides a summary remedy for avoiding illegal tax assessments, a court of equity is not thereby deprived of concurrent jurisdiction over the same matters.93 Provision for a remedy at law by which a party or his witness may inspect any real or personal property material to the question in dispute does not deprive equity courts of jurisdiction over the same matter through discovery.94 And, in one case, the court considered but found it unnecessary to pass upon the question of whether equity jurisdiction. for obtaining discovery in aid of actions at law was done away with by the enactment of statutes providing for interrogatories in law actions.95

In each of the foregoing cases, and in accordance with the rule previously stated, the decision was predicated upon the fact that the statute creating the legal remedy did not expressly provide that the concurrent jurisdiction of equity over the same matter was thereby abolished. However, it should not be overlooked that the power of the legislature to create legal remedies and at the same time abolish equity jurisdiction over the same matters is

But it is equally clear that the legislature cannot infringe upon the jurisdiction of the circuit courts over any matter which is inherently cognizable in equity and which is, therefore, assigned by the Constitution exclusively to them.97 

In other words, the power of the legislature to create legal remedies and at the same time abolish equity jurisdiction over the same matters is limited in its operation to the additional statutory jurisdiction of equity courts and it cannot be exercised to infringe upon the constitutional jurisdiction of those courts. 

§ 10. Effect of Concurrent Jurisdiction of Equity and Law Courts. 

It has previously been shown that courts of law and courts of equity have concurrent jurisdiction in many cases.98 In cases coming within this concurrent jurisdiction, the rule is that the court which first takes actual cognizance of a particular controversy should as a general rule be permitted to retain it to the end. 

When the subject matter of and parties to a controversy are before a court of law, an equity court cannot withdraw the case and parties from the jurisdiction of the law court where the latter is as competent to grant the proper relief as the former.99 This rule also applies between two equity courts of co-ordinate power. 100 

It has been stated that, when an equity case and a law case involving the same questions between the same parties are pending in the same court, and the legal questions will be determined in the equity suit, good practice suggests the continuance of the law case until the equity case is determined.101 But this statement may be explained as creating an exception to the general rule where the con-

Where a judgment at law has been entered in a particular controversy, it will bar a suit in chancery on the same cause of action between the same parties or their privies.102 A court of equity will not entertain a second suit in such a case merely because of some matter which the plaintiff could have availed himself of if he had first sued in equity, or because it has been made clear that justice has not been done at law, or because the judgment in the first suit was the result of an erroneous instruction to the jury. A judgment having been rendered by a court of the plaintiff's own choosing, it is not within the province of an equity court to review it. While the judgment remains in force it is conclusive upon the rights of the parties.103

§ 11.-Concurrent Jurisdiction of Equity and Probate Courts.- 

The Constitution of Florida, in addition to granting "exclusive original jurisdiction in all cases in equity" to the circuit courts, also confers upon those courts "supervision and appellate jurisdiction of matters arising before county judges pertaining to their probate jurisdiction, or to the estates and interests of minors."107 It is further provided that "the county judge shall have jurisdiction of the settlement of the estates of decedents and minors, to order the sale of real estate of decedents and minors, to take probate of wills, to grant letters testamentary and of administration and guardianship, and to discharge the duties usually pertaining to courts of probate." 108

The 

Neither the grant of jurisdiction over the estates of decedents and minors to the county judge, nor the grant of supervisory and appellate jurisdiction in such matters to the circuit courts, takes anything from the original and exclusive equity jurisdiction conferred upon the circuit courts. The grant of authority to the county judge is confined to probate or surrogate powers. circuit court having been invested with full original chancery jurisdiction, it is clear that the county judge cannot exercise any chancery power unless the power is of such a nature that it may be called a probate or surrogate power as well as a chancery power. 

Whenever, therefore, a probate or surrogate power is at the same time a chancery power, there is unquestionably concurrent jurisdiction in the two courts, but whenever the power is purely equitable, as distinguished from a probate or surrogate power, jurisdiction becomes exclusive in the circuit court.109 Nor were the inherent equity powers of the circuit court limited by the grant to it of supervisory and appellate jurisdiction in the settlement of estates of decedents and minors. This grant was merely a subordination of the powers of the county judge to the original equity

It must be conceded, however, that in the absence of special equities, the probate and equity courts have concurrent jurisdiction in cases of this nature and that the tribunal which first takes cognizance of the matter in controversy will retain it to the exclusion of the other, unless for some special reason it is made to appear that the probate court cannot administer adequate and complete relief between the parties.111

As one instance of a special equity which will give exclusive jurisdiction to an equity court, it is held that, where distributees file a bill against the administrators of an estate charging maladministration and praying for an accounting and distribution, equity has jurisdiction because the probate court, while it can remove the administrators, cannot grant the same relief as a court of chancery.112 Similarly, the circuit courts, as courts of equity, have jurisdiction to compel an accounting and discovery in cases of the mismanagement of estates because the probate court cannot administer the relief necessary to do complete justice in the premises.113 

And, where creditors seek to surcharge and falsify the accounts of an administrator, and to recover for waste and conversion of assets, and several of them hold mortgages upon the real estate of the decedent, a court of chancery will take jurisdiction because the powers of the probate court are not considered to be adequate or sufficiently comprehensive and flexible to render complete justice.114

§ 12.-Concurrent Jurisdiction of Florida and Federal Equity 

Courts. Except as judgments of state courts are subject to review in proper cases by the Supreme Court of the United States, or as to those actions originally brought in a state court which may lawfully be removed to a Federal court, the courts of the United States and of the several states are independent of each other, and the pendency of a suit in one of such courts is not a bar to a suit in the other involving the same controversy. However, as a matter of comity, one of the courts will not ordinarily determine a controversy of which the other court has previously acquired jurisdiction. 

Consequently, when a state and a Federal court have concurrent jurisdiction over the same parties or their privies and the same subject matter, the tribunal where jurisdiction first attaches retains it exclusively, and that court will be left to determine the controversy, to fully perform and exhaust its jurisdiction, and to decide every issue or question properly raised in the case. 

This jurisdiction continues until the judgment rendered in the first action is satisfied and it extends to proceedings which are ancillary or incidental to the action first brought. The usual practice is for the court in which the second action is brought, not 

115. Robarts v. Coram, 72 Fla. 225, 

72 So. 668; Redfearn on Wills, p. 145, 

§ 1.06. 

116. Fisher v. Guidy, 106 Fla. 94, 142 

So. 818. 

117. Constitution of Florida, Article V, Section 17. 

118. Ritch v. Bellamy, 14 Fla. 537.

§ 13] 

31 

to dismiss the action, but to suspend proceedings therein until the first suit is tried and determined.¹ 119

However, if either court disregards this rule and fails to suspend proceedings because of the prior action instituted in the other, a judgment entered in the second suit is none the less a bar to the further prosecution of the first. A final judgment entered in either court will be binding and conclusive in the other, without regard to the question of which suit was first commenced. Thus, where the defendants in a suit in equity in a Florida court for an accounting and settlement of a partnership, pending such action, bring suit against the plaintiff in a Federal court upon the same cause of action and procure a decree therein, that decree is a bar to the further prosecution of the state court suit. Of course, the state court may still proceed to an adjudication of all issues in the cause pending therein which were not settled and adjudicated in the prior Federal court decree. 120 

The rule that the judgment first obtained is conclusive, regardless of which suit is first commenced, applies only to suits in personam. Where the suits are in the nature of proceedings in rem, in that the object of the action requires the court to exercise control and dominion over the property involved in the litigation, that court which first acquires possession, or that dominion which is equivalent thereto, draws to itself the exclusive right to dispose of the property without interference from a court of co-ordinate power. And if the court in which the second action is begun nevertheless proceeds to a final decree, that decree will not be recognized in the court which first acquired jurisdiction of the res. A suit for partition is one in which it may be said, within the meaning of this rule, that the court, by the issuance and service of process, acquires dominion over the property involved.122 121

§ 14. Jurisdiction of Florida Equity Courts Over Land in Other 

States.- Florida equity courts have, of course, no jurisdiction over land in other states. They have no power to divest title to real estate situated in another state, 127 nor can they, through their officers, take possession of property beyond the territorial limits of the state. 128

§ 15.-Law Applicable.-As a general rule, both parties and courts are governed by the law of pleading, practice, and procedure as it exists at the time of their proceeding.' Thus, where the statutes in force when a bill of complaint is filed provide for one form of process but, prior to the issuance of process, a statute prescribing a different form takes effect, process is properly issued under the latter statute.2 And where, under the laws in force when a suit is instituted, a bill of complaint disclosing the existence of an adequate remedy at law should be dismissed, but prior to the dismissal of the suit a statute is enacted providing that such suits shall be transferred to the law court of competent jurisdiction, the court must act in accordance with the latter statute.3 

In accordance with the same rule, any advantage in pleading gained by a party under one law must yield when in conflict with a law subsequently becoming effective, with the duty on the court to exercise its powers upon application so as to avoid any injustice. 

Thus, any advantage which a defendant may have gained by filing a sworn answer must yield to a statute, taking effect after the

Under some circumstances a court of equity may be permitted or bound to apply statutes affecting simply the remedy and professedly enacted for the regulation of courts of law, but the extent of this permission or obligation has not been decided.5 

Of course, the power of the state to determine by what process and procedure rights may be asserted and determined is subject to the limitation that the procedure adopted, as applicable to the particular case, must not arbitrarily and unjustly discriminate against a party so as to deny him the equal protection of the law or deprive him of reasonable notice and a fair opportunity to be heard before his rights are decided. 

§ 16.-1931 Chancery Act.-Florida chancery practice was recently and completely revised by Chapter 14658, Laws of Florida, 1931.7 This statute provides that it shall be known and may be cited as the "1931 Chancery Act." The need for such legislation had long been felt due to the often too manifest tendency to procrastination, the confusing multiplicity of unessential details, and the consequent inefficiency in the State's system of administrative justice which prevailed under the former practice. As a result, the 1931 Chancery Act was prepared by the Florida State Bar Association, passed by the legislature without amendment, and approved by the Governor on June 4, 1931.9 The Act provided that it should be in force and effect on and after October 1, 1931, and should govern all proceedings in cases then pending or thereafter brought.10

The 1931 Chancery Act is designed to promote the ends of justice. Every opportunity is afforded to present all points involved in a case either in behalf of the plaintiff or defendant, but there is placed upon the solicitors in the case, as the representatives of the parties, the duty of presenting the questions involved speedily

The 1931 Chancery Act is, of course, controlling as to all matters of equity pleading and practice within its purview. Any questions not covered by the Act are governed by the applicable rules of practice. § 17.-Equity Rules. From the earliest period in the history of 

Florida the power to make rules for inferior courts has always been conferred by the legislature upon the highest appellate court of the state. The first statute to this effect was enacted in 1824 and the most recent in 1873.12 The latter statute provides that the Supreme Court of Florida shall have power to make, amend, annul, or modify the rules of pleading or practice of the Supreme Court, or of any other court, as it may see fit, not inconsistent with. law.13

Under the power thus conferred, the Supreme Court of Florida, in 1873, adopted a set of ninety-five rules governing the practice and procedure of the circuit courts of Florida in the exercise of their equity jurisdiction.14 Most of these rules were still in force when the 1931 Chancery Act was adopted. The provisions of that 

Act superseded and necessarily abrogated the equity rules previously in force which were inconsistent and in conflict with it, and the Supreme Court, on October 7, 1931, promulgated an order to that effect. Many of the rules are, therefore, no longer in existence.14A 

The statutes also provide that, in the absence of provisions of law or rules of practice of this state, the rules of practice in the courts of equity of the United States, as prescribed by the Supreme Court of the United States under the Act of Congress of May 8, 1792, shall be rules for the practice of the courts of this state when exercising equity jurisdiction and, when the rules of practice so

The circuit courts of Florida have no power to adopt rules of practice in equity. While it is true, in a general sense, that every court of record has inherent power to adopt rules of practice, yet it is equally true that in all matters not purely of a judicial nature, or forbidden by constitutional limitations, the legislature has power to prescribe general rules of procedure and pleading binding upon the parties and the court alike. The circuit courts being creatures of the Florida Constitution, 28 and their course of proceeding not having been minutely pointed out by the Constitution, it necessarily follows that the legislature has power to divest the circuit courts of their inherent right to adopt such rules of practice as are simply convenient and beneficial but not necessary to the court in the exercise of its constitutional jurisdiction. Of course, the legislature cannot deprive courts of the rule making power when its exercise is essential to the administration of their constitutional jurisdiction.

The real and substantial merits of the case were always looked to. Exceptions to formal minutiæ in the pleadings were never allowed by the court to prevent a hearing on the merits, for the court would, upon the discovery of any errors of this sort, allow an amendment of them. In many cases courts of equity would allow substantial defects to be amended if the cause was at such a stage that they could be amended without prejudice to the opposite party.32 In other words, equity looked always

Thus it has been held that, where the purpose of a bill of complaint was to correct an innocent mistake in a mortgage and decree of foreclosure, it was immaterial whether the bill should have been or in form was a bill of review, a bill in the nature of a bill of review, a supplemental bill in the nature of a bill of review, or of other technical character and form, for its purpose would be effectuated if no substantial rights were thereby inequitably affected.34 So also it has been held that an amended bill of complaint which was good in substance should not be dismissed regardless of its form.35 

Where a final decree was voidable because of the existence of jurisdictional facts not appearing on the record, it was held allowable to set it aside on motion with adequate notice to the opposite party. This practice was said to be simple, speedy, effective, and calculated to promote the interests of justice with the least cost and trouble to suitors.36 In accordance with the same principle, courts have refused to lay down any precise boundary line between motions and petitions and the cases in which each should be used.37 

The tendency of modern pleading and practice is toward simplicity.38 Accordingly, the spirit of the rule above discussed was broadened and incorporated in a statute by the 1931 Chancery Act. That Act provides that "all technical forms and classes of bills, answers and other pleadings in equity are hereby obolished."39 

The principal purpose of this provision is to eliminate any emphasis still placed on mere forms of chancery pleading and, while retaining the substance of the old procedure, to provide a few simple general forms adaptable for all purposes which previously required an adherence to nomenclature inconsistent with simplicity and directness.40 And, if the substantial rights of the parties may be

Under the 1931 Chancery Act it has been held that a supplemental bill in the nature of a bill of review is now permissible in the form of a petition.42 And though, under the 1931 Chancery 

Act, defenses in point of fact are properly raised by answer, it has been held permissible to present, by a motion to dismiss the cause, the defense that the plaintiff foreign corporation could not maintain suit because it had not paid certain taxes.43 § 19.-Method of Pleading. In a suit in equity, as in an action at law, the issues to be tried and determined are made by the pleadings, and, the object of all judicial proceedings being to ascertain and decide the disputed points, all pleadings should be certain, clear, and concise in order that the points in controversy may be evolved and distinctly presented for decision.44 

The object of an affirmative pleading is to state facts to which the court may apply the law in adjudicating rights.45 Therefore, facts must be pleaded. Allegations which amount to mere conclusions of law do not warrant relief in equity.46 But the facts should not be alleged in greater detail than is necessary. The virtue of a pleading does not consist in stuffing it with recitals and long digressions as to matters of fact wholly immaterial,47 but in the ultimate facts which constitute the case on which the demand or defense rests. Pleadings are not a war of words, and their allegations should be succinct and certain. They may often be crippled and their efficacy greatly impaired, if not wholly destroyed, by an overzealous effort to write into them with grammatical exactness every unimportant detail and collateral circumstance which might have a bearing upon the case.48 The pleader is only required to allege

The facts required to be alleged should be stated with as much brevity and precision as possible.50 There is no excuse for circumlocution, indirection, and innuendo. Certainty is the fundamental requirement of the art of pleading and when it is ignored confusion and often unnecessary expense is introduced into a perfectly simple case which otherwise might have been determined expeditiously and at a minimum of cost. No reason exists in logic or law, or in grammar or good pleading, why allegations should not be made in the phrases or sentences commonly employed to express their meaning.51 

The substance of the foregoing principles has been incorporated in the 1931 Chancery Act, which provides as follows: "All pleadings in an equity cause shall be expressed in as brief and succinct terms as reasonably practicable, and shall contain no unnecessary recitals of deeds, documents, contracts or other instruments in hæc verba, or other irrelevant, redundant or impertinent matter or scandalous matter not relevant to the suit. As far as practicable, all pleadings shall be stated in successively numbered paragraphs."52

The latter requirement enables a party to make brief and ready reference to any part of his adversary's pleading. 

§ 20.-Contents and Construction of Pleadings. It is incumbent upon each party to a suit in equity to allege in his pleading every fact, clearly and definitely, that is necessary to entitle him to the relief sought or to the benefit of the defense set up. If essential facts are omitted, or facts are alleged showing the insufficiency of the claim or defense, the pleader must suffer the consequences of so doing. 53

Where the pleadings in a case have been inartificially drafted and the proceedings loosely conducted, and the record is in a confused state, the court may, instead of attempting to disentangle the parties from the confusion in which they have become involved, and as the best method of putting them in a position to assert their rights, dismiss the entire proceeding of its own motion. 63 

§ 21.—Verification of Pleadings.—Where it is prescribed by stat ute or rule of court that an affidavit to a pleading be made by the party in person no one else can make it for him. Thus, where a bill of complaint in a partition suit is required to be sworn to by the plaintiff, an affidavit thereto by his attorney is insufficient to invoke the jurisdiction of the court.64 An oral oath to a pleading is sufficient unless a written oath is prescribed.65 

If an affidavit has been inadvertently omitted from a pleading the court may permit it to be filed at any time before a decree pro confesso has been entered for such failure. Even after a decree pro confesso has been entered, should the pleader apply to the court promptly for an order vacating the decree, making proper showing of mistake or inadvertence in the omission of the affidavit, it would be within the sound discretion of the court to open the decree upon such terms and conditions as might seem proper under all the circumstances. It is not the policy of courts to cut off substantial rights by hard and fast rules of technical pleading. 

But, where an affidavit to a pleading prepared by an attorney omits certain essential words, and there is no attempt to show that the omission was accidental, it may be taken by the court to have been intentional. And where the party insists upon the correctness of the affidavit as filed, the court cannot exercise any discretion in favor of opening a decree pro confesso based upon its insufficiency.66 § 22.-Exhibits.-The original rule of equity pleading was that an instrument of writing relied upon to establish a claim or defense should be pleaded according to its legal effect. It was not necessary to attach a copy of the instrument to the pleading as an

The foregoing rule was changed by a series of decisions beginning in 1928. These cases held that, where a party to a suit in chancery depended upon an instrument of writing as the basis of his right or defense, he must in his pleading state the substance of the instrument and file with or attach to his pleading as an exhibit the instrument itself or a true copy thereof, or assign by allegations in the pleading some satisfactory reason for its nonproduction.70

The 1931 Chancery Act, with reference to brevity and relevancy in pleadings, provides that they "shall contain no unnecessary recitals of deeds, documents, contracts or other instruments in hæc verba" and that "no papers shall be unnecessarily annexed as exhibits."71 The first of these provisions has been held to change the prior rule in one respect at least. Where a statute requires the instrument sued upon, or a copy thereof, to be annexed to the pleading and made a part thereof, and this is done, the pleading need not also allege the legal effect of the instrument nor the substance of the provisions thereof relied upon by the pleader.72 

There is no apparent reason why this rule should not also apply where the instrument relied on is properly attached to and made a part of the pleading, not because of a statutory requirement, but at the election of the pleader. 

It is an open question whether the second provision of the 1931 Chancery Act above referred to changes the prior rule making it

FLORIDA CHANCERY PLEADING AND Practice necessary to attach to and make a part of a pleading any instrument, or a copy thereof, relied upon as the basis for a claim or defense. The statute merely requires that no papers shall be "unnecessarily" annexed as exhibits. The 1931 Chancery Act was designed to expedite chancery procedure and, where a written instrument is relied upon as the basis for a claim or defense, the interests of justice would seem to make it necessary that the legal effect of that instrument be determined at the earliest stage of the proceeding possible. Where an instrument is the foundation of the pleader's case, and it is attached to and made a part of his pleading, its legal effect can be determined upon motion or other appropriate pleading before the trial of the cause. If the result of the litigation depends upon the legal effect of the instrument time and expense is thus saved. The cause of justice is not served by permitting a pleader to conceal the actual terms of an instrument behind his own perhaps erroneous allegations as to its legal effect, and to thus withhold it from the record until compelled to disclose its terms by a motion for better particulars, interrogatories, or other appropriate procedure. To permit such a practice is to encourage vexatious litigation. Furthermore, even though both parties to a cause may have copies of the controverted instrument, the court is without one, and it is obvious that the court may more intelligently and accurately pass upon questions raised by the pleadings if a copy of the instrument is in the record. 

Although an exhibit contains pertinent evidentiary facts it does not dispense with the necessity of alleging every fact necessary to the cause of action or defense. Thus it has been held that where bill is filed to foreclose a mechanic's lien against an estate by the entireties, and the essential allegation that the labor was performed with the "knowledge and assent" of the husband and wife is omitted, the deficiency is not supplied by a notice of lien, attached to and made a part of the bill of complaint, stating that the labor was furnished at the "instance and request" of the husband and wife, and this is true regardless of whether instance and request are synonymous with "knowledge and assent."73 

Of course, an exhibit containing merely irrelevant and evidentiary facts may be stricken from a pleading, and it is error to deny 

73. Allardice v. Weatherlow, 98 Fla. 

475, 124 So. 38.

§ 24] PRINCIPLES OF EQUITY PLEADING AND PRACTICE 47 

a motion to strike such an exhibit even though no material injury results to the adverse party from the denial.74 

§ 23.-Effect of Pleadings.-The issues to be tried and deter mined in a suit in equity are made by the pleadings. It is, therefore, an established rule of chancery practice, and of pleading and practice generally, that the allegata and probata must correspond. 

However full and convincing may be the proof as to any essential fact, unless the fact is averred, proof alone is insufficient. All the evidence offered in a case must correspond with the allegations and be confined to the issues made by the pleadings.75 

Allegations made in pleadings may sometimes be invoked as an estoppel against the party making them. It is a general rule that a party will not be permitted to assume inconsistent positions in legal proceedings,76 and when he has successfully made an allegation in pleading with reference to a certain fact he will be estopped to deny the truth of that allegation in a subsequent action between the same parties involving the same transaction.77 However, representations and declarations made in pleadings give rise to an estoppel only as between the parties and their privies to the case in which the pleadings are filed, and only those to whom the representation is made and who have been influenced by it, and their privies, may take advantage of the estoppel. If the act was inter alios there can be no estoppel.78 The pleadings of a party in one suit may be used in evidence against him in another, not as an estoppel, but as proof, open to rebuttal and explanation, that he admitted certain facts.79

They are, therefore, binding on the court and its clerk as on the litigants and their counsel.82

It should not be forgotten, however, that courts are established for the purpose of administering justice and that rules for the conduct of litigation are made to facilitate the trial of causes on their merits to the end that substance may not be sacrificed to form nor justice entangled in the meshes of an elaborate technique.83 Therefore, where the strict enforcement of the letter of the rules of practice would tend to prevent or jeopardize this end, the rules should yield to the higher purpose.84 Thus, the court has a wide discretion in the matter of extending the time prescribed for the filing of pleadings, and no exercise of this discretion will be interfered with unless it is plainly abused to the unjustifiable detriment of the other party.85 As yet no departure from the practice prescribed by the 1931 Chancery Act has been sanctioned, but it has been recognized that in an emergency, produced by conditions over which the parties have no control, the court may, upon a proper showing and after due notice, depart from the express rules prescribed by the Act in order that a cause may be completely presented and the court fully advised of all material points.86

Stipulations.-There is neither a statute nor equity rule governing the form or method of evidencing stipulations between solicitors for the parties to a suit in chancery. However, one of the rules of practice for the government of the circuit courts of Florida in common law actions provides that "no private agreement or consent between parties or their attorneys in respect to the proceedings in a cause shall be of any force before the court unless the evidence thereof shall be in writing, subscribed by the party or his attorney, against whom it is alleged." The rule further provides that "parol agreements may be made before the court."90 

This rule has been tacitly adopted by the circuit courts in equity proceedings.91 Thus, it has been held that an alleged agreement between solicitors for the parties to an equity suit extending the time for the filing of defendant's answer was of no effect because it had not been reduced to writing.92 And it has also been held in an equity suit that, while the rules require all stipulations and agreements between counsel or parties to a suit, the purpose of which is to vary the practice from that prescribed by the rules of court, to be in writing, it is competent for the court to recognize and approve such agreements when made orally, especially when no question as to the existence of the agreement is raised by either party.93 A stipulation in writing extending the time for taking testimony will be recognized and enforced.94 

The making of stipulations is encouraged by the courts rather than discouraged. They facilitate the progress of causes and save the time of the court. Generally, all stipulations of parties regarding the conduct of litigation will be enforced unless they are
