§ 27.-Accrual of Cause of Action.-The original equity rule, of almost universal application, was that the cause of action must exist at the time a suit is commenced.' The right of a plaintiff to the relief prayed was determined according to the facts existing when the original bill of complaint was filed,2 and the plaintiff could not supply the want of a valid claim at that time by the acquisition or accrual of one during the pendency of the suit.³ 

Under some circumstances it was permissible and proper, by means of a supplemental bill, to introduce into a suit matter that had occurred after the filing of the original bill, yet the new matter could not be such as to change the rights and interests of the parties before the court,4 and under no circumstances was a party who had no cause of action at the time of filing his original bill authorized to file a supplemental bill in order to maintain his suit upon a cause of action that accrued after the original bill was filed. 

This was true even though the cause of action shown by the supplemental bill arose out of the same transaction as the original bill.5 

Thus it was held that, where a city was enjoined from enforcing a certain ordinance, it could not introduce into the suit, by supplemental cross-bill, and for the purpose of vacating the injunction, another ordinance enacted after the suit was filed. And, in view 

1. Rose v. Henderson, 63 Fla. 564, 59 So. 138. 

2. Meredith v. Long, 96 Fla. 719, 119 So. 114. 

3. Marianna R. Co. v. Maund, 62 

Fla. 538, 56 So. 670. 

4. Ledwith v. Jacksonville, 32 Fla. 

1, 13 So. 454. 

5. Crump v. Perkins, 18 Fla. 353. 

6. Ledwith v. Jacksonville, 32 Fla. 

1, 13 So. 454.

[Ch. 4 

of the original equity rule that a creditor's bill to reach equitable assets of a debtor could not be maintained without a showing that an execution had been sued out at law and returned nulla bona, it was held that the suing out and return of an execution after a creditor's bill was filed could not be shown by supplemental bill for the purpose of making out a cause of action. Likewise, a bill in equity to recover for injuries to property of a permanent nature could not be maintained by showing in a supplemental bill that the plaintiff acquired title to the property after the original suit was filed. Nor could a bill to foreclose a mortgage be maintained by reason of a default in the payment of interest occurring after the suit was filed.

The foregoing rule was, however, changed by the 1931 Chancery Act. One of the provisions of that Act is that "facts occurring after the institution of the suit, if introduced by amendment, may be used in support of the equity of the bill." 10 

This statutory provision was enacted for the express purpose of changing the rule embodied in the cases above discussed, and it is now clear that facts occurring after a suit is filed may be introduced therein by amendment to the bill of complaint for the purpose of establishing a cause of action in the plaintiff. In accordance with this and other provisions of the 1931 Chancery Act, it has been held that a plaintiff foreclosing a mortgage for part of a debt may amend his bill of complaint to show that, subsequent to the filing of suit, his option to accelerate the maturity of the entire debt had accrued and that he thereby exercised the option." 

§ 28.—When Suit May Be Filed.—A suit in chancery may be filed at any time. A Florida statute provides that "the circuit courts, sitting in chancery, shall always be kept open for the issuing and return of process."12 In accordance with this statute, there are no terms of court for the purpose of chancery proceedings and courts of chancery are always open for the institution of proceedings therein.13

 § 29.-Venue.-Venue relates to and defines the particular county or territorial area within the state where a suit must be brought or tried. It commonly has to do with geographical subdivision, relates to practice or procedure, may be waived, and does not refer to jurisdiction at all.14

Under a Florida statute, all provisions of law governing locality of actions at law, when they can be made applicable, govern those in chancery.15 In regard to the locality of actions at law, the statutes provide: 

"Suits shall be begun only in the county *** where the defendant resides, or where the cause of action accrued, or where the property in litigation is. "If brought in any county *** where the defendant does not reside, the plaintiff, or some person in his behalf, shall make and file with the præcipe or bill in chancery, an affidavit that the suit is brought in good faith, and with no intention to annoy the defendant. This section shall not apply to suits against non-residents."16 "Suits against two or more defendants residing in different counties *** may be brought in any county ***in which any defendant resides."17 "Suits upon several causes of action may be brought in any county ***where either of the causes of action arose."18 "Suits against domestic corporations shall be commenced only in the county *** where such corporation shall have or usually keep an office for the transaction of its customary business, or where the cause of action accrued, or where the property in litigation is; and in the case of companies incorporated in other states or countries, and doing business in this state, suits shall be commenced in a county *** wherein such company may have an agent or other representative, or where the cause of action accrued, or where the property in litigation is situated."19 (Omissions in the quotation of the foregoing statutes are of references to courts of justices of the peace which are, of course, inapplicable to chancery proceedings.)

Originally all actions were local in character with respect to their venue and could be brought only in the county where the cause of action arose. They are now classified as local or transitory. An action is local if the transaction on which it is founded 

14. McGowin v. McGowin, 122 Fla. 

394, 165 So. 274. 

16. C. G. L. 4219. 

17. C. G. L. 4220. 

15. C. G. L. 4889; Pepple v. Rogers, 1.04 Fla. 462, 140 So. 205. 

18. C. G. L. 4221. 

19. C. G. L. 4222.

[Ch. 4 could only have happened or been consummated in the place where it actually took place, and an action is considered transitory if the transaction might have taken place anywhere.20 In this view, when the subject of the injury is real estate, whether in tangible form or as an easement or right of way, the action is local for the reason that the injury to that particular real estate or easement could not possibly have occurred at any other place than where the thing injured is actually situated. But, if the subject of the injury is an individual, then an injury to that individual person, no matter by what means occasioned or when accomplished, is essentially an injury to a subject not having a fixed, stationary, and immovable loca- `tion, and an action to recover damages for such an injury is necessarily transitory. In other words, the test of venue is not whether the direct effect of the action would be in rem or in personam, but whether the occurrence giving rise to the action could have happened only in one place or might have happened anywhere.2 21 At common law, the venue of a transitory action could be laid in any county where the court could get jurisdiction of the person of the defendant. The defendant had no privilege of being sued in any particular place. But, as service of process could not be had on a defendant outside the county where it was issued, the plaintiff necessarily had to bring his suit in the county where he could serve the defendant.

However, a Florida statute²² provides that all process shall run throughout the state, and therefore process may be issued in one county and be served in any other county in the state. Going on the common law theory that a transitory action could be brought in any county if the court got jurisdiction of the person, a suit on a transitory action in Florida could now be brought in any county and service had in any other county were it not for the provisions of the statutes above quoted which limit the places where suits may be brought and give the defendant the privilege of being sued in a particular county. This privilege is a creature of statute and not of the common law. The statutes providing it are in limitation of the common law rather than an enlargement of it.23

In Sanchez v. Haynes, supra, it was held that, where process was issued in one county and served in another, the service was a nullity, and a decree pro confesso entered by the clerk for failure to appear was void unless the record affirmatively showed that the county in which suit was brought was the county of defendant's residence, the county where the cause of action accrued, or where the property in litigation was. This case points out that prior to Chapter 3721, Laws of Florida, 1887, there was no law authorizing process to be served outside of the county where it was issued, and therefore suit could be brought in the county where the cause of action accrued only if the defendant could be found in that county. The 1887 Act remedied this by providing that, when any suit was brought in a county in which the defendant did not reside or could not be found, process could be served in the county where the defendant resided or could be found. But this Act contained a proviso that it did not authorize suits to be brought in any county other than that in which the defendant resided, or the cause of action accrued, or the property in litigation was. The decision in Sanchez v. Haynes was directly predicated on this proviso, the court construing it to mean that, if suit was not brought in one of the proper counties, there was no statutory authority for service in another county and any such service was void.

The only applicable part of the 1887 Act which was carried into the Revised Statutes of 1892 was the provision that any process issued in a suit instituted in a county where the defendant did not reside might be served by the sheriff of the county where the defendant was found. Yet in 

Chapman v. Reddick, supra, it was held that Sanchez v. Haynes, supra, was still law and that process to be served beyond the county in which it was issued must, in order to be valid, be issued by a court having jurisdiction of the subject matter by reason of the residence of the defendant, the accrual of the cause of action, or the situation of the property in litigation being within its territorial limits. In 

Baker & Holmes Co. v. Indian River

Bank, supra, it was held that, where process was issued in one county and served in another, and a default was entered against the defendant for failure to appear, the default was not void unless the record affirmatively showed that the suit was not properly brought in the county where process was issued. In that case, however, the defendant appeared when the question of damages was submitted to the jury and did not question the validity of the service and the decision was partly predicated upon the fact that this constituted a waiver of the venue. It is clear that the privilege of being sued in the proper county may be waived by failure to appear or, after appearing, by failure to raise the question.

inally enacted in 1895. It was, therefore, not in existence when Sanchez v. Haynes, supra, was decided. It was in existence when Chapman v.

C. G. L. 4234, suit on a transitory cause of action can now be brought in any county of the state and valid service had in any other county, the defendant, of course, still having the right to appear and plead his privilege under the venue statutes. The essential difference between Linger v.

Balfour and the rule of Sanchez v. 

Haynes is that the former case holds that statutes now authorize the issuance of process in one county and the service thereof in another, even where the venue statutes are not complied with, whereas the rule of the latter case is that there is no statute authorizing service outside of the county where the defendant resides or is found except where the venue statutes are complied with. The question involves the existence or construction of the statutes governing service of process and not the effect of the venue statutes. Since Linger v. Balfour is based upon a statute which was not in existence when Sanchez v. Haynes was decided and the effect of which was not specifically discussed in the subsequent cases apparently approv ing Sanchez v. Haynes, it seems more probable that Linger v. Balfour would be held to correctly state the law on this point if the question ever arises. 

The principle of Linger v. Balfour was followed in McGowin v. McGowin, 122 Fla. 394, 165 So. 274, although the former case was not cited in the latter.

In McGowin v. McGowin the plaintiff, a resident of Hillsborough County, sued defendant, a resident of Illinois, for a divorce and filed his suit in Hardee County. Summons was served on defendant in Hillsborough County.

No property involved was located in Hardee County and it did not appear that the cause of action arose in Florida. Defendant filed a plea of privilege. A decree of the lower court dismissing the suit was reversed on the ground that a cause of action for divorce was transitory and could be brought in any county in this state if the defendant was a non-resident thereof. The decision apparently recognizes the validity of service outside of the county where suit is brought where the venue statutes are not complied with or are inapplicable. 

However, the case of Bailey v. Crum, 120 Fla. 36, 162 So. 356, decided subsequently to Linger v. Balfour, contains several statements indicating that the rule of Sanchez v. Haynes is still the law although the effect given 

C. G. L. 4234 in Linger v. Balfour was not considered nor was the latter case mentioned.

Additional support for the conclusion that Linger v. Balfour, supra, correctly states the Florida law on this question may be found in the equal protection clause of the Federal 

Constitution. In Linger v. Balfour, supra, C. G. L. 4234 has been construed as authorizing service upon a non-resident in a county other than that in which he is sued even though he might have been sued in the county where he was found. It may be argued, therefore, that C. G. L. 4234 should also be construed as authorizing service upon a resident in a county other than that in which he is sued even though the venue statutes are not complied with. It is possible that a contrary construction of the statute

§ 29] 

57 

But the statutes governing the locality of actions affect only venue. 

The authority to bring an action in the county of the defendant's residence necessarily presupposes that the court in which the action. is brought possesses jurisdiction of the subject matter as well as of the parties. The statutes do not purport to confer extra-territorial jurisdiction as to subject matter located in another county, nor to change existing rules with reference to the locality of actions which in their essential nature are local and therefore must be brought in a court having jurisdiction of the subject matter as well as of the parties.24 Thus, where a present and continuing trespass upon real estate is the sole basis of a suit, and a determination of ownership is actually or potentially involved as a major issue, and the gravamen of the action is injury to the freehold and crops growing upon the land, and the principal relief sought is an injunction against the continuing acts of trespass which occasion the damage, the action is necessarily local in its nature and must be maintained in the county where the land lies. Even though the acts of trespass are in the nature of personal acts, the court looks to the underlying major question involved in order to determine whether the action is local or transitory.25 So also a proceeding in rem, or in the nature of a proceeding in rem, must be brought in the county where the land lies. Thus where, as in Florida, a mortgage is a mere lien and legal title remains in the mortgagor, and a foreclosure decree operates to deprive the mortgagor of that estate, the action is regarded as local and must be brought in the county where the land lies.

The fact that a deficiency decree is sought does not change this rule.26 

The only effect of the venue statutes is to create a privilege in the defendant. If the cause of action did not accrue, or if the property in litigation is not in, another county in Florida, the de- would be held to violate the equal protection clause. In this connection, it should be noted that the only question involved is the validity of service under C. G. L. 4234. The privilege of a resident defendant who is sued in one county and served in another to invoke the venue statutes is neither involved nor impaired. The question is whether service upon a resident defendant who is so sued is a valid predicate for a judgment against him where he waives his privilege under the venue statutes. 

24. Lakeland Drainage District v.

25. Lakeland Drainage District v.

[Ch. 4 fendant does, of course, have the right to be sued in the county where he resides.27 However, if the cause of action accrued in 

Florida, or the property in litigation is situated in this state, but in a county other than that of the defendant's residence, the statutes do not permit him to elect in which county suit shall be brought.28 

If the cause of action arose or the property in litigation is situated in a county other than that in which the defendant resides, it is the plaintiff who may select the county in which he shall sue and the privilege of the defendant is secured if he is sued in any one of the three.29 Thus a suit to compel the conveyance of land may be brought in any county in which part of the land lies,30 and a suit to enjoin an action at law may be brought in the county where the law action is pending even though the plaintiff therein resides elsewhere.31

The statutory provision that the defendant may be sued where the cause of action accrued relates to the cause of action and not to the right to sue. Thus, though the probate of a will and issuance of letters testamentary in a certain county give a right to sue the executor, this right is dependent upon a pre-existing cause of action and the executor may be sued in any other county than that in which he was appointed provided the cause of action arose there.32 

There is no statutory privilege provided for the non-resident of Florida to be sued at a particular place in the state on a cause of action arising in another state. Therefore, the common law rule must apply and a non-resident may be sued on a transitory cause of action in any county of this state if the court has jurisdiction of his person. 1.33 

The statutory provisions regulating venue are not limitations upon the constitutional jurisdiction of the circuit courts.34

Venue thus laid in the margin is sufficient even though it is not repeated in the body of the bill of complaint,36 or even though the wrong venue is inserted in the bill.37 The foregoing rules apply whether the action is local or transitory.38 Where local causes of action arising in different counties are joined it is sufficient to lay the venue in the county where suit is brought.39 § 31.-Waiver of Venue. In transitory actions it is entirely clear that the defendant has a statutory privilege of being sued in the county where he resides or where the cause of action accrued. 

This privilege or right is not founded upon, nor does it create, a lack of jurisdiction in the court where the defendant does not reside in the county where suit is brought or the cause of action. accrued. Personal actions against a defendant generally follow his person, and where process emanating from a court having jurisdiction of the subject matter is personally served on him in the county where suit is instituted, the court acquires jurisdiction of both the subject matter and the person. The statute has, however, conferred upon the defendant the right or privilege of being sued either in the county of his residence or the county where the cause of action accrued. But, when sued in a personal action, of which the court has jurisdiction, in a county other than the one in which he resides or the cause of action accrued, the defendant can waive the privilege given him by statute and, when he does not insist on it, a valid judgment can be rendered against him.40

When Suit Is Commenced.-While an action at law is considered as pending only from the time of the service of the writ, a suit in chancery is considered as filed and pending from the time of filing the bill of complaint.59 It is not necessary that a summons be issued.60 Thus, under a statute authorizing the transfer of pending suits in case of the disqualification of the judge of the original forum, a suit is considered as pending from the time the bill of complaint is filed. So also, a suit is filed, for the purpose of computing the statutory period of limitation, from the time the bill is filed in the clerk's office even though the summons is not issued or served until after the statute has run. 62 Upon a motion to dismiss a bill of complaint on the ground that the cause of action set forth therein is barred by the statute of limitations the time when suit was instituted may be shown by the file marks on the bill.63

A suit is commenced when the bill of complaint is filed even though the affidavit of good faith64 required by statute when the defendant is sued in a county other than that in which he resides is not filed at the same time as the bill.65 

§ 34.—Effect of Filing Suit.-When a bill of complaint is filed it becomes a court document and a part of the record in the cause. 

It becomes, from the moment it is filed, under the control of the court and in the custody of its officer, the clerk, and the statutes 66 provide that such papers may not be removed from the clerk's office without leave of court. § 35.-General Nature and Contents.-When a person seeks the aid of a court of equity to redress an injury which he has suffered or which is threatened against him, he must, in order to invoke the jurisdiction of the court, file therein a written statement of his case. This statement is in the nature of a petition to the court and is called a bill in equity or a bill in chancery.' 

The contents of a bill in equity are prescribed by the 1931 

Chancery Act as follows: 

"Hereafter it shall be sufficient that a bill in equity shall 

"First: The name, and when known, the residence of each plaintiff and defendant; and, if any party be under any disability, that fact shall be stated. "Second: A short and simple statement of the ultimate facts upon which the plaintiff asks relief, omitting any mere statement of evidence. "Third: A statement of and prayer for any special relief pending the suit or on final hearing, which may be stated and sought in alternative forms. If special relief pending the suit be desired the bill should be verified by the oath of the plaintiff, or someone having knowledge of the facts upon which such

§ 36.-Address. It was originally required that a bill in equity be addressed to the judge or judges of the court in which suit was filed. Thus, bills of complaint in Duval County, Florida, were usually addressed "To the Honorable Judges of the Circuit Court of the Fourth Judicial Circuit of the State of Florida, in and for 

Duval County, in Chancery sitting." However, while the practice of omitting the address was never approved, a bill properly entitled and complying with all other legal requirements was never held bad for want of the proper address unless the defect was raised by special demurrer.3 Under the 1931 Chancery Act no address to a bill of complaint is required and in the interest of brevity it should be omitted.4 

§ 37.-Statement of Parties.-Every bill of complaint must open with a statement of the name and, when known, the residence of each plaintiff and defendant. If any party is under a disability that fact must be so stated. These requirements are imperative. 

A failure to state the name of a defendant in the introductory part of a bill may, however, be cured by subsequent allegations if the defect is not taken advantage of at the proper time.7 

§ 38.-Statement of Case.-The primary purpose of a bill in equity is, of course, to state the facts upon which the complaining party bases his right to relief in a court of equity. The bill of complaint is the foundation for all subsequent proceedings in the cause. The plaintiff will not be permitted to prove any fact which is not alleged in the bill. The allegata and probata must reciprocally meet and correspond. And the plaintiff can derive no benefit from facts not charged in the bill even though such facts may

However, in accordance with the maxim that equity looks to substance instead of form, a bill of complaint which states any ground for equitable relief will not be dismissed by the court sua sponte or otherwise.22 Even though a bill may be subject to criticism as lacking in a high degree of clearness, yet if it is not wholly deficient and its allegations are broad enough to support a meritorious case, it will not be dismissed.23

In stating the facts upon which relief is sought, the general principles applicable to all pleadings29 in equity should, of course, be scrupulously observed. In stating his case, the plaintiff should plead only ultimate facts.30 As provided in the 1931 Chancery 

Act, a bill of complaint containing "a short and simple statement of the ultimate facts upon which the plaintiff asks relief" is sufficient.31 It is not necessary that the bill contain statements of evidence, or the details and circumstances that are comprised within or that go to prove the ultimate facts.32 No accurate and satisfactory definition of ultimate facts can be given. It is often said that they are conclusions reached by natural reasoning, or the results deduced from an inferential process in which the evidentiary facts become the premises and the ultimate facts the conclusions. 

If resort must be had to the artificial processes of the law to reach a final determination, the result is a conclusion of law. Ultimate

While a bill of complaint should contain allegations of ultimate rather than evidentiary facts, it should also avoid allegations of opinions and conclusions of law.34 Conclusions of law need not be alleged35 and, in the absence of sufficient allegations of fact, they cannot constitute a basis for relief in equity.36 Where the facts alleged in a bill of complaint are sufficient to warrant relief, conclusions of law, if pleaded, will be treated as surplusage and disregarded.37 Where a bill of complaint is replete with conclusions and allegations so general as a whole as to render a defense against them very difficult, if not impossible, it will be dismissed.38

A few examples of allegations which have been held to be conclusions of law will sufficiently illustrate what is included within the meaning of that phrase. An allegation that plaintiffs are the heirs at law of a certain person is only a legal conclusion. The facts establishing heirship should be set forth.39 An allegation that notice to the defendant of the application for an injunction will accelerate the injury is a conclusion of law. Facts showing how or why notice will accelerate or precipitate the injury must be alleged.40 An allegation that a contract made by an agent without authority has been ratified by his principal is insufficient. The acts constituting ratification must be alleged.41 An allegation that defendant failed to furnish an abstract showing merchantable title is a legal conclusion. The specific defects in the title must be set forth.42 Illegal acts cannot be charged in general terms. The particular acts claimed to be illegal must be described.43 Thus, an

However, an allegation that the defendant is insolvent is not a conclusion of law,46 nor is an allegation that the deceased, at the time of his death, was the owner of certain lands which, with his wife, he occupied as their homestead.47 An allegation that an agent was duly authorized is not a conclusion of law.48 So also, an allegation that a cause of action accrued in a certain county is not a legal conclusion.49

The line of demarcation between allegations of fact and conclusions of law is exceedingly difficult to draw. It is quite easy to say that the ultimate facts are but the logical conclusions deduced from certain primary facts evidentiary in their character, and that conclusions of law are those presumptions or legal deductions which, the facts being given, are drawn without further evidence. This does not, however, quite meet the difficulty. We deduce the ultimate facts from certain probative facts by a process of natural reasoning, and we draw the inference or conclusion of law by a process of artificial reasoning, but the latter process is often in such exact accord with natural reasoning that the distinction is scarcely appreciable. In the main it may be said that in distinguishing between ultimate facts and conclusions of law courts are governed more by precedent than by substantial differences in principle.

An allegation in a bill of complaint of the performance of conditions precedent must not consist of a conclusion of the pleader. 

Such performance may be alleged generally in actions at law,50 but the ultimate facts constituting performance must be alleged in a bill in equity. The failure of a bill to aver the performance of a condition precedent, or an excuse for non-performance, is fatal

So, if a person contracting to buy land announces his determination not to perform his contract, the vendor's bill for specific performance need not allege the tender of a deed.53 

§ 39.-Surplusage and Irrelevant Matter.-Where a bill of com plaint contains allegations or exhibits which are not essential to the relief prayed, but which do not destroy the effect of material allegations stating a cause of action, such non-essentials may be treated as surplusage and entirely disregarded.54 While allegations which amount to mere conclusions of law need not be alleged, they may, if alleged, also be treated as surplusage.55 Thus where the facts constituting fraud, accident, or mistake are contained in an original bill of complaint, an amendment thereto simply charging fraud, accident, or mistake as a conclusion of law may and should be treated as surplusage. Stating conclusions of law is bad pleading but its effect cannot be to destroy equities otherwise shown to exist.56

Any person prejudiced by surplusage or irrelevant matter in a bill of complaint may have the same stricken therefrom,57 but no matter should be stricken on this ground if it has any proper relation to the subject matter of the litigation.58 Surplusage does not render a bill of complaint subject to a motion to dismiss.59

[Ch. 5 1 Matter which may be regarded as surplusage cannot render a bill of complaint multifarious because multifariousness is the improper joining of two or more good causes of action in the same bill.60 § 40.-Construction of Bill of Complaint.-The facts and circum stances upon which a plaintiff bases his claim and right to relief are matters peculiarly within his own knowledge and he will, therefore, be presumed to have alleged them as strongly and favorably to himself as he could, and to have exercised his privilege of selecting his own language in which to state them.61 Accordingly, a bill of complaint, and any indefinite or uncertain allegations therein, will be construed most strongly against the pleader.62 

Where there are contradictory or inconsistent allegations in a bill, its equity will be tested by the weaker rather than the stronger allegations. 63 And when some allegations show a case entitling the plaintiff to relief, but they are contradicted by other allegations in the same bill, and it is impossible for the court to determine the true nature of the case sought to be made out, the bill will be subject to dismissal.64

Particular allegations in a bill should be construed with reference to any other allegations in the bill to which they relate so that the full effect and meaning of the particular allegations may be determined.65 But an allegation as to the legal effect of the facts stated in the bill is immaterial. The court will draw its own conclusion from the facts stated, and if the facts justify the relief sought it will be granted. Thus, where a will creating a trust is set forth in a bill of complaint, but the plaintiff's interpretation of the will is incorrect, the relief sought will still be granted if the provisions of the will warrant it.66

 § 41. Anticipating Defenses.-As a general rule, a bill of com plaint need not and should not, by its averments, anticipate a defense thereto and negative or avoid it. But, if the bill itself states a cause of action, the fact that it also attempts to negative or avoid a defense is not a fatal defect, and allegations made for that purpose are immaterial and may be treated as surplusage unless the defendant wishes to rely upon them. In that case he will be relieved from specifically setting up the defense and may accept the issue presented by the plaintiff.67

However, there is one class of cases in which the plaintiff must negative a defense to his suit. It is a well established rule that, where a bill of complaint shows upon its face long acquiescence and laches by the plaintiff in the assertion of his claim, then it becomes necessary for him, by way of excuse for his apparent acquiescence and laches, to allege some actual hindrance or impediment to the seeking of his rights, such as concealment or faultless want of knowledge of facts. If the plaintiff fails to allege an excuse or reason for his long delay, laches will be imputed to him and the court will refuse its aid.68 If a bill shows laches on its face without any allegations excusing it, the defect renders it subject to dismissal.69 

§ 42.-Joinder of Causes of Action and Multifariousness. In re gard to the joinder of causes of action, the 1931 Chancery Act provides: "The plaintiff may join in one bill as many causes of action, cognizable in equity, as he may have against the defendant. But when there is more than one plaintiff, the causes of action joined must be joint, and if there be more than one defendant the liability must be one asserted against all of the material defendants, or sufficient grounds must appear for uniting the causes of action in order to promote the convenient administration of justice. If it appears that any such causes of action cannot be conveniently disposed of together, the court may order separate trials."70

The foregoing statute has been construed as not prohibitive of

[Ch. 5 anything which was permissible under chancery practice before its enactment. It follows, therefore, that while the statute may have broadened and liberalized, it did not limit or restrict, the pre-existing rules governing the joinder of causes of action. Consequently, decisions rendered prior to the enactment of the statute may still be considered as controlling insofar as they permit the joinder of causes of action, although such decisions may be only persuasive insofar as they prohibit a joinder. For this reason, the prior rules as to multifariousness will be reviewed before considering the extent to which they may have been liberalized by the 1931 Chancery Act. 

Prior to the 1931 Chancery Act, it had been repeatedly held that, to render a bill multifarious, it must contain two or more distinct causes of action that could not properly be joined in one bill of complaint.72 It was also frequently stated that multifariousness was the joining of two or more distinct, separate, and independent causes of action that could better be adjudicated in more than one suit.73 The test of multifariousness was merely convenience in the administration of justice.74

It is apparent from the foregoing that no absolute rule can be formulated as to when it was permissible, under the old practice, to join two or more causes of action in one bill. And it has been recognized that there is no rule of equity pleading or practice in the application of which there has been less certainty and uniformity than that relating to multifariousness. This condition, flowing perhaps inevitably from the variety of modes and degrees

Accordingly, each case has been largely determined by its own peculiar features.75 But the decisions have laid down a number of secondary or subordinate principles for determining whether a bill is multifarious, and these principles, when considered in connection with the facts on which they are based, are helpful in deciding whether two or more particular causes of action may be joined in one bill of complaint.

In the first place, the decisions establish that there are two general and distinct forms of multifariousness. One occurs when distinct and disconnected subjects, matters, or causes of action are united in the same bill of complaint. The other occurs when there are joined in the same suit, either as plaintiffs or defendants, parties who have no common interest in the subject of the litigation and who have no connection with each other insofar as the issues in litigation are concerned.76

As to the misjoinder of distinct and independent causes of action, a bill in equity brought by a single plaintiff against one defendant, or several defendants jointly liable, is not necessarily multifarious because there may be united in it several causes of action between the same parties. The avoidance of a multiplicity of suits being in itself a ground of equitable jurisdiction, a bill will not be held multifarious if the matters contained in it can be disposed of together and a multiplicity of suits thereby avoided.77 Thus, where one of two tenants in common sold timber from the land held between them, the other owner may sue for a partition and for an accounting for the proceeds of the timber in one action.78 Likewise, causes of action for partition, an accounting for rents and profits, an injunction against the sale of land, and a receiver therefor, may be joined in one bill of complaint where the various causes of action are against all defendants jointly.79 A bill to

A bill of complaint to enjoin a continuing trespass to land and for an accounting for products removed therefrom brought against several defendants jointly liable is not multifarious.81 A bill for divorce and alimony, to declare a trust in real estate paid for with plaintiff's money, and to enjoin the sale of the real estate is not multifarious,82 at least where third persons have not acquired intervening rights in the real estate.83 A plaintiff may join in one suit against the same defendant causes of action to quiet title against a tax deed issued for state and county taxes and to quiet title against a tax deed issued for drainage district taxes.84

If several persons sue as parties plaintiff, or several persons are sued as parties defendant, the right to join different causes of action depends upon the existence of a common interest in a single subject matter. Thus, where the parties plaintiff have a common interest in the subject of the litigation and have some relation to each other growing out of the common interest, and the allegations are of a single, distinct equity as to which specific relief is prayed against one or more defendants, the bill of complaint is not multifarious.85 For example, creditors of the same debtor, each of whom is entitled to resort to equity, although their claims are severable and distinct, may, when other requirements are met, join in a creditors' bill.86 And several children may join with their widowed mother in a bill to set aside a decree of divorce obtained by her husband and to secure their interest in his estate.87

But where the plaintiffs have separate and distinct rather than common interests in the subject matter they cannot join their demands in one bill. Thus a general creditor of a surviving partner, and a partnership creditor, cannot join in a bill against the surviving partner, his fraudulent grantees, and the legal representatives of the deceased partner.89 And several fruit growers, each owning distinct parcels of land, cannot join in a bill against a state plant board to nullify a rule promulgated by it.90 

Where several persons are sued as parties defendant, a number of causes of action cannot be joined unless the determination of each cause of action affects all of the principal defendants.91 But different causes of action may be joined in the same bill if they all grew out of the same transaction and all defendants are interested in the same right.92 Frequently the fact that demands which are otherwise entirely distinct relate to the same subject matter affords a sufficient connection to justify their union in one bill and avoids an objection of multifariousness.93 Thus, some of the heirs of a decedent may maintain a bill against the remaining heirs for a partition of real estate and join in the same bill a claim against the administrator for an accounting as to the personal property.94 Even if the subject matter in controversy is encumbered with many conflicting claims equity will entertain a suit to determine and adjudge all the interests at once.95

In regard to the latter form of multifariousness it is held that, if the object of a suit is single, but it happens that different persons have separate interests in distinct questions which arise out of the single object, such different persons must be brought before the court in order that the suit may conclude the whole subject.96 

It is not necessary, in order to overcome the objection of multifariousness, that all the parties should have an interest in all the matters contained in the suit. The objection will be defeated if it appears that each party has an interest in some matters in the suit and that those matters are connected with the others. The inquiry is not whether each defendant is connected with every branch of the case, but whether the bill seeks relief in respect to matters separate and distinct in their natures. A bill in equity is not multifarious where one general right is claimed by the plaintiff, even though the defendants have separate and distinct rights.97 

The court will in such cases pursue the course which seems most likely to enable it to do complete equity in the particular case with the least expense, delay, and trouble, striving always to obviate the necessity of a multiplicity of suits.98 

The most common case of this kind is where several grantees, each claiming different portions of the property of a fraudulent grantor, are made defendants with him to a bill to set aside the conveyances. Such a bill is not multifarious. As against the creditor, the deeds to the property, whether there be one or many, or whether there be one grantee or many, are void. The entire property is treated in a court of equity as the property of the debtor. The object sought to be obtained is single, the subjection of the debtor's property to the payment of his debt.99 

Another case where various defendants may be joined because the object of a suit is single is where a husband is dead and there are children born as the result of cohabitation between the husband

An objection that a bill for the specific performance of a contract to make a lease is multifarious is not established because tenants of the property, not parties to the contract, but whose interest in the subject matter of the controversy may be conveniently settled in the suit, are made parties defendant, nor because the suit involves the enforcement of another contract between the principal parties for the sale of land where such contract grew out of the contract for the lease and formed part of the consideration therefor.102 And, where the case is one whose bona fide object is the partition of lands between the common owners thereof, one or more of whom are plaintiffs and the others defendants, and they or some of them are in possession, then all controversies between them as to the legal title and right of possession may and should be settled in one suit.103

A bill against a state plant board, as a body corporate, certain individuals as members of the board, and certain other individuals as a committee acting under the board, to nullify a rule adopted by the board, is multifarious as to parties defendant. 108 A cause of action for partition and to foreclose a mortgage may not be joined in one bill. The foregoing are the principal rules relating to multifariousness as they existed prior to the 1931 Chancery Act. It is apparent that they are reasonably liberal and promotive of the interests of

In regard to the joinder of causes of action, the previously quoted provision of the 1931 Chancery Act provides that, where there is only one plaintiff and one defendant, the plaintiff may, as of right, join in one bill as many causes of action cognizable in equity as he may have against the defendant.112 Thus a municipality may by one bill foreclose paving liens against two or more separate lots where all lots are owned by the same person.113 Likewise, a bill brought by a wife against her husband for divorce, alimony, custody of children, and confirmation of title to certain real estate is permissible.114 A comparison of these decisions with those rendered prior to the 1931 Act indicates that, where there is only one plaintiff and one defendant, the Act does little more than convert a permissible practice into a statutory right. 

The previously quoted provision of the 1931 Chancery Act also provides that, where various causes of action against one defendant belong to several plaintiffs jointly, they may also, as of right be joined in one bill of complaint.115 But two persons having separate and independent causes of action against one defendant cannot join both claims in one suit.116 The statutory right to join causes of) action in one bill also exists where there are several defendants if the liability is asserted against all of the principal defendants. Thus, a bill of complaint may combine two causes of action, one to foreclose a mortgage, and the other to remove a cloud upon title, where the property and defendants are identical in each cause of action.117 

And a defendant in a partition suit may maintain a counterclaim to foreclose a mortgage upon the entire estate in a part of the lands involved.118 

It has been held, however, that, even under the apparently clear provisions of the statute, causes of action cannot be joined as of

Thus specific performance of a contract to convey land and the foreclosure of a mortgage upon the same land have been held to be remedies so diverse in their nature that they may not both be incorporated in the same bill of complaint.119 

With this exception, the causes of action which may be joined where there is only one plaintiff and one defendant, where the causes of action belong to several plaintiffs jointly, or where the liability asserted is against all the principal defendants, may be wholly independent, separate, and distinct, and need have no connection or relation whatsoever with each other. 120 The only requirement for the joinder is that each cause of action must be cognizable in equity.12 However, since this statute is not prohibitive of anything which was permissible under chancery practice before its enactment, it seems clear that legal relief may be granted as incidental to any one of the causes of action so joined where, prior to the statute, such legal relief could have been obtained in a court of chancery as incidental to that particular cause of action. 122 121 It thus appears that, while the 1931 Chancery Act may to some extent broaden the prior rules as to the joinder of causes of action where they accrue to several plaintiffs jointly, or are asserted against. all of the principal defendants, in this instance also no substantial departure from prior decisions is indicated. And, under the terms of the Act, the court may, where the joinder of causes of action is as of right, order separate trials if it appears that the various claims cannot be conveniently disposed of together. 123 

It will be noted that, except in the limited classes of cases above discussed, the statute does not give an unrestricted right to join causes of action. Unless there is only one plaintiff and one defendant, unless the causes of action accrue to several plaintiffs jointly, or

unless the liability is one asserted against all of the principal defendants, different causes of action may be joined only where sufficient grounds are made to appear for uniting them in order to promote the convenient administration of justice. As convenience in the administration of justice was the principle which has always guided courts of chancery in determining whether several causes of action could be joined in one bill, the statute did not necessarily alter the existing practice in this respect. However, since it has been held that the object of the statutory provision is to permit mulifariousness, 124 it is possible that the statute will have the effect of liberalizing the rules as to the joinder of causes of action in cases where it is not a matter of right.

Under the 1931 Act, it has been held that several owners of lumber which has been commingled by the defendant into an unidentifiable mass have such a common interest in the subject matter as to justify their joinder in one bill. 125 And where a vendor received from fire insurers, under policies payable to the vendor and purchaser as their interest should appear, an amount equal to that due from the purchaser, and wrongfully transferred the property and the purchaser's notes to a trustee for the purchaser, the purchaser was held entitled to maintain a bill against the vendor and the insurers to compel a conveyance of the land involved, a surrender of the notes, and an accounting for the balance due on the insurance policies. 126

But indicative of the fact that the 1931 Chancery Act does not authorize any substantial departure from the pre-existing rules governing multifariousness, where there are several parties plaintiff or defendant, are several decisions in which a joinder was held not permissible. Thus, in a decision expressly applying the prior principles, it was held that two separate and distinct causes of action could not be set up in one bill against two persons neither of whom was interested in the other's transaction and neither case being affected by the evidence or relief in the other.127 

Likewise, for the reason that no sufficient ground for the joinder was shown, it was held not permissible to join a cause of action

against a husband for maintenance, suit money, and attorney's fees with a cause of action against a son to enjoin an unlawful possession and retention of plaintiff's property." 128 And a bill against an insurer by the insured's widow and minor child on two life insurance policies was held multifarious, especially since the widow's cause of action might be barred by limitations, laches, or estoppel, while, as to the minor child, the statute of limitations would not begin to run, nor could he be charged with laches or estoppel, until he reached his majority.129

It is thus apparent that, in order to justify the joinder of several causes of action under the 1931 Chancery Act, where there are several parties plaintiff or defendant, and such joinder is not as of right, sufficient ground therefor must appear. 130 If a sufficient ground is shown, causes of action which are wholly independent, separate, and distinct, and which have no connection or relation whatever with each other, may be joined.131 But, as clearly appears from the decisions which have been discussed, the application of the rule must depend largely upon the circumstances of each particular case and rest in the sound discretion of the court.132 

§ 43.-Bill With Double Aspect.-A bill in equity may be framed with a double aspect without being open to the objection of multifariousness. 133 By a bill with a double aspect is meant the statement of two sets of facts of a different nature but which entitle the plaintiff to exactly the same relief. Thus the plaintiff may allege as many different grounds for the rescission or cancellation of a contract as he may desire, and he is not confined to the proof of one of such grounds, nor will a failure to prove one prevent recovery on the others.134 So also, a bill for divorce may state a case for relief on the ground of extreme cruelty, habitual indulgence in a violent and ungovernable temper, adultery, and impotence.135

A somewhat different form of bill framed with a double aspect is found in cases where the facts give rise to two distinct though alternative rights, each of which entitles plaintiff to the same relief. 

Thus a bill of complaint seeking to foreclose a mortgage may also state a case in the alternative seeking the enforcement of a lien on the separate statutory property of a married woman in case the mortgage is found to be defectively executed.136 So also, where the exact debts secured by a mortgage are in doubt, a bill in equity may seek the foreclosure of the mortgage to secure a certain debt or, in the alternative, if the mortgage is construed as not securing that debt, its enforcement through the foreclosure of a mechanic's lien. 137

But a bill may not be so framed in the alternative where it is based on inconsistent sets of facts. Thus a suit in equity may not be maintained against the defendant on the allegation that he had either actual or constructive notice of plaintiff's rights.138 Nor may a bill in equity be maintained when two distinct collocations of distinct and different facts, each collocation presenting different rights and calling for different relief, are embodied therein. For example, specific performance of a contract to convey land and foreclosure of a mortgage upon the same land are remedies so diverse in their nature that they cannot be incorporated in the same bill of complaint. 139

Framing a bill in equity with a double aspect has always been. permissible in equity pleading and it is clearly sanctioned by the

The foregoing requirements have been materially changed by the 1931 Chancery Act which provides that a bill shall only contain “a statement of and prayer for any special relief pending the suit or on final hearing, which may be stated and sought in alternative forms." It further provides that "prayers for general relief and for subpoena shall be omitted" and that "every bill of complaint shall be considered to pray for general relief."146 A prayer that the defendant be required to answer is now unnecessary except as to nominal parties.147

The statute thus continued in force the prior requirements in regard to a prayer for special relief. As to that prayer the rule is that the relief sought must be predicated upon appropriate allegations of the bill and that the nature and extent of the relief granted is determined by the pleadings in the cause and the proof in support thereof.148 But, if an equity appears from the allegations of a bill, defects, if any, in the prayer do not render it insufficient for appropriate relief.149 A prayer for relief not based upon allegations in the bill creates no equity.150 But an improper prayer, or a prayer which may be mere surplusage, does not destroy other equities and proper prayers for relief based upon sufficient allegations in the bill.151

Signature and Verification.-The 1931 Chancery Act pro vides that: "Every bill or other pleading shall be signed individually by one or more solicitors of record, and such signatures shall be considered as a certificate by each solicitor that he has read the pleading so signed by him; that upon the instructions laid before him regarding the case there is good ground for the same; that no scandalous matter is inserted in the pleading; and that it is not interposed for delay. 59. Revivor. § 47.-In General.-There can be no suit without parties and where it is uncertain who the parties are the suit is fundamentally defective. The defect is not one of form but of substance.' 

It is the constant aid of courts of equity to do complete justice, hence the common expression that courts of equity delight to do complete justice, and not by halves.2 A partial or incomplete decree will not be entered. Consequently, it is a general rule of equity pleading that all persons who are materially interested, either legally or beneficially, in the subject matter of a suit must be made parties, either as plaintiffs or defendants, and however numerous they may be. By this means the court is enabled to make a complete decree between the parties, to prevent future litigation by eliminating the necessity of a multiplicity of suits, and to make it

When all the parties are before the court the whole case may be seen, but it may not be where all the conflicting interests are not brought out by the pleadings. The reason for the rule thus lies in the principle of public policy enforced in courts of equity that a decree should finally and completely determine the rights which all persons have in the subject matter so that the parties may safely obey and act upon the decree. It is one of the peculiar advantages of chancery jurisdiction that the court can bring before it at once all persons having any interest or concern in the subject of the controversy.7 Therefore, all persons whose interests will necessarily be affected by any decree that can be rendered in a cause, or whose actions with reference to the subject matter of the litigation are to be controlled by the decree, or without whose presence a complete settlement of the questions involved in the action could not be attained, are necessary and indispensable parties.8

The court cannot properly adjudicate the matters involved in a suit when it appears that necessary and indispensable parties to the proceeding have not been served with process or are not in some proper way actually or constructively before the court. Not only will the court refuse to proceed without them, 10 but it is error for the court to enter a final decree in a cause before all parties made defendants have been brought into court and the issues made up or a decree pro confesso entered against such defendants." It follows as a necessary corollary of the foregoing rule that the rights of persons who have an interest in the subject matter of the litigation, whether legal or equitable, cannot be adjudicated or affected by a decree in a suit to which they were not made parties.¹4 

Where the record discloses that there are persons, not made parties to the suit, who claim rights in the subject matter thereof, they are not bound by the decree no matter what may be the allegations of the bill or the evidence as to the nature of their claims. 15 Otherwise stated, the rule is that the rights and interests of necessary and indispensable parties cannot be adjudicated when they are not properly before the court.16

To sustain the character of a plaintiff it is necessary to show in the person so suing an interest, either legal or equitable, in the subject matter of the suit.19 Thus, if the distributee entitled to the personalty of an intestate should die, his administrator, or executor, if there is one, is the only person who may sue for such personalty. 

The husband and children of the distributee cannot maintain a suit growing out of the personalty.20

It is proper to join together as plaintiffs all persons who are together the owners of the entire interest in the cause of action brought before the court for adjudication. Thus the pledgee of a contract sought to be specifically enforced is a proper party plaintiff to the suit for specific performance.21 Where a bill of complaint brought to compel payment of a fire insurance policy shows that the loss, if any, is conditionally payable to a mortgagee; and that the amount of the mortgage is less than the face amount of the policy, both the mortgagor and mortgagee are necessary parties to the suit.22

A person has no standing as a plaintiff in a court of equity if he has no interest in the subject matter of the suit.23 Where it appears that a co-plaintiff has disposed of all his interest in the property in dispute before the commencement of the action, such person is neither a necessary nor a proper party.2 24 Thus, an assignor of an outstanding mortgage is not a necessary party plaintiff to a bill for redemption brought by the mortgagor.2

No person can be made a co-plaintiff without his consent,28 and, as provided in the 1931 Chancery Act, the established rule is that, when any one of several persons having a united interest in the subject matter refuses to join as a party plaintiff, he may for such reason be made a defendant.29 Persons so made defendants are entitled to share in the relief granted even though they complain of nothing and ask for nothing. They may remain passive and consequently be made parties defendant without being held to have waived or surrendered their rights in the premises.30 This is true even though a defendant does not claim in the same right as the plaintiffs, but actively opposes and denies their claims.31 

§ 49.-Necessary Parties Defendant. In regard to parties defend ant, the 1931 Chancery Act provides that "any person may be made a defendant who has or claims an interest adverse to the plaintiff" and that "persons having a united interest may be joined on the same side as plaintiffs or defendants."32 These provisions also are merely declaratory of settled law.33 It has always been a rule of equity pleading that all persons whose interests are adverse to those of the plaintiff should be made defendants where they are necessary or proper parties and their names are known.34 

The 1931 Chancery Act makes no material change in the preexisting rules of practice in regard to the distinction between necessary and proper parties defendant to a suit in equity. A necessary party defendant is one without whose presence no decree whatsoever can be entered, whereas a proper party defendant is one who may be joined because of his interest in the subject matter of the suit, or whose presence will enable the court to more com-

It has always been a settled rule of equity practice that all persons whose interests will necessarily be affected by a decree, whose actions with reference to the subject matter of the litigation are to be controlled by the decree, or without whose presence a complete settlement of the question involved in the action cannot be attained, are necessary parties defendant.35 So also, persons without whose joinder no effectual decree can be rendered in plaintiff's favor are necessary parties, for the court will not interfere at all except in a mode which will be effectual for the purpose of the decree.36 Of course, all those against whom relief is prayed are proper and necessary parties.37

Thus, when a bill for an accounting is filed by a creditor of a partnership against the representatives of a deceased partner, the surviving partner is a necessary party defendant. He has an interest in taking the account correctly, inasmuch as there may be a remedy over against him by the representatives of the estate by their being substituted in the place of the creditors.38 Where one of several wards brings a bill for an account against his guardian, any other wards who are interested in the general fund must be made parties to the suit.39

Whether the subject of an action is real or personal property, a plaintiff seeking to set aside fraudulent judicial proceedings in reference thereto should join as parties defendant all persons who were actors in such proceedings and who claim a present interest in the specific property.40

A bill seeking to set aside a conveyance by which a subsequently deceased person acquired title must name his heirs as parties defendant.41 Upon the death of the head of a family his heirs are necessary parties to all proceedings affecting his homestead.42 In

Persons charged with fraud and having made a fraudulent conveyance, which plaintiff seeks to have removed as a cloud upon his title, are necessary parties defendant to a suit for that purpose.46 

All joint mortgagors against whom a deficiency decree is specifically prayed, are necessary parties defendant to a foreclosure suit.47 In a suit to execute the trusts of a will, it is not necessary to make the heir at law a party, but the plaintiff is at liberty to make the heir at law a party where he desires to have the will established against him.48

Persons not shown by the record to have any present interest in the issues presented, or any future interest which may be affected by the final decree, are not necessary parties.49 Nor is it necessary to join as defendants persons whose presence is not essential to a complete settlement of the questions involved in the suit and whose rights will not be affected by the decree.50 

Thus the original vendee of an estate is not a necessary party to a suit against his assignee for specific performance of the contract to purchase.51 In a suit instituted to foreclose a mortgage, and to set aside a sale under an execution, it is not necessary to make the original owner of the judgment, who has parted with all

Where a bill is filed against an assignee for the benefit of creditors to enforce a lien upon the assigned property, and no relief is prayed against the assignor, the assignor is not a necessary party defendant to the bill.54

If a suit involves specific property which is well described in the pleadings, all persons purchasing such property from a party to the suit while the suit is in full prosecution do so at their peril. 

They take the risk of the suit and are concluded by the decree therein, and it is not necessary that they should be made parties thereto.55 A husband who is beyond the jurisdiction of the court and not amenable to its process, and against whom no relief is prayed, is not a necessary party to a suit to subject certificates of stock owned by his wife to the payment of a debt which she had pledged them to secure.56

The joinder of parties defendant in equity is largely a matter of discretion with the court and therefore a nonjoinder of parties in such suits cannot always be definitely determined. The general rule is that, if the interests of those present and those absent are inseparable, all must be joined or the case will fail, but if the interests of the parties present are separable, and a decree may be made without affecting the interests of those not present, the case may be decided on its merits as between those who are regularly before the court.57

The court has a broad discretion in forming its decrees in order to adapt the relief to the circumstances of particular cases. The primary object of a decree is to reach the ends of justice and equity procedure is usually elastic enough to accomplish this result. Generally, relief may be granted against some defendants and denied as to others. The rule in actions at law, that a judgment must be rendered against all defendants charged with a joint liability, or against none, has no application to suits in equity.59 The principle is incorporated into a provision of the 1931 Chancery Act that "in all cases in which the plaintiff has a joint and several demand against several persons, either as principals or sureties, it shall not be necessary to bring before the court as parties to a suit concerning such demand all the persons liable thereto; but the plaintiff may proceed against one or more of the persons severally liable."60 This statute does not, however, destroy the distinction between joint and several actions, and, where a decree joint in its nature is rendered against a defendant over whom the court has never acquired jurisdiction, it will be a cause for reversal.62 

Where there is a total absence of parties against whom a decree can be made, a suit in equity cannot be maintained.63 And, since it is an elementary principle that a court cannot adjudicate directly upon the rights of parties without having them actually or constructively before it, a decree for the plaintiff rendered in the absence of a necessary party will be reversed on appeal.64 However, in order to warrant this result the absent parties must have such an interest in the controversy that a final decree between the parties before the court cannot be made without affecting their interests or without leaving the controversy in such a situation that its final determination may be inconsistent with equity and good conscience.65

PARTIES § 50. Proper and Nominal Parties.-As previously stated, 66 

proper parties to a suit in chancery are those who may be joined because of their interest in the subject matter of the suit, or whose presence will enable the court to more completely settle the controversy before it, but whose absence will not preclude the entry of a decree between the parties who are in court. 

It is proper to join as plaintiffs all those who are together the owners of the entire interest in the cause of action brought before the court for adjudication. Thus the pledgee of a chose in action sued upon is a proper party plaintiff.67 But persons who, before the commencement of the suit, have disposed of their interest in the property in dispute, or who have no interest in the subject matter of the suit, are improper parties plaintiff.68 A statute69 providing that a person in whose name a contract is made for the benefit of another may sue without joining with him the person for whose benefit the action is brought does not prevent the joining of the latter. He is a proper party plaintiff.70 

As to proper parties defendant, it has been held that, where fraud is the gravamen of a plaintiff's right to relief, all those who participated in the alleged fraud, and those who will be the beneficiaries of it, are proper parties.71 Where a deed sought to be reformed covers land claimed by others than the grantor, it is proper to join them with the grantor as defendants.72 But a receiver of an estate, not being vested with legal title, is not a proper party to a bill to remove a cloud upon title.73 And the sheriff is not a proper party to a bill to enjoin a sale under execution.74

It will be noted that the 1931 Chancery Act provides that every action shall be prosecuted in the name of the real party in interest, whereas the prior statute which was held applicable to both actions at law and suits in equity was merely permissive. It will also be noted that both statutes apply only to the bringing of actions and not to their defense. § 52.-Suits By or Against Incompetents.-In regard to the bringing of suits by infants, the 1931 Chancery Act provides that "all infants and other persons so incapable may sue by their guardians, if any, or by their next friend; subject, however, to such orders as the court may direct for the protection of infants and other persons."85

The original chancery rule was that a suit could not be maintained by one "as guardian" of an infant. The suit had to be brought in the name of the infant by his next friend.86 The same rule necessarily resulted from a Florida statute providing that an infant may sue by his next friend in all cases whatsoever,87 although a provision of the same statute requiring the next friend to give bond upon the institution of suit was held inapplicable to chancery suits.88

Under the above quoted provision of the 1931 Chancery Act, however, and a pre-existing equity rule,89 an infant may sue by his guardian, if any, or by his next friend. The statute does not require the use of a next friend, at least in the absence of special circumstances shown to the court.90 Under both the statute and its general powers, a court of equity may enter such orders as are necessary to protect the interests of infants.91

In accordance with the principle that infant defendants are entitled to the special protection of a court of chancery,92 the 1931 Chancery Act provides that "guardians ad litem to defend a suit may be appointed by the court for infants or other persons who are under guardianship, or otherwise incapable of suing for themselves."93 This statute contemplates that the court will take care that the rights of those who in law are not sui juris will be protected.94 Therefore, when it is made to appear to the court, even though informally, that one of the parties defendant in a cause pending before it is a minor, whether a resident or non-resident, the court should appoint a guardian ad litem for the minor and direct him to file such pleadings as may be necessary to guard the minor's interests in the suit.95 Thus it is error to appoint an examiner or master to take testimony in a cause where, at the time of the appointment, no guardian ad litem had been appointed to represent minor defendants.96

Where a stranger to an equity cause interposes any pleading for and on behalf of minors interested in the issues thereof, as their guardian ad litem, and the record fails to show that such person has ever been appointed or authorized by the court to act in the cause as such guardian ad litem, all the pleadings interposed by the stranger are nugatory. They do not bind the minors and all orders and proceedings in the cause predicated upon those pleadings will be set aside as void.97 But it has been held that, where service is made upon the general guardian of an infant, and he appears and makes the defense required by law, and is heard by the court as the representative of the infant, such action is equivalent to his appointment as guardian ad litem.98

The appointment of a guardian ad litem is not an empty formality. He is designated by the court for the definite and positive purpose of safeguarding the rights of his ward by filing such pleadings as may be necessary or appropriate, and it is not to be anticipated that he will file an answer merely stating that he has no defense to present.99 The formal answer of a guardian ad litem should submit the infant's rights to the determination of the court and leave the plaintiff to make out the facts of his case by strict proof. 100

It is an established rule that a guardian ad litem cannot admit or waive anything adverse or prejudicial to the infant and he has no power to bind his ward by the admission or waiver of anything. 101 Questions of jurisdiction, or proof by competent evidence of material issues, or procedure in accordance with established rules, cannot, as against infant defendants, be waived.102 Thus a guardian ad litem is without power to waive service of process on a counterclaim as to infant defendants.103 And an answer filed by a guardian ad litem before the return day fixed in an order for constructive service upon minor defendants will not operate as an appearance as to them. An infant cannot against his will and interest be considered in court until the full period fixed in the order has elapsed and full opportunity for the notice to be brought home to him accorded. The infant may be of such years of discretion as to be entitled to be heard upon the choice of a guardian ad litem, or those naturally interested in the infant's welfare may wish to be heard in the selection.104 Nor can a guardian ad litem compromise or settle a suit on behalf of an infant. 105

It is also a general rule that an infant shall not be prejudiced. by any act, default, or admission on the part of his guardian ad litem. An infant is a ward of the court and therefore the court is bound to protect the rights of the infant notwithstanding a

Under the provision of the 1931 Chancery Act that "all infants and other persons so incapable may sue by their guardian, if any, or by their next friend,"112 a person of unsound mind who has been adjudged insane, for whom a guardian has been appointed, should sue by his guardian.113 A prior statute also provides that idiots and lunatics shall sue by their guardians.114 

It should be noted, however, that there is a difference in the civil status of one whose mind is not sound but is enfeebled or nearly destroyed from old age, bodily infirmity, or other physical causes, and who is for that reason incapable of managing his own affairs, and one who has been adjudged to be a lunatic or insane. Yet a person of the former class is as much entitled to the protection of the courts from the consequences of improvident dealings or the aggressions of deceitful and designing persons as one of the latter class. Therefore, it has always been the practice of courts of equity to authorize persons of the first class to apply to the court by next friend for relief against agreements or conveyances which they have been improperly induced to make or execute to the advantage or gain of some unscrupulous or designing person. To deny such relief would be a denial of one of the highest functions of a court of equity.115

There being no adjudication of insanity or appointment of a guardian in such cases the above quoted statute requiring idiots and lunatics to sue by their guardian does not apply. Furthermore, the purpose of the statute was not to abridge an equity rule

As a general rule, and in accordance with the provisions of the 1931 Chancery Act that infants and other persons so incapable may sue by their guardians, if any, or by their next friend, a married woman sues in equity by her next friend. 123 But there are several statutory exceptions to this rule. Thus, a married woman may interpose a claim to her personal property levied upon under legal process with all the rights, powers, and privileges of a femë sole.124 A married woman whose husband has become insane or has deserted her for six months may prosecute or defend any action at law or in equity as if she were a feme sole. 125 A married woman may also bring suits for or concerning her real estate without joining her husband or next friend, 126 and she may sue for and recover wages and earnings acquired by her in any employment separate from her husband as though she were a single woman. 127 

Where the general rule applies, and the married woman sues by next friend, the next friend may very properly be the husband when he is not adversely interested.128 But a next friend will be named only with the consent of the married woman.129
