PARTIES § 53. Suits By or Against Executors and Administrators.-The 

1931 Chancery Act provides that "every action shall be prosecuted in the name of the real party in interest, but an executor, administrator, guardian, trustee of an express trust, a party with whom or in whose name a contract has been made for the benefit of another, or a party expressly authorized by statute, may sue in his own name without joining with him the party for whose benefit the action is brought."142 Accordingly, an administrator or executor may sue without joining with him the next of kin, heirs, legatees or devisees. 

This has always been the rule as to personal property comprised within an estate.143 Thus a personal representative is the proper party to foreclose a mortgage.144 For a long period of time, however, the rule was otherwise as to real estate. 

The original Florida rule was based upon an 1828 statute providing that "real estate shall be considered assets in the hands of an executor or administrator." Under this statute the personal representative was entitled to the possession of real estate and could maintain ejectment to protect and preserve his possession.145 

An heir could not maintain ejectment against either the administrator146 or third persons.147 The personal representative and not the heir was the only necessary party to a mortgage foreclosure upon a decedent's real estate. 148

In 1892, however, the statute which was the basis of the foregoing rule was repealed and a new law was enacted providing that "real estate shall be liable for the debts of a decedent but shall descend to the heir or devisee and remain in his possession until the executor or administrator shall take possession of the same under the order of the court, or until the same shall be sold under execution by any creditor of the decedent."149 Under this statute a personal representative could only maintain ejectment as to real estate in his possession or authorized to be taken into his possession

The Florida Probate Act, enacted in 1933, reverts in part to the earlier doctrine with a new provision that the heirs or devisees may maintain actions of ejectment or suits to quiet title. This statute provides: "Personal representatives may bring and maintain actions or suits for the possession or recovery of real property of the estate, for the purpose of quieting the title thereto, for waste thereof and trespass thereto, and against cotenants of the decedent in real property for the partition thereof. Heirs or devisees of the decedent may themselves or jointly with the personal representative bring and maintain actions or suits for the possession or recovery of real property of the estate or for the purpose of quieting title thereto against anyone except the personal representative. In any suit to quiet title brought by an heir or devisee, the possession of the personal representative shall, for the purpose of such suit, be deemed the possession of the heir or devisee. In all actions or suits involving the title to real property, against an estate for the possession or recovery of real property or for the purpose of quieting title thereto, the personal representative and the heirs or devisees of such property shall be made parties."153

In a suit by an executor or administrator, in his representative capacity, he should describe himself and make his claim "as" executor or administrator only. Describing himself "executor" or "administrator" is mere descriptio personæ.154 And it is good practice for a personal representative, when he sues as such, to make profert of his letters testamentary or of administration. 155

The reason for this rule is that, no matter in which capacity a recovery is had, the judgment becomes an asset of the estate for which the personal representative is accountable, and the matter does not concern the defendant, whose liability is individual in any event. The same defenses are available to the defendant, the form of judgment is necessarily the same, and the liability will be discharged by payment regardless of the form in which the judgment may be obtained. 156 

It will be noted that the provision of the 1931 Chancery Act permitting an executor or administrator to sue in his own name, without joining with him the party for whose benefit the action is brought, has no application to suits against executors or administrators. 157 The nature of the suit determines whether the personal representative, or the heirs, or both, must be made parties defendant. 

In a suit on a contract made with a party since deceased, his legal representatives are necessary parties.158 But where services are rendered to a personal representative under a contract made with him he should be sued in his individual capacity.159 And, as previously noted, the 1933 Florida Probate Act requires that "in all actions or suits involving the title to real property, against an estate for the possession or recovery of real property or for the purpose of quieting title thereto, the personal representative and the heirs or devisees of such property shall be made parties."160 

While a personal representative should be sued "as" executor or administrator, where the word executor or administrator is used merely as descriptio personæ, and no exception is taken to the designation of the capacity in which he is sued, the action will be treated as one against him in his representative capacity.161

PARTIES § 54.-Class Suits.-The 1931 Chancery Act provides that 

"when the question is one of common or general interest to many persons constituting a class so numerous as to make it impracticable to bring them all before the court, one or more may sue or defend for the whole."167 This statute accords with the principle permitting such a suit where a number of persons have separate and individual claims and rights of action against the same party, but all arise from some common cause, are governed by the same legal rule, and involve similar facts, and where the whole matter may be settled in a single suit brought by all of these persons uniting as co-plaintiffs, or one of the persons suing on behalf of himself and the others, or even by one person suing for himself alone.168 In such cases, representation of all by certain of the parties in interest is permitted for convenience and is necessary to prevent a failure of justice. 169

In order to come within the statute, a common or general interest to many persons must be shown and the duty devolves on the court to determine whether the common or general interest exists before rendering a decree against those who are alleged to be in court by representation. 170 The court must also be satisfied that the party or parties who represent the class will adequately assert and protect the interests of all. Particularly where it is claimed that the defendant represents a class, the court should be certain that the defense is thorough and in good faith, and that the defendant was not chosen merely for the purpose of a friendly suit. If the requirements of a class suit are met the absent members, though they are not considered as parties to the suit, are bound by representation by any decree rendered therein.171 

In accordance with the statute it has been held that one or more members of an unincorporated association, whose members were so numerous as to make it impractical to bring them all before the court, may, as representatives of the whole class, sue to foreclose a mortgage.172 

167. C. G. L. Per. Supp. 4918 (7); 

McCarthy Chan. Act, p. 47, § 14. 

168. Chew V. First Presbyterian

169. Carnahan v. Peabody, 31 Fed.

Even where all of the members of the class are not in being at the time of the institution of suit, the decree will be binding upon them. Thus, where there is a remainder to a class, and there are remaindermen of the class in being who are made parties to a suit affecting the property, the decree rendered therein will bind all others who subsequently come into the class. This result follows from the doctrine of representation, it being assumed that the living representative will look after the interests of the entire class by bringing to the attention of the court the merits of the controversy so far as they affect the class. 173 

§ 55.-How Persons Are Made Parties.-Persons are made plain tiffs to a suit in equity by naming them as such in the bill of complaint and by clearly alleging their interests in the cause of action therein stated. 174 No one can be made a party plaintiff without his consent.175

To be made a defendant, a person must also be named as such in the bill of complaint and his interest in the subject matter definitely alleged.176 In addition, a person can only be made a defendant by being served with process, or by order of court upon his own intervention. 177 However, one not named as a defendant may become a party by voluntarily appearing to the bill and participating in the proceedings, or he may by stipulation to that effect make himself a party and be bound by the decree.178 A person who has been appointed an administrator after the institution of a suit cannot be made a party to it by mere suggestion, even though a copy of the record of such suggestion, and of his having been so made a party, is served upon him.179 

A substitution of parties may be procured, under the 1931 Chancery Act, by order of the court upon motion. No supplemental bill, or bill of revivor, or bill in the nature of either is necessary.¹

§ 59.-Revivor.-A suit in equity abates upon the death of the sole plaintiff and all proceedings must be suspended until his legal representatives have been brought in.212 Likewise, a suit in equity abates upon the death of a defendant who has appeared insofar as proceedings against him or his interest are concerned, and if he was an indispensable party to the suit all proceedings must be suspended until his representatives have been brought in. If, however, a decedent's interest wholly ceases by his death, or wholly survives to one of the other parties, no revivor is necessary.213 But where a defendant dies, the presumption is, in the absence of a contrary showing in the record, that a revivor must be had and his legal representatives properly brought into court.214 

Instances in which a revivor is not necessary are where the suit is by or against a husband and wife in the right of the wife and the husband dies under circumstances which admit of no demand by or against his representatives, where one of several creditors suing on behalf of themselves and other creditors dies, or where one of several joint tenants, parties to a suit, dies. But a revivor is necessary where the interest of the person dying passes to his heirs or legal representatives. Thus a suit must be revived where one of several tenants in common, parties to a suit, dies. 

And where one sues on behalf of himself and other creditors, and dies, there may be a revivor by his personal representatives. 

Where a defendant dies during the interval between the entry of a decree pro confesso and a final decree a serious problem is presented. Although the point has not been decided the more logical view is that by permitting the entry of a decree pro confesso the defendant has admitted the allegations of the bill of complaint and has nothing further to defend, thereby making it unnecessary to substitute his legal representatives or heirs.215 And, in any chancery case where a decree pro confesso has been entered against a defendant upon whom constructive service has been had, and

Where the legal representatives of a deceased party wish to appeal from a final decree rendered prior to his death, a revivor must be had in the lower court, and the presumption is that the deceased party died after and not before final decree.217 

As to when and how a revivor may be had, the 1931 Chancery 

Act provides: 

"In the event of the death of either party the court may, before or after final decree, in a proper case, upon motion, order the suit to be revived by the substitution of the proper parties. 

If the successors or representatives of the deceased party fail to make such application within a reasonable time, then any other party may, on motion, apply for such relief, and the court, upon any such motion may make the necessary orders for notice to the parties to be substituted and for the filing of such pleadings or amendments as may be necessary, including the appointment of an administrator ad litem."218

The 1931 Chancery Act219 also provides that no supplemental bills, or bills of revivor, or bills in the nature of either, shall be necessary to procure a substitution of parties, but substitution of parties shall be made in all cases where it becomes necessary by order of the court upon motion, and the cause shall then proceed in the same way as if there had been no occasion for a change of parties.

As a general rule a suit may be revived at any time before the cause of action is barred by the applicable statute of limitations. 

And, since a statute of limitations does not run in the absence of a person who is capable of suing, in case of the abatement of a suit

Since foreign personal representatives, who produce probate of wills or letters of administration obtained in any other state of the United States, are now authorized to maintain actions in the courts of this state under the same rules and regulations as other plaintiffs, it seems clear that suits may be revived in their favor.222 

Likewise, it would seem that suits may be revived against foreign personal representatives in any case where they may be sued in this state.223

Where a defendant files a suggestion of the death of the sole plaintiff, it is erroneous for the court to enter a decree pro confesso against such defendant, since the question of whether the proper plaintiff is before the court should be determined before any further proceedings are had in the cause.224 If a suit is brought in the name of a deceased person as sole plaintiff, and a decree pro confesso is entered against the defendant, and thereafter, without notice to the defendant, a real party is made sole plaintiff, the decree against the defendant is erroneous, since he has not had his day in court as to the amendment.225 Where, after the submission of a cause, a party dies, a revivor may be obviated by entering a decree nunc pro tunc as of the date of the hearing. 

But a decree nunc pro tunc presupposes a decree previously passed or allowed and not entered, or else a cause which has been heard and is under advisement. The expedient cannot be resorted to for the purpose of validating a proceeding which was void at the time it was had.226 The death of a party pending the process of advertising property for sale under a final decree does not, if no

He is successor to all the rights and interests of the trust company by virtue of his appointment.231

If any corporation becomes dissolved, by the expiration of its charter or otherwise, before a final decree in any suit pending against it, the suit does not abate, but the dissolution of the corporation being suggested upon the record, and the names of the trustees or receivers being entered thereon, and notice thereof being served upon them or the counsel of record in the case, the suit proceeds to a final decree against the trustees or receivers by the name of the corporation.232 Although the statutes provide that all corporations shall continue bodies corporate for three years after their dissolution, for the purpose of prosecuting suits by or against them, where a suit is prosecuted to submission for final hearing in the appellate court within three years from the dissolution of the plaintiff corporation, the appellate court may reverse the decree after the three year period.233

§ 60.-Necessity of Process.-Before potential jurisdiction of the subject matter can be exercised in a particular case, it must be lawfully invoked and called into action. In other words, the parties to the controversy and the subject matter thereof must be brought before the court in such a way that it acquires control and power The jurisdiction of courts of equity over the subject matter of controversies has previously been discussed.2 As to jurisdiction over the parties, process must be served on the party or parties defendant in order that they may have an opportunity to be heard, or the property, if that is the subject matter of the acto act.¹

[Ch. 7

Statutes which are hereinafter discussed point out the particular manner in which a court of equity may obtain jurisdiction over parties defendant, and no other mode of acquiring such jurisdiction can be recognized, except by the consent of the party concerned.4 In general, summons in chancery, or constructive service, when authorized, must be directed to each defendant named in the suit and it must be served on him in the manner required by law before the court acquires jurisdiction over his person. There is no statute in this state which authorizes a proceeding in chancery to be conducted on notice. There must be an actual or constructive service of process. A bare notice the defendant may disregard. However, the legislature is not prohibited by the requirements of due process of law from establishing a general rule of practice by which notice of the institution of a suit may be given by an attorney or party.7

A person not named as a defendant, or served with process, may become a party by voluntarily appearing to a bill of complaint and participating in the proceeding, or he may by stipulation to that

It is essential that the court acquire jurisdiction of the person of the defendant. If it proceeds without such jurisdiction, acquired either by the service of process or personal appearance, its decree can have no binding effect.10 A decree rendered where jurisdiction of the defendant has not been so acquired is not merely voidable, but absolutely void.11

Prior to 1931, a statute required the copy of the summons served upon the defendant to have endorsed upon it the name of the court from which it issued, the title of the cause, the words "copy of subpoena," and the name of the plaintiff's solicitor.17 

This statute was repealed by the 1931 Chancery Act, 18 but under its provisions it was held that, while the words "et al.," might be used in place of the names of some of the parties in stating the title of the cause, they could not be used in stating the names of the defendants in the body of the summons.19 There each and every defendant was required to be named with certainty.2 20 The 1931 Chancery Act apparently does not require the body of the summons to contain the names of all defendants in order to be a good summons to the defendants who are named therein. 

This conclusion is supported by the provision that, where there is more than one defendant, the clerk shall issue but one summons against all defendants unless otherwise directed by the plaintiff or his solicitor. The Act seems clearly intended to permit the issuance of more than one summons and to make each summons valid as against the defendant or group of defendants named therein.21

§ 63.-Issuance of Summons.-The summons in chancery is issued as of course by the clerk of the circuit court upon the filing of the bill of complaint. No summons may be issued until the bill is filed in the clerk's office.24 No prayer for process is necessary.25 

§ 64.-Return Day.-The summons in chancery must be made returnable to the rule day next after the date of its issuance unless there shall not be ten days intervening between the day of issuance and the next rule day. In the latter event, the summons must be made returnable to the rule day in the next succeeding month.26 The first Monday in each month is the rule day.27 

§ 65. Personal Service. By personal service of summons is meant service on the person of the defendant or some statutory substitute there for such as leaving a copy of the summons at his usual place of abode with some member of his family. The 1931 

Chancery Act provides that service of summons in chancery shall be as prescribed by law in the case of summons ad respondendum.28 

§ 66.-Time of Service and By Whom Made.-All process must be served at least ten days before the rule day to which it is returnable.29 Service of process on Sunday is void and the person making service or causing service to be made on that day is liable to the party aggrieved as if no service had been made.30 

All process must be served by the sheriff or a constable of the county in the district in which it is to be served.31 Service cannot be made by a private party.32

As regards service upon minors, the original chancery practice, where the infant did appear voluntarily, was to send an officer to bring him into court and then a guardian was appointed to defend his interests in the suit.47 From this practice grew the chancery rule that, where a minor is to be made a party defendant in a suit, a summons must be issued to the minor and regularly served upon him in the presence of his legal guardian or in the presence of the person who is charged with his legal care and custody. Then a guardian ad litem for the minor is appointed by the court, and the guardian ad litem is also served with a summons in the cause.

§ 68.-Manner of Service-Partnerships.-A Florida statute pro vides that, when suit is brought against several persons composing a mercantile or other firm, the service of summons on any one member of the firm is as valid as if served on each individual member thereof, and the plaintiff may, after service upon any one member of the firm, proceed to a judgment against them all.51 This statute provides a kind of constructive service on all of the members composing a mercantile or other firm by service on any one member of the firm, and its provisions should accordingly be strictly construed. But service on the one member must be in person in order to affect the other members. Leaving a copy of the summons at his usual place of abode with a member of the family above the age of fifteen years may bind him individually, but the statute has not made it sufficient to bind the others.52 

In a suit against a partnership, the service of summons upon one member of the firm is sufficient to authorize a judgment covering the partnership property and the interest therein of the partners not served. The latter are not thereby deprived of property without due process of law.53 And a judgment based upon such service is a lien, not only on the property of the partnership, but upon the individual property of each and every member who was

Another statute provides that, where any firm or partnership conducts or carries on a business or business venture in the state of Florida, or has an office or agency in the state of Florida, service of summons may be made upon any business agent or accredited representative of the firm or partnership, and such service is binding upon the partnership and the individual members thereof, but, in order to authorize such service, it must appear that personal service cannot be made upon the individual partners, or any of them, and that the firm or partnership is composed wholly of persons not resident in Florida.55

Since the statute authorizes a method of serving process in the nature of substituted service, it is to be strictly construed and, in proceeding under it, the summons must specifically state that the named defendants are sued as partners. The omission of the word "as" following the names of the defendants and preceding the description of them as partners renders the action one against the named persons as joint defendants but not necessarily as partners.56 

Furthermore, all of the partners and their residences must be shown by the record because, if a single partner is a resident of Florida, service under the statute is invalid and insufficient to confer jurisdiction.57 And it has been held that the statute refers only to an agent having some general supervision over the affairs of the partnership being carried on in Florida, or to some accredited representative of the partnership in Florida having general authority to act for it.58 While the constitutionality of the statute has been questioned, it has never been passed upon.59

Under this statute, a return showing service upon an inferior officer or agent of a corporation, in order to bind the corporation, must show the absence of all officers of each superior class designated in the statute as those upon whom service must be made before resort is had to service upon one of an inferior class. The absence of all members of a superior class is a condition precedent to the validity of service upon a member of an inferior class. This is the clear and explicit language of the statute.61 In referring to the absence of all of the members of a superior class, the statute means absence from the county where the suit was instituted and such service sought, and not absence from the state. 62 And, in order to sustain service upon a member of an inferior class, the return need only show absence from the county of all members of the superior class on the date service is actually made on a member of the inferior class. It need not show such absence up to the last possible moment in which service could be made.63 All officers of the same class are equal in standing for the purpose of service of process. 64 Personal service on a corporation under the statute is properly made in the county where the corporation is domiciled.65

Where service is made under the fifth section of the statute upon an agent of a foreign corporation in any county other than that in which suit is brought, the return must show the absence from the state of all of the officers designated in the first four sections of the statute and also that the service was made upon an agent transacting business for the corporation in Florida. Service upon a person described as an acting secretary and attorney is not service upon any officer designated in the statute.67 

Another method of serving process upon a corporation is provided by a statute enacted in 1927 which provides that it is cumulative of all other provisions of law and that it does not preclude the service of process upon a corporation in accordance with any statute then in force.68 Under the 1927 statute every domestic corporation, and every foreign corporation qualifying to do business in Florida, is required to designate an office or place of business for the service of process in this state. This office or place of business is required to be kept open on all business days and the corporation is required to keep there an officer or agent upon whom process may be served. The location of the office and the names. of the officers upon whom process may be served are required to be filed in the office of the Secretary of State of Florida, where the information is available to any person interested. Service of summons in chancery may be made upon any officer or agent of the corporation found at such office or place of business. The person designated by the corporation as its officer or agent for the service of process, although generally known as its "resident agent, is neither a business agent resident in the state nor an agent transacting business for the corporation in the state within the meaning of the prior statutes.69

The method of making service upon an incorporated college or academy, a municipal corporation, or a county, is specified in separate statutes.70 A number of other classes of corporations are excepted from the 1927 statute discussed above.71

[Ch. 7 § 70.-Return of Summons.-As to the return of summons, a statute provides that all officers to whom process is directed shall note thereon the time when it comes to hand, the time when it was executed, the manner of execution, and the name of the person upon whom it is executed, and, if that person is served in a representative capacity, the position occupied by him. A failure to state these facts in the return subjects the officer so failing to a fine not exceeding ten dollars, in the discretion of the court.72 The statute requires the method of service to be reported to the court by its officer in order that the court may determine whether the defendant is properly summoned and whether it has jurisdiction to proceed with the cause. The ordinary presumption that an officer has properly performed his duty does not arise where the particular acts constituting the service are required to be set forth in a return.73

A sheriff's return of due service of a summons in the manner prescribed by law is conclusive as to jurisdiction over the defendant unless the same is impeached, and it requires clear and convincing evidence to overcome the statements of a return made under the sanction of official oath and responsibility.74 If this burden is met, a judgment based upon a false return is subject to either direct or collateral attack.75

Where the sheriff's return is fatally defective, a judgment rendered thereon is void and will be reversd.76 A return stating that process was "served on the within named party" is fatally defective.77 And a return signed by a deputy sheriff in his own name, without disclosing the name of his official principal for whom he acted in making the service, is a nullity and furnishes no evidence that the court from which the process issued acquired that jurisdiction over the person of the defendant which would warrant it

for service by publication, and most of them apply to suits in equity. 

However, constructive service cannot be made the basis for a judgment or decree which is purely personal. It may be validly used only when the suit is one in rem or quasi in rem. In other words, constructive service can only authorize a decree affecting the defendant's interest in some property or other res which is within the jurisdiction of the court.86

As frequently stated by the Supreme Court of Florida, the purpose of constructive service statutes is to give non-resident, unknown, absent, or concealed defendants notice of a suit brought against them so that they may, if they care to, come into court and present their defense.87 Of course, constructive service, whether used against natural persons or corporations, is predicated upon necessity and, if personal service can be effected by the exercise of reasonable diligence, constructive service is unauthorized. The test, however, is not whether it was in fact possible to effect personal service in a given case, but whether the plaintiff reasonably employed the knowledge at his command, made diligent inquiry, and exerted an honest and conscientious effort, appropriate to the circumstances, to acquire the information necessary to enable him to effect personal service on the defendant.88 

Statutes authorizing constructive service of process must be strictly and exactly pursued in order to give the court jurisdiction to render a judgment by default. If there is a failure to pursue the essential requirements of the statute, a decree rendered upon constructive service is void as to parties who have not appeared or pleaded in the cause.89 This principle is especially applicable

The full text of the statutes governing constructive service is somewhat confused and overlapping due to numerous amendments. 

However, practice under them has been well established in accordance with the portions thereof above set out. A study of the full text readily reveals the repealed provisions. 

The general rule is that constructive service of process, valid and sufficient as to persons sui juris, applies to and is binding upon persons non compos mentis, infants, and persons under other legal disability, unless an exception is expressly created in favor of the classes last named. Beginning with the general chancery procedure act of November 7, 1828, and continuing down to and including the present time, statutes have existed in Florida providing generally for constructive service of process upon non-residents and designated classes of other absent defendants in suits in equity, including suits relating to or affecting title to real property. None of these statutes contain any exception or limitation excluding infants or persons non compos mentis from their operation. Under the general rule above stated, therefore, the statutes mentioned have always afforded a means of effecting constructive service upon non-residents, which, when properly invoked, is binding upon and applicable alike to all persons within the designated classes of defendants whether such persons be sui juris or infants or persons non compos mentis. 102

A prior case to the contrary has been expressly overruled. 103

Each of the four alternative situations above mentioned, including that in which the affiant states that the defendant's residence is unknown, are set off in the statute by commas and are separated by the disjunctive "or," indicating the legislative intent that each situation should furnish a distinct, independent, and substantive basis for the issuance of an appropriate order of publication.118 To construe the statute otherwise would lead to anomaly and uncertainty which are apparent on brief reflection. 

The required affidavit, in order to constitute the basis for constructive service, must substantially comply with the statute.119 Allegations of a categorical nature, which follow the words of the statute are sufficient. 120 It is unsafe to change the verbiage of the statute in matters of constructive service.121 It is not necessary, however, that the affidavit follow the exact language of the statute. It need only set up such facts as show a compliance with what the statute requires. 122 And the weight of authority is that, even if an affidavit is defective, but it nevertheless tends to show each material statutory fact necessary to be shown to make valid constructive service, and there is not an entire omission to state any required fact, though some facts are inferentially or insufficiently set forth, the proceedings upon such constructive service are merely voidable, not void, and are not subject to collateral attack, 123

What and how much evidence the court should require to satisfy itself as to due diligence in these matters rests largely in the discretion of the court issuing the order. 

Extraordinary steps to ascertain the whereabouts of the party are not required. But judgments should not be entered without actual notice when, by the exercise of reasonable diligence, actual notice can be given. Reasonable diligence in such matters is an honest effort, and one appropriate to the circumstances, to ascertain whether actual notice can be given and, if so, to give it. Such effort, however, need not embrace a search in remote parts of the state, and it is not essential that all possible or conceivable means should be used. But the effort should usually extend to inquiry of persons likely or presumed to know the facts sought.127

The word "residence," as used in the constructive service statute, should not be construed as synonymous with domicile in all cases, but it should be construed to carry out the intent of the statute to reach the defendant and impart notice of the pending proceeding to him as far as it is reasonably possible to do so. In order to do this, it would not in all cases be sufficient to allege the legal domicile of the defendant instead of his actual residence and place of abode. 

Thus, if a citizen and resident of Florida, whose legal domicile is in this state, has a summer home in North Carolina where he spends six months of the year, including the entire summer, it would be proper and more in consonance with the purpose of the statute, if constructive service were to be made upon him during the summer, to allege the summer home as his place of residence. 

On the other hand, the present mailing address of the defendant might not be at all synonymous with his residence. Thus, if a travelling salesman should be a party defendant, and the plaintiff knew that the salesman had a settled residence or place of abode in a certain town or city where he kept his belongings and to which he frequently returned after his various business trips, it would be obviously misleading and insufficient for the plaintiff to allege as the defendant's residence, or as his mailing address, some one of the many towns or cities which he visited in the course of his business, even though, at the time of making the affidavit, the defendant might in fact have been temporarily present in the town or city alleged. A copy of the order mailed to him at the transient address would not be at all likely to reach him. Of course, Of course, in many cases the residence and domicile of a defendant upon whom constructive service is sought may be one and the same.¹ 138 

The second alternative situation stated by the statute as supporting the use of constructive service is where defendant's residence is unknown. Subject to the requirements of truth, good faith, and reasonable diligence, hereinabove referred to, a sworn bill or affidavit by the plaintiff, his agent or attorney, that defendant's residence "is unknown," coupled with the requisite additional statement as to defendant's age, is a sufficient predicate for the issuance of an order to appear and satisfies in that respect the requirements of

The statement required in the preceding alternative situation, specifying defendant's address as particularly as it may be known, has no application whatsoever where defendant's residence is stated to be unknown. The punctuation and language of the statute, as well as the inconsistent results which would follow, repel the view that this requirement applies to the latter situation. 

The plaintiffs need not even state that the defendant is a resident of a state or country other than the state of Florida. Such a construction of the statute would require statements of doubtful consist ency.1 

139 An affidavit that the plaintiff believes that the defendant formerly resided at Orlando, Florida, that prior to the making of the affidavit the defendant left Orlando, that his present residence is unknown, but that the plaintiff believes he is a resident of the United States, is in effect an affidavit that defendant's residence is unknown. 140 An affidavit that the defendant is a non-resident of the state of Florida, and that his "address" is unknown, is sufficient to prevent a decree based thereon from being declared void on collateral attack, though its sufficiency on direct attack has not been decided.141

The third situation supporting constructive service is where defendant, if a resident, has been absent for more than sixty days next preceding the application for the order of publication and there is no person in the state the service of a summons upon whom would bind such defendant. An affidavit to this effect is sufficient, even though the defendant was within the state during the sixty day period, where the plaintiff in good faith believed the allegations of the affidavit to be true. This result necessarily follows from the provision of the statute that the plaintiff need only state his belief as to the required facts.142 In a divorce suit, where the defendant is a non-resident, it is not necessary for the affidavit to state that there is no person in the state the service of a summons upon whom would bind the defendant.143

To be entitled to constructive service against a domestic corporation, or a foreign corporation which is doing or has done business within this state, the sheriff's return on the writ must show the failure of such domestic or foreign corporation to elect officers or appoint agents, or, in the case of a foreign corporation, the failure to have within the state an officer or agent upon whom process could be served, or the absence from the state for the period of six months before the issuing of the writ of the officers or agents of any domestic or foreign corporation, or the fact that the officers or agents of a domestic corporation are unknown. 145 This includes, of course, the resident agent for the service of process which every domestic corporation, or foreign corporation doing business in the state, is required to appoint.146 Of course, constructive service against corporations, like constructive service against natural persons, is not authorized unless a diligent effort has been made to perfect personal service.147 § 74.-Order to Appear.-The order to appear is issued by the clerk or judge, depending on the statute under which constructive service is sought.148 But, regardless of statutory provisions, an

The requirements of a "newspaper" within the meaning of the constructive service laws have been prescribed by statute. It must be a paper printed and published periodically once a week or oftener, wholly or in large part in the English language, entered as second class matter at a post office in the county where published, for sale to the public generally, available to the public generally for the publication of official or other notices, and customarily containing information of a public character or of interest or value to the residents or owners of property in the county where it is published, or of interest or value to the general public. In addition, the newspaper must have been continuously published at least once a week and entered as second class mail matter at a post office in the county where published for a period of one year next preceding the first publication of the constructive service order, or the newspaper must be a direct successor of a newspaper which has been so published.167 The latter requirement does not apply, however, in

One sued by a wrong name may appear by his correct name. 

Where a party sued by a wrong name appears and pleads to the merits by his true name, and by proper averments shows that he is the party actually sued, he is not in default and a decree pro confesso cannot be entered against him. This rule applies to both natural persons and corporations. Under such circumstances the pleadings may be amended to correspond with the name by which the defendant appears. 195

Where the clerk enters the defendant's appearance by an attorney, and the attorney shows that he did not authorize the clerk to enter his appearance for the defendant, the clerk's entry cannot bind either the attorney or the party.196 However, where an attorney has entered an appearance for the defendant, it is presumed to have been authorized. And if a judgment is entered on an unauthorized appearance, and the statute of limitations has run on the original cause of action, the defendant is bound by the judgment unless he can show that he had a meritorious defense to the action and that the attorney who entered the unauthorized appearance is insolvent. 197

§ 80. Taking Advantage of Defective Service.-Persons who are named as defendants in an equity suit, where process has been issued and returned as served upon them, when in truth and in fact no legal service was made, have the right to contest the validity of the service without submitting their persons to the jurisdiction of the court for an adjudication of the merits of the controversy. 

While the proper procedure for this purpose has been prescribed by statute for actions at law,202 this statute is apparently inapplicable to suits in equity and the Federal practice has been adopted in such suits.203 Accordingly it is well settled, under the 1931 

Chancery Act as well as under the prior practice, that the correct procedure to test the jurisdiction of the court over the person of the defendant in an equity suit is for the defendant to file a special appearance and a motion to set aside or quash the return.204 This practice is simple, speedy, and effective and promotes the interests of justice with the least cost and trouble to suitors. The special appearance and motion should be filed on or before the rule day upon which the defendant is required to plead or answer,205 and it is safer practice to confine the motion to one to quash the service and return rather than the summons.206 Substantially the same procedure may be used where constructive rather than personal service has been had, except that in the former case the motion should be to quash the constructive process or orders to appear based thereon.207

Where a party appears specially for the purpose of contesting the jurisdiction of the court over his person he must restrict his motion to the question of jurisdiction, and he must not include in it some other ground which recognizes the jurisdiction of the court over his person and amounts to a general appearance in the If he does so, his motion will be held to be a general appearance notwithstanding the fact that it purports to be made in pursuance of a special appearance.208 However, an appearance is not controlled by the designation given it by the appearing party and, if an appearance is for the sole purpose of establishing a lack of jurisdiction over the defendant, the appearance is special whether so designated or not. On the other hand, if a party files a motion asking for relief that can be granted only by a court having jurisdiction over his person, his appearance is general regardless of his intention and even though the appearance is designated as special.209 But, as long as a special appearance and motion filed pursuant thereto, whether filed personally or through counsel, is confined solely to jurisdictional matters and asks nothing except that the court determine for itself its own want of jurisdiction under the law, the special appearance and motion must be regarded as limited in character and conferring no jurisdiction to proceed to a trial on the merits.210 Such an appearance and motion do not waive service of process, or cure irregularities therein, nor do they authorize a judgment on the merits.211

If, after appearing specially and moving to quash the return, and appealing from the court's denial of his motion, the defendant moves the court to extend the time for answering the bill, the latter motion will not be deemed a waiver of the jurisdictional question if it is expressly stated in the motion that it is made without waiving any of the defendant's rights with reference to the jurisdiction of the court, or any rights that may have been acquired by reason of the appeal.230 But if a defendant, who has taken no steps to question the jurisdiction of the court over his person, moves for and obtains an extension of time for answering the bill, this constitutes a general appearance. 231 The prosecution of an appeal from a final decree on the merits operates as a general appearance and when the cause is remanded the lower court will have jurisdiction to proceed even in cases where it originally obtained no jurisdiction over the person of the defendant.232 This rule does not, of course, preclude the taking of a special appeal from an order denying a motion to quash made after a special appearance.233

The doctrine of waiver of defects in the service of process is a salutary one, and the rule ought to be rigidly applied in every case where the acts of the party can be fairly construed as a waiver, but it would be proceeding with too great strictness to apply the doctrine in any case where it appears that the objecting party took every reasonable precaution to guard against his special appearance being construed as a general appearance.234 Nor, can a general appearance by a defendant who was not properly served with process relate back and validate proceedings taken against him before he was legally in court.235

91. Proceedings in Lieu of Decree Pro Confesso. § 82.-Prerequisites to Entry. In regard to the entry of decrees pro confesso, the 1931 Chancery Act provides: "If the defendant shall fail to file his appearance or shall fail to file his answer or other defense to the bill of complaint, within the time prescribed by law, or within such other time as shall have been fixed by the court, then the plaintiff may at his election take an order to be entered by the clerk or the judge, as of course, that the bill be taken pro confesso; and thereupon the cause shall proceed ex parte and the matter of the bill may be decreed by the court accordingly if the same can be done without an answer and is proper to be decreed."1 

The object of a statute authorizing decrees pro confesso is to provide a just and reasonably expeditious mode of obviating the delays and difficulties to which plaintiffs are subjected by the neglect of defendants and their disobedience to the mandates of the court, and no construction of such a statute should be indulged which would encourage defendants in their neglect of the process of the court.2

Under the 1931 Chancery Act, a decree pro confesso can be entered for the failure of the defendant either to appear or plead to the bill of complaint within the time prescribed by law or order of the court. In this respect the Act follows an earlier statute, 1. C. G. L. Per. Supp. 4939 (1); Mc 

Carthy Chan. Act, p. 108, § 42. 

2. Prout v. Dade County Security 

Co., 55 Fla. 816, 47 So. 12; Encyc. Dig., V. 8, p. 113, § 22. 

3. C. G. L. 4940.

[Ch. 8 

enacted in 1917, permitting the entry of a decree pro confesso for failure to appear on the rule day fixed in the summons. Under the practice prior to 1917, a decree pro confesso could not be entered for want of appearance on the rule day to which the process was returnable, but only on the next succeeding rule day, and then, not for want of appearance, but for want of an answer or other pleading.4 

Of course, a decree pro confesso cannot be legally entered against a defendant unless the sheriff's return shows that the defendant has been served with process, unless constructive service has been perfected against him, or unless it appears that the defendant has in some way submitted himself to the jurisdiction of the court. If constructive service has been used, a decree pro confesso cannot be entered unless the clerk has filed with the papers in the suit a certificate of compliance with the constructive service statutes. But, where no decree pro confesso is actually entered, the filing of the clerk's certificate is not necessary to the entry of a final decree against the guardian ad litem of an infant," or against the guardian ad litem of unknown persons in suits relating to or affecting the title to real estate, unless it is also shown that the constructive service statutes were not complied with. Decrees pro confesso cannot be entered against infant defendants.9 Nor can a decree pro confesso be entered where the defendant has filed any sufficient pleading in the cause.10 If a motion to dismiss the bill is on file and undisposed of, a decree pro confesso is unauthorized. Whether the filing of a motion to strike part of a bill of complaint precludes the entry of a decree pro confesso depends upon the scope of the motion. If the portions of the bill moved to be stricken would, if eliminated, put an end to the plaintiff's right of recovery, no decree pro confesso may be entered. But, if the motion to strike is addressed to merely immaterial portions of the bill, a decree pro confesso may be entered unless a stay order is obtained.18A 

Since the 1931 Chancery Act19 provides that the filing of an amended bill or an amendment to the bill before answer or motion does not extend the defendant's time for pleading, such an amendment has no effect upon the plaintiff's right to a decree pro confesso. 

But if, after an answer has been filed, the plaintiff files an amended bill without leave of court, the failure of the defendant to notice it does not authorize the entry of a decree pro confesso thereon.20 

If pursuant to leave of court, an amended bill is filed after motion or answer by the defendant, it seems clear that no decree pro confesso can be entered for failure to replead to the amended bill. 

This necessarily results from the provision of the 1931 Chancery Act21 that, if the defendant fails to replead within ten days after receipt of a copy of the amended bill, the original motion or answer shall be considered as pleaded thereto.

Under the old practice it was said that a decree pro confesso should not be entered where the defendant failed to answer after his demurrer to the bill was denied, or after his original answer was stricken for insufficiency and he failed to answer further, and that the proper judgment under these circumstances was a final decree on the pleadings.22 But, even under the old practice, it was nevertheless several times expressly held that, where a defendant failed to answer after his demurrer was denied, a decree pro confesso might be entered against him.23 It is difficult to reconcile the conflicting decisions on this question, but the matter has now been settled by a provision of the 1931 Chancery Act24 that, if a motion to dismiss is denied, the defendant must file his answer within ten days, or such further time as the court may fix, or a decree pro confesso may be entered against him by the clerk or the judge. Under this statute, it has been held that, where no supersedeas has been obtained, a decree pro confesso for failure to answer may be entered after the entry of an appeal from an order denying a motion to dismiss the bill of complaint.25

Under the former practice, if the defendant filed an answer not signed by him,26 or a plea not properly verified,27 his pleading could be ignored by the plaintiff and a decree pro confesso entered against him. But this is not true under the 1931 Chancery Act 28 since, under its provisions, 29 defensive pleadings need only be signed by the defendant's solicitor. Likewise, under the former practice, affidavits on file in the cause have been held not to preclude the entry of a decree pro confesso for failure to answer even though they may have set up a complete defense to the bill.30 It is entirely possible, however, that such a strict rule would not be

§ 83.-Rendition and Entry.-The 1931 Chancery Act provides that, if the defendant fails to appear or plead within the time prescribed by law or fixed by the court, a decree pro confesso may be entered against him "by the clerk or the judge, as of course."32

While the statute appears to give the clerk and the judge equal powers in regard to the entry of such decrees, it may be doubted if the prior limitations on the clerk's powers in this respect have been thereby removed.

Before the 1931 Chancery Act, it was well settled that, while a decree pro confesso could be entered by the judge at any time during the continuance of the default, such a decree could be entered by the clerk only upon a rule day.33 This was true whether the service of process had been personal or constructive. The preservation of the rule day system in the 1931 Chancery Act may indicate that this limitation upon the clerk's power still exists. 

However, where a decree pro confesso is entered because of the failure of the defendant to answer after his motion to dismiss has been denied, the 1931 Chancery Act 34 expressly provides that the decree pro confesso may be entered by the clerk or the judge. 

Where constructive service is used, and the return day named in the order to appear is not a rule day, the defendant is not required to appear until the rule day next succeeding the return day fixed in the order.35 Therefore, under such circumstances, a decree pro confesso for failure to appear may be entered by the clerk on any rule day after the return day during the continuance of the default, or by the judge on the rule day next succeeding the return day or any day thereafter during the continuance of the default. The clerk may, however, be authorized or directed by the judge to enter a decree pro confesso on a day other than a rule day.37 

Likewise, a decree pro confesso entered by the clerk on a day other than a rule day may be ratified by the judge.38 A decree pro confesso cannot be entered by the clerk if the plaintiff's right to its entry is dependent upon a judicial question which must be submitted to the judge.39 And a decree pro confesso cannot be entered by the plaintiff's solicitors.40 Where a judge enters a decree pro confesso in a cause, and thereafter disqualifies himself by reason of having acted as counsel for the plaintiff before becoming a judge, the decree is void.41

As previously pointed out, decrees pro confesso may be entered on the first rule day upon which the default in appearing or pleading occurs, or on any day thereafter. Of course, a decree pro confesso entered before the day fixed for appearance or pleading is void.42 

Under the former practice, where the bill of complaint was amended before the filing of an answer, a decree pro confesso could not be entered until the second rule day after the amendment.43 

But, since the 1931 Chancery Act44 provides that the filing of an amended bill or amendment to the bill, before answer or motion, does not extend the defendant's time for pleading, this rule is no longer applicable.

A decree pro confesso merely filed by the clerk with the papers in the cause is invalid. Like other chancery decrees,45 it must be recorded in the chancery order book in order to be effective.46

However, where a defendant actually in default is not prejudiced by the failure to take and enter a decree pro confesso, the defect may not be sufficient to justify the reversal of a final decree based thereon47 and, in any event, the final decree is not void and subject to collateral attack.48 The failure to enter a decree pro confesso against one defendant does not affect the rights of another defendant so as to require a reversal of the final decree.49 Thus, in a suit to charge a married woman's separate property, the failure to enter a decree pro confesso against her husband is not reversible error.50 § 84. Decree Pro Confesso on Counterclaim.-In regard to the entry of decrees pro confesso on counterclaims, the 1931 Chancery 

Act provides: 

"If the cross defendant shall fail to file his reply or other defense to an answer asserting a counterclaim and specially praying relief at the time prescribed by law, or within such other time as shall have been fixed by the court, a decree pro confesso may be taken and like proceedings had thereon as in case of failure of the defendant to answer or file defensive pleadings to the bill of complaint."51

Of course, as a prerequisite to the entry of a a decree pro confesso on a counterclaim, the parties defendant to the counterclaim must have been served with notice thereof in accordance with other requirements of the Act.52

A decree pro confesso cannot be entered on a counterclaim where there is on file and undisposed of a motion to strike portions of the answer in which it is included, which motion, if well founded, would destroy the basis for the counterclaim.53 Likewise, a decree pro confesso should not be entered on a cross-bill or counterclaim to which a motion to strike, not frivolous on its face, has been filed and is pending.54

Since an answer containing merely affirmative matter, as distinguished from a counterclaim, requires no reply without a special order of the court, the new matter being considered as denied by the plaintiff,55 a decree pro confesso cannot be entered upon such an answer even where it contains a prayer for affirmative relief.56 

However, if the plaintiff is in doubt as to whether an answer contains a counterclaim or merely defensive or affirmative matter, he must submit the question to the court by a motion to dismiss the counterclaim filed within the time allowed for an attack thereon. 

The failure of the plaintiff to so proceed is at his own risk. If the matter does in fact constitute a counterclaim, and the plaintiff files no pleading thereto, a decree pro confesso may be entered against him.57 

§ 85.-Effect of Decree-As An Admission.-Where a valid decree pro confesso has been entered, the defendant is held to have admitted the allegations of fact and the fair inferences and conclusions of fact which may be drawn from the allegations contained in the bill of complaint.58 This rule has been variously stated. It is sometimes said that a decree pro confesso admits only facts which are well pleaded and which the law will allow to be proved by competent evidence if put in issue.59 It is also said that such a decree admits the truth of the definite and certain allegations of fact contained in the bill which tend to establish the equities of the case, and that the allegations of the bill and the exhibits properly made a part thereof may then be considered in ascertaining the rights and interests of the parties.60

In any event, it follows that, after the entry of a decree pro confesso, the defendant is precluded from contesting the facts alleged in the bill.61 As a general rule it is not necessary, though

However, a decree pro confesso determines nothing except as to the facts alleged in the bill. It does not admit conclusions of law, facts not well pleaded, or forced inferences.63 Nor does it admit facts which the law will not permit to be confessed on the part of the particular defendant, for such facts, if provable at all, must be established by competent evidence.64 And a decree pro confesso does not aid or supplement a bill which does not state a good cause of action,65 and it is not to be taken as an admission of the equity of the bill.66 The court can grant no relief, notwithstanding the entry of a decree pro confesso, where the plaintiff's own uncontradicted statement demonstrates a want of equity in his prayer.67 And the defendant has a right to attack the sufficiency of the bill of complaint to state a case against him even after the entry of such a decree.68 Likewise, a decree pro confesso does not bind a defendant as to matters not properly adjudicated in the suit.69

§ 87.-Setting Aside Decree Pro Confesso.-The rules govern ing the setting aside of a decree pro confesso should be distinguished from those governing the setting aside or vacating of a final decree rendered upon a bill so taken as confessed, although many of the rules applicable in the one case are also applicable in the other.7 

Under the 1931 Chancery Act,79 as well as the statutes previously in force, a final decree rendered upon a decree pro confesso cannot ordinarily be vacated or set aside except upon motion filed within twenty days after its entry. But courts of general equity jurisdiction possess the inherent power, and it is their duty, of their own motion, to correct or set aside any order or decree made or entered improvidently or through inadvertence, unless such order or decree, by lapse of time, or for some other reason, has passed beyond the control of the court. A decree pro confesso, being interlocutory, remains within the control of the court, in the absence of intervening appellate jurisdiction, at least until final decree and may, for good cause shown, be set aside at any time prior to the entry of a final decree.81

Before a decree pro confesso properly entered can be set aside on motion of the defendant, the movant must not only show reasonable diligence but also a meritorious defense.82 A showing of reasonable diligence without a meritorious defense, or of a meritorious defense without reasonable diligence, is unavailing.83 

Furthermore, the question of setting aside a decree pro confesso is addressed to the sound discretion of the court, which will be exercised according to the circumstances of each case, and the exercise of this discretion will not be interfered with on appeal unless it has been grossly abused. But a decree pro confesso will never be set aside where it is a consequence of the defendant's own negligence.84 However, where an application is made to set aside a decree pro confesso, and an answer is offered disclosing on its face a meritorious defense, any reasonable doubt in the matter should be resolved in favor of allowing a trial on the merits.85 

The usual procedure for setting aside a decree pro confesso is to file a motion supported by an affidavit as to the facts relied upon to establish reasonable diligence, and at the same time tender an answer showing a meritorious defense.86 A motion not supported by an affidavit has been held to be insufficient.87

From the foregoing cases it may safely be concluded that reasonable diligence is not so much dependent upon the time within which the motion is filed as it is upon the actions and good faith of the defendant and his solicitors in complying with the orders of the court. 91 Thus where the defendant filed a motion to strike an amended bill from the files on the September rule day, which motion was denied on October first and recorded on October twenty-sixth, a motion to vacate a decree pro confesso entered on November seventh was justly denied. The court charged the defendant with knowledge, on the September rule day, that the amended bill required an answer and his failure to plead thereto even after his motion to strike had been denied was considered a lack of reasonable diligence.92 But if a bill is materially amended after the entry of a decree pro confesso, a motion to vacate should be granted.93

§ 90. Appeals From Default Decrees.-An appeal will not lie from a decree pro confesso itself. The appellate court will refuse to hear the defendant out of respect for the court below, to whose order he has refused obedience. Furthermore, since the setting aside of decrees pro confesso is addressed to the sound judicial discretion of the lower court, the defendant is first required to seek to purge himself of the contempt there before he can be heard upon the matter in the appellate court.143 

It is also a general rule that no appeal will lie to the action of a court in the exercise of a discretionary power. However, where the discretion is not absolute, but is a legal discretion to be exercised in accordance with established principles of equity, the decision of the court is reviewable to the extent of determining whether there has been a gross abuse of discretion affecting a substantial right of the complaining party. Therefore, and in accordance with the statute144 permitting appeals from interlocutory orders and decrees in chancery cases, an appeal will lie from an order denying a motion to set aside a decree pro confesso.145 But the scope of the appeal is limited to determining whether a gross abuse of discretion has been shown.146

It is well settled in Florida, however, that an appeal may be taken from a final decree rendered upon a decree pro confesso.147 

Under the English system such an appeal did not lie. This was

The scope of an appeal from a final decree based upon a decree pro confesso is limited to two general questions.149 First, the legality of all proceedings prior to the decree pro confesso is open for review and the defendant can take advantage of any reversible error apparent upon those proceedings. § 91.-Proceedings in Lieu of Decree Pro Confesso.-The 1931 Chancery Act provides: 

"The plaintiff may, instead of causing a decree pro confesso to be entered, if he requires any discovery or answer to enable him to obtain a proper decree, have process of attachment against the defendant to compel the answer; and the defendant shall not when arrested upon such process be discharged therefrom unless upon filing his answer or otherwise complying with such order as the court may direct as to pleading to or fully answering the bill within a period to be fixed by the court and undertaking to speed the cause."163

This provision of the 1931 Act is exactly the same as a prior statute which had been in force since 1847.164 

The procedure permitted by these statutes has been little used. 

It is sometimes necessary, in order that the plaintiff may have a proper decree, to compel a discovery by the defendant in his answer even though the allegations of the bill are admitted. For example, where the plaintiff, as principal, brings a bill of complaint against the defendant, as his agent, the plaintiff may find it necessary to compel a complete discovery of the accounts between them. 

While it has been held that the subject of discovery, interrogatories, and the production of documents is controlled by other sec-

CHAPTER IX  Effect of Motion. 

In General. 

Grounds. 

Judgment on Motion. 

§ 92.-In General.-Prior to the 1931 Chancery Act, a motion to dismiss a bill of complaint for want of equity was unknown to Florida chancery practice.' The proper method of testing the legal sufficiency of a bill was by demurrer.2 But this practice was changed by the following provision of the 1931 Act: 

"Demurrers are abolished. Every defense in point of law arising upon the face of the bill, whether for misjoinder or nonjoinder or by reason of insufficiency of fact to constitute a valid cause of action in equity, which might heretofore have been made by demurrer or plea, shall be made by separate motion to dismiss or by a motion to dismiss contained in the answer; and every such point of law must go to the whole of the cause or causes of action stated in the bill and such motion incorporated in the answer may be called up and disposed of before final hearing at the discretion of the court."3

Thus the sufficiency of a bill of complaint to state a cause of action in equity must now be tested by a motion to dismiss.4 For most purposes a motion to dismiss is the substitute for and the equivalent of a general demurrer under the former practice. The

But a motion to dismiss admits only facts which are well pleaded. 

It does not admit conclusions of fact not justified by the facts alleged, or assertions of ultimate facts that are not sustained by the facts alleged.28 Nor does a motion to dismiss admit conclusions of law, for the law is to be ascertained by the court.29 So also, a motion to dismiss does not admit facts which are contradicted by records of which the court will take judicial notice, 30 or facts which the law will not allow to be proved, or which are inconsistent with law.31

These principles are illustrated by a number of decisions. Thus, an allegation of the ownership of land below the high water mark of a navigable stream is not admitted by a motion to dismiss. Since the private ownership of land usually stops at the high water mark, those claiming ownership below that mark must show the sources and muniments of title from an authority competent to make a grant against the rights of the public in the shores of navigable waters.32 An allegation of fraud in general terms, without stating the facts constituting the fraud, is not admitted by a motion to dismiss.33 In a suit to remove a cloud upon title, a motion to dismiss does not admit general allegations of ownership so as to cure defects in the plaintiff's statement of his title.34 

Where plaintiff's bill contains a description of his land according to an official government survey, and alleges that it is not in a certain drainage district, a motion to dismiss does not admit the latter allegation because the court will take judicial knowledge of land so described and determine for itself whether it is located within the drainage district in question.35 Allegations as to the legal effect of an instrument not sustained by the instrument itself made a part of the bill are not admitted by motion to dismiss.36 

An allegation in a bill of complaint that a certain document purporting to be an Act of the legislature is invalid because it was never presented to the Governor is not admitted by a motion to dismiss. 

The allegation is only susceptible of proof by public records in the office of the Governor or Secretary of State, and not by parol evidence. The bill must therefore allege the existence of such public records.37 Allegations which seek to lay the foundation for the introduction of parol evidence to contradict the terms of a written instrument are not admitted by a motion to dismiss.38

Although a motion to dismiss admits the allegations of a bill of complaint, the admission is only for the purpose of passing upon the legal sufficiency of the bill to state a cause of action. A motion to dismiss must be founded upon some certain and absolute proposition, destructive of the entire relief sought by the bill.49 The 1931 Chancery Act50 requires that every point of law made the basis of a motion to dismiss "must go to the whole of the cause or causes of action stated in the bill." Therefore, in passing on the motion, only grounds applicable to the whole bill will be considered.51

Under the former practice, where a bill set forth various claims against the defendant, he was permitted to put in his demurrer separate and distinct grounds applicable to each claim, for the same grounds frequently would not apply to the whole bill, though the whole might be subject to demurrer. In such a case, the demurrer might be sustained as to one cause of action and overruled as to another.52 It may be doubted if the 1931 Chancery 

Act is to be so literally construed as to terminate this practice as applicable to motions to dismiss. Such a construction would require each ground of the motion to go to all causes of action stated in the bill and would further require the motion to be overruled unless it was well founded as to all causes of action. In any event, where a bill asserts several causes of action, and one of them is not well founded, it may be eliminated from the bill by motion to strike.53 And, in view of the fact that the 1931 Chancery Act54 abolishes technical forms of pleadings, it seems reasonably clear that, where one of several distinct causes of action contained in a bill is insufficient, it may be eliminated therefrom regardless of the name given the motion used to attack it. 

One of several defendants may in his exclusive interest move to dismiss a bill the allegations of which, however good they may be as to the remaining defendants, state no cause of action against him.55

The most frequent ground of a motion to dismiss is that the bill is without equity. If a bill is so vague and indefinite that it does not state any case upon which a court of equity will grant relief, it is subject to dismissal.56 Likewise, when some of the allegations in a bill show a case entitling plaintiff to relief, but they are contradicted by other allegations in the same bill, and it is impossible for the court to determine the true nature of the case sought to be made, a motion to dismiss will be granted.57 But no objection addressed solely to the prayer of a bill can be raised by motion to dismiss.58 An improper prayer for damages will not render a bill subject to motion to dismiss.59 Where the plaintiff is in doubt as to whether he is entitled to one kind of relief or another, he may frame a prayer in the alternative and if, in such a case, he is entitled to either kind of relief the defendant cannot move to dismiss because he is not entitled to the other. Under the former practice a bill of complaint which showed on its face that the plaintiff had an adequate remedy at law was subject to demurrer.61 But this is not a proper ground for a motion to dismiss under the 1931 Chancery Act. That Act provides for transferring to the law side of the court cases erroneously brought in equity.62 Therefore, when a bill shows on its face that the plaintiff has an adequate remedy at law, the proper remedy is a motion to transfer the case to the law side.63 However, a motion to dismiss will be treated as a motion to transfer the case to the law side if the remedy at law is adequate.64 

The law is well settled that, where it is clearly apparent upon the face of a bill of complaint that the plaintiff has slept so long upon his rights as to be guilty of laches in the assertion of them, and no circumstances are stated as an excuse for the delay, the question of laches may be raised and determined upon a motion to dismiss for want of equity.65 But a motion to dismiss will not ordinarily be granted on this ground unless the showing of laches on the face of the bill is incontrovertible as a matter of law.66 Allegations in a bill which merely show a few years between the accrual of a right and its assertion, but do not show a change in value or other circumstances substantially changing the relationship of the parties or the status of the property rights involved, do not render it subject to a motion to dismiss.67 However, where a bill in chancery

A motion to dismiss is the proper method of reaching a defect of parties appearing on the face of a bill in equity.69 Where it does not appear that the right and interest of the plaintiff entitles him to maintain the suit a motion to dismiss on this ground will be sustained.70 Thus, if a bill is brought by the next friend of a party, and it does not appear that the party is a minor or married woman or otherwise entitled to sue by next friend, the bill is subject to a motion to dismiss.71 Conversely, a motion to dismiss is the proper method of attacking a bill of complaint brought by a married woman not suing by her next friend.72

The want of necessary parties defendant is also properly raised by motion to dismiss.73 For misjoinder of parties only those who are improperly joined can move to dismiss.74 

Under the former practice, a failure to state the name of the defendant in the introductory part of the bill was not a proper ground of a motion to dismiss.75 The 1931 Chancery Act76 still requires the names of the defendants to be contained in the introductory part of the bill but it seems clear that under this Act also. a failure to meet this requirement does not render the bill subject to a motion to dismiss.

Therefore, where the court has jurisdiction of the subject matter and the parties, a defendant cannot wait until the hearing to raise the question of the expediency of including all of the matters in a single suit.82 If the objection of multifariousness is not raised by motion to dismiss, or ore tenus, at the argument thereon, it is waived.83
