It has been held that,94 under the 1931 Chancery Act, a motion to dismiss is for all practical purposes the equivalent of a general demurrer under the former practice. It follows that the principles above discussed, governing the action of the court on a general demurrer to a bill of complaint, are now applicable to the action of the court on a motion to dismiss. Accordingly, it is clear that, if there is any equity in a bill, a motion to dismiss it will be denied.95 And where a bill is not entirely without equity, a motion to dismiss will be denied even though the bill might be subject to compulsory amendment and to a motion for better particulars because of indefiniteness.9 96 Likewise, as under the former practice, a motion to dismiss a bill will be denied if there is any equity in the bill even though particular paragraphs or claims therein may be insufficient or unfounded.97 Under the former practice a special demurrer to that part of a bill setting up a distinct and separate claim might be sustained and the balance of the demurrer overruled. The 1931 

Chancery Act does not authorize a motion to dismiss part of a bill. 

However, as previously pointed out,98 it is entirely possible that, where a bill sets up several claims, one of which is bad, that part of a motion to dismiss directed to the insufficient claim will be treated as a motion to strike and the insufficient claim thus eliminated. 

Where a motion to dismiss a bill in equity filed by two defendants is joint and several it may be good as to one and bad as to the other. In such a case the motion may be granted as to the one and denied as to the other.99 But where the motion is joint, it must be good as to each of them or it will as a general rule be bad as to each.100 If the interests of two or more defendants are

Under the former practice it was held that the question of whether there was "any equity in the bill," so as to justify the overruling of a general demurrer thereto, was a matter determinable on the face of the pleadings and no discretion could be accorded the court in its action in this respect.106 But under a Federal equity rule similar to the section of the 1931 Chancery Act authorizing motions to dismiss, it has been held to be within the sound discretion of the court, when promotive of justice, to decline to decide a suit on a motion to dismiss the bill, to deny the motion, and to require an answer. Where a final decree is rendered for the defendant on a motion to dismiss, the plaintiff is estopped from maintaining a similar suit for the same cause and upon the same grounds that were disclosed in the first suit. Such a final decree determines the merits of the cause as presented by the bill. 109 A decree rendered on a motion to dismiss is as conclusive, by way of estoppel, of the facts confessed by the motion as a decree containing a finding of the same facts. 110

But where a motion to dismiss is granted because essential allegations of fact are omitted from the bill, a final decree on the motion concludes the plaintiff only as to the sufficiency of the facts alleged to state a cause of action. It is not a bar to a second suit between the parties for the same cause where the bill in the second suit supplies the essential allegations omitted in the first suit, though the conduct of the plaintiff in not presenting the case when an opportunity was first afforded may under special circumstances operate as an estoppel in pais.111 A final decree of dismissal on a motion to dismiss a bill for multifariousness should ordinarily be without prejudice to any equities which the plaintiff may be entitled to otherwise assert.112

When a motion to dismiss a bill is granted, the court should briefly state in writing which grounds of the motion are sustained and which are overruled,113 but the failure of the court to do so is harmless error if any one of the grounds is well taken.114 If a motion to dismiss a bill is filed but not formally disposed of, and the parties proceed to take testimony and submit the cause to the court on its merits, and a decree is rendered thereon, the motion. to dismiss will be treated as having been denied.115

§ 96.-Time of Filing.-Unless the time is enlarged by the court, and whether the service was personal or constructive, the defendant must file his answer in the clerk's office on the rule day next succeeding that fixed for the entry of his appearance.' The court is vested with a wide discretion in the matter of extending the prescribed time for the filing of pleadings, and this discretion will not be interfered with by the appellate court unless it has been plainly abused to the unjustifiable detriment of the complaining party.2 

Where a motion, such as one to strike the bill from the files, is interposed, and the defendant takes no steps to have the motion disposed of or get an extension of time for filing his answer or other defensive pleading, and the motion is not well founded, a decree pro confesso for failure to answer may be entered against him.3

If the defendant files a motion to dismiss, which is denied, his answer must be filed within ten days thereafter or such other time as may be fixed by the court. Otherwise a decree pro confesso may be entered against him.4 But the court has a wide discretion in fixing the time for filing the answer under these circumstances.5

§ 97] ANSWERS As a general rule, defenses in an equity cause should be interposed promptly when they are due. A party who offers them at a late stage of the proceeding must abide the discretion of the court as to whether they will be allowed." 

§ 97.-Function of Answer.-The function of an answer under the 1931 Chancery Act is materially different from its function under the former practice. Prior to the 1931 Act an answer was both a discovery and a pleading. The plaintiff could call upon the defendant to make a discovery under oath of the charges contained in the bill. But if the defendant was thus put upon his oath by his adversary, and the parties proceeded to a hearing, the defendant's sworn answer was considered as evidence in his favor and was taken as true and conclusive unless overcome by the testimony of two witnesses, or the testimony of one witness and corroborating circumstances. In order to have this effect, and in addition to being under oath, the averments of the answer were required to be within the personal knowledge of the defendant, and to be direct, positive, and certain,10 and responsive to the allegations of the bill. Furthermore, the denials of an answer, in order to make it evidence, had to be denials of facts stated in the bill and not merely denials of conclusions or arguments flowing from those facts. 12 Not all averments of a sworn answer were evidence in the defendant's favor. Only those which were responsive to the allega-

Under that Act an answer in equity is merely a defense. It is not a discovery for the benefit of the plaintiff. Requirements of Answer.—In regard to answers in equity, the 1931 Chancery Act provides: 

"The defendant in his answer shall in short and simple terms set out his defenses to each claim asserted by the bill, omitting any mere statement of evidence and avoiding any general denial of the averments of the bill, but specifically admitting or denying or explaining the facts upon which the plaintiff relies, unless the defendant is without knowledge, in which case he shall so state, such statement operating as a denial. Averments other than those of value or amount of damage, if not denied, shall be deemed confessed, except as against an infant, lunatic or other person non compos and not under guardianship, but the answer may be amended, by leave of the court upon reasonable notice, so as to put any averment in issue, when justice requires it."22 

If the defendant desires to set up any defense in point of fact, based upon matters de hors the bill of complaint, he must do so in his answer.23 This is the proper and only method of making such defenses even though, as previously noted, the answer may also in-

The requirement that defenses in point of fact be raised by answer carries with it a right in the defendant to so make such defenses. 

This is not a mere formal or technical right. It is a substantial and duly prescribed right that cannot be lawfully taken from the defendant except by due course of procedure.25 But if the defendant is summoned into court, and assumes to determine for himself that the bill of complaint is insufficient and requires no answer, his right is waived and he has no ground for an appeal from an adverse decree.26

Where the defendant does exercise his right to answer the bill of complaint, he is required to make full, true, direct, and perfect answer to each fact alleged in the bill. The answer must contain no evasion or doubtful terms. The defendant must, as to all material allegations, either admit them or deny them, or, if he has no knowledge of the facts alleged, he may disclaim such knowledge and require strict proof. But if the facts are within the defendant's knowledge he must answer positively. An evasive or qualifying answer is not sufficient. If the defendant knows that the facts are true he must admit them.27

An answer should consist of allegations of fact, stated with as much brevity and precision as possible. It should not contain inferences, arguments, or recitals and long digressions as to matters of fact wholly immaterial.28 However, the defendant need not answer inferences or conclusions of law drawn from the facts stated in the bill, nor need he answer immaterial or irrelevant matter alleged in the bill.29

Like any other pleading in equity, an answer should not contain matter which is scandalous, impertinent, or irrelevant. Such matter may be stricken from an answer by the court of its own initia-

If the court strikes matter from the record it is gone and the party may have no opportunity of placing it there again. But if it is left in the record, and is prolix and oppressive, the court may at the hearing do justice between the parties in the imposition of costs. The court should, therefore, always give the answer a liberal construction on the point of irrelevancy and impertinence and consider whether the matter in question can have any real and proper influence upon the suit. If the matter can have any influence on the decision of the suit, either as to the subject matter of the controversy, the particular relief to be given, or as to costs, it should not be stricken as impertinent or irrelevant.31 A few unnecessary words in an answer do not render the pleading impertinent unless they would lead to the introduction of improper evidence by putting in issue matters which are foreign to the cause.3 32 And matter should not be stricken as impertinent or irrelevant even though it is so indefinite that better particulars may properly be required.33

It will be noted that the statute requires the defendant to either admit, deny, or explain the facts alleged in the bill unless he is without knowledge, in which case he shall so state, and the statement operates as a denial.34 Accordingly, it is not sufficient for the defendant to merely state that he neither admits nor denies the allegations of the bill, but demands strict proof thereof. If the defendant is without knowledge of the facts he must so state and that statement will operate as a denial. But an allegation that defendant neither admits nor denies, without an allegation that he is without knowledge, will not operate as a denial. It will be construed as an admission of the facts in question even though the defendant also calls for strict proof thereof.35 The same is true

If the facts alleged in the bill are known by the defendant to be true he must positively admit them. He is not permitted to shelter himself behind equivocal, evasive, or doubtful terms, and thus mislead the plaintiff. An evasive and qualifying answer will be treated as an admission.37 An answer which neither denies or avers that the defendant is without knowledge will also be treated as an admission.38

Furthermore, it will be noted that the statute requires the defendant to either admit, deny, explain, or aver that he is without knowledge as to each claim asserted by the bill. The defendant, in pleading to the bill, is not permitted to group several claims in one paragraph of his answer. He must plead to each claim separately. This does not mean, nor was it contemplated by the statute, that the defendant should in substance copy in his answer each allegation or paragraph of the bill and expressly aver that he admits, denies, or is without knowledge as to each such allegation or paragraph. But, in order to simplify the method of reaching an issue as to each fact set up by the bill, each paragraph alleging a separate fact should be answered separately without grouping paragraphs of the bill in one averment of the answer. Averments of the answer not conforming to this practice are subject to a motion to strike.39

The foregoing requirement is contrary to the original chancery practice in this state. Under that practice, the defendant could answer by saying he denied or was without knowledge as to each and every item of the bill of complaint. It was also customary to conclude an answer with a general denial and this denial was sufficient to put in issue all material allegations of the bill of complaint.40 But the provision of the 1931 Chancery Act now under discussion, like a prior statute enacted in 1915, requires the defendant to admit the allegations which he knows are true and to

The statute thus authorizes the practice of incorporating a motion to dismiss in an answer. Of course, this procedure does not operate as a waiver of the defendant's rights under the motion and it is immaterial whether the motion is on a separate paper filed at the same time as the answer.49 The preferable practice is to dispose of a motion to dismiss contained in the answer before final hearing. The taking of testimony and the consideration of questions of law and fact raised by the answer can be obviated if the case can be disposed of on a question of law arising on the face of the bill. Where a motion to dismiss contained in an answer is not called up for disposition at or prior to the final hearing, its merits cannot be considered on appeal in the absence of jurisdictional defects.50

Under some circumstances, facts alleged in an answer containing a motion to dismiss may be considered in passing upon the motion. 

Thus, where a bill seeks to rescind a sale of personal property, and it is sought by motion to dismiss contained in the answer to take advantage of the failure of the bill to allege delivery of the property, the defendant is considered bound by an allegation in his answer that the property was delivered to him and dismissal of the bill is thereby precluded.5 51 The making and disposition of a special defense formerly presentable by plea will no doubt be governed largely by the rules applicable to pleas and their disposition under the former practice, particularly where such a defense is to be separately heard and disposed of before the trial of the principal case. It is, therefore, necessary to review the rules applicable to pleas as they existed prior to the 1931 Chancery Act.

The function of a plea in equity was to bring forward some one distinct matter of fact which was a complete defense to the whole bill, or some distinct part of it to which the plea applied. The plea did not deny the equity of the bill, but brought forward a fact

Its office was to confess the right and avoid it by matter de hors the bill.52 Pleas introducing no matter de hors the bill were overruled.53 The necessity of a plea arose from the original equity rule that, if the defendant once consented to answer, he must answer fully and respond to all of the charges contained in the bill. Therefore, if a defendant had a single affirmative defense which would be decisive of the controversy, he could avoid giving discovery as to the case made by the bill by setting up this defense in a plea. This was the reason for filing a plea rather than an answer.54 But the reason for the rule is now gone. The answer no longer serves the purpose of discovery. 

That is obtained by interrogatories.55

A plea in equity was required to set forth the ultimate facts offered as a bar to the suit. Its averments had to be direct and positive, and not by way of argument, inference, or conclusion. 

And it was required to state facts necessary to render it a complete equitable defense to the case made by the bill. If a plea did not state a full and complete defense, or the necessary facts had to be gathered by inference alone, it was overruled.56 

A common ground of a plea in equity was res judicata. Such a plea was required to show that the former suit was substantially between the same parties and for the same subject matter. It had to set forth so much of the former bill and answer as sufficed to show that the same point was then in issue, and it had to aver that the allegations as to the title to relief against the defendant were substantially the same in the second bill as in the first. A plea of another suit pending was very similar to a plea setting up a former judgment or decree, the one being in abatement and the other being in bar of the proceeding. As a general rule the pendency of a prior suit in equity could be pleaded in abatement to the prosecution of a subsequent suit in equity in the same jurisdiction, between the same parties, and upon the same cause of action.63 

The plea was required to set forth the general nature, character, and objects of the former suit and the relief prayed, and it was required to state, not only that the same issue was joined in the former suit as in the suit before the court, but also that the proceedings in the former suit were taken for the same purpose. The plea generally failed where there was a substantial difference in the relief sought in the two suits.64 

A plea of a prior pending suit applied only where the plaintiff in both suits was the same person and both suits were commenced by him. It did not apply where the plaintiff in the subsequent suit was a party defendant maintaining a cross-bill in the prior suit.65

The foregoing is an outline of the rules applicable to pleas in equity as they existed prior to the 1931 Chancery Act. That Act abolished pleas and provided that defenses previously presentable by plea must be made in the answer and may be separately heard and disposed of before the trial of the principal case in the discretion of the court. As in the case of motions to dismiss incorporated in the answer, it would in many cases probably be more expeditious and in the interests of justice to have a special defense in the nature of a plea disposed of prior to the trial on the merits. 

The time and expense of a trial on the merits can thereby frequently be saved.

Where there is a separate hearing on a special defense contained in an answer, the rules governing the disposition of pleas under the former practice will very probably, in their fundamental characteristics, be applied.89 There is now no limitation on the number of special defenses which the defendant may interpose, as there was on the number of pleas which he could file. But in the main, the legal sufficiency and truth of a special defense can and probably will be determined in much the same way as in the case of a plea.

[Ch. 10 § 100.-Inconsistent Defenses.-The original equity rule was that a defendant was not permitted to set up contradictory facts as a substantive defense. The reason for the rule was that, the answer being under oath, such a practice would encourage perjury in its worst and most dangerous form.90 The answer under oath has been definitely abolished by the 1931 Chancery Act and, as the reason given for this rule is gone, it is possible that inconsistent facts may now be alleged.

But a distinction may properly be drawn between inconsistent facts and inconsistent defenses. Even under the 1931 Chancery 

Act it would seem that allegations of inconsistent facts should not be permitted. Such a practice is obviously inappropriate to a court of equity and would ordinarily serve only to confuse the issues and delay the determination of the cause. It is conceivable that a defendant might have one defense if a certain fact was true, and another defense if it was not true. But that should not justify an allegation that the fact was true for one purpose and untrue for another. The defendant could aver his lack of knowledge of the particular fact and set up his two defenses in the alternative, claiming the benefit of the one or the other as the particular fact was found to be true or untrue. 

Defenses which are merely inconsistent in point of law, and based upon facts definitely alleged or not necessarily contradictory, should always be permitted. In such cases, the particular defense which is applicable usually depends upon a conclusion or question of law. To compel a defendant to elect one defense and abandon the other, and to suffer an adverse judgment if he selects the wrong one, would be to introduce into modern equity the technical severity of the earliest common law pleading. This restriction upon the scope of defensive pleading has long since been abolished at the common law. Contradictory pleas in law actions have been permissible in Florida since 1828,91 and they were permissible in England long prior to that date.92 Certainly, the 1931 Chancery Act, which was designed to promote the ends of justice,93 cannot be construed as reviving the restriction in modern equity practice.

The Federal equity rules, after which much of the 1931 Chancery Act was patterned, expressly permit inconsistent defenses.94 

Likewise, inconsistent defenses were expressly permitted by the Florida statute 95 governing answers in chancery which was in effect prior to 1931. Under these circumstances, it may be contended that the failure of the 1931 Act to expressly authorize inconsistent defenses is an inferential prohibition of them. Yet the 

1931 Act96 provides that the defendant in his answer shall set out his "defenses" to each claim asserted by the bill, whereas the Federal equity rule and the Florida statute previously applicable merely provide that the answer shall contain his "defense" to each claim. The express permission granted by the 1931 Act to set out more than one defense to each claim asserted by the bill, with no express prohibition of inconsistent defenses, would seem to indicate with reasonable certainty that inconsistent defenses are now permissible, particularly when they are so frequently necessary in order to do complete justice between the parties. 

§ 101.-Affirmative Defenses.-The defendant may, of course, set up affirmative defenses in his answer. When an answer contains averments of new matter not stated or inquired of in the bill of complaint, or not inseparably connected therewith, and such new matter is in opposition to or avoidance of the allegations of the bill, the burden is upon the defendant to prove such matter by a preponderance of the testimony.97 An affirmative defense is not made out as a matter of pleading by demanding proof of a fact alleged positively in the bill.98

But affirmative relief cannot be decreed in favor of defendant, except in matters of accounting, upon the facts stated in the answer. 

Where a defendant seeks affirmative relief he should file a counterclaim or cross-bill, and if he seeks any relief from one who is not a party to the proceedings he should make that person one of the

§ 102.-Form of Answer. Since the 1931 Chancery Act¹º¹ abol ished all technical forms of bills, answers, and other pleadings in equity, the answer of the defendant need not conform to any prescribed form. The intention of the statute is to leave the court free to do substantial justice between the parties unhampered by technical definitions and distinctions. 102 Therefore, if the substantial rights of the parties can be ascertained and determined from the allegations contained in the pleadings, it is the duty of the court to consider and decide them without regard to the form in which they are presented. 103 Even an error in the title of a pleading, or the lack of a title, is now immaterial.104

Under the former practice it was customary to conclude an answer with a general denial. This was sufficient to put in issue all material allegations of the bill not admitted in the answer and to which no direct response was made. Such allegations then had to be proved by a preponderance of the testimony.117 

But the 1931 Chancery Act118 requires the answer to avoid any general denial of the averments of the bill, and to specifically admit, deny, or explain the facts on which the plaintiff relies, unless the defendant is without knowledge, in which case he must so state and the statement operates as a denial. Averments other than those of value or amount of damage, if not denied, are deemed confessed, except as against an infant, lunatic, or other person non compos and not under guardianship. The statute does not require the defendant, in his answer, to copy the substance of each allegation of the bill, or paragraph thereof, and expressly admit, deny, or state that he is without knowledge as to each such allegation. But, in order to simplify the method of reaching an issue as to each fact set up in the bill, each paragraph alleging a separate fact must be answered separately without grouping paragraphs of the bill in one averment of the answer. 119

§ 103] 221 ANSWERS "At the expiration of ten days from the filing of the answer, if there be no counterclaim, or, if there shall be a counterclaim, then at the expiration of ten days from the filing of the reply thereto, the cause shall be deemed at issue. If, however, within such period of ten days a motion is filed to strike the whole of the answer or reply or to dismiss the counterclaim, or if the cause is set down for hearing on bill and answer, the cause shall not be deemed at issue until the points of law so presented shall have been ruled upon by the court."120 

While the foregoing statute clearly states that the cause shall be deemed at issue at the expiration of ten days from the "filing" of the answer, there is a substantial doubt as to whether this provision can be construed literally. Another section of the 1931 Act121 grants to the defendant ten days from the time the answer is required to be filed within which to file a motion to strike. Construing the two sections together it would seem that the cause would not be deemed at issue until ten days after the day the answer is required to be filed even though it actually is filed before that day. 

Where an attack is made upon an answer, the cause is not at issue until the points of law so raised have been disposed of.122 

While the ten day period intervening between the filing of the answer and the day the cause is deemed at issue would seem to be for the benefit of the plaintiff, and for the purpose of giving him an opportunity to attack the answer, it has been held that the plaintiff alone cannot waive the lapse of this period as a prerequisite to the cause being at issue. If the plaintiff proceeds to a trial within the ten day period, making no attack upon the answer, it is reversible error unless the defendant expressly or by conduct also waives the ten day period. 123

Since general replications have been abolished, the filing of such a replication does not affect the statutory provision that the cause shall be deemed at issue ten days after the filing of the answer. 124

§ 105.-Cross-bills. -A defendant in an equity suit cannot, except in matters of accounting, obtain affirmative relief merely upon the facts stated in his answer. Under the original equity practice he was required to seek affirmative relief either by a cross-bill or an independent suit in equity.' Thus, upon a bill by a vendee in possession of land under a contract to purchase seeking to set aside the contract as a cloud on title, the vendor could not, without a cross-bill, have a decree for the specific performance of the contract.2 Upon a bill by a mortgagor to redeem, there being no prayer for the sale of the land and no cross-bill, it was irregular to decree a sale.³ And it was held that, where a suit was filed to foreclose a purchase money mortgage, the mortgagors could not set up facts justifying a rescission as a defense to the suit. Their remedy was to file a bill or cross-bill for rescission after offering to reconvey the land."

Under the modern practice, a defendant may also seek relief through a counterclaim, but neither the 1931 Chancery Act nor any prior statute has ever abolished the cross-bill and it may still be used in appropriate cases. The 1931 Chancery Act expressly

provides that "in lieu of a counterclaim in an answer, a defendant may file a cross-bill." A cross-bill is a bill brought by a defendant in a suit against the plaintiff in the same suit, or against other defendants in the same suit, or against both, touching the matters in question in the original bill. Its function is to secure affirmative relief for the defendant in regard to the matters in controversy and to obtain a complete determination, among the parties, of all the elements involved in or connected with the suit. It is primarily a defense and must be restricted to matters of equity germane to or growing out of the original suit.7

A cross-bill is considered as an auxiliary suit and as dependent upon the original bill, and it can be sustained only on matter growing out of the original bill. While it may set up new matter arising subsequently, still the new matter must constitute part of the same defense or relate to the same subject matter. Without this restriction, new matter might be introduced into litigation by crossbills without end. As a complete defense to the original suit, a cross-bill may be necessary and proper, but it cannot be converted into a separate and distinct suit relative to other and different matters or become the foundation of a decree concerning matters not embraced in the original suit.8

Thus where a suit in ejectment is pending between two parties, and the plaintiff brings a bill in equity to restrain the defendant from cutting timber from the land involved, and the defendant in his answer alleges that title to the land is in himself, he may maintain a cross-bill to enjoin the plaintiff from further prosecuting the suit in ejectment. Purely defensive matter in a cross-bill is objectionable. It must contain averments sufficient to show some ground for affirmative equitable cross relief. If it does not seek affirmative relief and sets up no defense other than would be available by answer it is insufficient." Thus, the question of usury in, and payments made upon, a note and mortgage sought to be foreclosed are matters of defense to be pleaded in the answer, and they are improperly raised by cross-bill where the amounts so claimed are less than the mortgage debt. 12

A cross-bill may, however, be filed to answer the purpose of a plea puis darrein countinuance at the common law, as where, pending the suit, and after issue joined, the defendant obtains a release. 

The release not being in issue, the defendant will not be permitted to prove it, and hence the necessity of making it an issue by crossbill. But any new matter so brought into a suit must be so related to the original suit as to be in defense of it. Nor can unrelated new matter be brought into the suit by supplemental cross-bill. 13 

It is not generally permissible to maintain a cross-bill for relief which the defendant could obtain by insisting on the filing of a proper original bill or an amendment to the original bill.14 

Where a cross-bill is filed setting up matters of defense that have previously been adjudicated as insufficient in an answer, the crossbill should be eliminated and striking it is not an inappropriate remedy.15 But, where the plaintiff sets a cause down for hearing on bill and answer, and obtains a decree in his favor, this is not a hearing or disposition of a cross-bill even though it is incorporated in the same pleading as the answer. 16

A cross-bill cannot be maintained on a cause of action purely legal in its nature. 19

As in the case of an original bill, the cross-plaintiff must allege, clearly and definitely, every fact that is necessary to entitle him to relief, and if he omits essential facts, or states such facts as show that he is not entitled to relief, he must suffer the consequences of his so doing.20 In addition, a cross-bill should state the purport of the original bill, that is, the parties, prayer, and objects of it, and the proceedings thereon, as well as the rights of the original plaintiff which are necessary to be made the subject of cross litigation, or the ground on which the original bill is resisted, if that is the object of the cross-bill. It must appear from the cross-bill that it is confined to such new facts and issues as relate to the subject matter of the original bill. And it should make all persons entitled to be heard parties defendant thereto, and contain prayers for the relief sought.21 Persons not already parties in the original cause, whose presence is essential to a complete determination of the matter, may be added as parties defendant to the cross-bill.22 

However, it is not permissible to join as parties plaintiff in a crossbill persons who were not made parties defendant in the original bill, and where this is done the cross-bill is subject to a motion to strike.23

§ 106.-Nature and Requirements of Counterclaim.-In modern equity practice, the cross-bill has been largely superseded by the counterclaim. The counterclaim is a creature of statute. 

In re- gard to it, the 1931 Chancery Act provides: "The answer must state, in short and simple form, any counterclaim arising out of the transaction which is the subject matter of the suit, and may, without cross-bill, set out any counterclaim against the plaintiff which might be the subject of an independent suit in equity against him; and such counterclaim so set up shall have the same effect as a cross suit, so as to enable the court to pronounce a final decree in the same suit on both the original and cross claims."32

This section of the 1931 Act is in all respects now material exactly the same as a prior statute on this subject enacted in 1915.33 

Under the 1931 Act, any matter that could formerly be set up in a cross-bill may now be set up by a counterclaim included in an answer and it will have the same effect as if set up by cross-bill.34 

The counterclaim permitted by the statute is probably of broader scope than the cross-bill in chancery.35

There is a plain distinction between a defense and a counterclaim. 

A counterclaim must state a cause of action and seek affirmative relief, while a defense merely defeats the plaintiff's cause of action by a denial or confession and avoidance and does not admit of affirmative relief. A defense cannot be turned into a counterclaim merely by attaching a prayer for relief. The same facts may, however, constitute both a defense and ground for a counterclaim. But, in such a cause, if it is intended to insist upon the matter as a counterclaim, it must be pleaded as such and not as a

[Ch. 11 mere defense. A pleading cannot be at once both an answer and a counterclaim. But if an answer sufficiently, in apt words, and in substance and in fact, sets up a counterclaim, it must be so treated. So also, if the facts stated constitute a defense only, they will be so treated, regardless of the name which the defendant gives to his pleading.36

Under the 1931 Chancery Act a prayer for relief is necessary to a counterclaim. The Act provides: 

"If the answer contains a counterclaim, appropriate special relief shall be expressly prayed in respect to the counterclaim, otherwise the answer shall be regarded as defensive only; but such prayer for special relief shall also be held to include any relief grantable under a prayer for general relief."37

A counterclaim, as that word is used in the statute, includes both recoupment and set-off, and it is broader than both because it includes matters which do not fall under either head, as, for example, equitable demands.38 A set-off is a mode of defense whereby the defendant acknowledges the justice of the plaintiff's demand, but sets up a demand of his own, based upon an independent contract, to counterbalance the plaintiff's demand either in whole or in part.39 

A recoupment implies an admission of the plaintiff's claim, but it goes only to reduce or extinguish the claim and no affirmative judgment can be had upon it. Furthermore, it must arise out of the contract or transaction on which the plaintiff's claim is founded.4° 

A counterclaim is intended to secure to a defendant all the relief which either an action at law, a bill in equity, or a cross-bill would have secured on the same facts. The object of the statute authorizing counterclaims is to enable parties to settle and adjust all their cross claims in a single action, thus avoiding circuity of action and a multiplicity of suits. The statute should be liberally construed to effect this end.41

To constitute a counterclaim, the answer in an equity case must not only set up new affirmative matter which is a defense to the bill of complaint, but it must set up such an independent right in the defendant as will make his claim a proper matter of counterclaim as that term is understood in the law.42 An answer designed for affirmative relief by way of counterclaim should set forth the cause of action and conform to the other essentials of pleading with the same exactness employed in an original bill even though the counterclaim arose out of the same transaction as the original suit.43 If the answer contains a counterclaim, the special relief sought must be prayed, otherwise the answer is regarded as defensive only, but the prayer for special relief includes any relief grantable under a prayer for general relief.44 Where a counterclaim is set up in an answer, it has the same effect as a cross suit and enables the court to pronounce a final decree in that suit on both the original and cross claims.45 Of course, a counterclaim must be pleaded and exist in favor of the defendant in the same right in which he is sued.46

Where the parties stipulate that the court shall make a final disposition of all matters involved in a suit, a final decree may be entered granting affirmative relief to the defendant on his answer alone without a cross-bill or counterclaim.47 

§ 107.-Subject Matter of Counterclaim.-As to the subject mat ter of a counterclaim the 1931 Chancery Act48 specifically provides that "the answer must state, in short and simple form, any counterclaim arising out of the transaction which is the subject matter of the suit, and may, without cross-bill, set out any counterclaim against the plaintiff which might be the subject of an independent suit in equity against him.' This provision is almost exactly the same as a prior Florida statute49 enacted in 1915, and decisions

The statute thus divides counterclaims into two classes. The first class includes those which arise out of the transaction which is the subject matter of the suit. These must be set up in the answer in the interest of an end of litigation. If the defendant fails to set up such a counterclaim his cause of action will nevertheless be considered as res judicata. The second class of counterclaims created by the statute includes those which might be the subject of an independent suit in equity against the plaintiff. Counterclaims which may be set up under this provision are allowed, at the option of the defendant, in order to quickly settle all equitable issues properly capable of trial between the parties in one suit. But there is no penalty if the defendant does not set up a counterclaim of this class.50 51 In regard to counterclaims which must be set up in the answer, because they arise out of the subject matter of the suit, the word "transaction" is of a flexible meaning. It may comprehend a series of many occurrences, depending not so much upon the immediateness of their connection as upon their logical relationship.5 

Thus a counterclaim setting up a road construction lien as superior to that of a mortgage in a foreclosure suit has been held proper as arising out of the transaction which was the subject matter of the suit.52 It has also been held that the defendant in a suit to foreclose a materialman's lien may maintain a counterclaim for damages resulting from a delay in furnishing the materials, since the counterclaim arose out of the same transaction as the subject matter of the suit.53

In regard to counterclaims which may be set up in the answer, because they might be the subject of an independent suit in equity against the plaintiff, the statute has not been given as broad a construction as its language would permit. 

50. Tilton v. Horton, 103 Fla. 497, 137 So. 801, 139 So. 142. 

51. Moore v. New York Cotton Ex change, 270 U. S. 610, 46 S. Ct. 371, 70 L. ed. 757. 

52. Clermont-Minneola Country Club v. Loblaw, 106 Fla. 122, 143 So. 129. 

53. Southern Concrete Co. v. Fed eral Terra Cotta Co., 79 Fla. 376, 84 

So. 171.

§ 107] 233 

Similar language is contained in one of the Federal equity rules54 and there is a diversity of opinion upon its proper construction in the Federal courts. Under the liberal construction, the defendant is required to set out in his answer any counterclaim arising out of the subject matter of the original bill, and he may, if he wishes, set up any other equitable causes of action against the plaintiff even though they have no relation to the subject matter of the suit. 

Under the strict construction, any counterclaim arising out of the transaction which is the subject matter of the suit must be set up, but the counterclaims which the defendant may set up at his option are restricted to those which have some connection with or are germane to the subject matter of the suit.55 

The Supreme Court of Florida has adopted the strict construction of the statute and it requires that there be some legal or equitable connection between the matters pleaded as a counterclaim and the matters alleged in the original bill. The court holds that the words "any counterclaim arising out of the transaction which is the subject matter of the suit" underly and give color to the entire section, and that the further language regarding "any counterclaim against the plaintiff which might be the subject of an independent suit in equity against him" is not in conflict therewith because innumerable instances might be cited wherein the matter set up as a counterclaim, while connected with the subject matter of the original bill, might also afford ample grounds for an independent. suit in equity by the defendant against the plaintiff. Thus, while the term "counterclaim," as used in the statute, probably covers a broader scope than the familiar cross-bill, it is analogous to a cross-bill in that a defendant is not permitted to set up in his answer a counterclaim based on an entirely distinct cause of action foreign to and not in any way connected with the subject matter of the original bill.56

This construction of the statute is more consistent with the prior existing equity practice in this state and is productive of a more orderly and efficacious procedure. It is the purpose and intent of the statute to afford a simplified and expeditious method 

54. Federal Equity Rules of 1912, Rule 30. 

55. Turner v. Utley, 93 Fla. 910, 112 

So. 837. 

56. Lovett v. Lovett, 93 Fla. 611, 112 

So. 768; Encyc. Dig., V. 12, p. 118, § 12.

[Ch. 11 

of presenting in the answer matters previously presentable by crossbill. Since the former practice was grounded upon the principle that the scope of the litigation was limited to the subject matter of the original bill and matters germane thereto, there is no good reason for placing upon the statute the liberal construction. To do so would permit a defendant to file, by way of counterclaim, an original bill based upon extraneous matters. Thus the defendant could fully answer the plaintiff's original cause of action, but the plaintiff could not assert his right, if any, to affirmative relief against the defendant's original and extraneous cause of action without undue prolixity of pleading and a hopeless confusion of issues, if, indeed, it could be done at all. For example, under the liberal construction, a plaintiff might bring suit to foreclose a mortgage, and the defendant might file a counterclaim for the specific performance of a contract wholly unrelated to the subject matter of the original bill. In this manner the litigation might be indefinitely protracted, the plaintiff indefinitely postponed in the enforcement of his original right, and all manner of equitable controversies foreign to the plaintiff's original demand injected into the suit.57 And further, in connection with the hypothetical case just stated, if the plaintiff had a right to the reformation of the contract sought to be specifically enforced, there is no way that it could be set up in the suit because there is no provision in the 1931 Chancery Act permitting a counterclaim to be pleaded in the plaintiff's reply.58

In accordance with the rule of strict construction it has been held that, in a suit to foreclose a mortgage, the defendant could not maintain a counterclaim seeking relief in connection with a contract between him and the plaintiff having no connection with the mortgage, the transaction in which the mortgage was given, or the mortgaged property.59 Likewise, it has been held that one defendant to a suit for the foreclosure of a municipal tax lien cannot maintain a counterclaim against another defendant for the purpose

In an early case it was held that the defendant in a mortgage foreclosure suit could maintain a counterclaim for an accounting for moneys embezzled from him by the plaintiff even though there was no connection between the two transactions.65 This case is difficult to reconcile with the strict construction of the counterclaim statute subsequently adopted. 

There are indications in one decision rendered since the 1931 Chancery Act that the strict construction of the statute governing counterclaims is being relaxed. Finally, it is necessary to note one limitation which is applicable to both those counterclaims which must, and those which may, be set up in the answer. With one exception hereinafter discussed, it is imperative that in either case the counterclaim be one which could be made the subject of an independent bill in equity. In other words, with one exception, the counterclaims referred to in the statute, though not expressly so stated, include only causes of action of equitable cognizance. The reason for the rule that a defendant may not and may not be compelled to set up a legal counterclaim is that such a construction of the statute would conflict with the constitutional guaranty of a trial by jury. The Federal Constitution69 provides that in suits at common law the right of trial by jury shall be preserved. The Florida Constitution70 provides that the right of trial by jury shall be secured to all and remain inviolate forever. If the 1931 Chancery Act were construed to require a defendant to counterclaim on causes of action not of equitable cognizance, or to permit him to set up such counterclaims over the objection of the plaintiff, it would violate both of these constitutional provisions.71

Thus, where a bill is filed to foreclose a mortgage, the defendant cannot, over the objection of the plaintiff, maintain a counterclaim for money due for personal services, the counterclaim being legal in its nature and there being no connection between the two transactions. The counterclaim may be stricken on motion of the plaintiff.72 Likewise, a counterclaim for moneys received by the plaintiff for the use of the defendant will, on motion of the plaintiff, be stricken from the defendant's answer to a bill to foreclose a mortgage.73 Nor can a counterclaim for breach of covenant be interposed in a suit to foreclose a purchase money mortgage.74 And a counterclaim to recover a statutory penalty against a lessee hold-

Of course, counterclaims which are legal in their nature may be maintained where each party waives his right to a trial by jury. 

The defendant is held to have waived his right to a jury trial of any purely legal counterclaim by pleading it in the equity suit. But the plaintiff has the same guaranty of a jury trial as the defendant. 

Therefore, unless the plaintiff also waives his right, and the waiver appears of record, expressly or by necessary implication, a legal counterclaim is not maintainable in a suit in equity under the 1931 Chancery Act.76 It would seem, however, that if a counterclaim has no connection with the cause of action asserted in the bill, the court may of its own motion dismiss a legal counterclaim even though both parties do waive their right to a jury trial.77 

As previously mentioned, there is one exception to the rule that a legal counterclaim is not maintainable in a suit in equity. This exception is based upon the principle that, when a court of equity has, by virtue of its original jurisdiction, cognizance of a cause for one purpose, it will proceed to a complete adjudication of the entire case, including the settlement of legal rights and the granting of legal remedies which would otherwise be beyond the scope of its authority. It is a prerequisite to the granting of such legal relief, however, that not only must some substantial ground of equity jurisdiction be alleged in the bill, but it must also be proved at the hearing. And further, in order to authorize an equity court to grant legal relief under the foregoing rule, the legal demand must constitute some part of and be incidental to the equitable demand.78 

Since a plaintiff may obtain legal relief in an equity suit when such relief is incidental to equitable relief to which he has proved himself entitled, it logically and necessarily follows that a defendant may obtain legal relief through a counterclaim under the same cir-

Of course, as in the case of granting legal relief to the plaintiff, if it appears at any stage of the proceedings that there is no cause of action of equitable cognizance upon which to predicate the jurisdiction of the court, the defendant's counterclaim will fall with the bill of complaint even though it may be meritorious as a legal cause of action. In one case the plaintiff sought to enjoin the defendant from making use of certain personal property, such as books and keys, belonging to the plaintiff corporation. The defendant answered and filed a counterclaim seeking a receiver for the corporation and to be restored to his office therein. Likewise, where a bill was brought to recover purchase money on a land sale contract, it was held that a legal counterclaim seeking damages for breach of the contract to sell was not maintainable. The court, in stating its reasons, said: "The bill in the instant case does not state a case for relief in equity nor does the answer set up a counterclaim that could be made the subject of an independent bill in equity. Therefore, * a decree could not be rendered herein on a cause of action, if any, triable in a court of law."81 

The rules applicable to the granting of legal relief on counterclaims filed in suits in equity may be summarized as follows: 

1. A legal counterclaim not arising out of the transaction which is the subject matter of the suit cannot be maintained over the objection of the plaintiff because of the constitutional guaranty of a trial by jury in common law cases; 

2. Even though a legal counterclaim arises out of the transaction which is the subject matter of the suit, no relief can be granted thereon unless there is some cause of action of equitable cognizance stated in the pleadings and proved at the hearing as a predicate for the jurisdiction of the court; and 

3. Where a legal counterclaim arises out of the transaction which is the subject matter of the suit, the court may, as incidental to any equitable relief which it may grant, also grant the legal relief sought by the counterclaim. It would seem clear that legal relief may be granted to the defendant as incidental to equitable relief granted to either the plaintiff or defendant. 

Where the defendant sets up a legal counterclaim, and the bill of complaint is dismissed as without equity, the decree is not a bar to a subsequent action at law on the cause of action asserted in the counterclaim unless it appears that the cause of action was actually adjudicated in the chancery suit under circumstances which

amounted to a waiver of a jury trial by both parties.82 And when a bill is dismissed as having no equity, and the defendant's counterclaim is dismissed without prejudice, it becomes immaterial whether the counterclaim was an equitable one which could have been litigated in a chancery suit.83 

§ 108.-Parties and Procedure.-The 1931 Chancery Act84 pro vides that "when in the determination of a counterclaim complete relief cannot be granted without the presence of parties other than those to the bill, the court may order them to be brought in as defendants."

Under this statute, a defendant may seek relief against either the original plaintiff solely, or against the original plaintiff and other persons, regardless of whether the latter are or are not already parties to the action. But, in either event, in order to maintain a counterclaim, relief must be claimed against the original plaintiff or the matters set up must affect the original plaintiff's rights.85 Thus a junior mortgagee, who is a party defendant in a suit to foreclose a first mortgage, cannot maintain a counterclaim to foreclose his junior lien.86

As permitted by the statute, the defendant may, when it is necessary to the granting of complete relief on his counterclaim, require that persons not then parties to the suit be brought in as defendants.87 But the general rule is that the defendant cannot maintain a counterclaim which requires the bringing in of third persons who may have independent claims against the plaintiff.88 

Nor is it permissible to join as parties plaintiff to a cross-bill persons who were not made parties defendant to the original bill. 89

§ 110.-General Replications.-Under the original practice, the plaintiff was required to file a replication to an answer duly filed and not excepted to and, if he failed or refused to do so, the defendant was entitled to an order as of course for the dismissal of the suit.¹ The failure to file a replication was waived, however, by the defendant proceeding to trial as though the cause was at issue,2 or consenting to the filing of evidence which amply supported the final decree.3

A general replication was a general denial of the truth of the defendant's answer and of the sufficiency of the matter alleged in it, and an assertion of the truth and sufficiency of the bill. When a replication was filed to an answer it therefore put in issue all the matters alleged in the bill and not admitted in the answer, as well as those matters alleged in the answer which were not responsive to the bill of complaint.4 When the answer concluded with the general denial usually found in answers in chancery, that was sufficient to make an issue on material allegations in the bill not admitted in the answer and to which no response was made.5 Such statements were not taken as admitted to be true but, where the oath to the answer was waived, were required to be proved by at least a preponderance of the testimony. Matters set up in the answer that were not responsive to the bill of complaint, such as new matter in

In regard to general replications, the 1931 Chancery Act provides: "General replications to answers are hereby abolished. Unless the answer assert a counterclaim with a prayer for affirmative relief no reply shall be required without a special order of the court, and any new or affirmative matter therein shall be deemed to be denied by the plaintiff. If the answer include a counterclaim with a prayer for affirmative relief, each party against whom it is asserted shall file his reply thereto within the time prescribed by law. The reply shall state the facts relied upon in answer to such counterclaim."8

The foregoing statute is substantially the same as a prior statute enacted in 1915.9 In accordance with its terms, no replication to an answer is required without a special order of the court unless the answer asserts a counterclaim with a prayer for affirmative relief. 

The cause is deemed at issue at the expiration of ten days from the filing of the answer. 10 Even though a general replication is filed to an answer which does not assert a counterclaim, this does not affect the rule that the cause is deemed at issue ten days after the filing of the answer.¹¹

The abolition of general replications does not deprive the plaintiff of any benefit which accrued to him under the former practice. 

A general replication merely placed in issue all the matters alleged in the bill and not admitted by the answer as well as those matters alleged in the answer which were not responsive to the bill. Since responsive in this sense meant by way of denial, 12 the effect of the old rule was to place upon the plaintiff the burden of proving the allegations of his bill not admitted in the answer and to place upon the defendant the burden of proving any allegations of his answer which were not in the nature of denials. § 111. Special Replications.-A special replication was occa sioned, under the original equity practice, by the defendant introducing new matter in his plea or answer which made it necessary for the plaintiff to put in issue some additional fact on his part in avoidance of such new matter. A special replication usually required a rejoinder, which in turn might require a surrejoinder. 

The court was thus drawn into the nicety of special pleading as used. in courts of law. The inconvenience, expense, and delay of such proceedings caused special replications to be discontinued at an early date in chancery practice. Amendments to the bill were substituted for them. 118. Judgment on Motion. § 113.-In General.-There is inherent in courts of chancery power to prevent the abuse of their procedure. The court has power, of its own motion, to purge pleadings of prolixity, tautology, scandal, and impertinence, and it cannot, therefore, be held in error for striking such matter on motion of a party to the cause.¹ 

Likewise, a pleading may be stricken if it is sham or frivolous or wholly irrelevant to the cause, or if it violates a rule or order of the court, or if it is a palpable attempt to impose upon or trifle with the court, as by merely repeating or reiterating to no better effect and with no additional new matter the same facts already presented and adjudged immaterial or insufficient.2 But striking a pleading or any part thereof is a severe remedy and should be resorted to only in cases clearly requiring it for the proper ad ministration of justice.3 

Motions to strike have long been recognized as one means of attacking pleadings for frivolity and impertinence and for palpable and serious defects in form.4 The 1931 Chancery Act contains two provisions based upon this established practice and declaratory of the existing law. The first of these is as follows: "All pleadings in an equity cause shall be expressed in as brief and succinct terms as reasonably practicable, and shall contain no unnecessary recitals of deeds, documents, contracts, or other instruments in hæc verba, or other irrelevant, redundant

If any pleading or other paper filed in the cause shall violate the provisions of this section to the prejudice of the opposing party affected the court may, on motion to strike or of its own motion, expunge the objectionable matter at the cost of the offending party, upon such terms and conditions as shall be fixed by the court. 115 The second provision of the 1931 Act above referred to provides: "Exceptions to bills, answers and other pleadings for scandal, impertinence or irrelevancy are abolished, but the court may, upon motion to strike or upon its own initiative, strike out any redundant, impertinent, irrelevant or scandalous and impertinent matter which is prejudicial to the opposing party, upon such terms as the court shall think fit."6

Matter should not be stricken from a pleading under the foregoing statutes unless it is wholly irrelevant, or is otherwise improper, and can have no bearing on the equities of the case and no influence upon the decision either as to the relief to be granted or the allowance of costs.8 And it is a well established rule that allegations will not be stricken as irrelevant unless it clearly appears that they are wholly immaterial and impertinent. If the court strikes matter from the record, it is gone, and the pleader may have no opportunity of placing it there again. But if it is left on the record, and is prolix or oppressive, the court may, at the hearing of the cause, set the matter right in the imposition of costs.⁹ 

The court should always give the pleading sought to be stricken a liberal construction on the point of irrelevancy and consider whether the matter can have any real and proper influence upon the suit.10 Thus, while ambiguity in a pleading should be construed against the pleader, yet where, under the allegations of the

A motion to strike a bill of complaint or counterclaim should be distinguished from a motion to dismiss and the two remedies should not be indiscriminately applied as they are governed by essentially different rules of procedure. A bill or counterclaim in proper form duly filed should not be stricken for insufficiency. Its sufficiency as a pleading should be tested by motion to dismiss. The summary disposition of pleadings by motion to strike is the exercise of a necessary but delicate power which should be cautiously applied. 

A motion to dismiss goes to the bill or counterclaim as an entirety for insufficiency, while a motion to strike is applicable to such pleadings where the whole or any part thereof is wholly irrelevant or for any reason improper.20 A motion to strike is properly used, however, to test the legal sufficiency of an answer to a bill of complaint or a reply to a counterclaim.21 

§ 114.-Motion to Strike Answer or Part Thereof.-A motion to strike, as applicable to an answer in chancery, may be used for two distinct purposes. As in the case of other pleadings, it may be used to eliminate from an answer any portions thereof which are irrelevant, impertinent, redundant, or scandalous. And a motion. to strike may be addressed to the answer as an entirety to test its legal sufficiency.

While a motion to strike an answer or any part thereof has, for some purposes, succeeded the remedy by exceptions to an answer, the two should be carefully distinguished. Exceptions have been abolished by the 1931 Chancery Act22 but they were formerly used to eliminate scandalous or impertinent matter from an answer or to compel a further and more complete answer to such allegations of a bill of complaint as the plaintiff conceived were not sufficiently answered.

If an answer went out of its way to state scandalous matter, or matter which was not material to the defendant's case, it was subject to exceptions as to such matter.23 The exceptions were required to definitely designate the matter alleged to be impertinent

An exception to an answer had to be supported in toto, and it failed if it covered any part of the answer which was relevant and material.26 Thus it was erroneous to sustain exceptions to an entire paragraph of an answer if the paragraph contained any averments which were responsive to the bill or set up a valid defense thereto.27

If an answer contained an insufficient or evasive response to the allegations or interrogations of the bill, the plaintiff could take exceptions thereto, specifying the parts of the bill which were not sufficiently answered and praying that the defendant be required to make a further and full answer thereto.28 But excep- tions for insufficiency did not lie to an answer to a bill that was not essentially one for discovery and that expressly waived an answer under oath.29 Nor did exceptions for insufficiency lie to an answer setting up a defense in bar of the suit. Exceptions were proper only when the answer did not sufficiently respond to the allegations, charges, and interrogatories of the bill.30 Thus, an exception for insufficiency would not be sustained when the answer denied a material allegation of the bill of complaint.31

Since, under the 1931 Chancery Act, the answer is only a defensive pleading and no longer serves the purpose of giving discovery to the plaintiff,33 the reason for permitting exceptions for insufficiency has been abolished with the remedy. Even prior to the 1931 Act, a motion to strike, as well as exceptions, could be used to eliminate impertinent, irrelevant, or scandalous matter from an answer. The effect of the provision in the 1931 Act abolishing exceptions is, therefore, no more than to make a motion to strike the exclusive remedy for that purpose.34

As in the case of exceptions for impertinence, a motion to strike any part of an answer which may be deemed impertinent, redundant, or scandalous is controlled by the rule which requires the denial of the motion unless the matter sought to be stricken is wholly irrelevant, can have no bearing upon the equities, and no influence upon the decision in the cause, either as to the relief to be granted or the allowance of costs.35 And a motion to strike a portion of an answer must not be too broad, for if the portion assailed contains any matter material to the issue, it will not be stricken.36

The question of pertinency depends in some degree upon the frame of the bill. If the bill alleges unnecessary facts by way of inducement or otherwise, and especially if it tends to cast reflections upon the integrity of the defendant, an answer responsive to such allegations is not impertinent. Where the averments of an answer make issues that should be determined upon a consideration of evidentiary matters, not concluded as a matter of law by the pleadings as they stand, a motion to strike the answer should be denied.48 And where a bill of complaint is filed putting a particular construction upon the transaction which forms the subject matter of the suit, an answer asserting a different construction of the transaction is not subject to a motion to strike and is properly left for the consideration of the court in making its final decree on the merits.49 

A motion to strike a part of an answer setting up a single complete defense to the bill, like a motion to strike an entire answer, should not be granted unless the matter assailed is wholly insufficient as a defense.50 Thus, in a suit to have mortgage participation certificates adjudged to be liens prior to receiver's certificates, that part of an answer setting up a subordination agreement should not be stricken.51

Since special defenses to the bill formerly presentable by plea are now to be included in the answer, it seems clear that the legal sufficiency of such a defense is to be tested by a motion to strike that part of the answer in which it is set up and that such a motion will have the same effect as setting the plea down for argument under the former practice.52 

§ 115.-Motion to Strike Reply or Part Thereof.-A motion to strike a reply to a counterclaim, or any part of such a reply, is in all material respects the same as a motion to strike an answer, or part thereof, and is governed by the same rules and principles. 

Where the motion is addressed to the entire reply, it is used in the same way that a motion to dismiss a bill of complaint is used and it admits to be true those allegations of the reply which are well pleaded.53

§ 116.-Time of Filing. In regard to the time for filing a motion to strike an answer or reply, or any part thereof, the 1931 

Chancery Act provides: 

"In the absence of a special order of the court, ten days and no longer shall be allowed the complainant in which to move to strike the answer or any part thereof *** ; and the defendant shall have a like period of ten days (unless the time be extended by special order of the court) in which to move to strike the whole or a part of the reply to a counterclaim. The period of ten days shall begin to run from the time the answer is required to be filed, * * "'54 No mention is made of the time from which the ten day period begins to run in the case of a motion to strike a reply but, by analogy, it seems clear that the ten days begin to run from the time the reply is required to be filed.

There is an apparent conflict between the foregoing provision of the 1931 Chancery Act and a subsequent section providing as follows: 

"At the expiration of ten days from the filing of the answer, if there be no counterclaim, or, if there shall be a counterclaim, then at the expiration of ten days from the filing of the reply thereto, the cause shall be deemed at issue. If, however, within such period of ten days a motion is filed to strike the whole of the answer or reply * * * the cause shall not be deemed at issue until the points of law so presented shall have been ruled upon by the court."55

The foregoing provision might be construed as requiring a motion to strike an entire answer or reply to be filed within ten days. after the actual filing of the pleading so attacked regardless of when the pleading was required to be filed. However, in view of the clear and specific statement in the section of the 1931 Act first above quoted, that the ten day period begins to run from the time the pleading is required to be filed, there can be little doubt but that this section controls. If this were not true, the defendant, by filing his answer more than ten days before it was required to be filed, could place upon the plaintiff the burden of continually watching the court file or be precluded from moving to strike the 

54. C. G. L. Per. Supp. 4902 (19); Mc 

Carthy Chan. Act, p. 103, § 38. 

55. C. G. L. Per. Supp. 4902 (20); Mc 

Carthy Chan. Act, p. 104, § 39.

§ 117] 259 

answer if it was filed more than ten days before the required time. without his knowledge. It is safe to conclude that no such result was contemplated by the 1931 Act. 

It should be noted that, while a motion to strike a part of an answer or reply may be filed within the ten day period, only the filing of a motion to strike the entire answer or reply prevents the cause from being deemed at issue at the expiration of the ten day period. 56 

Except in case of an emergency, notice should always be given to the opposing party of an application for an extension of time for filing a motion to strike an answer or reply.57 

§ 117.-Effect of Motion.-Like a motion to dismiss a bill of complaint, a motion to strike an answer or part thereof admits the assailed allegations which are material and well pleaded to be true. 58

The admission is, of course, only for the purpose of passing on the motion.

The 1931 Chancery Act provides that a motion to strike an entire answer or reply, filed within ten days after the day upon which the answer or reply is required to be filed, prevents the cause from being deemed at issue until the points of law so presented have been ruled upon by the court.59 While this ten day period would seem to be entirely for the benefit of the party who might wish to file a motion to strike, it has been held that, even where no motion is filed, it may be necessary for both parties to waive the ten day period in order to proceed with the taking of testimony or the final hearing before its expiration.60

The 1931 Chancery Act also provides that a motion to strike part of a pleading does not stay the progress of the cause unless it is so ordered by the court. Such a stay order may be entered without notice to the opposite party.61 This rule gives the court an opportunity to discourage the use of motions to strike for dilatory purposes.

The rule that a motion to strike part of a pleading does not stay the progress of the cause is not construed with literal exactness. If, for example, a motion is filed to strike a part of a counterclaim which, if eliminated, would put an end to the entire cross demand, the progress of the cause is stayed to such an extent that, either no decree pro confesso can be entered against the plaintiff for failure to reply to the counterclaim, or a decree pro confesso, if entered, would be set aside upon proper application by the plaintiff.62 But, if a motion to strike is addressed to immaterial parts of a bill of complaint which, if eliminated, would not affect the plaintiff's right of recovery, a decree pro confesso may be entered unless a stay order is obtained. 62A § 118. Judgment on Motion.-If a motion to strike an answer, or part thereof, is denied the cause is ordinarily then at issue.63 If such a motion is granted, the court may, in accordance with its general power in that regard, permit the answer to be amended or an amended answer to be filed.64 

There is some doubt as to the proper judgment to be entered where a motion to strike an entire answer is granted without leave to amend, or with leave to amend where no amended answer is filed. Under the former practice it had been said that it was improper to enter a decree pro confesso under these circumstances and that the proper judgment was the entry of a decree on the pleadings.65 However, even prior to the 1931 Chancery Act this practice was not generally followed.66

It is probable that, under the 1931 Chancery Act, the proper procedure is to enter a decree pro confesso where a motion to strike is granted without leave to amend, or with leave to amend which is not exercised. The 1931 Act specifically provides that a decree pro confesso may be entered if the defendant fails to file his answer within the time prescribed by law "or within such other time as shall have been fixed by the court."67 This provision is broad

§ 119.-In General. It is a well established principle, in courts of equity, that mispleading in matters of form is never allowed to prejudice any party. The real and substantial merits of the cause are always looked to. The court will, upon the discovery of errors of form, allow an amendment or wholly overlook them at the hearing as waived. And in many cases, courts of equity will allow substantial defects to be amended if the cause is at such a stage that they can properly be amended.¹

In accordance with these principles, the 1931 Chancery Act, in regard to amendments generally, provides: "The court may at any time, in furtherance of justice, upon such terms as may be just, permit any process, proceeding, pleading or record to be amended, or material supplemental to be set forth in an amended pleading. The court, at every stage of the proceedings, must disregard any error or defect in the proceedings which does not affect the substantial rights of the parties."2

Since statutes relative to the amendment of pleadings are liberally construed to facilitate the administration of justice, the trial court is, under the foregoing statute, vested with a wide discretion 

1. Spencer v. Dell, 55 Fla. 790, 46 So. 729. 

2. C. G. L. Per. Supp. 4902 (7); Mc 

Carthy Chan. Act, p. 68, § 26.

[Ch. 14 

in permitting amendments to pleadings. And, where no settled rule of law or procedure is plainly violated, or a sound judicial discretion grossly abused, the action of the court in permitting amendments will not be disturbed on appeal.3 Scarcely any right of procedure is more important to suitors, or more frequently called into exercise in actual practice, than that of amending their pleadings. 

The right to amend is substantial, and its denial has been held, in extreme cases, to amount to an illegal departure from the essential requirements of the law. In Florida, the liberal practice of permitting all timely and proper amendments to present the real points of a cause of action or ground of defense is not only ratified by statute, but is also grounded upon many decisions of the Supreme Court. These decisions have operated to reverse more cases for refusing amendments in proper cases than for allowing them in improper cases. In other words, judicial discretion is more likely to be abused by refusing to permit an amendment than by allowing it.4

Since a pleading in a cause, after it is filed, becomes a court document, it should not be altered, amended, or destroyed without the permission of the court upon due notice to the opposite party. 

Thus an interlineation of a prayer for an injunction in a bill of complaint, made without notice to the opposite party and without leave of court, is an unauthorized and an invalid act.5 Amendments should be effected by filing amended pleadings, or amendments to pleadings, as separate documents. 

As provided by the 1931 Chancery Act, amendments may be permitted at any time. During the taking of testimony, the chancellor has authority to confine the evidence to the issues duly made, or to permit amendments in furtherance of justice. Amendments are not usually allowed at such a late stage of the proceedings, 3. Morgan v. Eaton, 59 Fla. 562, 52
