however, except for the purpose of conforming the pleadings to the proof. Therefore, when the chancellor has set a date for a hearing and entered upon a trial before himself in open court of the issues made, and the hearing has substantially proceeded, the denial of an application by the defendant to amend his answer so as to broaden the issues will not be disturbed on appeal in the absence of a clear showing of an abuse of discretion under the circumstances. Even upon the final hearing, when it clearly appears from the evidence that the plaintiff has a case which entitles him to relief, but which by reason of some defect or omission in the allegations of the bill is not brought fairly within the issues, he will generally be permitted to amend the bill and adapt its allegations to the case as proved. But when such an amendment would change the issue, or introduce new issues, or materially vary the grounds of relief, it is not generally permissible.9

Pleadings may be amended even after an appeal has been taken or decided. Thus, where the appellate court has decided that the plaintiff is entitled to no relief on the facts alleged by him, the plaintiff may amend to introduce new facts which would change equitable issues already decided.10 But the plaintiff cannot, by amendment after an appeal, depart from the cause of action originally brought." Thus, where plaintiff seeks the rescission of a contract to sell land, and the defendant counterclaims seeking specific performance, and the appellate court affirms an interlocutory decree holding the counterclaim sufficient, the plaintiff cannot file an amended bill, based upon a new and inconsistent theory of his case, which will deprive the defendant of the benefit of the prior ruling on appeal. Likewise, when a party appeals from an order in a chancery case, and the order is affirmed and the cause remanded for further proceedings consistent with the appellate court's opinion, the lower court has no authority to reopen the case, or to permit amendments to be made inconsistent with the state of

It will also be noted that the statute permits "material supplemental matter to be set forth in an amended pleading."13 In regard to such matter, another section of the 1931 Chancery Act further provides: "Upon application of either party the court may, upon notice and such terms as are just, permit him to file and serve an amended pleading, alleging material facts occurring after his former pleading, or of which he was ignorant when it was made, including the judgment or decree of a competent court rendered after the commencement of the suit determining the matters in controversy or a part thereof."14

Under the original chancery practice, amendments to pleadings could not set up facts occurring after the filing of suit. It was the function of a supplemental bill to set up facts which had occurred, or at least been discovered, since the filing of the original bill and affecting the rights of the parties or the subject matter of the controversy.' In regard to the amendment of bills of complaint, the 1931 

Chancery Act provides: 

"The plaintiff may, as of course, amend his bill before the defendant has filed his answer thereto, but if such amendment be filed after the defendant has appeared the plaintiff at his own cost shall furnish to each opposing party affected, a copy of the amended bill, or of the amendment, as the case may be, unless otherwise ordered by the court. After answer filed by any defendant, plaintiff may amend by consent of such defendant or leave of the court."19

Under this statute, it is clear that bills cannot be amended as of course after the answer has been filed.20 It is not error to disregard an amended bill filed after the answer without leave of court.21 

As is the case of amendments generally, the matter of allowing amendments to a bill of complaint, other than those which are allowable as of course, is one solely in the discretion of the chancellor and his rulings thereon will not be disturbed unless his discretion is abused.22 Thus, where a bill is amended three different times, and the plaintiff still fails to state a cause of action, it is not error to refuse leave to file further amendments, although the dismissal of the bill should be without prejudice.23 And where, after the sustaining of a motion to dismiss with leave to amend, the plaintiff files an amendment containing no new matter to meet the objections already determined, the amendment may properly be stricken.24

If the public is interested in the suit, the chancellor should give every opportunity to amend the bill where there is any reasonable ground upon which relief may be prayed.25 Thus the dismissal of a bill seeking an adjudication that harbor bonds are invalid, without permitting the public prosecutor to amend so as to state a case for relief appropriate to taxpayers whose property might

§ 121.-Amendment of Bill-Stating New Case.-The provi sions of the 1931 Chancery Act in regard to the amendment of bills of complaint do not alter or abolish the long established chancery rule that an amended bill which is in effect the institution of a new and materially different suit, palpably inconsistent with or repugnant to the original pleading, should be rejected as an inappropriate pleading in the cause.29 Therefore, when a proposed amendment to a bill of complaint would change the issue, introduce new issues, or materially vary the grounds of relief, it is not generally permissible.30 Thus a bill to foreclose a mortgage cannot be amended so as to make it a bill to enforce a resulting trust. 31 But whether an amended bill constitutes a departure in pleading depends upon whether the ultimate purpose of both the original and amended bills is identical.32 Where an original bill seeks to quiet title and to restrain a trespass, and an amended bill seeks the same relief, the amended bill is not in effect the institution of a new and materially different suit.33 Likewise, where the original bill on a note alleged that the money loaned constituted the plaintiff's separate property, an amended bill alleging that the plaintiff had loaned the money as guardian of her minor children did not materially change the cause of action.34 And an amendment stating

§ 122.-Amendment of Bill-Facts Occurring After Suit.-Under the former equity practice, facts occurring after the institution of suit could only be introduced by a supplemental bill. 

The function of a supplemental bill was to bring before the court facts which had occurred, or at least been discovered, after the filing of the original bill and which affected the rights of the parties or the subject matter of the controversy. It could be resorted to where an amendment was not available, since it was not permissible to introduce into the bill by amendment facts occurring after the filing of the original bill. But the new matter which might be introduced by supplemental bill was restricted to such matter as constituted part of the cause of action set up in the original bill and referred to and supported the rights and interests asserted therein.40 Thus a supplemental bill could be filed to subject rents accruing after the filing of an original bill of foreclosure to the payment of the mortgage debt.41 Matter which changed the rights and interests of the parties already before the court, or which attempted to show a cause of action in the plaintiff which he did not have at the commencement of the suit, could not be introduced by

§ 123. Amendment of Bill-As to Parties.-In regard to the addition of parties to a suit in equity, the 1931 Chancery Act49 contains the broad provision that "any person may at any time be made a party if his presence is necessary or proper to a complete determination of the cause." Parties may be added at any time. before final decree, 50 or even afterward.51 Of course, any party brought in as a defendant after the cause is at issue has a right to be heard on all matters affecting his interest.52 

Though it has been said that one may be made a party by stipulation,53 the proper method of bringing in new parties is by amendment to the bill.54 Thus a married woman may be permitted to amend her bill at any time so as to sue by her next friend.55 And an amendment stating that the plaintiff sues in a representative capacity, and not individually, is permissible.56 

Where the defendant alleges that other parties not plaintiffs have an interest in the subject matter of the suit, the plaintiff may, with the consent of the court, amend his bill so as to add such parties plaintiff. When this is done the defendant is estopped to question the propriety of the amendment.57 And when a petition for intervention is filed, and the intervenor is specifically made a party by decree of the court and thereafter participates in and becomes the main party defendant in the cause, he cannot afterwards complain because the bill was not physically amended to make him a party. 58 Where the plaintiff does not amend his bill to meet an objection as to parties, and proceeds to a hearing without securing a ruling

§ 124.-Amendment of Bill-Prayer.-Under the former prac tice, it was usual for a bill in equity to contain a prayer for the relief specifically sought and also a prayer for general relief. The purpose of the latter prayer was to enable the court to do complete justice between the parties in case the plaintiff mistook the relief to which he was entitled or the special prayer did not embrace all the relief to which he was entitled.62

Under the 1931 Chancery Act63 every bill is construed to pray for general relief and the prayer for such relief may be omitted. 

Therefore, no question as to the right to amend or broaden the prayer for general relief can arise. The 1931 Act also requires the plaintiff to pray for any special relief sought pending the suit or on final hearing. Under the former practice, the prayer for special relief could be amended provided the relief so sought was within the scope of the pleadings and proof, and did not take the defendant by surprise.64 This is also the undoubted rule under the present practice.

Of course, the interlineation of a prayer in a bill of complaint after it is filed, without leave of court and without notice to the opposite party, is an invalid act.65

 § 125.-Amendment of Bill-At What Stage of Proceedings.-In general, the bill may be amended at any stage of the proceedings. 

The 1931 Chancery Act66 permits such amendments at any time, in furtherance of justice, upon such terms as may be just.67 Though applications to amend should be made promptly after the necessity for the amendment has been discovered, 68 the time at which amendments are allowed is in the sole discretion of the chancellor and his rulings thereon will not be disturbed unless an abuse of discretion is shown.69

The plaintiff may amend his bill as of course before the defendant has filed his answer but, if the amendment is filed after the defendant has appeared, the plaintiff must, at his own cost, furnish to each opposing party affected a copy of the amendment or amended bill.70 After an answer has been filed by any defendant, the plaintiff may amend only with the consent of the defendant or by leave of court.71 Under the former practice, notice to the defendant of an application for leave to amend after answer was not necessary.72

The 1931 Chancery Act makes no specific requirement of such notice.

Under the former practice, when a demurrer to a bill of complaint was sustained, the plaintiff was entitled to amend unless it was clear that the defects in the bill were incurable, and such leave to amend could be granted without a formal motion by the plaintiff.73 And, where a bill did not wholly fail to state a cause of action, it was error to dismiss it for an excusable failure to file an amended bill within the time fixed by the court.74 Under the 1931 

Chancery Act, the court has the same power to permit amendments to the bill after sustaining a motion to dismiss, and the bill should not be dismissed without first granting leave to amend.75 If it is

Amendment of the bill is even permissible on the final hearing when it then clearly appears from the evidence that the plaintiff has a case which entitles him to relief, but which, by reason of some defect or omission in the allegations of the bill, is not brought fairly within the issues. The statutory rule that the defendant's original motion or answer shall be considered as interposed to the amended bill unless he files a new pleading does not, of course, affect the defendant's right to plead anew to the amended bill. In allowing amendments to bills and permitting amended bills to be filed, courts do not pass upon the legal sufficiency of such amendments or amended bills. 

An amended bill is not the same bill as the original bill. Therefore, its legal sufficiency can only be adequately tested, and the question saved for review on appeal, by permitting a motion to dismiss the amended pleading.89 The circumstance of the amendment being of the most trifling character will not make any difference.90 And, where the defendant desires to test the legal sufficiency of an amended bill, the court cannot deprive him of this right by requiring him to file an answer instead of a motion to dismiss.91 

§ 128. Amendment of Answer. The rules for the amendment of pleadings generally apply, of course, to answers, 92 and the 1931 Chancery Act93 specifically provides that the answer may be amended, by leave of court upon reasonable notice, so as to put any averment in issue, when justice requires it. The allowance of an amendment to an answer rests in the sound judicial discretion of the court and its action will not be reversed on appeal in the absence of an abuse of discretion.94 But an amendment should be allowed where it will further the ends of justice.95 An amended answer filed without notice or leave of court is properly stricken from the files.96

§ 130.-Better Particulars.-Under the original equity practice, a motion for better particulars was unknown and could be ignored by the court.112 But the 1931 Chancery Act contains the following provision in regard to the obtaining of better particulars: "Better particulars of any matter stated in any pleading may in any case be ordered upon such terms, as to costs and otherwise, as may be just."113

This section of the 1931 Act has been taken from an analogous provision of the Federal equity rules and the Supreme Court of Florida has held that it bears the same construction as the Federal equity rule.114

The object of the statute is to enable the party asking for better particulars to know what case he has to meet at the trial. CHAPTER XV HEARING ON BILL AND ANSWER § 131. Before Cause At Issue. 

132. After Expiration of Time for Taking Testimony. 

§ 131.-Before Cause At Issue.-Under the former practice, if an answer in chancery was in substance bad as a defense, and raised no issue requiring proof of the allegations of the bill, the proper procedure was to set the cause down for hearing on bill and answer.¹ 

This could be done immediately after the answer was filed and before the cause was at issue by reason of the filing of a replication. 

But where the plaintiff set the cause down for hearing on bill and answer before the filing of a replication, and consequently before the cause was at issue, he was, in thus cutting the defendant off from proving the truth of his answer, held at the hearing to have admitted the truth of all of its allegations.2 The admission applied to all pertinent allegations of the answer,3 whether they were responsive to the bill or in confession and avoidance of it, and whether the answer was sworn to or not. Of course, on such a hearing, all allegations of the bill not sufficiently denied by the answer were taken as true. Even the enactment of a statute dispensing with replications in certain cases, and providing that the cause was at issue on the filing of the answer, did not change the foregoing rules as to hearing on bill and answer. Only the plaintiff was authorized to set the cause down for hearing on bill and answer before the cause was at issue or before the time for taking testimony had expired. The defendant had no such right because, of course, he was not entitled to thus have the

The foregoing practice, with the exceptions hereinafter noted, is incorporated in the following provision of the 1931 Chancery Act: "The plaintiff may, within ten days after the filing of the answer, or within such further time as the court may allow,.move for a decree on bill and answer, and if the motion be overruled, the plaintiff shall have the right to proceed to trial notwithstanding the motion or order thereon; and if the answer be found insufficient as a defense but amendable, the court may permit it to be amended on such terms and conditions as may be equitable."9

It will be noted that, under this statute, a motion for decree on bill and answer must be filed within ten days after the filing of the answer. In other words, the motion must be filed before the cause is at issue.10 Since the purpose of the motion is to test the legal sufficiency of the answer, it is improper to proceed to a hearing on the motion if it is filed after the cause is at issue.11 

In one respect the 1931 Chancery Act materially alters the former practice. Prior to the Act, it was usual for the court to enter a final decree for the prevailing party at the hearing on bill and answer. Now, however, if the motion is not well founded, the plaintiff may, if he wishes, proceed to the taking of testimony, and if the motion is well founded the court may permit the defendant to amend his answer. But, if the answer is insufficient and not amendable, a final decree may then be entered against the defendant. 

§ 132.-After Expiration of Time for Taking Testimony.—While a hearing on bill and answer before the cause is at issue is an interlocutory hearing, there is another kind of hearing on bill and answer which is a final hearing. No specific provisions as to a final hearing on bill and answer are contained in the 1931 Chancery Act.

If there are several defendants, one defendant as to whom the time for taking testimony has expired cannot set the cause for final hearing when there are other defendants as to whom the time for taking testimony has not expired. The court will not make as many final decrees as there are defendants. If there has been inexcusable delay, the proper remedy for a defendant as to whom the time for taking testimony has expired is to move to dismiss the bill for want of prosecution.21 However, a defendant may waive his right to object to a final hearing on bill and answer before the time for taking testimony has expired by participating in the hearing without objection or by setting down the cause himself.22 

The general rule is that when an equity cause is set down for final hearing on bill and answer, no testimony having been taken by either party, all allegations of the bill of complaint that are admitted by the answer are taken as true and require no proof. 

Material allegations of the bill that are denied by the defendant and are not proved cannot avail the plaintiff. And averments in the answer of new matter that are not proved cannot avail the defendant.23 A general denial in the answer is sufficient to deprive the plaintiff of the benefit of material allegations of his bill not specifically admitted by the defendant,24 and where the answer is responsive and in denial of the bill, the allegations of the bill must fall when they are not sustained by proof.25 This is on the proper reasoning that, because the plaintiff has neglected and refused to submit evidence in proof of his bill, he should only have the benefit of the allegations therein which the defendant has admitted. 

By the same reasoning, it is only responsive allegations of the answer which are taken as true at the hearing on bill and answer.26

§ 133. 

CHAPTER XVI INTERVENTIONS Who May Intervene. 

134. Status of Intervener. 

135.

Procedure. 

136. Time of Intervention. 

§ 133.-Who May Intervene.-The 1931 Chancery Act' contains a provision, adopted from the Federal equity rules,2 that "anyone claiming an interest in the litigation may at any time be permitted to assert his right by intervention." However, interventions had always been recognized in Florida equity practice. 

Under the statute, as well as prior thereto, persons having an interest in the subject of a suit in equity, and who are either necessary or proper parties to the suit, if not made so by the plaintiff, may come in by way of application to intervene and be made parties plaintiff or defendant to the end that their interests may be adjudicated and protected in the suit. The interest which will entitle a person to intervene must be in the matter in litigation, and of such a direct and immediate character that the intervenor will either gain or lose by the direct legal operation of the decree. In other words, the interest must be that created by a claim to the demand, or some part of the demand, in suit, or a claim to or lien upon the property, or some part of it, which is the subject of the litigation.4 

However, if the real merits of the cause can be determined without affecting the interests of absent persons, the cause may proceed without them even though they are proper parties.5 

There are numerous decisions illustrating these general principles and the interest necessary to support an intervention. Thus, in a suit by one partner against another for an accounting, a person claiming a lien on part of the partnership property may intervene.® 

In a suit in which certain property is to be sold, the state has a

If any of the parties wish to question the validity of the tax, they may do so by answer. Where the plaintiff in a partition suit claims an interest in the land as the widow of the former owner, a person denying the plaintiff's marriage, and claiming under an alleged valid marriage to the former owner, may intervene on the ground that she is a necessary party to the suit in the first instance.Ⓡ 

A person in adverse possession of property at the time a mortgage thereon is executed by another, who had no notice of the mortgage until after it was executed, is entitled to intervene and defend in proceedings for the foreclosure of the mortgage.9

Generally, those having an interest in a fund in the custody of the court may intervene. 10 Thus, where a sale has been had in a partition suit and the property converted into money, a proper and usual mode of bringing forward the demands of creditors who have a right to satisfaction out of the funds is to intervene.11 But the fact that one may be a contract creditor of a partnership does not entitle him to intervene and be made a party to a suit brought to dissolve the partnership. 12 And the rule is that, where a court has appointed a receiver and taken possession of the property of an insolvent for administration, creditors have the right to intervene and contest the validity as well as the priority of other claims or asserted liens. 13 However, in corporate mortgage foreclosures the rule is that the trustee, being a party to the suit, represents all the bondholders, and the latter will not be permitted to intervene unless a showing is made that the trustee is not unexceptionable, as, for example, that the trustee has represented or is representing a financial interest in the litigation opposed to that of the bondholders, that he is conspiring with someone to bring about unfair results, or that he is guilty of fraud or is not acting in good faith.14 

Ordinarily, one cannot intervene and be made a party defendant to a suit in personam over the objection of the plaintiff. Thus, upon

In a suit for an accounting, a receiver, and an injunction, an intervention was allowed by one who had advanced money to the defendants and who also sought the reformation of a contract made by them for the sale of certain lands.16

Prior to the 1931 Chancery Act, the rule was that a purchaser pendente lite from a party to the suit could not intervene.17 A purchaser pendente lite who did not claim under a party to the suit might be permitted to intervene.18 Under the 1931 Chancery Act, a purchaser pendente lite claiming a superior title to the plaintiff may, in the discretion of the court, be permitted to intervene even though his interest is acquired from a party to the suit after the filing of a lis pendens. 19 

§ 134. Status of Intervener.-As provided in the 1931 Chancery 

Act, 20 an intervention must be "in subordination to, and in recognition of, the propriety of the main proceeding, unless otherwise ordered by the court in its discretion." He cannot be heard to raise any new issue. § 137.-Appointment and Qualification. The 1931 Chancery 

Act' provides that evidence shall be taken by depositions before or after issue, or before an examiner or master to be appointed, by the court, or orally before the court. Obviously, the statute does not require a reference to a master, for the testimony may be taken before the court or an examiner. But the reference to a master is for the convenience of the court and it is the practice followed in the great majority of chancery cases.2 However, where the questions in issue are matters of mere computation, or of ready ascertainment, that can usually be settled under the supervision of the chancellor without interfering with his public duties, the parties should be saved the expense of a reference. Thus, a reference is not necessary, for example, to ascertain the amount of principal and interest due on a note, or to state an account, where the items are few and not complicated, or to determine what is a reasonable attorney's fee to be allowed in the case.³ 

Masters in chancery may be either general or special. The judges of the circuit court are empowered to appoint in writing, from among the members of the bar in their respective circuits as many general masters in chancery as they may find necessary. A general master continues in office until removed by the court.4 The court may also appoint, for any particular service required by it, from among the members of the bar of the court in active practice, special masters in chancery. Special masters are governed by

Where the court appoints or orders some person to take the testimony in a chancery case it makes no material difference whether that person is designated in the order as a master, examiner, or by any other appropriate name, or whether any official title is given him in the order. The 1931 Chancery Act19 requires an order appointing a general master to be recorded in the chancery order book. Under the former practice it was also held necessary to record an order appointing a special master. The then existing statutes required orders appointing general masters to be recorded, and also provided that special masters should be governed by the provisions of law governing general masters. It was held that, construed together, these two statutory provisions required the recording of orders appointing special masters, that a special master was without authority to perform the functions designated in the order of appointment until the order was recorded, and that testimony taken before him prior to the recording of the order could not be considered as a basis for a final decree.20

In 1927, a statute21 was enacted dispensing with the requirement of recording orders appointing general and special masters and examiners.22 This statute was not specifically repealed by the 1931 

Chancery Act, though that Act readopted the provisions of the earlier statutes requiring orders appointing general masters to be recorded in the chancery order book and making all provisions of law governing general masters applicable to special masters. It would seem, therefore, that the decisions rendered on the statutes in effect prior to the 1927 statute would apply to the 1931 Chancery Act and that orders appointing special masters should be recorded. 

But this construction has not been placed on the 1931 Act and the Supreme Court of Florida has held that the specific provision requiring orders appointing general masters to be recorded, coupled with the absence of such a requirement in regard to orders appointing special masters and examiners, necessitates a construction that the latter orders need not be recorded.23 While this decision overrules the earlier cases on the question, it is based on the sounder reasoning. 

Parties to a suit may waive all provisions relating to the appointment of a master or examiner and submit their case to the court on an agreed statement of facts, or upon evidence taken before some person agreed upon by them, which would in effect be an agreed statement of facts. Where such a waiver appears the parties are bound by a decree based upon the facts so agreed upon or the testimony so taken.24

A party moving for an order of reference cannot, on appeal, complain of an order made in accordance with his motion.25

Under the foregoing statutes, a master has power to speed the cause before him,31 to postpone or continue a hearing,32 or to reopen the case for the taking of further testimony.33 However, a master has no power to do those things which only the chancellor can do. § 139.-Procedure Before Master.-After an order of reference to a master has been entered, a hearing should be had. In regard to the hearing, the 1931 Chancery Act provides: "Whenever any reference of any matter is made to a master to examine and report thereon, the party at whose instance or for whose benefit the reference is made shall cause the same to be presented to the master for a hearing with all reasonable dispatch. If he shall omit to do so, the adverse party shall be at liberty forthwith to cause proceedings to be had before the master, at the cost of the party procuring the reference.' 

As to procedure for setting the case for a hearing, the 1931 

Chancery Act further provides: 

1138 "Upon every such reference, it shall be the duty of the master, as soon as he reasonably can after the same is brought before him, to assign a time and place for proceedings in the same, and to give due notice thereof to each of the parties; and if either party shall fail to appear at the time and place appointed, the master shall be at liberty to proceed ex parte, or, in his discretion, to adjourn the examination and proceedings to a future day, giving notice to the absent party of such adjournment; and it shall be the duty of the master to proceed with all reasonable diligence in every such reference, and with the least practicable delay, and either party shall be at liberty to apply to the court for an order to the master to speed the proceedings and to make his report, and to certify to the court the reason for any delay. 

The evidence in all examinations shall be taken down in writing by the master or by some other person by his authority in his presence and filed with his report.

1140 The statutory requirement of notice of the time and place of the master's hearing is fundamental. In all proceedings where the rights of a party are to be adjudicated, it is necessary that he be given due notice, for it is a maxim of the law that every man is entitled to his day in court. The rule extends to proceedings before a master as well as proceedings before the court. A court might as well proceed to enter judgment in a cause where there has been no service, as for a master to pass upon the rights and interests of a party without due notice to him. It is, therefore, the right of every party in interest to notice and a hearing on the matters referred to the master, and not only is it the duty of the master to see that all parties entitled to notice are duly summoned and to preserve the notices with proof of service, but his report should show these facts.41 Where the findings of a master are challenged on the ground that notice of the hearing was not given, and it appears that this ground of objection is well founded, a decree rendered on the master's findings will be reversed.42 Of course, a party against whom a decree pro confesso has been entered cannot complain that he received no notice of the master's hearing.43

"All affidavits, depositions and documents which have been previously made, read or used in the court upon any proceeding in the cause or matter may be used before the master of the court.' "44

§ 140.-Master's Report.-The report of a master in chancery must contain all of the evidence taken before him.48 form of such reports, the 1931 Chancery Act provides: "In the reports made by the master to the court, no part of any statement of facts, account, charge, affidavit, deposition, examination or answer brought in or used before him shall be stated or recited. When a reference is made to a master to ascertain a fact depending upon testimony, his report should show the basis of his finding so that the court may see the correctness of his conclusions.50 Thus a decree for attorney's fees, predicated upon a master's report containing no testimony as to what was a proper fee under the circumstances of the case, will be set aside.51 And when a reference is made to a master to state a partnership account, his report should state the account in such a manner that the court may see that it is correct. are allowed and which disallowed.

thereon.52 Likewise, where the master in his report simply recapitulates immaterial portions of the testimony, without stating an account, no decree can be based upon his report.53 

On appeal, if the master's report and other matters in the record do not justify the decree, it will be reversed, and the appellate court may examine the master's report in order to ascertain whether any good would be likely to result from sending the case back for further proceedings.54 However, where the testimony taken before the master is lost, so that it cannot be transcribed in the record going to the appellate court, the latter is bound to presume everything in favor of the decree of the lower court and, unless the appellant can show that no case could have existed if the testimony had been present, he cannot prevail.55 

After hearings before the master have been completed, and his report is prepared, the procedure should be in accordance with the following provision of the 1931 Chancery Act: 

"The master, as soon as his report is ready, shall return the same into the clerk's office, and the day of return shall be noted by the clerk in the progress docket. Immediately upon returning his report, the master shall give written notice of the filing thereof to counsel for the respective parties, and file a copy of such notice together with his certificate as to the service upon each counsel and the manner of such service. The parties shall have ten days from the time of the receipt of such notice within which to file exceptions to said report. The said time may be enlarged by the court for good cause shown upon application of either party and said application may be heard by the court ex parte. 

If no exceptions are filed within the said period by either party, the report shall be confirmed by order of the court or in or by the final decree. If exceptions are filed they shall stand for hearing before the court upon reasonable notice by either party."56

Under the English and perhaps the Federal equity practice, a master was required to prepare a draft of his report, and to give notice to the parties that his report was ready, in order that they might attend before him, inspect the report, obtain copies, suggest changes, and file objections thereto, for, under that practice, after

Therefore, notice was required to be given to the parties so that they might have an opportunity to object, and have their objections made of record, before the report was signed and settled and passed beyond the control of the master.

However, while that practice may be proper and unobjectionable in Florida, it is clear that under the 1931 Chancery Act a party may file his exceptions to the master's report within ten days after the receipt of notice that it has been filed in the clerk's office and that he cannot be debarred of this right by any failure of the master to give him notice and an opportunity to object to the report either before the time of its filing or by his own failure to take advantage of such an opportunity if it is offered.57 But, where a party wishes to file exceptions to a master's report on the ground that certain evidence was inadmissible, he must first lay the foundation therefor by making timely objections before the master.58 

However, if the master is not authorized to make findings, objections to testimony on the ground of irrelevancy or immateriality need not be taken down or reported by him. Such testimony may be stricken on motion at or before the final hearing.59 

Where the master's report is filed before the time for taking testimony has expired, a decree entered thereon will not be reversed unless it appears that the complaining party did not have ample opportunity to present his case to the master and did not receive notice of the filing of the master's report. 60 

Notice by the master to the parties of the filing of his report in the clerk's office is absolutely essential.61 It is a fundamental principle of all judicial procedure that in subordinate courts the parties shall have an opportunity to make objections and reserve exceptions for the purposes of a review by an appellate tribunal.

This right is secured in the master's office by a statute requiring him to give notice of the filing of his report, and the master cannot disregard this requirement without having his report set aside or referred back to him by the court with directions to observe the procedure prescribed by the statute. If proper notice of the filing of the master's report is not given, the report should not be confirmed and no decree should be entered upon it without the consent of all the parties expressly or impliedly given.62 

As required by the statute, exceptions to a master's report must be filed within ten days after receipt of notice of the filing of the report, unless further time is granted by the court. Exceptions taken after the entry of an appeal from an order made by the court on the report cannot be heard.63 The exceptions must definitely and specifically point out the findings of fact or rulings of law to which objection is made. However, a stipulation that an order confirming a master's report, to which no exceptions have been filed, shall be set aside on the final hearing, if it is made to appear that there are grounds of exception to the report, may be given effect.64 And the report of a master showing on its face material errors may be inquired into without exceptions.65

The practice of filing a large number of exceptions to a master's report has been emphatically disapproved by the Supreme Court of Florida because it is unfair to the chancellor and casts an enormous and unnecessary burden upon him. In such a case the court is justified in refusing to pass upon any of the exceptions until they have been reduced to a reasonable number.66 Where an exception is filed to a master's report on the ground that the cause was referred to him to take an accounting before the equities of the case were settled, the exceptions, though well taken, will be overruled when the complaining party consented to the order of reference.67

Where the appointment of a master is without the consent of the parties, his report is merely advisory to the court, to be adopted only to the extent that it may accord with the judgment

Such a reference is a submission of the controversy to a judge of the parties' own selection, to be governed in his conduct by the ordinary rules applicable to the administration of justice in tribunals established by law. The master's findings are to be taken as presumptively correct, subject to review when there has been manifest error in the consideration given to the evidence or in the application of the law, but not otherwise. In other words, such findings of fact are entitled to the same weight and effect as the verdict of a jury and they should not be set aside unless they are clearly in conflict with the weight of the evidence upon which they were made.69

It is also a rule of long standing that a master's findings of fact, if approved by the chancellor, will not be disturbed on appeal unless it appears that they are clearly wrong.70 In case of a simple conflict in the testimony, the court cannot direct a finding for one party rather than the other.”¹

In view of the ten day period allowed by law for the filing of exceptions to a master's report, the cause cannot proceed to a final hearing until the ten day period has expired. Of course, the parties may waive the right of exception and the time allowed by law for filing exceptions and proceed accordingly. And such a waiver may be given by a guardian ad litem for infant and unknown defendants.72

Whenever exceptions will lie to a master's report, it must be regularly confirmed before any decree can be entered upon it.73

The provision of the 1931 Chancery Act79 relating to the filing of master's reports and exceptions thereto obviously applies only where the master is reporting upon the performance of judicial functions by him. Where he is no more than an instrumentality of the court in carrying out its decree, as when he sells property at a mortgage foreclosure sale, the procedure prescribed by the foregoing statute does not apply, although all parties should have notice of an application to confirm the report of his actions in such matters.80

The duties of an examiner are limited to taking the testimony of witnesses, after giving notice to the solicitors for the parties to the cause to attend and interrogate them, and to reducing the testimony to writing and returning the same to the clerk's office.91 Objections to testimony, except on the ground of irrelevancy and immateriality, should be taken down and reported by the examiner, but he has, of course, no authority to make rulings thereon.92

The provisions of the 1931 Act for the filing of exceptions to a master's report have no application to examiner's reports.93 Exceptions cannot be filed to an examiner's report and it is therefore unnecessary for it to remain on file in the clerk's office for ten days before further proceedings can be had upon it.94

§ 143.-Time for Taking.-In regard to the time within which testimony in equity causes is to be taken, the 1931 Chancery Act provides: "When any chancery cause shall be at issue and shall not have been set for trial before the court, the court of its own motion or upon application of either party after due notice to the opposite party, shall enter an order fixing the time within which the testimony of the parties shall be taken. After the entry of such an order, the court may, upon good cause shown by either party, enlarge the time; and no testimony taken after such period shall be allowed to be read in evidence at the hearing. All such orders shall be entered by the clerk in the Chancery Order Book. 

In the absence of any order by the court extending or limiting the time otherwise, three months from the time a cause is at issue and no longer shall be allowed for the taking of testimony in any cause, unless the case has been set for trial before the court. The time for taking testimony may be extended by special order of the court in its discretion or by written stipulation of the parties filed in the cause, or by oral stipulation evidenced by the record. "The foregoing limitation of the time for taking testimony shall not apply to a cause proceeding ex parte consequent upon the entry of a decree pro confesso, or to a party against whom a decree pro confesso shall have been entered, but in such cases testimony may be taken at any time."1 

1. C. G. L. Per. Supp. 4921(2); Mc 

Carthy Chan. Act, p. 126, § 46.

§ 143] 309 

TAKING TESTIMONY 

When the court fixes the time within which the testimony of the parties shall be taken, the period of time allowed is wholly within the chancellor's discretion.2 The period of time so fixed begins to run, not from the date appearing on the order, but from the time the order is filed and recorded.3

If the time for taking testimony is not fixed by the court, the three months allowed by the statute begins to run from the time the cause is at issue and, in determining when that time expires, the first day when the cause is at issue is to be excluded from the calculation. The cause is at issue at the expiration of ten days from the filing of the answer, or, if there is a counterclaim, at the expiration of ten days from the filing of the reply to the counterclaim. If, within the ten day period, the answer or reply is attacked by appropriate motion, or if the plaintiff moves for a decree on bill and answer, the cause is not at issue until the points of law so raised have been ruled upon by the court. As a matter of fact, where no motion is filed, the ten day period probably begins to run, not from the time the answer is actually filed, but from the time it is required to be filed."

If, before the cause is at issue, the parties proceed to the taking of testimony without objection, the defect will be deemed to have been waived. Contrary to the rule under the former practice,7 the 1931 Chancery Act imposes no limitation on the time for taking testimony as against a party who has suffered a decree pro confesso to be entered against him.

The matter of extending the time for the taking of testimony is within the sound judicial discretion of the chancellor, and ordinarily his determination of the question will not be disturbed by the appellate court. Yet the chancellor's ruling on this question is reviewable on appeal and, where it is plainly made to appear that there has been an abuse of discretion, it is the duty of the

The 1931 Chancery Act, it will be noted, also provides that the time for taking testimony may be extended "by written stipulation of the parties filed in the cause, or by oral stipulation evidenced by the record." Where such a stipulation has been made, and testimony taken within the extended time, neither party should be permitted to repudiate the stipulation or suppress the testimony, 21 and the court should likewise be bound by it.22 The making of such stipulations should be encouraged rather than discouraged as they facilitate the progress of causes and save the time of the court.23 And where a party consents to the appointment of an examiner after the time for taking testimony has expired, he will be held to have waived any defect in the testimony by reason of its having been taken too late.24 A final decree based on testimony taken after the expiration of the time allowed by law or by the court is erroneous but not void.25

Of course, the court may, of its own motion, remand the cause for the taking of further testimony. Where the testimony submitted to a chancellor is, on some material point, insufficient to authorize a just decree in the cause, and it clearly appears from the record that sufficient testimony does exist to authorize a decree, the cause should be re-opened with directions to take further testimony on that point.26 Likewise, where the chancellor, upon examination of the pleadings and the evidence, concludes that the transaction out of which the litigation grew was subsidiary to and dependent upon another transaction, and he desires to be more fully informed of all the details of both transactions, he may remand the cause for such proceedings as will fully advise him.27

Where, through inadvertence or negligence, the plaintiff has omitted to prove some fact which is necessary to support his case, the court will sometimes give him liberty to supply the defect by proving the fact at the hearing. This permission is, however, cautiously granted. It would be dangerous practice to permit every party, whose case broke down at the hearing, to go into further evidence. The practice is usually confined to cases of proof by documentary evidence, or to proof of the execution of deeds and other papers where the attending dangers are not great.29 After a decree pro confesso has been entered, the chancellor may himself hear such evidence as is necessary to determine the amount due on a mortgage, the amounts advanced by the plaintiff for taxes, and the reasonableness of an attorney's fee.3 30 While the parties have, in the absence of an order to the contrary, three months after the cause is at issue within which to take testimony, that right is not absolute. § 144.-How Taken.-The 1931 Chancery Act34 provides that 

"evidence shall be taken by depositions before or after issue, as provided by law or rules of court for actions at law or suits in chancery, or before an examiner or master to be appointed by the court, or orally before the court." Evidence must be taken by one of the methods prescribed by the statute. It should not be pleaded either in the bill of complaint,35 or in the answer,36 and even a verified answer is not evidence for the defendant.3 37 The usual procedure in chancery cases is to take the testimony before a master or examiner, though there is no rule or statute requiring it. Such a reference is made solely for the convenience of the court.38 Where testimony is to be taken before a master or examiner, his appointment is jurisdictional and testimony taken before him prior to his appointment is without authority of law and is not entitled to consideration by the court as a basis for a final decree.39 Testimony taken before a master or examiner prior to his appointment cannot be validated by an order of appointment nunc pro tunc.40 But the parties to a cause may waive the appointment of a master and take their testimony before some person agreed upon between them, in which case the testimony will be considered as an agreed statement of facts.41 

It is irregular and improper to appoint a master or examiner for the purpose of taking testimony before all the issues in the cause are made up.42 It is likewise improper to appoint such an officer after the time for taking testimony has expired. But the defect in either case will be considered as waived where the complaining party proceeds with the taking of testimony without objections.43

When an order is entered to that effect, testimony may be taken in open court before the chancellor. However, as previously noted, the question of whether the chancellor will hear the evidence himself or refer the cause to a master or examiner is one of his convenience. In equity, parties do not have and never did have the right to a trial by jury.44 The chancellor may, where the evidence is particularly conflicting direct an issue out of chancery to be tried by a jury. But an issue out of chancery is usually at the suggestion of the chancellor himself. It is intended to aid him in arriving at a satisfactory conclusion in regard to a particular fact. It is not a matter of right and the verdict of the jury is not binding upon the chancellor.45

A chancery cause may also, under the Florida Constitution and statutes, be tried before a referee.46 In such cases, the referee acts in the place and stead of the circuit judge and testimony taken before him is equivalent to testimony taken before the court. A chancery case may not be tried before a judge ad litem.47

After a master has been duly appointed, the cause should be brought on for hearing before him with all reasonable dispatch. 

The primary duty of setting the case for hearing before the master is upon the party for whose benefit the reference is made, but if he does not cause proceedings to be had before the master the adverse party may do so, at the cost of the party procuring the reference.48 

The master must assign a time and place for the hearing and give due notice thereof to all parties. If either party fails to appear, the master may proceed ex parte or adjourn the proceedings to a future day, giving notice of the adjournment to the absent party. 

The master should proceed with the least practicable delay in every reference and either party may apply to the court for an order to the master to speed the proceedings before him.49 Testimony taken at a hearing of which one of the parties had no notice cannot

Testimony before a master or examiner must be taken orally, and it must also, unless the court otherwise directs, be reduced to writing by the master or examiner, or by some other person by his authority and in his presence, and filed with his report.53 The purpose of the latter provision is to enable the chancellor to determine the correctness of the master's findings.54 There is no requirement in the 1931 Chancery Act that the testimony taken before a master or examiner be subscribed by the witnesses. The presence in the Act of an express requirement to that effect where testimony is taken by deposition55 indicates with reasonable certainty that there is no such requirement where testimony is taken before a master or examiner.

When testimony is taken before the court it is, of course, also taken orally, but it must, on motion of either party, or by order of the court, be reduced to writing and filed in the cause.56 However, the failure to reduce the testimony to writing, even when that is required, does not render a decree based thereon void.57 

When deemed necessary by the court or officer taking testimony, a stenographer may be designated to take down testimony in shorthand and, if required, transcribe the same. The stenographer's fee is to be fixed by the court and ultimately taxed as costs.58

The testimony submitted to a master, examiner, or the court may consist of the oral statements of witnesses, depositions, and the answers to interrogatories. In interlocutory matters the court may also accept affidavits.59 All parties accounting before a master must bring in their respective accounts in the form of debtor and creditor, and any of the other parties who are not satisfied with the account so brought in may examine the accounting party orally, or upon interrogatories, or by depositions, as the master may direct.60 

§ 145.-Agreed Statement of Facts.-Parties to a suit may waive the provisions of law in regard to the taking of testimony and submit their case to the court on an agreed statement of facts.61 

A distinction exists between a case which is agreed to be decided by the court on an agreed statement of facts after the issues are made up, and a case where the only office served by an agreed statement of facts is that of a substitute for testimony. Undoubtedly, when a case is submitted to the court on an agreed statement of facts, all questions of the sufficiency of the pleadings and their legal effect are waived and the want of an answer becomes immaterial and no findings of fact are necessary to a review. But when an agreed statement of facts is entered into merely as a substitute for the taking of testimony, and the case is submitted for decision, not on the agreed statement of facts, but on the pleadings and the agreed statement of facts, the effect of omissions and admissions in the pleadings is not disturbed by what may be contained in the agreed statement of facts, and the court is warranted in giving the pleadings their ordinary effect in determining the equities, notwithstanding what may be contained in the stipulation of facts filed in lieu of testimony.62

An agreement between parties to a suit in equity to submit the case to the court on the bill and answer and affidavits attached to the agreement will be construed as an agreement to consider the affidavits as evidence in the case.63

§ 146.-Witnesses and Their Examination.-In regard to the sum moning of witnesses to appear and testify before a master or examiner, the 1931 Chancery Act provides: "Witnesses who live within the State, and whose testimony may be taken out of court, may be summoned to appear before a commissioner appointed to take testimony, or before a master or examiner appointed in any cause, by subpoena in the usual form, which may be issued by the clerk in blank and filled up by the party praying the same, or by the commissioner, master or examiner, requiring the attendance of witnesses at the time and place specified, who shall be allowed for attendance the same compensation as for attendance in court; and if any witnesses shall refuse to appear to be sworn or give evidence it shall be deemed a contempt of the court, which being certified to the clerk's office by the commissioner, master or examiner, an attachment may issue thereupon by order of the court, in the same manner as if the contempt were for not attending, or for refusing to give testimony. Witnesses may be summoned to appear and testify before the court by subpoena as in cases at common law.' 

Under the 1931 Chancery Act a master also has full authority to examine the parties in the cause, upon oath, touching all matters contained in the reference, to require the production of all books, papers, writings, vouchers, and other documents applicable thereto, and to examine on oath, orally, or by deposition or otherwise, all witnesses produced by the parties before him.65 Process issued by a master should be directed to all and singular the sheriffs or any constables in the state of Florida.66 ."64 

The foregoing statutes do not authorize a master to issue a subpoena duces tecum to a party to a cause, as the subject of discovery, interrogatories, and inspection and production of documents in chancery causes, as applied to the parties themselves, is controlled by other specific provisions of the 1931 Chancery Act.

§ 147.-Admissibility of and Objections to Evidence. It is an es tablished principle of chancery practice, and of pleading and practice generally, that the allegata and probata must correspond. However full and convincing may be the proof of an essential fact, unless the fact is averred, proof alone is insufficient. All evidence offered in a case should correspond with the allegations of the pleadings and be confined to the issues so made.71 The court is confined, in its consideration of evidence, to proof of facts alleged in the pleadings, and evidence offered in proof of other facts is inadmissible.72 The requirement that the cause of action or affirmative defense must be stated as it actually is, and that the proofs must be confined to and establish it as stated, is involved in the very theory of pleading. A litigant has a right to rely upon his adversary's pleading as indicating the case he is to meet. Otherwise, pleadings

The plaintiff cannot have the benefit of facts not charged in his bill even though such facts may be proved by the testimony.74 Relief cannot be based upon facts proved but not alleged.75 Thus, where plaintiff prays for a decree adjudging that the defendant is indebted to him in a certain sum, and that a lien be enforced against certain property in default of payment, he cannot have a decree for a larger sum than that claimed in his bill.76 

However, proof of a fact not specifically alleged, but embraced substantially within the case made by the bill and answer, is admissible. The mode and method by which a fact is to be proved need not be alleged.77 And the chancellor has authority to permit amendments to pleadings in furtherance of justice when it appears from the evidence that the plaintiff has a case which is not brought fairly within the issues.78 Of course, where all the allegations of a bill upon which relief is predicated are expressly admitted, no proof is necessary to sustain the bill.79

The rules of evidence are the same in suits in equity as in actions at law.80 Thus a party cannot, either in law or equity, vary or contradict the terms of an unambiguous written contract by showing that, even though he signed the contract, it was with the oral understanding that he was not to be bound by its terms.81 And in a suit in equity against the representative of a deceased person, the plaintiff is not a competent witness to testify as to any transaction or communication between himself and the deceased person. 82 In equity as well as at law, a well connected train of circumstances is as conclusive of the existence of a fact as the greatest array of positive testimony. Testimony merely conjectural is wholly inconclusive and will not be received in equity suits.84

But, courts of equity do not restrict themselves by the same rigid rules as do courts of law in the investigation of fraud and in the evidence and proofs required to establish fraud. It is equally a rule in courts of law and courts of equity that fraud is not to be presumed but must be established by proof. Circumstances of mere suspicion, leading to no certain results, will not, in either of these courts, be deemed a sufficient ground to establish fraud. On the other hand, neither court insists upon positive and express proofs of fraud. Each deduces such proof from circumstances affording strong presumptions. But courts of equity will act upon circumstances, as presumptious of fraud, in cases where courts of law will not deem them satisfactory proof.85 And, where relevant testimony is offered which will assist in knowing which party speaks the truth upon the issues of a suit in equity, it is admissible when to admit it does not override other formal rules of evidence.86 

Where a written instrument offered in evidence in equity contains enough to sustain the substance of a material allegation of the bill, the instrument is admissible to sustain the allegation even though it varies on its face in immaterial particulars from the description given in the bill.87

§ 148.-Burden of Proof.-The general rule is that the substance of the case, as made by the pleadings, must be proved. In considering the question of what matters are to be proved in a cause the first point to be ascertained is upon whom the burden of proof lies. As a general proposition, it may be said that the point in issue is to be proved by the party who asserts the affirmative, 106

Accordingly, the burden is on the plaintiff to make clear proof of his case,107 and he must prove every material allegation of his bill, which is not admitted in the answer, by a preponderance of the evidence.108 Thus, where the answer of the defendant sets up a failure of consideration for the obligation sued upon, the burden of proving a consideration is on the plaintiff in the bill. 109 

Where a bill alleges that the plaintiff is seised and possessed of certain land, and the answer denies this allegation, the burden is on the plaintiff to prove seisin and possession. 110 An answer denying the existence of the relation in which the defendants are sued casts upon the plaintiff the burden of proving the relationship."11 

An answer denying that certain liens were allowed against the purchase price of land puts the burden of proving these facts on the plaintiff.112

In general, it may be taken for granted that, whenever a prima facie right is proved, the burden of proof is always on the person calling the right in question. Thus when a defendant asserts a purchase for a valuable consideration without notice of plaintiff's claim, the fact of the defendant having had notice must be proved by the plaintiff.114

Facts alleged in the bill and admitted by the answer require no proof.115 Consequently, when an answer in chancery admits the truth of certain allegations of the bill, the facts so alleged and admitted are not in issue, and the plaintiff is entitled to a decree on those allegations though he produces no proof of them and even though the defendant has produced evidence tending to show that they are untrue. 116 The rule in chancery is that whatever is well pleaded and not denied is admitted.117 The 1931 Chancery Act118 provides that averments in the bill, other than of value or amount of damage, if not denied, are considered as admitted. An answer which does not deny an allegation of the bill, or state that the defendant is without knowledge of the fact alleged, is construed as admitting it.119

While a motion to dismiss admits the allegations of a bill, this is only for the purpose of testing its legal sufficiency and of itself has no effect upon the proof required to sustain the bill.120

Accordingly, when an answer in equity sets up an affirmative defense, the burden of establishing it is on the defendant.130 Thus the burden of proving an answer pleading payment or partial payment is on the defendant. 131 The defense of res judicata must

§ 149.-Depositions De Bene Esse.-One of the methods of tak ing testimony in an equity suit authorized by the 1931 Chancery Act is by deposition de bene esse. Such depositions may be taken before or after issue as provided by law or rules of court for actions at law or suits in chancery.137 

The 1931 Chancery Act provides one method of taking depositions de bene esse. The method is substantially the same as that prescribed by the Federal statutes and equity rules.138 

It is "The testimony of any witness may be taken by deposition de bene esse, either within or without the United States, when the witness resides out of the county in which the cause is pending, or is bound on a voyage to sea, or is about to leave the state of Florida, or to go out of the county in which the cause is pending before the time of trial or final hearing, or when he is old or infirm. The deposition may be taken before any notary public or judicial officer or before any officer authorized by the statutes of the state of Florida to take acknowledgments of proof of execution of deeds. The officer before whom such deposition shall be taken shall not be of counsel or solicitor to either of the parties or interested in the event of the cause. The statute thus confers upon either party to a cause the absolute right, upon mere notice in the manner prescribed, to take the deposition of a witness where one of the prescribed situations exists. No leave of court is required.140 No opportunity is given the adverse party to be heard upon the matter of selecting the officer before whom the deposition is to be taken. The responsibility for selecting an officer in accordance with the requirements of the statute rests entirely upon the party taking the deposition.141 

Probably, however, where the opposite party wishes to contest the right to take a deposition, he may do so by an application to vacate the notice instead of waiting until the deposition has been taken and then moving to suppress it.142

The statute merely requires that the notice be reasonable. What constitutes reasonable notice depends entirely upon the facts of each case.

After a deposition has been duly taken, the procedure prescribed by the 1931 Chancery Act is as follows: 

"Every such deposition, together with a certificate of the reasons aforesaid of taking such deposition and the notice, if any, given to the adverse party, shall be by such officer sealed up and directed to such court and shall remain under his seal until opened by the judge or the clerk of such court or by consent of the parties. The mere taking of a deposition and filing it among the papers in a cause does not make it a part of the record so that the master or the court before whom the case is being tried must take judicial notice of it. Depositions are only instruments of evidence. If the party who has taken a deposition desires the benefit of it, he must offer it in evidence. If not offered in evidence, it is not a part of the record before the lower court or on appeal.155 However, the court cannot order a party to file in evidence a deposition taken by him any more than it can order him to examine a witness whom he has brought into court by subpoena. The adverse party may offer such a deposition in evidence, but he cannot compel the other party to do so.156 A deposition is deemed published when filed unless otherwise ordered by the court. 157 

The provisions of the 1931 Chancery Act in regard to the taking of depositions do not modify or repeal any other law or rule of court providing other methods of taking depositions, but the method therein prescribed is merely an additional and optional method of taking depositions in equity cases. 158 Depositions upon a commission,159 and depositions in rei perpetuam, 160 may be taken under other statutes of the state of Florida.161

Statutes governing the taking of depositions must be substantially complied with and no material deviation therefrom will be allowed except by agreement or waiver of the parties.162

The requirement of a motion, with notice to the adverse party, implies that facts must be shown at the hearing thereon which establish that the books, records, or papers sought to be required to be produced either contain evidence pertinent to the cause of action or defense or that the movant has reasonable grounds for believing that they contain such evidence. The statutory procedure is merely a substitute for obtaining discovery that could formerly be realized only under a formal prayer therefor. 166

The foregoing statute is substantially the same as one of the Federal equity rules and it should probably be construed and applied in the same general way as the Federal rule. 187 

The distinction between discovery incident to a bill for equitable relief and a pure bill of discovery is elementary and is not affected by the statute. In the former case discovery is sought in aid of specific relief prayed in the bill. In the latter case, the sole object of the suit is to obtain discovery in order to protect or preserve some legal right of the plaintiff. In such a suit there is ordinarily no proceeding beyond the answer by which the discovery is obtained. The case is never brought to a hearing and there is no decree on the matters set forth in the bill.188 The foregoing provisions of the 1931 Chancery Act in regard to interrogatories did not abolish bills of discovery.189 

The purpose of the statutory provision for interrogatories was undoubtedly to enable the court to make a summary disposition of

In view of this purpose, it cannot be successfully contended that discovery by means of interrogatories is limited to facts within the exclusive knowledge of the adverse party and will not be permitted if the facts can be otherwise procured. A party should not be put to unnecessary labor or difficulty in making out his case and he is entitled to admissions, if he can get them, so as to render it unnecessary to produce other evidence.191 

At the same time, an undue burden should not be placed upon the adverse party in requiring him to make discovery.192 Ordinarily, however, this is not a good objection to answering an interrogatory unless the burden upon the party interrogated would more than offset the benefits from the discovery accruing to the court and counsel at the trial.193

The question also arises, in the construction of the foregoing provisions of the 1931 Chancery Act, as to whether interrogatories may be maintained where they seek the discovery of facts which relate exclusively to the case of the interrogated party. Although the decisions construing the analogous Federal equity rule are divided on this question, 194 the more probable construction of the Florida statute is that discovery of such facts may not be obtained by interrogatories.

The Supreme Court of Florida has held, with reference to the 1931 Chancery Act, that statutes authorizing interrogatories in equity cases before trial are usually construed as providing a substitute for the discovery in equity which has always been permitted under accepted equity practice. It was a fundamental of equity practice that discovery could not be obtained where the facts sought 195

There are several provisions in the 1931 Chancery Act itself which support the restrictive construction. The fact that the plaintiff is given the right to file interrogatories at any time after his bill is filed, although the answer may not yet have been filed, indicates that the interrogatories can relate only to his own cause of action. Then too, the defendant is given no right to file interrogatories until after his answer has been filed, thus indicating that the discovery to which he is entitled is to relate only to the defense set up in the answer and not to the plaintiff's cause of action. Interrogatories by the defendant as to the plaintiff's case might have been filed before the answer, if such a right had been contemplated by the rule. 198 While it may also be contended that the provision giving the plaintiff twenty-one days after issue in which to file interrogatories indicates that he may inquire concerning the defense, 199 the terms of the statute, on the whole, give more support to the restrictive than to the liberal construction. 

The provisions of the 1931 Chancery Act200 in regard to the compulsory production of books, records, and other documents also support the restrictive construction. Such production can be compelled only when the papers sought to be obtained contain evidence pertinent to the cause of action or defense of the movant. 

There is no apparent reason for restricting the compulsory production of books and documents to cases where they support the case of the movant, and permitting interrogatories, not only as to facts pertaining to the movant's case, but also to those pertaining to the case of the adverse party. If the statute was intended to permit interrogatories as to the opponent's case exclusively, it probably

However, even under the restrictive construction, the right to discovery as to matters material to the cause of action or defense of the interrogating party is not defeated by the fact that such matters also involve the ground of defense or cause of action of the interrogated party.201 But it is doubtful if a party having the negative may obtain discovery.202

It is reasonably clear that interrogatories may be used to obtain the discovery of evidentiary facts.203 The Supreme Court of Florida has held that, under the 1931 Chancery Act, the production of books and records may be compelled so that the plaintiff may obtain proof of how and when the wrong complained of in his bill was committed.204 In view of this decision it would seem that interrogatories could be used for the same purpose. If the restrictive construction of the statute is adopted, it necessarily follows that interrogatories cannot be used to obtain the evidence of the adverse party or the names of his witnesses.205 

In addition to the limitations upon interrogatories already noted, they are also subject to the same restrictions to which discovery was subject under long established chancery practice.206 Thus interrogatories are not maintainable when they are of a mere "fishing" character, are not reasonably relevant to the issue, are unnecessary or useless, seek to establish a forfeiture strictly so called, seek to contradict a written instrument, or seek the disclosure of privileged information. But interrogatories may be maintained even though they expose other persons to actions, expose the interrogated party to penalties, seek secondary evidence of lost documents, inquire into confidential communications that the party interrogated would not be privileged from disclosing on oral examination, seek to disprove the bona fides of a prima facie defense, 201. An interrogatory filed under the 1931 Chancery Act should embrace a single question and be so framed that it may be clearly seen what the interrogated party is called upon to answer. If this is not done, the court may, in its discretion, direct that the interrogatory not be answered. It is not justified in ordering a party to answer interrogatories not clearly framed and compelling him to assume the burden of being in contempt if he fails to answer fully.208

The provision that each interrogatory shall be answered separately forbids the making of one answer a response to more than one interrogatory. But it does not forbid several persons to whom an interrogatory is propounded from joining in the making of one separate answer thereto. The provision does not require the duplication or multiplication of answers when the parties interrogated desire to make the same answer.209

In regard to interrogatories to corporations, the 1931 Chancery Act provides: "If any party to the cause is a public or private corporation the interrogatories may be addressed to the corporation alone, and in such case the answers shall be made on the oath of an officer or agent of the corporation having personal knowledge, if any there be; or any opposite party may apply to the court for an order allowing him to file interrogatories to be answered by any officer of the corporation, designated either by name or his office, and an order may be made accordingly for the examination of such officer as may appear to be proper upon such interrogatories as the court may think fit."210 

Under this provision, it is obvious that interrogatories addressed to a corporation may be filed as a matter of right. A corporation cannot refuse to answer interrogatories on the ground that the answers might incriminate it, or, if a bank, that its records are privileged.211 An officer of a corporation must answer interrog-

166. Costs. § 153.-Definition and Kinds of Decrees.-A decree is a judgment of a court of equity. All decrees are either interlocutory or final.2 

An interlocutory decree is one which is rendered in the middle of a cause, upon a motion, answer, default, or other proceeding which is only intermediate, and which does not finally determine or complete the suit.³ Decrees containing rulings on the pleadings which contemplate further proceedings are interlocutory. A decree directing a reference to a master for the purpose of ascertaining any material fact in the case is interlocutory because questions are reserved until the filing of the master's report. The report may be excepted to and disapproved or confirmed and made absolute by order of the court. This being the case, it follows that there must be a final decree upon the report and that the order of reference is only interlocutory.4 Consequently, a decree directing an accounting or declaring the existence of a lien is interlocu-
