A decree adjudicating the rights and interests of the respective parties in a partition suit, ordering a partition, and appointing commissioners to make a partition, is an interlocutory decree.7

A final decree is one which disposes of every question involved in the case, leaves nothing open for future decision, and contemplates no further action in the cause other than the enforcement of the decree. A decree which does not dispose of the whole matter in controversy between the parties is not final. When a decree decides the right to property in controversy and directs that it be delivered up by the defendant to the plaintiff, or directs that it be sold, or directs the defendant to pay a certain sum of money to the plaintiff, and the plaintiff is entitled to have the decree carried immediately into execution, it must be regarded as final even though the bill is retained for the purpose of adjusting by further decree the accounts between the parties.10 Thus a decree determining litigation between creditors and an administrator as to the possession of a certain fund is final notwithstanding that distribution of the fund among the creditors was thereafter to be made.¹¹ 

A decree ordering a sale of property in a partition suit, the relative interests of the parties having been previously determined, is final. 12

Occasionally decrees, both interlocutory and final, are entered by the consent of the parties to the cause. Such decrees, not being the result of judicial action, cannot be set aside upon a rehearing, an appeal, or other similar action. Decrees so entered may be set aside only by the consent of the parties thereto.14 

§ 154.-Final Hearing.-Prior to the 1931 Chancery Act, a 

Florida equity rule required that a cause be set down for final hearing by an entry to that effect in the chancery order book. Another rule provided that, after the cause had been so set down, either party might, upon notice to the adverse party, have the cause heard upon a day to be named in the notice.15 

By order promulgated after the enactment of the 1931 Chancery Act, the Supreme Court of Florida revoked and annulled all equity rules inconsistent or in conflict with the 1931 Act.16 There is no apparent conflict between the equity rules above mentioned and the 1931 Chancery Act and it seems probable that these rules are still in effect. This seems to have been assumed in at least one decision of the Supreme Court rendered under the 1931 Act. 17 

However, the requirement that a cause be set down for final hearing by an entry in the chancery order book seems to be a technical rather than a substantial requirement. The mere failure to comply with it does not necessarily result in injury to the adverse party or require the final decree to be reversed on appeal. Where the complaining party accepts notice and is present at the final hearing, and objects to the entry of a decree only on the ground that the cause has not been set down by an entry in the order book, it is not error for the court to overrule the objection and enter a final decree. It will be assumed, in the absence of a contrary showing, that the failure to make the entry was not harmful to the opposite party.18 Likewise, where the complaining party is present at the final hearing and argues the cause on its merits, he cannot successfully assign as error the failure to set the cause down for final hearing.19 And on appeal, where the record is silent

However, the requirement that all parties shall have notice of the final hearing is fundamental and required by the simplest principles of justice. A final decree rendered without notice to the adverse party will be reversed.21 

But the requirement of notice may be waived. Thus where a defendant is present at the final hearing and argues the case on its merits he cannot successfully assign as error the failure of the plaintiff to give notice of the hearing.22 And, if the notice is sufficient to procure the presence of opposing counsel at the hearing, and he argues the merits, it is immaterial how the notice was served.23 

When the pleadings and the evidence in a chancery case are submitted to the chancellor the case is then before him for disposition and he may exercise his own pleasure and discretion as to whether he will hear argument from counsel on the merits of the case. If the chancellor feels that no good purpose would be served and no different result accomplished by indulging counsel in their desire to be heard in the matter, he is within his legal rights to so hold and to enter such a decree as appears to him justified by the pleadings and the evidence.24 § 155.-Requisites of Valid Decree.-For a decree in equity to be valid it must be shown by the record that the court had jurisdiction of the subject matter and of the parties to the suit.25 When it is said that a court has jurisdiction of the subject matter and the parties to a cause this implies, generally speaking, that the court

When a court does not have jurisdiction of the subject matter and of the parties affected by its judgment or decree, the adjudication is void and subject to collateral attack. But, if the court has jurisdiction of the subject matter and the parties, the adjudication is binding, even though erroneous, unless it is reversed or modified by direct appellate proceedings. Where the court has jurisdiction of the subject matter and of some of the parties, the adjudication may be binding on the parties over whom the court has acquired jurisdiction by the proper service of process or by appearance, and not binding as to other persons over whom the court has acquired no jurisdiction. In proceedings in rem, where proper notice is given, the adjudication is in general binding on all the world where the court has jurisdiction of the subject matter and the rem.27 

In regard to jurisdiction over the subject matter, the term jurisdiction in its general sense should be distinguished from what is usually referred to as equity jurisdiction. Jurisdiction is the power or authority to hear and determine a cause. Equity jurisdiction is the power to hear and determine certain classes of civil cases according to certain methods of procedure and certain principles of jurisprudence. If a court, such as a Florida circuit court, having general jurisdiction of actions at law and suits in equity, should hear and decide, according to equitable methods, a case which was properly cognizable at law, the judgment, though it would be subject to reversal, would not be void. Whether relief should be sought in equity or at law does not involve the power to enter a judgment. The question is one of procedure unless the right to a jury trial is unlawfully denied.28 Thus, where an equity court predicates the existence of a lien upon an instrument which has no

In regard to jurisdiction over the parties, both the Florida and Federal Constitutions provide that no person shall be deprived of property without due process of law, and this requires that every defendant be given notice and an opportunity to be heard in every suit brought against him. Accordingly, jurisdiction of the defendant is predicated upon the giving of notice and an opportunity to be heard, and is obtained by the service of process, either actual or constructive, or by the defendant's voluntary appearance. The plaintiff consents to the jurisdiction of the court over his person by filing his suit. If jurisdiction of the parties is not obtained, the decree is void and may be set aside on appeal or by collateral attack.31 But the mere failure to enter a decree pro confesso against a defendant who has been properly served with process will not render void a final decree thereafter entered.32

Another requirement of a valid decree in equity is that it be entered by a duly qualified judicial officer. The proper officer to enter a decree is, of course, the circuit judge of the circuit wherein the suit is brought.48 However, this circuit judge may be disqualified by reason of his being related to a party to the cause or his attorney, or of his being a material witness to or interested in the result of the cause. In such a case, he should enter an order disqualifying himself and upon receipt of a copy of this order the Governor of the state must designate another judge to hear the cause. But, if a temporary injunction is sought in the cause, an application therefor may be made to any other circuit judge without waiting for the Governor's designation of a judge to hear the cause.

An order by which a judge disqualifies himself is not appealable or subject to collateral attack. If the judge refuses to disqualify himself upon a suggestion thereof duly filed, his order is appealable but not subject to collateral attack. But orders entered by a judge in a cause in which he is a party are absolutely void.49 

A circuit judge may also become disqualified because of bias or prejudice and in this event a successor may be designated in the same manner as where he is disqualified for other reasons.50 In case of inability of a circuit judge to discharge the duties of his office, any other circuit judge may, on the application of either party, act in the cause.51

Under the Florida Constitution a valid decree in a chancery cause cannot be rendered by a judge ad litem nor can a person appointed as a judge ad litem be considered a referee. It seems clear that a chancery cause may be tried before a referee appointed under the Constitution and statutes of Florida and that a valid final decree may be entered by him.52 § 156.-Form of Decree. In regard to the form of a decree in equity, the 1931 Chancery Act provides: 

"In drawing up decrees and orders, neither the bill, nor answer, nor other pleadings, nor any part thereof, nor the report of any master, nor any other prior proceeding, nor any finding of law or fact need be recited or stated in the decree or order; but the decree and order shall begin, in substance, as follows: 'This cause came on to be heard (or to be further heard, as the case may be), and was argued by counsel; and thereupon, upon consideration thereof, it was ordered, adjudged and decreed as follows, viz:' (Here insert the decree or order).' 1153 A final decree in a chancery cause should be clear and definite in its terms and certain as to those protected by it.54 Though its scope is limited to the relief sought in the bill of complaint and matters appurtenant thereto, it is not necessarily limited as to its form by the language of the prayer. Thus in a suit to quiet title, though the prayer for relief is general in its terms, the final decree may describe the clouds and other defects decreed against with as much particularity and detail as the chancellor considers necessary or desirable.55 In order that the relief may be adapted to the circumstances of particular cases, the court has a broad discretion in forming its decrees.56

The above quoted section of the 1931 Chancery Act expressly provides that the chancellor need not incorporate findings of fact or law in a final decree. And it is not reversible error for the court to deny a motion that findings be incorporated in the decree.57

When a court makes two decrees upon the same matter in a pending cause, a number of days apart, it is the better practice, when the second one is made, to refer to the first one and state in what particulars the later decree is intended to modify, supplement, or supersede the first decree. However, this is not essential.59 § 157.-Rendition and Entry.-A court of equity will not make as many final decrees in a cause as there are defendants, but it will usually insist that one decree dispose of the rights of all parties.60 

Consequently the court will not proceed to a final decree before all parties, necessary or proper, have been brought into court and the issues made up, or decrees pro confesso entered against such defendants, or the cause dismissed as to unnecessary parties. In any event, before proceeding to a final decree, the court should strike or dismiss as to all unnecessary parties made defendant, and this should be done whether such parties have been served with process or not.61 

Of course, where the final decree dismisses the bill of complaint, there is no prejudicial error in not previously dismissing absent defendants.62

Since no court can adjudicate upon the rights of persons without having them actually or constructively before it, a court of equity will not proceed to enter a final decree in a cause in the absence of indispensable parties defendant. Being indispensable parties, a decree would necessarily affect their rights, and this will not and cannot be done in their absence. Therefore, where it appears on final hearing that necessary parties defendant are not before the

It is provided by statute that the circuit courts, sitting in chancery, shall always be kept open for making, hearing, and deciding motions, presenting, arguing, and deciding upon petitions, granting injunctions, and passing interlocutory and final decrees and orders. Any action of a circuit court in such matters in vacation has the same force and effect as if done in term time.65 In other words, decrees in equity are rendered in chambers and there are no sessions of court except in the broad sense that courts of equity are always open.66

A final decree should not ordinarily be entered until the time allowed by law for taking testimony has expired. An order or decree may be considered as having been rendered. when the chancellor pronounces in open court that which determines the issues in the suit even though a final decree is not then entered in the sense that an execution or appeal may be based thereon.76 

The formalities attending the entry and enrollment of a final decree under the practice of the English High Court of Chancery do not obtain in Florida. When a decree is pronounced by the chancellor a draft is usually prepared by the solicitor for the prevailing party. 

This draft is examined by the chancellor and, if found by him to be correct, he signs it. The document is then delivered to the clerk who records it in the chancery order book.77 

It is provided by statute that decrees may be signed when pronounced, and may be recorded at once.78 It is also provided by statute that all decrees shall be recorded in the chancery order book of the court without any other enrollment and that no process shall be issued or other proceedings had on any final decree or order until it is so signed and recorded.79 The statutory requirements of

The failure to record an order will render erroneous any proceedings had upon it notwithstanding that the order has been signed by the chancellor.82 Thus an order granting a writ of assistance to enforce an unrecorded decree is subject to reversal on appeal.83 

And, before the enactment of the statute providing that orders appointing special masters need not be recorded, a final decree of divorce was reversed because the testimony was taken before a master prior to recording of the order appointing him.84 

However, where an order has been signed by the chancellor and actually filed in the clerk's office, proceedings had upon it are not void and subject to collateral attack. Thus a master's sale under an unrecorded final decree of foreclosure is not subject to collateral attack where it is shown that the decree was signed and filed in the clerk's office.85 Likewise, a sale of real estate by the guardian of an insane person cannot be set aside on collateral attack because of the clerk's failure to record an order appointing the guardian which was actually filed with him.86

But where the order or decree, though signed by the chancellor, is never filed in the clerk's office for recordation, the decree and all subsequent proceedings upon it are void. In such a case, the failure to record is not a mere clerical misprision. The person obtaining the order may have withheld it from the files for some purpose of his own, or through carelessness may have misplaced it and never presented it for filing and record. The document never became a court record and proceedings upon it are void and subject to collateral attack.88

For the purposes of the foregoing rule, an order or decree is considered in law as filed when it is delivered to the clerk of the court and received by him to be kept in his official custody. The usual file marks are but one evidence of filing.89 The clerk is not authorized to receive papers for filing at his personal residence and a paper received there is not considered as filed until he takes it to the place at the court house assigned for its official custody.90 

An order or decree may, under some circumstances, be rendered and recorded nunc pro tunc. For example, where a delay in rendering a decree after the hearing or submission of a cause is necessary for the convenience of the court, or results from the press of other business or the intricacy of the questions involved, or is due to any other reason not attributable to the laches of the parties, a decree may be entered retrospectively as of the time when it should or might have been entered.91 And where, after the submission of a cause, a party dies, a revivor may be obviated by entering a decree nunc pro tunc as of the date of the hearing.92

A court of chancery has authority to make all appropriate orders for the enforcement of its decrees. Where it sets aside a conveyance of property as fraudulent, it may appoint a receiver for the land and the proceeds arising from payments on mortgages and contracts.128

A court of equity, having full jurisdiction over the enforcement of its decrees until they have been actually executed, may also stay or modify their enforcement when that is necessary to prevent a miscarriage of justice. Likewise, the method of enforcement may be altered to accord with any special and peculiar equities which may arise. This extraordinary power is vested in the court solely for the purpose of preventing inequitable consequences from following the enforcement of an admittedly proper decree. It cannot be invoked as a matter of right, but its exercise depends upon the demonstration of some special and peculiar equity and may be conditioned on the applicant doing equity on his part so as to prevent a miscarriage of justice on either side. Thus, even after the affirmance of a decree of foreclosure by the appellate court, the chancellor may in his discretion, and in accordance with special

A decree by default or upon confession is just as conclusive as a decree upon motion to dismiss or trial before the court or a master.137 

A decree rendered by a court having jurisdiction of the subject matter and of the parties, even though it may be erroneous, is binding and conclusive between the parties and it will not be set aside, reversed, or modified except by direct appellate procedure. 138 

Unless reversed, it is not open to contradiction or impeachment in respect to its validity, verity, or binding effect by the parties or their privies in any collateral action or proceeding. 139 Thus, for example, a decree cannot be attacked collaterally by a party to the suit in which it was rendered because of alleged mistakes made by the chancellor in construing the testimony.140 And when the decree is one that the court had jurisdiction to render, the presumptions are all in favor of its regularity and validity.141 If a decree is binding upon the parties to the proceeding, it is binding upon their privies. The term "privity" denotes mutual or successive relationship to the same rights of property.142

[Ch. 19 same parties for the same subject matter.143 This is the doctrine of res judicata, and the principle upon which it is founded is that parties ought not to be permitted to litigate the same issue more than once, and that, when a right or fact has been judicially tried or determined by a court of competent jurisdiction, or an opportunity for such a trial has been given, the decree of the court, as long as it remains unreversed, should be conclusive between the parties and those in privity with them in law or estate. 

Public policy and the interest of litigants alike require that there be an end to litigation, and the peace and order of society demand that matters distinctly put in issue and determined by a court of competent jurisdiction should not be retried between the same parties in any subsequent suit in any court. The doctrine of res judicata not only puts an end to strife, but produces certainty as to individual rights and gives dignity and respect to judicial proceedings which otherwise would be endless.144 Thus where, in an equity cause, the legal and equitable title to land is adjudicated between the parties, the decree in the cause will constitute res judicata between the same parties and their privies in a subsequent action at law involving the title to the same land. 145 

When the second suit is between the same parties as the first, and on the same cause of action, the decree in the first suit is conclusive in the second, not only as to every question which was decided, but also as to every other matter which the parties might have litigated and had determined within the issues made or tendered by the pleadings, or as incidental to or essentially connected with the subject matter of the litigation, whether such matters, as a matter of fact, were or were not considered. This rule applies to every question falling within the purview of the original action, both as to matters of claim and defense, which could have been presented by the exercise of due diligence. Thus, where a decree has been entered cancelling a contract to sell as a cloud upon the title to certain land, it is res judicata in a second suit brought by the

But when the second suit is upon a different cause of action, though between the same parties as the first, the decree operates as an estoppel only as to those points and issues which were actually litigated and determined in the first suit, and it is not conclusive as to other matters which might have been, but were not, litigated or decided. The test of the identity of causes of action, for the purpose of determining the question of res judicata, is the identity of the facts essential to the maintenance of the actions. 

Thus a decree denying a divorce on the ground of violent and ungovernable temper is not a bar to a second suit seeking a divorce on the grounds of extreme cruelty and desertion where different facts are alleged.147 The burden of proving the defense of res judicata, and the identity of the causes of action, is on the party claiming the benefit of the former decree.148 

Judgments and decrees, as estoppels, conclude only the parties to the suit and their privies.149 The rights of persons who have an interest in the subject matter of the litigation, whether legal or equitable, cannot be adjudicated or affected by a decree rendered in a suit to which they were not parties.150 Where the bill and evidence disclose that there are persons, not made parties, who claim rights in the property in litigation, they cannot be bound by the decree no matter what may be the allegations of the bill or the evidence as to the nature of their claims.151 And it is well settled that no one is in privity to a decree whose succession to the rights of property thereby affected occurred previously to the institution of the suit in which the decree was rendered. A party who has obtained a decree in his favor is bound by its terms equally with the party against whom it is rendered. Thus a purchaser who has obtained a decree of specific performance cannot, in a collateral proceeding, and upon finding that he cannot comply with the decree, question its validity for the purpose of securing a return of payments already made on the purchase price.153 And a decree vests no rights in a person who was not a party to the proceeding in which it was rendered.154 

A clear distinction exists between decrees which are merely voidable and those which are void insofar as their binding effect is concerned. As has been stated, a decree rendered in a suit where the court has jurisdiction of the subject matter and parties, even though erroneous, is only voidable and is binding upon the parties and their privies unless reversed or modified on appeal or other appropriate direct attack. But where the court does not have jurisdiction of the subject matter or of the parties, its decree is absolutely void and it may be set aside or stricken from the record at any time by any interested party.155 

Every decree in equity for the payment of money is a lien upon. the real estate of the defendant in the county where the decree is rendered. 156 Such a decree will create a lien upon the real estate of the defendant situated in any other county if a certified copy of the decree is recorded in the county where the real estate sought to be bound is situated. 157 The lien of a money decree in equity exists by virtue of statute. 158 It may be enforced in the same manner as the lien of a judgment at law. 159

§ 161.-Rehearings.-The 1931 Chancery Act contains the fol lowing provisions in regard to petitions for rehearing: "Every petition for rehearing shall contain the special matter or cause on which such rehearing is applied for, shall be signed by counsel, and the facts therein stated, if not apparent on the record, shall be verified by the oath of the party, or by some other person. No rehearing shall be granted unless the petition is filed within twenty days after the recording of the decree."161 

Under the English chancery practice, a petition for a rehearing could not be entertained after the final decree was enrolled, although enrollment could be delayed by filing a caveat after the entry of the decree in the registrar's book. Since recording under the Florida law is equivalent to enrollment under the English practice, a petition for a rehearing could not be filed after the recording of a final decree were it not for the provisions of the foregoing statute. 162

A petition for rehearing must be filed within twenty days after the recording of the decree on which a rehearing is sought.163 

After the expiration of the twenty day period the court loses jurisdiction of the cause and is without jurisdiction to enter an order granting a rehearing. 164 A motion to amend a final decree, filed after that time, and which is in effect a petition for a rehearing, should be denied.165 Under the statute, a final decree does not become absolute as long as the court may hear and determine a petition for a rehearing. Therefore a stipulation for reinstating a cause which had been dismissed by consent, if filed within the required time, may be treated as a petition for rehearing and

A petition for a rehearing in equity is the equivalent of a motion for a new trial in an action at law. § 162. Correcting, Amending, and Vacating Decrees.-There must be some point in every court proceeding when the cause is finally disposed of, its thread cut, and the parties out of court unless brought in again by some new process served upon them. The public welfare requires that there be some definite end to litigation,a point sometime, somewhere, when every case is terminated. This is especially true where, as in Florida, courts of equity have no stated term but are regarded as always open. Insofar as the trial court is concerned, this point of finality is reached twenty days after the entry of the final decree. If the final decree is based upon a decree pro confesso, no motion to set it aside may be filed after that time,181 and if the final decree is entered on the merits, 176. Smith v. A final decree may, however, be opened or vacated by the trial court within six months from the date of its entry where an error of law appears on the face of the record. Under the well established equity practice, a party aggrieved by a final decree may file a bill of review for the purpose of having it reopened on this ground. Such a bill cannot be predicated upon mere formal irregularities or matters resting in the discretion of the court. It is necessary to show that the decree complained of was contrary to some principle or rule of law or equity recognized and acknowledged or settled by decisions, and in order to determine whether there is error in the decree there can be no further examination of matters of fact, 186

But since a bill of review is substantially similar in its nature to an appeal, it cannot be maintained after the time for taking an appeal has expired.187

The foregoing rules apply only to final decrees which are erroneous as a matter of law. They have no application where the decree is either voidable or void upon grounds other than errors of law. Voidable and void decrees may, under some circumstances, be opened or vacated at any time. A voidable decree is one which is apparently valid but which may, by reason of matters not appearing of record, be set aside. A void decree is one which may be set aside or ignored because of matters appearing on the face of the record. 188

Among decrees which may properly be considered as voidable and, within certain limitations, subject to be set aside at any time, are those which may be reopened because of newly discovered evidence. The customary procedure for reopening a final decree on this ground is by a bill of review. Such a bill must show the discovery of material matters of fact which, by the exercise of reasonable diligence, could not have been known at the time of the original suit. The bill can only be filed with leave of court. It is not restricted by the time allowed for taking an appeal but it may be barred by laches. 189 One example of such a bill, though not strictly based on newly discovered evidence, is one filed to set aside a decree enforcing a special assessment lien based upon a statute subsequently declared unconstitutional by the appellate court in another suit. 190

Most numerous among decrees considered as voidable are those which have been entered through fraud, collusion, deceit, or mistake. Such decrees may be opened, modified, or vacated at any time on proper showing by the party injured.191 They are not void, but only voidable because their invalidity must necessarily be established by facts not appearing on the record. 192 

Thus decrees may be set aside as voidable where they have been based upon false allegations of jurisdictional facts. 193 A decree of divorce may be invalidated where the plaintiff's allegations as to the required residence in Florida are false.194 A decree quieting title, where the plaintiff's allegations as to the land being wild, unoccupied, and unimproved are untrue, will be set aside on a proper application. 195 A final decree entered on a decree pro

A decree that is shown by the record in the case to be absolutely void may be collaterally attacked.216 A direct attack on a decree is an attempt to defeat it in a proceeding provided by law for that purpose, whereas a collateral attack is an attempt to avoid or defeat its effect in some manner not provided by law for that purpose.217 A direct attack, for example, may be made by petition for rehearing, motion to vacate, or appeal. An instance of a collateral attack is where the validity of a decree is denied when it is used to support a plea of res judicata. 

When a decree is attacked collaterally, the scope of the inquiry is confined to jurisdictional infirmities which would render it void.218 The decree of a court having jurisdiction of the subject matter and parties cannot be collaterally impeached for mere irregularity or error.219 And in collateral proceedings, jurisdiction of the subject matter and the parties will be presumed until the contrary appears.220 A finding of the court that it had jurisdiction will be considered as correct,221 unless a lack of jurisdiction affirmatively appears on the face of the record.222

Equity courts are authorized by statute to dismiss causes for want of prosecution. The statute260 provides that all suits in equity in which it does not affirmatively appear from some action taken by the filing of pleadings, order of court, or otherwise, that the same is being prosecuted, for a period of three years, shall be deemed abated for want of prosecution and shall be dismissed by the court having jurisdiction of the cause upon motion of any person, firm, or corporation interested, whether a party to the suit or not, without revivor or notice. But suits dismissed under the statute may be reinstated by petition upon good cause shown by any party in interest within six months after the order of dismissal. 

Under the provisions of the statute the failure to take any affirmative action for three years automatically abates the cause and it may be dismissed upon the motion of any interested party. 

In the absence of such a motion, the cause stands abated, and before any action may thereafter be taken in the cause, proper proceedings for a revivor must be instituted.261 

It is also provided by a Florida equity rule262 that any cause not disposed of within three years from the filing of the bill shall be dismissed by the court at the cost of the plaintiff unless otherwise directed for cause shown. Reinstatement may be had within one year in the discretion of the court. This rule, like all others vesting a wide discretion in the chancellor, is to be enforced with caution. But the plaintiff is required by the rule to exercise reasonable diligence in all matters designed to expedite litigation and delay is justified only by considerations of his own safety and the duty he owes his adversary. Failure on the part of the plaintiff to prosecute his suit for an indefinite period of time operates as an abandonment of the suit and is fatal to his right to renew and carry it on.263

The statute provides as follows: 

"Any person or corporation claiming to be interested under a deed, will, contract in writing, or other instrument in writing, may apply by bill in chancery to any court in this state having equity jurisdiction for the determination of any question of construction arising under the instrument and for a declaration of the rights of the person or corporation interested, whether or not further relief is or could be claimed, and such declaration shall have the force of a final decree in chancery."264

It is further provided265 that all proceedings instituted under the statute shall be in conformity with the law and rules of court governing other proceedings in chancery, as far as the same may be applicable, and that the Supreme Court of Florida is authorized and empowered, whenever it shall be deemed necessary, to prescribe additional rules applicable to proceedings under the statute. 

It has been held that the foregoing statute is not in conflict with the Constitution of Florida. The Constitution provides266 that the circuit courts shall have exclusive original jurisdiction in all cases in equity, and "of such other matters as the legislature may provide." The latter clause can have reference to none other than judicial matters or functions. The legislature therefore had power to authorize the entry of declaratory decrees whether the power to enter such decrees is considered one of jurisdiction or of practice and procedure.267

Rendering a declaratory decree is no less a judicial act because it is entered before a right is invaded and no consequential relief is sought or given. Many decrees already authorized under the laws of this state are no more than declaratory. They merely declare the rights of the parties and are not followed by a decree for damages, injunction, specific performance, or some other form of coercive relief. Except for the coercive element, there is no difference between a declaratory decree and any other decree between opposing parties. And under the statute it is possible to pray for a declaration of rights and also coercive relief.268 

264. C. G. L. 4953. 

265. C. G. L. 4954. 

266. Constitution of Florida, Article V, Section 11. 

267. Sheldon v. Powell, 99 Fla. 782, 128 So. 258. 

268. Sheldon v. Powell, 99 Fla. 782, 128 So. 258.

[Ch. 19 

The purpose of a declaratory decree is to serve as an instrument of preventive justice, to render practical help in determining issues, and to adjudicate the rights or the status of parties without the peril of committing a wrong to put the legal machinery in motion. It is inhibitory of injury. Within the sphere of anticipatory and preventive justice, its use should be extended, its scope kept wide and liberal, and its boundaries elastic. But it does not fit every occasion and does not call for the scrapping of the balance of the system of remedies and actions. The declaratory decree merely contemplates that, when parties are in doubt as to their rights, they may have a judicial determination of them before a wrong has been committed or damage done.269

The statute places one clear restriction upon the right to enter declaratory decrees. Such a decree can only be obtained by a person interested under a deed, will, contract in writing, or other written instrument. And the proceeding may be maintained only for the determination of a question of construction arising under the instrument and for a declaration of the rights of the person interested. Other restrictions are that the question raised must be real and not theoretical, that the person raising the question must have a bona fide interest in it, and that there must be a defendant with a bona fide right to defend. In addition, a decree will generally be refused where it would serve no useful purpose, where special tribunals have been provided to handle the controversy, or where the facts sought to be litigated are hypothetical, present a made case, or are uncertain of occurrence.270 

The statute vests in the Supreme Court of Florida the power to prescribe rules for bringing suits to secure and enforce such decrees. However, the court has elected to exercise its authority on this matter sparingly and with caution and to lay down rules by the gradual process of judicial inclusion and exclusion rather than by specific orders.271

The most common use of the statute thus far has been for the construction of wills. A declaratory decree has been rendered construing the provisions of a will as creating an estate in fee

In regard to the construction of wills, however, the court will not, where there is no matter in dispute, undertake to declare future rights, nor will it undertake to decide upon and determine contingencies which may never arise unless such a determination is necessary to the decision of some immediate relief to be granted and which it can enforce by a decree. The jurisdiction of a court of equity in respect to testamentary construction will never be exercised for the purpose of determining hypothetical, abstract, or moot questions. As to an executor, it is only when he is under a present necessity of acting, or where he has reason to believe that he will soon be called upon to proceed under the doubtful provision, that he is entitled to a declaratory decree.274 

As to jurisdiction to entertain suits for the construction of wills, it has been held that the trustees under a testamentary trust created by the will of a Florida resident, and probated in Florida, may obtain a declaratory decree adjudicating the rights of the parties in the trust estate even though the trust res is not physically in Florida. Decrees Consolidating Causes.-The 1931 Chancery Act contains the following provision for the consolidation of suits in equity: "Upon the motion of any interested party and after notice to all other parties affected, the court may order two or more causes in equity to be consolidated upon such terms and conditions as may be just, and to prescribe the time and method of pleading and procedure and the effect of the decrees to be rendered in the cause when so consolidated. Complete identity of parties or subject matter shall not be requisite to the consolidation of causes. In any decree of consolidation the court may order that the consolidated causes shall preserve their separate existence or be merged into a single suit."278 

Suits in equity should not generally be consolidated when they differ both as to parties and subject matter, when the various questions presented are so confused as to make it proper that the suits be heard separately, or when conflicting objects are sought to be accomplished. But circumstances may arise when it would be feasible to consolidate causes having different parties and involving different rights.279 Under the 1931 Chancery Act, as well as under the former practice,280 it seems clear that consolidation may be effected at any stage of the case and that two causes may be consolidated and litigated to a decree as one.281 

It has been held proper to consolidate a suit for partition and a suit to quiet title, the parties and the subject matter being the same.282

It has also been held that an application to consolidate two foreclosure suits should be granted where the parties are identical and there is no difference in the two suits except as to the number of lots and the face amount of the mortgage involved in each.283

The general rule in regard to costs in equity is that they follow the result of the suit. But this rule is departed from when the failing party can show to the court any circumstances which would render it unjust that he should pay the costs of the proceeding.286 In such cases, it is within the discretion of the court to award or prorate costs as justice may require, and the appellate court will not interfere unless an abuse of discretion is shown.287 Where a suit is necessary to wind up a partnership, it is proper to divide the costs.288 Costs should be borne equally where neither party is blameless in the proceeding.289

The general rule which gives the costs of the suit to the victorious party applies equally to cases in which parties are suing or defending in a representative capacity. It is not, however, always applicable to trustees and other representatives who necessarily or fairly sue or defend for the protection of estates and funds. In such cases, the estate or fund will be charged.295 But these cases are exceptional, and in no case will an allowance be made to a trustee, failing in his suit, where the property belongs to and is in the possession of the defendant.296 Nor will the court allow a trustee or other representative to take advantage of this rule where he sets up an improper defense in an attempt to defeat the claims of a cestui que trust.297

§ 167.-Right to Appeal.-The right to an appellate review of a case which has already been heard in a trial court is not a natural, absolute, or unqualified right, but it is a right created by law, either organic or statutory.' The Constitution of Florida2 provides that "the Supreme Court shall have appellate jurisdiction in all cases at law and in equity originating in circuit courts." It 

1. Reed v. State, 94 Fla. 32, 113 So. 

630; Hines v. Noel, 110 Fla. 457, 149 

So. 17. 

2. Constitution of Florida, Article V, Section 5.

has been held that the right to utilize the appellate jurisdiction of the Supreme Court is in substance secured by this provision.3 

While it is also provided by statute that "appeals in chancery shall be matters of right,"4 the time and manner in which an appellate review may be obtained are subject to statutory regulation, as long as the right is not unduly restricted, and, to enjoy the benefit of an appeal, a party must comply with the conditions precedent and other applicable requirements prescribed by law. The adversary party has a right in the due observance of these statu tory regulations.7 

The right to an appeal is generally governed by the laws in force when the decree appealed from is rendered. Statutes giving and regulating the right of appeal are remedial in their nature and should receive a liberal construction in furtherance of the right.9 

It is provided by statute¹o that "appeals in chancery, whether from final decrees or from interlocutory orders or decrees, must be taken within six months after the entry of the order or decree appealed from." At the expiration of this period a final decree in chancery becomes absolute and cannot be corrected by an appeal." Where an appeal is taken after the lapse of six months, the Supreme Court acquires no jurisdiction over the cause and the appeal will be dismissed.12

The right to an appeal may be surrendered by agreement or it may be waived. Where competent parties, upon a sufficient consideration, enter into an agreement to waive errors and not to appeal from the decree of the court of original jurisdiction, their object being to settle their differences and terminate the litigation, and the agreement is seasonably brought to the attention of the appellate court by appropriate proceedings, it will be recognized

and given effect.13 It is also a general rule that one cannot ordinarily accept a benefit under a decree and then appeal from it, when the effect of his appeal may be to annul the decree as a whole. 

Thus a party cannot appeal from a decree cancelling a tax certificate held by him when he has accepted money paid into court by the adverse party as a condition precedent to the relief granted.14 

But the right to appeal is not waived where the decree is severable into distinct parts, so that the acceptance of benefits under one part is not inconsistent with an appeal from another, or when the amount found due the plaintiff and accepted by him is due in any event, so that the only question to be determined by the appellate tribunal is whether he is entitled to a greater sum.15 

A party is entitled to only one appeal from a single decree. It is irregular for a party to enter a second appeal from a decree while a prior appeal from the same decree is still pending and effective, and for such an irregularity the second appeal will be dismissed. There can be no necessity for a second appeal in such cases, as the first can be made to accomplish the same purpose as the second. Successive appeals of this nature would burden the docket of the appellate court, and cause trouble and expense to parties litigant, for no useful purpose.16 But if the first appeal is ineffectual to confer jurisdiction on the appellate court,17 or has been abandoned or dismissed without having been determined on the merits, a second appeal will be allowed, if it is not prosecuted in bad faith, and if it is entered within the time allowed by law. 18

The payment of all costs which have accrued up to the time an appeal is taken is not a prerequisite to the appeal as it is to the granting of a writ of error. 19

An appeal may be taken from a decree rendered in an ex parte proceeding.22 A party may also appeal from, and obtain a reversal of, a void judgment.23 Errors committed by the chancellor in granting or denying discovery or inspection and production of documents in the hands of the adverse party himself are redressible by appeal and not by mandamus.24 A final decree, entered pursuant to a writ of mandamus ordering the chancellor to proceed with the trial, is not reviewable by a supplementary mandamus proceeding. An appeal is the proper remedy.25 But where the remedy by appeal from an interlocutory order in a chancery suit is not plain, speedy, and adequate, the issuance of a writ of prohibition to stop further proceedings in the cause is authorized.26 

An appellate review in a statutory proceeding to re-establish lost papers or files in a pending suit must be by appeal if the suit is pending in equity and by writ of error if the suit is pending at law. But in other cases where statutory remedies are given, and it is not expressly provided that the method of reviewing orders therein shall be by appeal, then the only method of obtaining a review is by writ of error.27 Thus, statutory proceedings for the stay of an execution and the suspension of proceedings thereon, even though the execution may have been issued on a decree in equity, may be reviewed by a writ of error but not by an appeal.28

An appeal does not lie from an order punishing a party for contempt for the violation of an injunction issued in a chancery case. 

The remedy, if any, is habeas corpus for illegal imprisonment.29

Since an appeal lies only from an order or decree which was the result of judicial action, a consent decree cannot be reviewed by appeal. Such a decree may be set aside only by consent.30 

§ 169.-Definition of Appellate Jurisdiction.-The Constitution of 

Florida provides that "the circuit courts shall have exclusive original jurisdiction in all cases in equity." It confers upon the 

Supreme Court only "appellate jurisdiction" of cases in equity originating in the circuit courts.32 An appeal is a proceeding by which a party submits to the decision of a superior court a case which has already been tried in an inferior court.33 Consequently, it would be inappropriate, if not actually beyond its jurisdiction, for the Supreme Court to undertake the determination of an equity suit where it affirmatively appears that the issues involved have never been considered or determined by the circuit court as a court of first instance.34

Thus, where a suit is filed attacking the validity of a testamentary trust and seeking the appointment of an administrator ad litem, and the chancellor refuses to appoint the administrator ad litem but does not pass upon the validity of the trust, the Supreme Court, in reversing the order, will not pass upon the merits of the suit in the absence of a ruling thereon by the chancellor.35 On an appeal from an order permitting the filing of an amended bill, the Supreme Court will not rule on certain questions not ruled on by the chancellor, since anything it might say thereon would not necessarily be conclusive if the questions arose in subsequent proceedings in the lower court.36

Likewise, where the chancellor, in entering a final decree, recites that he has sustained a motion to dismiss the bill, and has given no consideration to the evidence or to the defendant's answer, the appellate court will not affirm the decree on the theory that it was justified by the evidence and the answer.

Under some circumstances, however, evidence de hors the record is admissible in the appellate court in connection with proceedings before it. Thus where the plaintiff has an election between inconsistent remedies, such as foreclosure and replevin, and he prosecutes a foreclosure suit to an appeal in the Supreme Court, evidence is admissible in that court to show that, subsequent to the appeal, he recovered the property in a replevin suit and thereby abandoned his appeal.41

There must be some action by the lower court making him a party.45

The general rule also is that a party to a suit is not entitled to appeal from a decree wholly in his favor.46 Thus a defendant to a chancery suit in whose favor the bill of complaint was dismissed, and against whom no relief was granted or any liability adjudged, cannot appeal. An appeal by such a party will be dismissed.47

But a party may appeal from a decree in his favor when the court has, without his consent, committed some error prejudicial to him.

For example, if a decree in favor of the plaintiff is for a smaller amount than it ought to be, he may appeal. Likewise, it is well settled that a plaintiff may appeal from his own decree for irregularities which may have intervened in the trial court and which render the decree invalid or unenforceable. The rule that a party may not take advantage of errors for his benefit does not apply to errors of the court. Therefore, he may obtain a reversal of an invalid decree in his favor in order that he may commence another suit and obtain a legal and valid decree.48

Where a party to a suit entitled to appeal from an adverse decree dies, the procedure for taking an appeal by his successors in interest depends upon whether his death occurred before or after the taking of the appeal. If the death occurred prior to the appeal, the suit must be revived in the court of original jurisdiction and the appeal taken by the successors or representatives of the deceased party. If the death occurred after the appeal, the revivor must be had in the Supreme Court.4 49 Where the death occurred prior to the appeal, the revivor must be effected in accordance with the provisions of the 1931 Chancery Act.50 The mere filing of letters testamentary by a personal representative does not enable him to appeal from a decree against the decedent.51 An appeal prosecuted by personal representatives without a revivor will be dismissed.52 

Where the death occurred after the appeal the method of revivor is prescribed by the rules of the Supreme Court. The proper representatives of the deceased party may voluntarily come in and be admitted as parties. But no revivor is necessary where the appeal has been perfected and the briefs have been filed.5 53 

§ 171.-Necessary Parties to Appeal.-Prior to 1927, there were definitely established rules in regard to necessary parties to appeals and to the method of making such parties. If all necessary parties were not joined, the appeal was dismissed. In 1927, however, a statute 54 was enacted providing that no appeal should be dismissed for want of proper parties if the notice of entry of appeal was recorded within the time allowed by law and identified with reasonable certainty the decree sought to be reviewed. Under this statute, it has been held that, where a properly recorded notice of appeal clearly, definitely, and correctly designates the date and book and page of record of the decree appealed from, all parties signing the notice, and in whose name the appeal is purported to be taken, are to be deemed appellants, and all other parties to the decree appealed from are deemed appellees and as such properly

In accordance with the foregoing principles, it is a well settled rule that unless all of the parties against whom a joint decree is rendered unite in an appeal therefrom, or unless the appeal is taken in the names of all such parties, with summons and severance, or unless equivalent proceedings are had as to those who refuse to join, the appeal will be dismissed.68 Thus where two defendants file what is in reality a joint answer, and part of it is stricken on motion of the plaintiff, and only one of the defendants appeals from the order, and the appellate court is unable to say to what extent the interests of the defendant who has not appealed are affected by the decree, the appeal will be dismissed.69 And where a suit is brought by a creditor to set aside a conveyance made by his debtor to her children, and the relief is granted as prayed, the children are vitally interested in a reversal of the decree and an appeal will be dismissed unless they are joined as appellants or a severance is had as to them.70

By this procedure the plaintiff below is brought into the appellate court by a proper record of the entry of appeal. The defendants in whose favor the decree is rendered are brought in by making them appellants in the entry of appeal.

It operates to suspend the action and power of the inferior court in the matter appealed from.9 A supersedeas is not essential to the acquisition or preservation of appellate jurisdiction.96 95 Where an appeal without a supersedeas is taken from an interlocutory decree, the power of the lower court to proceed with the cause toward an adjudication upon the merits is not affected by the appeal. Thus an appeal from an order denying a motion to dismiss the bill does not prevent the circuit court from proceeding with a determination of the cause on the merits where no supersedeas is taken.97 Likewise, an appeal from such an order does not prevent the entry of a decree pro confesso.98 

The limitation upon this rule extends only to the point of depriving the lower court of power to finally dispose of the cause by dismissal or otherwise so as to, in form or effect, interfere with the power and authority of the appellate court under the Constitution to make its jurisdiction and orders effective in the cause.99 

After an appeal without supersedeas the trial court cannot permit or require any proceedings in the cause that would impair the appellate jurisdiction of the Supreme Court or defeat the efficacy of an appeal already taken. Thus a decree dismissing the bill of complaint, made after an appeal from an interlocutory order does not affect the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court and, should the interlocutory order be reversed, the decree and mandate of the Supreme Court is effectual to restore the dismissed cause to the docket of the trial court. Whatever the trial court does after an appeal from an interlocutory order without supersedeas is, of course, subject to the ultimate exercise of the appellate jurisdiction of the Supreme Court. 101 

A contrary result would nullify the constitutional powers of the Supreme Court. 102 But the reversal of a decree, after an appeal without supersedeas, has no effect on what is done under the decree insofar as third persons are concerned. Thus, where a receiver has money sequestered by him under a decree finding such moneys applicable to the plaintiff's demand, and a portion of the money is applied by order of the court to the plaintiff's attorney for services in the suit, a subsequent reversal of the decree and of the order on an appeal without supersedeas gives the defendant no claim against the attorney. If there is no supersedeas, then action of the court in accordance with the decree can only be remedied by proceeding against the parties. 103 

The effect of an appeal with supersedeas is to suspend the power of the court of original jurisdiction to make any order tending towards an execution or enforcement of the order or decree appealed from.104 Thus, so long as an appeal with supersedeas from an order granting an injunction is pending, the power of the court to enforce the injunction, or to punish as contempts acts committed in violation of its terms, is suspended.105 Where an appeal is pending from a final decree authorizing a sale, and a supersedeas order becomes effective after the sale but before its confirmation, the order of confirmation is invalid.106 When there is an appeal with supersedeas from an order denying a motion to dismiss the bill, the appellant should not be required to plead to an amended bill thereafter filed in the cause. When an appeal with supersedeas is taken from an interlocutory order appointing a receiver, the supersedeas does not have the effect of discharging the receiver. It simply suspends his authority pending the supersedeas. It is the duty of the receiver to at once cease all action as such and to restore the property that may have come into his hands to the possession of the party from whom it was taken by the decree appealed from. The power of the chancellor over the receiver and the property in his hands is likewise suspended. Until the appellate court has acted in the case, the chancellor has no authority to make any further order relative to the property involved and no order of the chancellor while the supersedeas is in effect will excuse the receiver for a violation of the supersedeas.108

Where a supersedeas has been properly effected, neither the chancellor nor a master appointed by him may ignore or refuse to recognize it. And the appellate court has power to enforce the supersedeas by issuing a writ of prohibition to restrain further proceedings in the cause below, as well as to enforce the supersedeas by contempt proceedings. 109

A supersedeas does not, however, interfere with the power of the chancellor to make any further orders and decrees in the cause which do not tend toward an execution or enforcement of the decree appealed from. § 173.-Injunction in Aid of Appeal.-The Supreme Court of 

Florida has no power to grant an injunction in the exercise of original jurisdiction 169 because the writ of injunction is an equitable remedy and exclusive original jurisdiction in all cases in equity is conferred upon the circuit courts. But the Constitution of Florida does give the Supreme Court power to issue "all writs necessary or proper to the complete exercise of its jurisdiction."170 Consequently, the Supreme Court can issue a writ of injunction where such a writ is necessary or proper to the complete exercise of its appellate jurisdiction in an equity case.171

As will be noted from the language of the Constitution, the power of the Supreme Court to issue constitutional writs is not limited to those which are merely necessary to protect its jurisdiction but it extends to the issuance of such writs as may be proper to the complete exercise of its jurisdiction. It is therefore within the province of the court to grant a writ of injunction if it is found that the granting of the writ is either necessary or proper to the complete exercise of its jurisdiction to decide a matter brought before it on appeal. But, as in all other cases involving the right of the Supreme Court to interfere with the orderly administration of justice in the circuit courts, extraordinary relief of this character will not be granted except in cases of extreme urgency where it is necessary to protect the appellant from irreparable injury during the interim between the entry of the appeal and the final decision of the appellate court. 172

Thus, where an appeal is taken from the denial of an injunction against the destruction of bearing citrus trees and the taking of land for the construction of a highway, and it is made to appear that the trees are of such a peculiar nature that, in order to preserve the value and usefulness of the land until the merits of the appeal can

Application for an extraordinary writ of injunction should be made by petition to the Supreme Court. 178 Its issuance may, in proper cases, be conditioned on the giving of a bond to pay costs, damages, and attorneys' fees.179 When an application for a constitutional writ raises only questions of law involving the public good, and the cause is by consent argued fully on the merits, the court may, in the public interest, determine the merits of the appeal without passing on the application for the injunction. 180 § 174.-Entry of Appeal.-It is provided by statute 181 that "appeals in chancery, whether from final decrees or from interlocutory orders or decrees, must be taken within six months after the entry of the order or decree appealed from."

While the Supreme Court of Florida has appellate jurisdiction in all cases in equity, that jurisdiction can only be invoked in a particular case by compliance with the applicable statutory requirements.182

It is provided by statute 193 that when a married woman is a party to a judgment at law she shall be allowed two years in which to sue out a writ of error, and it is also provided by statute194 that the provisions of law relating to writs of error and governing the filing of transcripts, and proceedings thereon, and the filing of assignments of error, shall be applicable to appeals in chancery. The method of taking an appeal in a chancery cause is prescribed by the following statute: "Notice of entry of all appeals in chancery causes, whether taken in open court or in vacation, shall be filed with the clerk of the court whose order or decree is to be reviewed, and by such clerk shall be forthwith entered in the chancery order book; and no other or further notice of such appeal shall be required to be given or served in order to give the Supreme Court complete jurisdiction over the person of the appellee, but the record of such entry in the chancery order book shall be taken and held to be sufficient notice to the appellee of the taking of said appeal and of the pendency thereof in the Supreme Court."196

One of the strictest requirements of a notice of appeal is that it shall designate a proper return day. The return day in appeals in chancery is governed by the statutes regulating writs of error. Accordingly, the appeal must be returnable to a day, either in term time or vacation, more than thirty days and not more than ninety days from the entry of the appeal.206 Of course, a notice of appeal which specifies no return day is fatally defective. 

The record of such a notice does not inform the appellee of any time at which he is to appear before the appellate court. 

It cannot, therefore, be effectual as notice of the appeal and, in such a case, the appeal will be dismissed.207

Likewise, a notice of appeal designating a return day not within the statutory limits is void, confers no jurisdiction of the subject matter on the Supreme Court, and an appeal so taken will be dismissed by the court sua sponte.208 In numerous cases, notices of appeal designating a return day less than thirty days209 or more than ninety days210 from the date of their entry have been held void and the appeal dismissed. And, where an appeal is thus made returnable in violation of statute, the appearance of the appellee cannot confer jurisdiction of the subject matter on the Supreme Court and will not preclude the dismissal of the appeal.211 Obviously, the parties litigant have no power to waive a statutory requirement which the Supreme Court itself has no authority to change or modify.

While Sundays are included in the statutory period of more than thirty days and not more than ninety days from the date of entry of the appeal, the statute contemplates that the appeal shall be returnable on a day within the stated period when the Supreme Court is open for appearances and the transaction of business. An appellee cannot appear in court on Sunday, and when the notice of appeal is returnable on a Sunday it requires what the law does not permit. A notice returnable on a Sunday is therefore ineffectual to subject the appellee to the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court.212 And such a notice cannot be amended to state a proper return day after the time for taking an appeal has expired.213 

Where an entry of appeal in a chancery cause is void because it is made returnable contrary to law, a proper entry may be made without any disposition of the void entry. The latter, being a nullity, may be ignored.214

Another essential requirement of a notice of appeal is that it must be sufficiently full and explicit to advise the parties entitled to notice, as well as the appellate court, that an appeal is being taken by certain definitely named parties against other definitely named parties.215 However, a simple and expeditious method of satisfying this requirement was provided by a statute216 enacted in 1927. 

This statute provides that no appeal "shall be dismissed for want of proper parties if the *** notice of entry of appeal recorded within the time allowed by law shall identify with reasonable certainty the judgment or decree sought to be reviewed." It also provides that "in case of numerous parties it shall be sufficient designation to identify the cause by its usual title in the inferior court and the abbreviation 'et al.' may be used to designate parties other than those expressly named." To this end, the appeal is considered a step in the cause.

The object of the statute is to make the entry of an appeal sufficient for the purpose of transferring the cause to the appellate court if the decree sought to be reviewed is identified with reason-

able certainty. The words "proper parties" are used in the statute in their broad appellate sense and they embrace all parties whom it is proper to bring into the appellate court. They are not limited in their meaning to those merely formal parties who, prior to the statute, could have been omitted from an appeal without entailing the penalty of a dismissal for want of necessary parties. If thus narrowly construed, the statute would do nothing more than forbid the dismissal of an appeal for want of parties proper but not necessary to it, a thing which the Supreme Court never did prior to its enactment. The statute should not be construed so as to attribute to the legislature a futile act.217 

The effect of the 1927 statute upon the designation of parties in a notice of appeal has been thoroughly considered by the Supreme Court of Florida and, in a well reasoned opinion, it has been held that the statute precludes the involuntary dismissal of an appeal in chancery for any omission of parties if the notice of appeal, as filed and recorded, definitely and correctly states the date, book, and page of record of the decree appealed from. It has been further held that, where these requirements are met, the parties signing the notice, and in whose names the appeal purports to be taken, are deemed appellants, and that all other parties to the decree appealed from are deemed appellees and, as such, properly before the court. Under this construction of the statute, all parties to a decree of the lower court are required to take notice of a subsequently filed and recorded entry of appeal from that decree, and any party not among those taking the appeal may, as an appellee, file cross assignments of error if he desires to make complaint against the decree in the nature of an appeal from it.218 

The foregoing construction of the 1927 statute has not, however, been uniformly followed by the Supreme Court of Florida in subsequent decisions, but the rules for the designation of parties in a notice of appeal as they existed prior to the 1927 statute appear to have been applied. And, in any event, where the notice of appeal does not state the date, book and page of record of the decree appealed from, the rules as to the designation of parties

The recording of the notice is jurisdictional and absolutely necessary to confer upon the appellate court jurisdiction over the parties.

The transcript of the record on appeal should affirmatively show the record of the notice of appeal and, where it fails to do so, and the appellee has not appeared, the appeal will be dismissed for want of jurisdiction over his person.235 However, if the transcript fails to show a proper record, the omission may be supplied by competent evidence de hors the transcript.236 In the absence of contrary proof, it will be presumed that the record of the notice as it appears in the transcript is a true and correct transcription of the original notice.237

A notice of appeal under the statute serves the double function of conferring upon the Supreme Court jurisdiction over the subject matter of the cause and over the person of the appellee.238

Even though the appellate court may acquire jurisdiction over an appellee by a voluntary or implied appearance made after six months from the entry of the decree appealed from, an amendment of a notice of appeal for the purpose of bringing in new parties will not be allowed subsequent to the expiration of that time. An amendment of the notice to bring in new parties is, as to such parties, an appeal entered for the first time. Consequently, it will not be permitted after the lapse of the time allowed for taking an appeal.246 For the same reason, a notice of appeal recorded after the six months' period, either nunc pro tunc or otherwise, will not give the appellate court jurisdiction over the appellee.247 An entry of appeal cannot be amended in the appellate court.248 

§ 175.-Assignments of Error.-The office of an assignment of error is not only to inform the appellate court of the exact grounds upon which the reversal of a decree is sought, but also to inform the appellee of the precise errors relied upon in order that he may take proper steps and give proper directions in his own behalf for making the transcript of record exhibit to the appellate court what might otherwise be insufficiently shown.249 As a general rule, the consideration of the appellate court will be confined to the questions raised by the assignments of error,250 but where a jurisdictional or other fundamental error is apparent on the face of the record it may be considered by the appellate court even though it is not assigned. Thus the court may, of its own motion, notice the total failure of a bill of complaint to state a case for equitable relief,251 or the absence of a necessary party.252

It is the duty of an appellant, when he applies to the clerk for a transcript of the record in a chancery cause, to file with the clerk of the court whose decree is appealed from a complete assignment of all the errors he intends to rely upon for a reversal in the appellate court. At the same time, the appellant must file written directions to the clerk for making up the transcript. A copy of the assignments of error and written directions must be served upon the appellee or his attorney within five days after they are filed with the clerk. The assignments of error, and any assignments of error filed by the appellee, are the guide by which the transcript of the record is made up. Any failure of the appellant to comply with the foregoing requirements will result in a dismissal of his appeal by the appellate court.253 But an appellee who moves to eliminate assignments of error from the transcript on the ground that a copy was not served upon him must affirmatively show that fact.254

In preparing assignments of error, each error relied upon should be clearly and distinctly specified and separately assigned. A single assignment of error attacking a plurality of rulings of the trial court, whether upon the pleadings, the admission or rejection of evidence, or otherwise, will be unavailing unless all of the rulings grouped en masse are erroneous. A determination by the appellate court that one of the rulings so attacked is correct disposes of the assignment.255 Thus, where an assignment of error is that "the court severally erred in overruling the several exceptions of the defendants to the several findings and conclusions of the special master's report in said case, to wit," and then follows a copy of the exceptions taken by the defendants to the master's report, a determination by the appellate court that one of the exceptions was correctly overruled is sufficient to dispose of the assignment.256 But, in framing assignments of error based upon the sustaining of exceptions to a master's report, there is no occasion to frame an assignment as to the sustaining of each ground

Since the appellate court reviews the action of the chancellor on the report of a master in equity cases, and not the action of the master per se, an assignment of error that "the master erred in the report which he made to the court" cannot be considered.258 

An assignment of error that the court erred in making the master's findings a part of its final decree is without force when the decree does not recite that the findings were adopted and incorporated therein.259 Assignments of error based upon a motion to strike parts of an answer will not be passed upon when the transcript fails to identify the portions of the answer attacked.260 261 Assignments of error based upon the rejection of evidence will not be considered unless the record affirmatively shows that the evidence was offered before the chancellor and rejected by him. 

Assignments of error based upon the admission of evidence will not be considered unless it appears that the objection taken to the evidence was presented to and expressly ruled upon by the chancellor in the court below at or before the final hearing of the cause. 

While, in common law cases, an assignment of error that "the court erred in rendering judgment for the plaintiff" is too general to be considered, an assignment of error on an appeal in chancery that "the court erred in the entry of its final decree" is sufficient to call for a review of every error that may appear in the decree.262

However, such an assignment will not be considered where it appears that all the evidence is not included in the transcript.263 

Where several interlocutory decrees are made in a cause and only certain specified ones are appealed from, assignments of error based upon those not appealed from cannot be considered. But, on appeal from a final decree, errors may be assigned upon prior interlocutory orders even though they are not embraced in the

The practice of assigning a large number of errors is reprehensible, as it tends to hinder, delay, and make difficult the administration of justice. The assigning of from sixty to one hundred errors has been held to be unjustified. It is a violent presumption that any judge could make that many separate and distinct errors in the trial of a case, but, even if he should, it is not necessary to assign every one of them as error in order to secure a reversal of the decree.266

§ 176.-Transcript of Record. It is the duty of the appellant, on or before the return day of his appeal, to file in the Supreme Court a duly certified transcript of the record of the case in the court below.271 In addition, the appellant must also serve the opposite party or his attorney with a true copy of the certified transcript and file in the Supreme Court either a receipt for such a copy or an affidavit showing its service upon the opposite party. 

Where there are several appellees, only one copy of the transcript is required to be furnished to them.272 

Where the appellant neglects to file the transcript of the record as aforesaid, or to serve a copy thereof upon the opposite party, it is the duty of the appellate court, either upon motion of the appellee or its own motion, to dismiss the appeal unless good cause is shown to the contrary. A motion by the appellee to dismiss the appeal on this ground should be supported by a certificate from the court below that an appeal has been sued out and proof that the transcript has not been filed in the Supreme Court or served upon him.273

But the right to have an appeal dismissed on this ground may be lost by undue delay and laches in exercising it, as where the motion to dismiss is not made until after the transcript is filed.274

The Supreme Court may, upon proper and timely application and for good cause shown, extend the time for filing the transcript of record.275 The pendency of a motion to quash the appeal does not dispense with the filing of the transcript on the return day, nor is a mere request, contained in the appellant's brief resisting a motion to quash, a proper motion for an extension of time within which to file the transcript. Furthermore, even the filing of a
