This is done in the following manner: 

When the appellant applies to the clerk for the transcript of the record, he must file with the clerk written directions indicating the papers and proceedings that are to be copied and made a part of the transcript of record, and those that are to be recited therein, and also those that are to be omitted therefrom. The directions must indicate a date on which the clerk is to commence making up the transcript, which date must not be less than fifteen days after the filing of the written directions. A copy of the directions must also be served on the appellee or his attorney within five days after they are filed with the clerk. If, at the time fixed in the written directions, the appellee has not filed additional directions to the clerk requiring him to include in the transcript matters not designated in the appellant's directions, the clerk must prepare the transcript as directed by the appellant. But if the appellee, within the time fixed, files additional directions, the clerk must also include the matters therein directed.2 278 The appellant cannot evade his duty in the preparation of the transcript by a general direction to the clerk to copy everything on file.279 His written directions must show the papers and proceedings to be copied and made a part of the record, those to be recited, and those to be omitted. However, if the transcript should contain copies instead of recited proceedings, this alone would not constitute sufficient grounds for a dismissal of the appeal. Likewise, a variance between the original directions for making up the transcript and the copy served on the opposite party does not authorize a dismissal ipso facto, though it may furnish a cause for dismissal. The clerk of the circuit court, in making up the transcript of the record for the Supreme Court, has no authority to omit anything which he is directed by either party to insert therein if it is a paper or proceeding in the cause having relation or leading up to the decree appealed from, even though the opposite party directed him to omit it as not being necessary for the full and clear presentation of any question raised by the assignments of error.2 283

The rules of the Supreme Court288 provide that the transcript shall be printed, typewritten, or prepared by the use of photostatic copies of original papers. In order that the transcript may be easily read, requirements as to paper, lettering, and spacing are also prescribed. No photostatic copy of any document written in long hand may be embraced in the transcript unless accompanied by a certificate of the chancellor that a facsimile reproduction thereof is necessary to a consideration of the case. These rules should be followed by the clerk in making up the transcript.289 If they are not observed, the court may exercise the discretion vested in it and dismiss the appeal.290 

There is no authority in the statutes or court rules for transposing testimony from question and answer to narrative form for the transcript of record. Nevertheless the practice is of material assistance to the Supreme Court and it has been definitely approved. 

But the testimony in its final form must be certified by the chancellor as correct, either upon notice to the opposite party or by stipulation.291

Since no assignment of error will be heard or considered unless it is properly based upon the transcript of the record,292 it is the duty of the appellant resorting to the appellate court to see that the transcript is properly prepared so as to make the errors complained of clearly appear.293 The rules do not contemplate that the entire proceeding in the lower court shall be transmitted to the Supreme Court on appeal,294 but there are certain essential requirements as to the contents of the transcript. 

Obviously, the powers of the Supreme Court cannot be exercised unless there is an actual cause pending in the court below. Therefore, the transcript must contain a sufficient part of the record to show the existence of such a cause.

In the preparation of transcripts, redundancies, repetitions, and the unnecessary inclusion of papers should be avoided. It is provided by statute that, if necessary, original papers, books, documents, maps, pictures, or other exhibits may be transmitted from the circuit court to the Supreme Court for consideration in connection with an appeal.309 But an original master's report and accompanying testimony cannot be transmitted to the Supreme Court to save the cost or inconvenience of copying it into the transcript. This is not within the purview of the statute because it is part of the record proper and not merely an incident to the record as an exhibit.310

§ 177.-Briefs and Argument.-The appellant must, within thirty days after the return day of the appeal, file with the clerk of the Supreme Court three copies of his brief together with a receipt by opposing counsel for a copy of the brief or an affidavit showing service of a copy on opposing counsel. The appellee must file his brief within twenty days after the filing of the appellant's brief. 

As in the case of the appellant's brief, three copies must be filed with the court together with an affidavit or receipt showing service of a copy on the appellant's counsel. The appellant must then, within ten days after the filing of the appellant's brief, file three copies of such reply to the latter brief as he may desire to make together with proof of service of a copy on the appellee's counsel.326 

It is the duty of both the appellant and appellee to file briefs with the Supreme Court. If the appellant fails to do so the appeal may be dismissed or the decree affirmed. If the appellee fails to file a brief, the court may decide the case on its merits.3 But

A violation of the rules as to form and style, when no correction is seasonably made on application made and granted, will result in a dismissal of the appeal and the imposition of costs when the violation is by the appellant, and in the imposition of costs, or the striking of briefs, when the violation is by the appellee.331 

The contents of the briefs are also clearly prescribed by the Supreme Court rules. The appellant's brief should consist of three major divisions: first, a statement of the questions involved; second, a concise history or statement of the case, that is, a condensed summary of the pleadings and evidence on which the appellant relies to support his contentions; and third, the argument. 

The intention of the rule is that the statement of the questions involved shall be framed in such a manner that, by reading it, the court, without being compelled to examine any other part of the brief, may quickly see the nature of the legal issue and what points it will be called upon to decide. The statement of the questions involved must show the precise point of law at issue and its applicability to the facts at hand. Thus, a question such as, "Did the court err in sustaining defendant's motion to dismiss the bill of complaint?" is insufficient. But a question, "Does the conversion of private dwellings into apartment houses violate a restrictive covenant that there shall not be erected on the land any building designed for any other purpose than a private dwelling?" answers

The history or statement of the case is intended as an aid to or explanation of the questions involved and it should contain a closely condensed chronological statement of the essential pleadings, proceedings, and facts which are necessary to be known in order to determine the points in controversy. In this division the decree appealed from should be briefly stated. 

The third division of the brief should be devoted to the argument. In this division it should be pointed out what assignments of error present the questions previously stated in the brief. When the appellant fails to refer to the assignments of error the rule is not complied with.332

Under repeated decisions of the Supreme Court, assignments of error which are not argued or considered in the brief will be treated as abandoned.333 An argument which is no more than an assertion of the assignment of error is equivalent to an abandonment.334 Where assignments of error are grouped in a brief, and one fails, they all fail.335 In passing upon an assignment of error based upon the denial of a motion to dismiss the bill, the appellate court will consider only such grounds of the motion as are argued in the brief and will treat the others as abandoned.336

As to the contents of the appellee's brief, it need not contain a statement of the questions involved or a history of the case, but it may point out any error contained in these portions of the appellant's brief and add any further statement of the pleadings and facts that may be deemed necessary to a fair determination of the case.339 The appellee's argument should be clearly subdivided and addressed to the same major points as the argument of the appellant where this can be done without prejudice to the presentation of the merits of his case.

§ 178.-Frivolous and Dilatory Appeals.-Authority is conferred upon the Supreme Court, by a statute 343 which is applicable to equity cases,344 to quash an appeal in any cause where it is taken against good faith or merely for delay, and to decree damages against the appellant not exceeding ten per cent, even though the case has not been reached for final hearing on the regular call of the docket.345

It is not the purpose of the statute to require the court, upon a motion to quash an appeal on the ground that it is taken merely for delay, to enter into an examination of, or to decide or determine, doubtful or debatable questions properly raised by the assignments of error. The purpose of the statute is to enable the court to quash an appeal where the assignments of error are so plainly and palpably without merit as to lead to the conclusion that the proceedings were taken merely for delay. The absence of error in the proceedings must be apparent from a short and cursory examination of the record requiring neither investigation of authorities nor argument to show the untenableness of the assignments of error. If the assignments of error raise doubtful or debatable questions of fact, the court will not investigate or decide them on a motion of this character, but will deny the motion and hold the case for hearing in its regular order on the docket.346 

But if a short and cursory examination of the record discloses that the assignments of error are so obviously without merit as to lead to the conclusion that the appeal was taken merely for delay, a motion to quash should be granted.347

Upon a motion to quash an appeal taken merely for delay, the moving party will not be heard, either orally or by brief, because the assignments of error must, on an examination of the record. only, be so wholly devoid of merit as to require no argument to show that they are untenable.348 If the moving party files a brief or seeks an argument in support of his motion, the court may treat this as an admission that an arguable proposition inheres in the appeal which should not be summarily disposed of.349

The party opposing the motion will, however, be heard orally or by brief.350 

Although the court makes only a superficial examination of the record to determine whether an appeal should be quashed as

A motion to quash an appeal as frivolous must be prepared and a copy thereof served upon the opposite party or his attorney within ten days after the return day of the appeal. The rules of the Supreme Court contain appropriate provisions for a hearing on the motion, although they expressly provide that the mover is not entitled to be heard.352 If the motion is made prior to the return day, it must be accompanied by a complete transcript of the record in the court below. The Supreme Court obviously cannot act on such a motion in the absence of a transcript of the record.353 A subsequent motion by the appellant for a voluntary dismissal of the appeal does not preclude a hearing on a motion to quash.354

A motion to quash an appeal as frivolous should be distinguished from a motion to dismiss an appeal. The inquiry on the latter motion is ordinarily limited to whether an appeal lies in the particular case, and whether it has been regularly taken and perfected.355 But a motion to dismiss an appeal that is properly framed may be treated as a motion to quash.356 

The statute authorizes the Supreme Court, on a motion to quash, to assess damages against the party taking the dilatory appeal not exceeding ten per cent. 

The limitation mentioned in the statute obviously refers to the amount in controversy as determinable from evidence submitted to the court or from the record in the case. The penalty has usually been applied in cases involving money judgments, but it may also be applied to any other case

§ 179.-Voluntary Dismissals.-The Supreme Court rules provide that the appellant in any equity appeal, or the appellant and appellee jointly, where the appellee has assigned errors, may dismiss the appeal at any time by filing with the clerk of the Supreme Court a præcipe signed by his or their attorneys of record dismissing the appeal and paying the costs thereof. Upon the appeal being thus dismissed, it is the duty of the clerk to certify the fact of the dismissal to the lower court.358 The dismissal of an appeal must be in the Supreme Court, and an attempted dismissal by the circuit court is a nullity.359 However, where the appellant attempts to dismiss his appeal in the circuit court, and then enters and perfects a second appeal, which the appellee does not move to dismiss, on the ground of the pendency of the first, until after briefs had been filed and the second appeal called for oral argument, the rule will not be strictly applied. The appellant having unmistakably abandoned his first appeal, and the appellee having been guilty of great delay in moving to dismiss the second, the first appeal will be dismissed for failure to file a transcript, and the second appeal will be allowed to proceed to a disposition on its merits.360

The appellant has a clear right to the dismissal of his appeal unless it appears that the rights of the appellee would be prejudiced thereby, or unless the cause is ready for final disposition. Thus the appellant may, even after the cause is set down for oral argument, move to dismiss his appeal, and if the appellee has filed no cross assignments of error, the court is bound by the provisions

Where, pending an appeal, a cause has been settled by compromise or otherwise, it is the duty of both parties to notify the Supreme Court of the settlement, and the appellant is required, within ten days after the settlement, to file in the Supreme Court a præcipe for dismissal of the cause, which will then be dismissed.364 And where the parties have agreed upon a settlement and dismissal, and the Supreme Court is advised of the matter, it will dismiss the appeal of its own motion.365 Such a settlement renders the appeal moot, and where the appeal is from a final decree, the usual procedure is to reverse the decree with direc tions to dismiss the proceedings below without costs to either party.366

However, where appropriate, the settlement may be put into effect by a final decree embracing its terms.367 If the appeal was from an interlocutory decree, the decree should be reversed without prejudice and the cause remanded for appropriate disposition in accordance with the stipulation of the parties for a settlement, especially where the parties have acted upon the agreement between them.368

Where the appellee files a confession of error, serving notice thereof on the appellant, the Supreme Court will reverse the decree appealed from, without giving any views as to the extent of the error, and remand the cause for the elimination of the errors confessed and for further appropriate proceedings.369

§ 180.-Duty of Appellate Court.-A statute makes it the duty of the Supreme Court, on an appeal, to examine the record, to reverse or affirm the decree of the court below, or to give such decree as the court below ought to have given or as it may appear according to law.370

In general, when it appears that the cause was tried and determined by the chancellor in the lower court in accordance with the established rules of law and procedure, and the evidence amply sustains the chancellor's findings of fact when viewed in the light of the authorities, the decree appealed from will be affirmed.371 

On appeal from an order granting a motion to dismiss the bill of complaint, if any one ground of the motion is well taken, the order will be affirmed.372 When a motion to dismiss a bill for multifariousness is incorporated in an answer, and the motion is denied at the final hearing, the ruling will not ordinarily be reversed.373

§ 181.-Presumptions and Burden on Appellant.-It is well settled that in equity, as well as at law, every presumption is in favor of the correctness of the rulings of the trial judge, and it is the duty of the party resorting to an appellate court to make the errors complained. of clearly appear, if they in truth exist.394 It has also been frequently stated that, on an appeal, the rulings of the chancellor who tried the cause are presumed to be correct, and the burden is on the appellant to make it clearly appear that such rulings are erroneous. 

If the appellant does not meet this burden, the decree will be affirmed.395

These principles are particularly applicable to findings of fact, and the rule is that a final decree based largely or solely upon questions of fact will not be reversed unless the evidence clearly shows that it is erroneous.396 This is especially true where the testimony was taken before the chancellor,397 and it is true even though there

The 

Supreme Court will take judicial notice that, under the rules for the preparation of transcripts, the entire record below need not be brought up to the appellate court, but only such parts of the record as may be designated by the parties. Therefore, the absence from the transcript of any evidence that some necessary step or action was taken in the lower court is no evidence in the appellate court that such step or action was not in fact taken. It will be presumed that the proceedings below were correct.404

And while a correct result will not be reversed because it is based upon an incorrect reason, yet the appellate court will and should reverse a decree that has demonstrably resulted from the chancellor's misconception of the application of a rule of law to the facts of the case and where it is made to appear that, but for the misconception, a contrary decree would probably have been entered.440 Likewise, a decree will be reversed where there is a substantial doubt as to whether the chancellor's decision was the result of a correct or erroneous view of the principles of law applicable to the case.441 § 185.-No Reversal for Harmless Error.-A Florida statute442 provides that no judgment shall be set aside or reversed by any court of this state in any cause, civil or criminal, on the ground of the improper admission or rejection of evidence or for error as to any matter of pleading or procedure unless, in the opinion of the court to which application is made, after an examination of the entire case, it appears that the error complained of has resulted in a miscarriage of justice. The statute further provides that it shall be liberally construed. 

The Florida courts, therefore, follow what is known as the orthodox English rule rather than the rule announced by the Court of Exchequer in 1830 that injury will always be presumed from error committed. The latter rule led to such absurd results that it was subsequently abolished in England in 1875.443 But the orthodox rule had obtained in chancery causes long prior to the enactment of the foregoing statute. The statute merely extended the rule to other causes.444

It is established by a long line of cases that a final decree in equity will be affirmed where alleged errors in pleading and procedure are merely technical, formal, and unimportant irregularities and have not resulted in a miscarriage of justice, or where it is

§ 186.—Appeals from Interlocutory Decrees.-Under the original equity practice in Florida an appeal would lie only from a final decree.453

This rule was changed, however, by a statute enacted in 1852 providing as follows: "Appeals may be taken and prosecuted from any interlocutory order, decision, judgment or decree of the circuit courts of this state, when sitting as courts of equity; but the conferring of the right shall not be construed so as to deprive either party from deferring and postponing the entry of his appeal until after the entry of the final decree, or end of the cause as prescribed by law; nor shall such postponement of the appeal be decreed, held or taken to be an acquiescence in the propriety of any interlocutory order or decree made in the progress of the case, or any waiver of any error therein."454

The object of the statute permitting interlocutory appeals in chancery cases was to expedite the administration of justice by providing a means by which questions of law involved in the procedural steps of an equity suit might be finally and authoritatively settled by an appellate court and become the law of the case with reference to subsequent proceedings.455 It was also the purpose of the statute to permit separate appeals from interlocutory orders without interfering with the right to have all prior interlocutory decrees opened up for consideration on an appeal from the final decree.456

In accordance with the statute it is well settled that an appeal will lie from an interlocutory order.457 Thus an order denying

Where the appeal is not from a final decree, but from one or more interlocutory decrees, errors based on other interlocutory decrees not specifically appealed from will not be considered by the appellate court.465 Likewise, upon an appeal from one interlocutory decree, it is necessary, in order to entitle the appellee to the consideration of cross assignments of error based upon another interlocutory decree, that he enter a cross appeal from the latter decree.466

Where an appeal from an interlocutory order is taken after a final decree has been rendered in a cause, and no appeal is taken from the final decree, the appellate court will dismiss the appeal from the interlocutory order. This is done, not because of a want of jurisdiction in the appellate court, but because any error in the interlocutory order may have been cured or rendered immaterial by the final decree rendered before the appeal from the interlocutory order was taken. In such a case, the appellant is at fault in bringing only a portion of the cause to the appellate court when the whole cause has been adjudicated and disposed of by a final decree.468 Thus there can be no separate appeal from an order dissolving an injunction while there is a standing order dismissing the bill.469

But where an appeal is taken from an interlocutory order before a final decree is rendered in a cause, the appellate court will not dismiss the appeal merely because the appellant did not also take an appeal from the final decree subsequently rendered. In such a case, the jurisdiction of the appellate court having attached by virtue of the appeal from the interlocutory order taken before the entry of the final decree, all subsequent proceedings, including the final decree, are subject to the decision made on the appeal from the interlocutory order. To dismiss an appeal under such circumstances would be to constitute the lower court the sole and final arbiter of the correctness of interlocutory orders and divest the Supreme Court of its power to review them. It is true that the plaintiff had the right to take an appeal from the final decree, but his failure to do so does not deprive him of his rights and status under the interlocutory appeal previously taken.470

However, even though an interlocutory appeal has been taken before a final decree, the final decree subsequently entered may sometimes cure the errors in the interlocutory orders. Therefore, when the final decree has also been appealed from, the appellate court will first examine it to determine if any errors in the interlocutory orders have been cured and, if they have, the interlocutory appeal will be dismissed as moot.471 And where separate appeals from a final decree and two interlocutory decrees are pending, and the Supreme Court finds it necessary to affirm the final decree on its merits, it need only consider such questions raised by the two preceding interlocutory appeals as, had they been decided differently, would have changed the result reached in the final decree.472

An appeal from an interlocutory order does not, in the absence of a supersedeas, deprive the lower court of the right to proceed with the cause until the appeal is decided and the cause remanded. 

Of course, a party who proceeds with a cause after his adversary has taken an interlocutory appeal assumes the risk of the effect of an adverse decision of the appellate court on his rights.473 If a final decree is entered before the interlocutory appeal is decided, it is not erroneous, but it is subject to the decree made by the appellate court on the interlocutory appeal.474 But the reversal of an interlocutory order for errors therein does not render invalid subsequent decrees into which the errors have not been carried.475 

The affirmance of an interlocutory order on appeal conclusively fixes the status of that order as an adjudication of the propositions of law embraced in it so far as those propositions have been discussed and decided on the appeal. Such an adjudication necessarily precludes a change or amendment of the record in the lower court, after the mandate has gone down, which would defeat in whole or in part the effect of the appellate court's decision.476

Not only will an appeal lie from an interlocutory decree, but an appeal may also be taken from a decree rendered subsequent to a final decree wherein the court has taken judicial action in regard to the rights litigated in the main suit. But such an appeal must be prosecuted on some new and distinct ground not covered by the final decree. Only matters arising subsequent to the final decree can be reviewed.477 Thus a decree confirming a sale and entering a deficiency judgment in a mortgage foreclosure is appealable.478 § 187.-Scope of Review.-An appeal in equity is not a new suit, but it is regarded as a continuation of the suit below. In the language of the statute,479 it is regarded "as a step in the cause."480 

Consequently, the effect of an appeal is to transfer the whole record to the appellate court,481 to subject the facts as well as the law to review and retrial,482 and to open the whole case for consideration on its merits without reference to strict requirements as to assigning and considering errors in the appellate court.483 

This power follows from the statutory authority484 conferred upon the Supreme Court to reverse or affirm the decree of the court below, to award a new trial, or to give such decree as the court below ought to have given. It is very clear that the power to give the decree which the court below ought to have given could never be exercised if the Supreme Court did not possess the right to look into the whole case as it is presented by the record, and to consider it as the court below should have considered it. Accordingly, while the appellant may show that the view taken by the lower court was erroneous, the appellee may argue and show, if he can, that upon the whole case the same result must be reached on appeal. On an appeal from a final decree which has been entered upon a decree pro confesso, the scope of the review is limited to two general questions. The first is the correctness of the proceedings prior to the decree pro confesso. The second is the sufficiency of the bill of complaint to state a case warranting equitable relief. 

It is well settled that on an appeal from a final decree entered upon a decree pro confesso the regularity of all proceedings anterior to the order taking the bill as confessed may be questioned.494 Thus where a decree pro confesso is entered against a defendant for failure to answer after his motion to dismiss the bill is denied, he may, on appeal from a final decree subsequently entered, bring before the Supreme Court the correctness of the order denying his motion to dismiss.495 Likewise, an appellant may obtain a review of orders, entered prior to a decree pro confesso, adjudging his answer to be insufficient as a defense.496 But after a decree pro confesso is entered, the proceedings are ex parte, and they cannot be reviewed on appeal no matter how irregular or erroneous they may be.497

It is also clear that, on appeal, a final decree consequent upon a decree pro confesso may be examined to determine if it is warranted by the case made by the bill.498 If the bill does not state a case warranting equitable relief, or if there is an adequate remedy at law, the final decree will be reversed with appropriate directions notwithstanding the decree pro confesso.499 Likewise, the final

§ 189.-Effect of Decision of Appellate Court.-All points adju dicated by the Supreme Court on an appeal become the law of the case and are no longer open for discussion and consideration.517 

The "law of the case" means that the decision of a question of law by a court of last resort must govern the trial court in all subsequent proceedings in the same case and that such a decision will seldom be reconsidered or reversed, even though it appears to have been erroneously decided.517A Consequently, a subsequent appeal does not open up matters that have thus become res judicata. It is also the general rule that, where a party to a suit has assumed a position on a former appeal, and carried his case to an appellate court on a particular theory asserted on the record, he is estopped to assert, in a subsequent pleading or appeal, any other and inconsistent position towards the same parties and subject matter. This is not the doctrine of res judicata, but the doctrine of estoppel against inconsistent positions in judicial proceedings. 

It is based upon the theory that, where a party has made a record of the facts on which he bases his case, and has sought and obtained a final judicial judgment upon them, he is estopped to thereafter deny those allegations, and set up a new and different state of facts wholly inconsistent with them, to the prejudice of the adverse party.538

There is no doubt of the proposition that upon the reversal of a decree, where no supersedeas has been had, the law raises an obligation in the party to the record who has received the benefit of the erroneous decree to make restitution to the other party, the mode of restitution to be varied according to the circumstances of the case. In a perfectly plain case, where there can be no dispute about the facts, restitution may be ordered by the appellate court. But, ordinarily, application should be made by petition or motion to the lower court, which will investigate the facts and order the appellants to be restored to all things that they have lost by reason of the decree which was reversed.539 But anything done under a decree subsequently reversed, and the enforcement of which has not been superseded, is valid insofar as third parties are concerned.540

Where the Supreme Court has rendered a decision on an appeal in one suit which is applicable to an appeal then pending in another suit, the court will take notice of the decision and dispose of the latter appeal accordingly.541

§ 190.-Costs of Appeal.-Costs on appeals in chancery cases are not taxed as of course against the losing party but are taxed under the order of the court and the amount thereof should be entered in the body of the judgment or order. 542 It is the duty of the parties to a cause in the Supreme Court to file a statement of the items of costs they are entitled to recover. If they fail to do so, the court will not, after the expiration of the term at which the appeal was disposed of, order a retaxation of the costs so as to include items not shown by the record to have been erroneously omitted.543

Items which may properly be taxed as costs on an appeal include the cost of the transcript of record, all costs incurred in the proceedings in the cause in the lower court after the entry of the appeal which are properly a part of the appeal, and the costs shown to be due by the files of the clerk of the Supreme Court.544 

The cost of a copy of the opinion of the court to be certified to the clerk of the circuit court is also includible.545 The premiums paid for a supersedeas bond may be taxed as costs only when the bond is given by a fiduciary.546 

Where costs incident to an appeal do not follow the judgment, they are usually apportioned so as to do equity.547 Where neither party is diligent in avoiding the necessity of litigation, the costs. will be imposed equally upon them.548 Where the plaintiff's recovery is considerably reduced on appeal, the costs thereof will be imposed on the appellant and appellee in equal shares.549 On appeal from a decree foreclosing a lien, the allowance of excessive interest has been held to authorize the taxation of one-half the costs against the appellee.550 Where both parties appeal from

§ 191.—Rehearing in Appellate Court.-Rehearings before the 

Supreme Court must be applied for within fifteen days after the filing of the judgment, decree, or order of the court, unless further time is allowed by the court. The petition must not assume any new ground or position not taken upon the argument or in the points made upon which the case was submitted, but must set forth concisely the particular omission or cause for which the judgment is supposed to be erroneous. The court will consider the petition without argument.556

The proper function of a petition for a rehearing is to present to the court in clear, concise terms some material point that the court failed to consider. § 192.-Nature and Purpose.-A bill of review is in the nature of a writ of error, and its object is to procure an examination and alteration or reversal of a decree rendered upon a former bill.' 

A bill of this character can be brought only upon an error of law appearing on the face of the decree, without further examination of matters of fact, or upon some new matter which has been discovered after the decree and which could not possibly have been used when the decree was made.2 

The decisions distinguish between bills of review, bills in the nature of bills of review, and supplemental bills in the nature of bills of review. Although the decisions are not entirely clear on the exact line of demarcation between these classes of bills, it may in general be stated that a bill in the nature of a bill of review is one filed after a decree has been pronounced, but before it has been entered, and having the same object as a bill of review.³ A bill to impeach a decree for fraud is also usually referred to as an

So far as the necessity of entitling a bill as being in one or the other of these classes is concerned, the distinction between them has undoubtedly been abolished by the 1931 Chancery Act. But, insofar as different requirements as to time of filing and obtaining leave of court to file such bills is concerned, it is equally clear that the 1931 Chancery Act has effected no change in the former practice.7 

A bill of review should be distinguished from a motion to vacate a decree. Where a decree is shown by the record in the case to be absolutely void, it may be vacated or stricken from the record at any time, and it is subject to collateral attack. § 194.-Grounds-Error Apparent. One of the two grounds upon which a bill of review may be brought is to procure the alteration or reversal of a decree made in a former suit for an error apparent upon the face of the decree without an examination of the matters of fact upon which it is based. Such a bill cannot be maintained where the error is in a mere matter of form, or where the propriety of the decree is questioned. The decree complained of must be contrary to some principle or rule of law or equity recognized and acknowledged or settled by decisions. In order to ascertain if there is error in the decree, the general practice is to look back of the decree into the whole record of the pleadings and proceedings. The error must be apparent on the face of the record, that is, upon the bill, answer, and other pleadings and proceedings and the decree. It is not allowable to look into the evidence.14 

The purpose of a bill of review for error apparent is to have the court rendering the decree give the same relief that the appellate court would have given under the same circumstances.15 Thus, for example, a bill of review for error apparent will lie to correct a final decree in which a personal judgment for the recovery of money is entered against a married woman.16 It will also lie to procure the amendment of a decree for the specific performance of a contract to convey land so as to require the vendor to convey a merchantable title, free of encumbrances.17 

Likewise, where a final decree for the foreclosure of a mortgage upon partnership property erroneously construes the mortgage to include property afterward acquired by one of the partners in

Where the bill does not justify the final decree which has been entered it may be corrected by bill of review in the court rendering the decree, or by an appeal.1 19 

§ 195.-Grounds-Newly Discovered Evidence.-The second ground upon which a bill of review may be maintained is for newly discovered evidence.

In order to be a ground for a bill of review, the newly discovered evidence must be relevant and material, and of such weight and character that on a rehearing it will probably produce a different result and one more beneficial to the plaintiff than the original decree. As a general rule, a bill of review cannot be grounded on new evidence of a merely cumulative character. But the rule as to cumulative evidence is not absolute, the matter being, in its final analysis, one of discretion. This discretion will be exercised sparingly and cautiously, but affirmatively to entertain the bill, where the evidence, though cumulative, is decisive of the case.20 

Similarly, a bill of review cannot ordinarily be founded upon evidence which goes merely to the impeachment of witnesses. But the discovery that the evidence upon which a decree rests is perjured or forged is a recognized ground of a bill of review, as where the newly discovered evidence of the perjury is written, or record evidence of a witness' conviction of perjury is offered.21 

There is some indication, in the early cases, to the effect that, where the new evidence relates to issues previously tried, it must be of a permanent and decisive character, such as a document or

It has also been said, in an early case, that the new matter must be in proof of what was previously in issue, and not in proof of a title not previously in issue. In other words, the newly discovered evidence was required to establish the old case, and not make a new one.23 But the modern and better rule is that any evidence, whether written or oral, and whether relating to matters in issue on the former hearing or entirely new matters, will sustain a bill of review if it is material to the merits of the case and of sufficient probative force to justify the conclusion that it will change the result if a new hearing is had. This rule is borne out by the fact that the recent cases declaring newly discovered evidence to be a ground for a bill of review contain no requirement as to the character of the evidence or the nature of the issues to which it relates.24 

Another essential requirement of a bill of review on the ground of newly discovered evidence is a showing that the matter was not discovered until after the rendition of the decree attacked and could not, by the exercise of reasonable diligence, have been discovered before the hearing or the rendition of the decree.25 Mere forgetfulness is no excuse for not producing witnesses in the original cause. The same is true of poverty, or ignorance of the party, and of his counsel's negligence or erroneous advice. Matters of public record cannot be made the basis of a bill of review on the ground of newly discovered evidence. Where persons were known to have knowledge regarding the matters in controversy, their mere refusal to state what their testimony would be is no excuse for not calling them as witnesses in the original cause. But prior concealment of all knowledge by them does excuse the failure.26

§ 196.-Grounds-Fraud.-Although there are some indications in early decisions to the contrary, 28 a bill to impeach a final decree for fraud, being a direct attack upon the final decree, is usually referred to as a bill in the nature of a bill of review.29 

Thus a bill attacking a final decree upon the ground of fraud perpetrated by counsel in the case, and by officers of a corporation which was a party to the case, has been held to be a bill in the nature of a bill of review.30 Likewise, it has been held that a bill in the nature of a bill of review is the proper method of attacking a final decree of foreclosure which was entered as a result of a fraudulent agreement between the original mortgagor and a grantee of the mortgaged property who had issued a second mortgage, whereby they were to extinguish the second mortgage by defaulting on the first and bidding in the property at the foreclosure sale.31 And, a bill in the nature of a bill of review has been used with approval for the purpose of vacating a consent decree which was entered in pursuance of an agreement obtained by fraud.32

§ 198.-Time and Place of Filing.-There is no statute in Florida fixing the time within which bills of review must be filed. But the analogy between an appeal and a bill of review for error apparent on the face of the record is so apparent that the latter may be considered as necessarily comprehended within the equity of the statutory provisions governing the time for taking an appeal. For, if a bill of review for error apparent could be filed after the expiration of the six months allowed for taking an appeal, an original decree might, in effect, be brought before the appellate court for re-examination, after the period prescribed by law for an immediate appeal therefrom, by appealing from the decree on the bill of review.38

Consequently, the general rule, both in England and the various jurisdictions of the United States, is that, except for some very clear reason, such as the plaintiff's disability, a bill of review for error apparent on the face of the record must be brought within the time allowed by law for taking an appeal. It is likewise well settled in Florida that a bill of review for error apparent on the face of the record must ordinarily be filed before the expiration of

A bill of review based upon newly discovered evidence is not, however, subject to the same restrictions as to the time of filing as a bill of review for error apparent. Bills of the former class are controlled largely by the discretion of the court and they are not limited in the time of filing to the six months allowed for taking an appeal.40 But such a bill should be filed as soon after the discovery of the new matter as it reasonably may be.41 A sound rule is that a bill of review for newly discovered evidence should be brought within the time for taking an appeal after the discovery of the new facts or evidence.42 Accordingly, it has been held that a bill of review to set aside a decree of foreclosure and sale under a special assessment lien is maintainable where it is brought within six months after the statute under which the special assessment was levied was held unconstitutional and void.43

§ 202.-In General.-While courts of law have jurisdiction to enforce contract demands that involve an accounting, yet courts of equity also have jurisdiction of cases in which contract demands between litigants involve extensive mutual or complicated accounts.¹ But it is not every account which will entitle a court of equity to interfere. It must be such an account as cannot be justly and fairly taken in a court of law.2 The jurisdiction of courts of equity is predicated upon the greater facility and more improved methods of taking the account therein, and it can only be defeated by showing that, in the particular case, the remedy at law is as full, adequate, and complete as it is in equity.4 Suits for an accounting are most commonly brought to settle and wind up the affairs of partnerships and where a fiduciary relation exists. The question of liability on a bond is purely a matter of common law cognizance, and a court of equity has no jurisdiction of it unless there is some extraneous matter which gives it jurisdiction. 

But this general rule is subject to the equally well recognized exception that, where a court of equity has acquired jurisdiction to compel an accounting from a fiduciary, the sureties on the fiduciary's bond may not only be made parties defendant to the suit, but their liability on the bond may be enforced therein. However, before the liability of sureties may be enforced in equity, it must appear that equity has jurisdiction to compel an accounting on the facts stated in the bill, and that a fiduciary relationship exists between the plaintiff and the principal obligor. When these requirements are met, equity may give judgment against both principal and sureties, the only limitation being that, in the decree rendered, execution must be so limited as to require satisfaction first against the principal, unless he is shown to be insolvent, and secondarily against the sureties.41

§ 206.-Parties.-Where a bill for a general accounting and settle ment is filed by heirs and distributees against an executor, all the distributees are necessary parties to the suit.45 Likewise, where one of several wards brings a bill for an accounting against his guardian, the other wards who may be interested in the general funds must be made parties to the suit.46. In a suit for an accounting on the bond of a deceased guardian who left no estate, his legal representative need not be joined.47

A corporation substantially owned by a decedent, and the assets of which are being dissipated by an executor pending a proceeding to have the will declared spurious, is a proper party plaintiff to a suit against the executor for an accounting.48

Where a bill primarily seeks an accounting, and the remaining relief asked is incidental and germane thereto, the bill is proper for the consideration of a court of equity.62 Thus a surviving partner may demand an accounting from the administrator of a deceased partner and, where there are no partnership assets, he may join an independent claim against the deceased in the same bill.63 But a bill against an administrator and widow for an accounting of the assets of an estate received by them should not be joined with a demand against the widow for an accounting of the rents and profits of the homestead. There is no requirement that a bill for an accounting be verified by the oath of the plaintiff. It need only be signed by his counsel.65 

§ 208.-Answer and Counterclaim.-As respects an accounting, as long as the fiduciary relation exists between guardian and ward, the statute of limitations does not run and the doctrine of laches is inapplicable. Nor is the ward's right to an accounting defeated by mere lapse of time after marriage or becoming of age. 

The possession of the trust funds by the guardian is not adverse to the equitable title of the ward, but consistent with it. The guardian could have terminated the trust relation when the ward married or became of age by obtaining a legal discharge or making a direct settlement. His duty to account continues until this is done.66 

Likewise, a ward is not barred by laches from maintaining a suit for an accounting on the bond of a deceased guardian where the ward was of immature years when the transactions complained of occurred and the guardian failed to make full disclosures to the county judge in regard thereto.67

While the rule is well established that affirmative relief cannot be decreed in favor of a defendant except upon a counterclaim or cross-bill,70 suits for an accounting are a recognized exception to the rule. In such suits both parties are deemed actors and the defendant may have affirmative relief on the facts alleged in his answer.71 The court has authority to determine what is due from. one party to the other under the pleadings and proof, without a counterclaim, and to enter a money decree for that amount against the party found to be indebted.72 § 209.-Taking of Testimony.-On a bill to dissolve a partnership and for an accounting, the fact of a co-partnership should be decreed before the defendant is required to account.73

§ 212.— Appeals.—Accounting suits are generally single, not severable, controversies as respects the right to appeal from one portion of a decree while accepting benefits under another portion.104 

The rules and principles governing all equity appeals apply equally to appeals in accounting suits. Accounts which went before the master without exception cannot be objected to on appeal.105 An appeal opens the whole case for review by the appellate court. 106 The burden is on the appellant to make it clearly appear that the rulings of the chancellor in rejecting credits claimed in the course of the accounting are erroneous. 107 And, upon an accounting in a case where a master has taken and reported the evidence, in which there is some conflict, and where the chancellor has reviewed the evidence and entered a decree for an amount found to be due one party by the other, and there is sufficient evidence to support the decree as to the amount found due, it will not be reversed.108 A final decree of accounting will not be reversed because some items of relatively small amount, taken by themselves and without regard to the entire record, may appear doubtful.109 

In matters of account, where books are used before a master, the appellate court will not affirm a decree in their absence on the presumption that they contain evidence in addition to that reported by the master which will support the decree. If there is anything in the books which is material to the appellee's case, it must be copied in the record or otherwise brought before the court.110

§ 213.-Definition of Creditor's Bill.-A creditor's bill is one brought by a creditor who has secured a judgment at law, who has in vain attempted to satisfy it at law, and who sues in equity for the purpose of reaching property which cannot be reached by execution at law.¹

The original concept of a creditor's bill was a suit in equity brought by the creditors of a deceased person for the administration of his estate, or by creditors and claimants of a trust fund for the distribution of the fund. A like name has also been applied to proceedings by creditors to set aside a fraudulent conveyance or to remove encumbrances hindering an execution at law. As now applied, however, a creditor's bill is one brought by a party who has secured a judgment which he is unable to satisfy at law and who sues in equity for the purpose of subjecting to the payment of his judgment property which cannot be so subjected by execution at law.2

The nature, purpose, and scope of a creditor's bill is to invoke the equity powers of the court to enforce the satisfaction of a judgment by means of an equitable execution because execution at law cannot be enforced. It is in the nature of an equitable execution, 1. Armour v. First National Bank,

or equitable relief, which is granted solely on the ground that there is no remedy at law. Creditors' bills originated in the ineffectiveness of legal execution and were designed to aid creditors who had exhausted their legal remedies without obtaining satisfaction of their judgments and who sought to reach property of their debtors not reachable by ordinary legal process.³ § 214. Meaning of Equitable Asset.-A creditor's bill may only be maintained where it is sought to reach an equitable asset of the judgment debtor. If the property sought to be reached is subject to an execution at law, a creditor's bill will not lie.4 

There are numerous kinds of equitable assets which may be reached by a creditor's bill. The Florida statutes5 provide that lands and tenements, goods and chattels, equities of redemption in real and personal property, and stock in corporations, shall be subject to levy and sale under execution. Any kind of property not designated in the statute is considered as an equitable asset and it can only be reached by a creditor's bill. Thus a real estate mortgage, being merely a lien upon land, is not, under the statutes, subject to an execution at law, but it may be a proper subject for a creditor's bill in equity. An interest in a trust fund, whether created by the debtor or another, must be reached by a creditor's bill, and this applies equally to a debtor's interest under a resulting or constructive trust.7

Where a husband incurs debts for property used for the benefit of his wife's separate estate, and judgments against him on the debts cannot be satisfied out of his own property, a creditor may, on a bill filed for that purpose, obtain satisfaction out of the separate property of the wife. Had the husband paid these debts, he would have been entitled to reimbursement out of his wife's property and, the husband being without means, the creditor is. entitled to the same equity. The most common type of equitable asset sought to be reached by a creditor's bill is a debtor's interest in real or personal property which he has purchased but title to which has been taken in the name of another. It is well settled that, if real or personal property is bought and paid for by one person, but by his direction title is conveyed by the vendor to another, creditors of the person buying the property cannot reach it by an execution at law. They must seek relief in equity.10

This rule applies especially to cases where title to the property is taken in the name of the debtor's wife. Where property is purchased and paid for by the husband, and a deed is taken in the name of his wife, it is not subject to an execution at law. Property of a debtor which stands in the name of his wife may even be reached by subsequent creditors. Proof of prior debts, insolvency at the time of the purchase, becoming insolvent by reason of the purchase, or the design and purpose of hindering and delaying those to whom he is about to become indebted, are some of the indicia of fraud which will enable a subsequent creditor to reach such property. Proving payment of prior debts amounts to nothing if it appears that the debtor is acquiring other debts.¹4 

It should be noted, however, that there is a clear distinction between cases where a debtor buys property and takes title in the name of another, and cases where he has title to property and conveys it to another for the purpose of defrauding his creditors. In the latter class of cases the property may be reached by an execution at law. A bill in equity may also be maintained to remove the conveyance, as an obstruction to the full enforcement of a judgment lien, and to subject the property to the payment of the judgment, but such a bill is not a creditor's bill within the present meaning of that term.15

The right to maintain a creditor's bill to reach equitable assets is not defeated by a discharge in bankruptcy where the property involved was not administered by the bankruptcy court.16 

Where a debtor had good legal title by deed and adverse possession, but the title deed has been lost and the record thereof destroyed by fire, a creditor's bill will not lie. The whole matter is cognizable in a court of law.17 Where a husband contracts to buy land, enters into possession, makes improvements, and pays part of the purchase price, but is unable to complete his payments, and such payments are completed by his wife with her own money, the husband has no equitable interest in the land which can be subjected to sale under a creditor's bill for the payment of his judgment debts.18

In fact, the very nature of a creditor's bill often negatives the objection of multifariousness that might ordinarily apply to other bills in chancery as to parties plaintiff, as the very purpose of such a bill is to prevent a multiplicity of suits by allowing several creditors, although having unrelated claims, to join in one suit. 

It must appear, however, that each creditor seeks substantially the same relief and that the same defenses are applicable to each.21 

A trustee in bankruptcy is vested with all the rights, remedies, and powers of a judgment creditor having an execution at law returned unsatisfied, and he may maintain a creditor's bill to reach equitable assets of the bankrupt and to have them sold and the proceeds applied to the payment of the debts proved against the bankrupt. 22 However, such a right in the trustee is not exclusive, and a creditor may maintain a bill to reach equitable assets notwithstanding that the debtor has been adjudicated a bankrupt and that the fund obtained must be administered by the bankruptcy court. 23

§ 217.-Necessity for Judgment and Execution at Law.-Under the original Florida rule, a creditor's bill could not be maintained unless it was shown that the plaintiff had recovered a judgment against the defendant at law and that an execution had been issued on the judgment and returned nulla bona.28 The creditor's right to relief in such cases depended upon the fact of his having exhausted his legal remedies without being able to obtain satisfaction, and the best, if not the only, evidence of this was the actual return of an execution unsatisfied.29 The assumption was that if the debtor had legal title to property, which he then held or had fraudulently conveyed, an execution at law could be satisfied without the necessity of a suit in equity, while, if the debtor had only an equitable title, that fact could not be properly ascertained until an execution at law was actually served and returned unsatisfied.30 

Under the original rule, a judgment obtained subsequent to the filing of a creditor's bill was not sufficient to support the equitable jurisdiction.31

The foregoing rule was altered, however, by a statute enacted in 1903. That statute provides: "A creditor's bill may be filed in the courts of this state, having chancery jurisdiction, before the claims of indebtedness of the persons filing the same shall have been reduced to judgment, but no such bill shall be entertained by such court, unless the complainants therein shall have first instituted suits in the proper courts at law for the collection of their claims; and no final decree shall be entered upon such creditor's bill until such claims shall have been reduced to judgment."32

The effect of the foregoing statute is to permit a creditor's bill to be maintained before the claims of indebtedness of the persons filing it have been reduced to judgment. But an action at law must have been instituted for that purpose prior to the filing of the bill, and no final decree can be entered in the creditor's suit until the claims of indebtedness have been reduced to judgment at law.33 

Institution of a suit at law is a jurisdictional prerequisite to the entertainment of a creditor's bill.34

The statute does not change the prevailing rule that, before a creditor can have the relief afforded by a creditor's bill, he must first secure a judgment at law and show that an execution issued upon the judgment has been returned nulla bona. The provision in the statute that "no final decree shall be entered upon such creditor's bill until such claims shall have been reduced to judgment" indicates that no change in the existing law was intended other than to allow a creditor's bill to be filed before judgment at law is rendered. In other words, a creditor's bill may be filed before judgment in the law action, but the creditor cannot obtain relief in the creditor's suit until after the judgment at law is rendered and the legal means of satisfying that judgment have been exhausted. A creditor's bill is not an alternative method of collecting a debt, but the remedy thereby afforded can be resorted to

The rule that the institution of a suit or the entry of judgment at law will support a creditor's bill is not without its restrictions. 

A void judgment will not support a creditor's bill.36 The mere institution of a suit at law for damages not involving a claim of indebtedness does not warrant a creditor's suit or the granting of extraordinary relief, such as an injunction or receiver, therein.37 

A suit at law is not pending, within the meaning of the statute, where it appears that no service of process has been had and cannot be had.38 But a deficiency decree entered by an equity court in a suit for the foreclosure of a mortgage will support a creditor's suit.39 And a judgment against a non-resident defendant in a law action instituted by attachment will support a creditor's bill.40 

The rule that a creditor must obtain a judgment at law before he can be granted relief in a creditor's suit is not without its exceptions. It has been seen that a judgment at law and an execution returned unsatisfied is required as proof that legal remedies have been exhausted and that the intervention of equity is necessary to reach an equitable asset. But this is not the only method of proving the ineffectiveness of the legal remedies and, where the necessity of resorting to a court of equity is otherwise made to appear, it will not require meaningless formalities. Thus, where the defendant is a non-resident, and personal service upon him cannot be had, and he has no property in the state which could be reached by an attachment proceeding, a creditor's bill may be maintained without the institution of a suit or the recovery of a judgment at law.41 Likewise, where the creditor of a partnership seeks the satisfaction of a partnership debt out of the estate of a deceased partner, no action at law will lie, and therefore a creditor's bill may be maintained directly upon the claim.42

§ 218.-Bill of Complaint.-The plaintiff in a creditor's bill must allege in his bill every fact, clearly and definitely, that is necessary to entitle him to relief, and if he omits essential facts therefrom, or states facts which show that he is not entitled to relief in a court of equity, he must suffer the consequences of his so doing.46 

The rules of equity pleading apply with the same force to a creditor's bill as to any other kind of a bill of complaint. Since a court of equity will not aid a plaintiff in a creditor's bill where there is an adequate remedy at law, a creditor's bill, like every other bill, must allege facts sufficient to invoke the jurisdiction of equity. The allegations relating to jurisdiction cannot be general, such as that the plaintiff has no remedy, or no adequate remedy, without the assistance of a court of equity, but facts must be alleged showing that only in equity will the plaintiff's remedy be full, adequate, and complete.46A Thus, among other things, a creditor's bill must allege that the plaintiff's claim has been reduced to judgment and an execution returned nulla bona, or that an action at law has been instituted on his claim.47

When a creditor's bill makes no reference to any property that could properly be classed as an equitable asset or interest of the judgment debtor it does not state a case for equitable relief.48

Reference to property to which the debtor had legal title, but which he has fraudulently conveyed, will not support a creditor's bill within the present meaning of that term. There is provided by statute a specific remedy at law for all judgment creditors against property to which the judgment debtor had legal title but which he subsequently conveyed.49

A bill to reach equitable assets of a judgment debtor, brought by one not a party to the judgment, must show the plaintiff's title to or ownership of the judgment. An allegation of ownership of the execution issued thereon, which has been returned unsatisfied, is insufficient.50

A creditor's bill is not multifarious because it seeks discovery and relief against several who are not united in interest and who are strangers to each other where the object of the bill is to reach various assets of the principal debtor in their several possessions.51 

Likewise, a creditor's bill is not subject to dismissal for the joinder of causes of action, in some of which particular defendants have no interest, when the case presented by the bill is so entire that it cannot be prosecuted in several suits, and when each of the defendants is a necessary party to some part of the case stated.52 

§ 219.-Priority of Complaining Creditor.-In a suit filed by a judgment creditor to discover and reach assets not subject to an execution at law, the rule is that the creditor who first institutes suit and serves his summons, or otherwise entitles himself to the law of lis pendens, acquires a lien upon the assets which his bill seeks to reach, and upon obtaining a decree he is entitled to the fruits of his diligence. But, if the property is subject to an execution at law so that the plaintiff can levy on it, it is not, before it vests in a receiver, so bound by a bill that it cannot be levied on and sold under an execution issued by another creditor.53 Each creditor is, however, entitled to appear before the master and there contest the claim of any other creditor.54

[Ch. 23 § 220.-Final Decree.-The proper decree in a creditor's suit is for the sale of the equitable asset sought to be reached and the application of the proceeds of the sale to the payment of the plaintiff's judgment.55 Any surplus would be payable to the defendant or to such other creditors as establish their right to payment therefrom. Pending a final decree, it is proper for the court to appoint a receiver to take charge of and hold the property involved in the suit.56 Of course, no final decree can be entered until the plaintiff's claim has been reduced to judgment at law.57 

A discharge of the judgment debtor in bankruptcy does not preclude the entry of a final decree for relief in a creditor's suit. A bankruptcy proceeding does not discharge or abrogate the vested liens of judgment creditors, acquired more than four months before the bankruptcy proceedings, on property which the debtor had and fraudulently kept from his creditors in the bankruptcy proceeding. 

This is true even though the creditor could not enforce his lien by execution at law since he had, long prior to the bankruptcy proceeding, an equitable lien on the property. Consequently, a state court of equity may at least decree that the property be subjected to the proper demands of lien holding creditors even though the funds derived from the property are to be administered by the bankruptcy court.58 § 221.-Appeals.-To an appeal by one creditor in a creditor's suit, all other creditors are necessary parties.59 However, where a suit is brought by one definitely named creditor as a representative of all other creditors who may thereafter come into the suit, an entry of appeal by that creditor, as representing the class, against all other parties to the cause, whether defendants, interveners, or creditors, is sufficient to confer jurisdiction of the parties and the subject matter on the appellate courtso even where such jurisdiction is not conferred by a proper designation of the decree appealed from.61

§ 222.-In General.-The marriage relationship is a matter of contract between the parties entering into that status.' But the marital relation, unlike ordinary contractual relations, is regarded by the law and the state as the basis of the social organization, and the preservation of the relation is deemed essential to the public welfare.2 Consequently, though marriage is defined in law as a civil contract, it differs very materially from ordinary bilateral 

1. McGowin v. McGowin, 122 Fla.. 

394, 165 So. 274. 

2. Gallemore v. Gallemore, 94 Fla. 

516, 114 So. 371.

[Ch. 24 contracts in that it cannot be terminated by mutual consent, by performance, or by the will of either party.3 

The only method by which a marriage contract may be terminated, other than through the death of one of the parties, is by a judicial decree of divorce. While the power to grant a divorce is a statutory and not a common law power, it is likewise a judicial and not a legislative power.4 The granting of divorces is a proper subject of legislation when either of the parties is a resident of the state at the time of the divorce, but the power of the legislature is confined to prescribing the grounds for divorce and the procedure under which they may be obtained. An inquiry into the facts upon which a divorce is sought is a judicial function which must be exercised by the courts, and a statute which attempts to dissolve the marriage relationship in a particular case impairs the obligation of the contract and conflicts with the provisions of the Constitution of the United States.6 In Florida, the power to grant divorces has been conferred by the legislature upon the circuit courts as courts of equity.7

In view of the public interest in the marriage relationship, the husband and wife are not considered as the only parties concerned in a marriage or divorce. A suit for divorce is in reality a triangular proceeding in which the husband, the wife, and the state are parties, and the court, representing society, must see that the public welfare is protected. In accordance with these principles, it is not the policy of the state to permit the dissolution of the marriage relation by any agreement between the two contracting parties, and it is well settled that contracts intended to facilitate the procurement of a divorce are contrary to public policy and void. 

Even the incorporation of such an agreement into a final decree of divorce cannot impart validity to it.10

Nor is it the policy of the law to grant divorces for post-nuptial causes short of marital infidelity when such causes do not in fact render one of the parties incapable of performing the duties incident to the marriage status. Relief is given in such cases only on the ground that the conduct of one party renders it impracticable for the other party to perform the marital duties."1 

In suits involving the marital status and rights, strict rules of procedure are not required. Where the rights of the parties are in substance protected, the proceedings are largely in the discretion of the trial court.12 But where minor children are involved, the rules governing the granting of a divorce should be more strictly applied, and their welfare becomes the paramount consideration to which the claims and personal desires of the parents, and even the wishes of the child, must yield." 13 A suit for divorce is a purely personal action which cannot survive the death of either party.14 § 223. However, the great weight of authority supports the rule that, when it becomes proper or necessary, a wife may acquire a domicile separate from that of her husband for the purpose of a suit for divorce by her.16 Thus, a wife may acquire a separate domicile for purposes of divorce when her refusal or failure to live with her husband is justified or through no fault of hers.17 Whether the actions of the husband which give the

The Florida statutes provide that, in order to obtain a divorce, the plaintiff must have resided in the state of Florida for ninety days before the filing of the bill of complaint.19 The requirement of the statute, that the plaintiff must have resided in the state for ninety days before bringing suit, refers to the legal residence of the plaintiff, that is, to his place of domicile or permanent abode as distinguished from a temporary residence.20 The requirement as to residence is jurisdictional and the ninety days' residence must be both alleged in the bill of complaint and established by proof in order to give the court authority to grant a divorce.21 If the required residence is questioned, the burden of proving it is upon the plaintiff.22

§ 225.-Service of Process.-Where the defendant to a divorce proceeding is a resident of the state of Florida, personal service should be had upon him. Where the defendant is not a resident of Florida, constructive service may, under some circumstances, be made the basis for a valid decree of divorce. 

The Florida statutes provide that bills for divorce may be brought against defendants residing out of the state, and service may be effected upon them as in other cases in chancery.28 It has been seen, however, that a valid personal judgment or decree cannot be predicated upon constructive service. Constructive service only authorizes a decree affecting the defendant's interest in some property or other res which is within the jurisdiction of the court.29 

In divorce proceedings, the matrimonial domicile is considered as the res which authorizes the court of the jurisdiction in which it is located to determine the defendant's rights in the marriage relationship after constructive service of process upon him. 

Ordinarily, the matrimonial domicile is the permanent residence of the husband. If the wife without justification leaves him or refuses to live with him, the matrimonial domicile nevertheless remains with the husband and a valid decree of divorce can be rendered only in the jurisdiction of his residence. On the other hand, if a husband leaves his wife without justification, or if the wife has sufficient cause for leaving the husband and refusing to live with him, the matrimonial domicile remains with her and a valid decree of divorce can be rendered only in the jurisdiction in which she resides.30 Consequently, the state in which the matrimonial domicile, as thus defined, is located, may render a valid decree of divorce based upon constructive service against the defendant. 

It has been seen that statutes authorizing constructive service are strictly construed and must be exactly pursued in order to give a court jurisdiction to render a judgment by default against a party who does not appear or plead in the cause.31 This principle is especially applicable to constructive service in divorce cases. That a husband is not a citizen or resident of the state of Florida, except insofar as military duty requires his residence on a military reservation ceded to the United States under a statute whereby the state retained concurrent jurisdiction for the purpose of executing process, does not immunize him from process in his wife's suit for divorce or separate maintenance.42 

§ 226. Grounds for Relief-Desertion. One of the grounds of divorce, under the statutes of Florida, is the willful, obstinate, and continued desertion of the plaintiff by the defendant for one year.43 

Desertion, within the meaning of the statute, consists of three things: an actual cessation of cohabitation for the period specified, the willful intent of the absent spouse to desert, and the desertion by that spouse against the will of the other.44 The essence of the wrong of desertion thus consists in the refusal of a husband or wife to live with the other, when that other wants the deserting spouse to live with him or her.45

As used in the statute, the word willful means intentional, and obstinate means determined, fixed, and persistent.46 Thus, where a husband by his own act intentionally brings cohabitation to an end, and keeps it at an end for the statutory period, showing no evidence of a purpose to renew the marital relation, he is guilty of desertion. and the wife is entitled to a divorce on that ground. But the husband may, without the wife's consent, establish the family domicile, and it is her duty to live with him at the family domicile if it is reasonably possible for her to do so.47

While a wife who has been deserted by her husband without cause will not be denied a divorce on the ground of desertion because she

It is very doubtful, however, if this principle requires an affirmative effort at reconciliation by the husband. It certainly does not in cases where the wife's conduct shows that such an effort would be unavailing.49 The furthest the principle has been applied in practice is to hold that, if the wife makes it clear that she would return if the way were open to her, the husband will be denied a divorce on the ground of desertion where, for the purpose of making her absence a ground of divorce, he refrains from doing anything to induce her to return.50

But this decision does no more than require a husband to respond in good faith to his wife's attempts at a reconciliation. 

On the other hand, it has been held that, where one spouse intentionally and wrongfully deserts the other, the willingness for, or tacit acquiescence in, the desertion, on the part of the deserted spouse, will not defeat a suit for divorce.51 The case stating that rule involved the desertion of a husband by a wife, and no affirmative effort by the husband to restore marital relations appeared. It is reasonable to conclude, therefore, on all the cases, that a husband need make no affirmative effort to bring back a deserting wife unless the circumstances at least indicate that she desires to return. 

Where an offer of reconciliation is made by either party, it must be made in good faith and be free from improper qualifications and conditions. Thus a husband has no right to make it a condition of the renewal of marital relations that his wife shall convey to him her separate property.52

In a suit for divorce on the ground of desertion, it is immaterial which of the parties leaves the marital home. The one who intends bringing the cohabitation to an end commits the desertion. The party who drives the other away is the deserter, and either may drive the other away.57 Where a wife severs the marital relation, and leaves her husband, a very strong showing of a willful and determined effort to force her to leave, or by wrong doing, rather than poverty, to make life so unbearable that she cannot continue to live with him, must be established in order to justify a divorce.58 

Where there has been a willful, obstinate, and continued desertion by either a husband or wife for a period of one year, there is no obligation on the part of the deserted spouse to thereafter resume marital relations, and the refusal to do so does not extinguish the cause of action for divorce.59
