The guiding principle in considering a divorce on the ground of extreme cruelty is safety for the future, and not retribution for the past. 63

Where physical violence is relied upon to establish extreme cruelty, the marriage relation must be shown to have been defeated by grave and serious misconduct. Isolated or single acts of violence, repeated at long intervals, may be insufficient. A divorce is not authorized for every slight violence which a husband may commit against his wife, and much less will slight acts of violence by a wife, from which the husband can easily protect himself, constitute cruelty entitling him to a divorce.64

Where extreme cruelty is predicated upon mental injury, it is not necessary to show any single instance of conduct which, standing alone, will sustain the charge. The conduct which will be sufficient to justify a divorce on the ground of extreme cruelty must necessarily depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case.66 Where physical violence is involved, the court should look to the mental and physical condition of the person upon whom the violence is inflicted. An act which might be lightly regarded by a woman of firm and vigorous mind and person, whose sensibility to insult was dull and obtuse, might be an act of extreme cruelty to a woman in poor health and of acute sensibilities. The court should also use the greatest caution and discrimination in case of a single act of violence, where the parties had previously lived quietly and peacefully, and there is no just reason to fear a repetition of the act of violence or danger to the woman in a continuance of the cohabitation. And the court should consider whether the act was caused or provoked by the wife, and the degree of provocation, or whether the act was wholly unprovoked. 67

§ 228.-Grounds for Relief-Violent and Ungovernable Temper.- 

The Florida statutes provide that a divorce may be granted on the ground of habitual indulgence by the defendant in violent and ungovernable temper.71 In order to warrant a divorce on this ground the violent and ungovernable temper must have been displayed toward the plaintiff, and habitually, with the effect of rendering life an oppressive and intolerable burden, making it impracticable to discharge the marital duties.72 Occasional outbursts of passion, petulance, readiness to anger, frequent and unreasonable complaints, though made in a loud voiced, boisterous manner, which render the relations between the parties only unpleasant and disagreeable, or simply unhappy, do not furnish cause for divorce.73 

§ 229.-Grounds for Relief-Habitual Intemperance.-A divorce. 

may also be granted on the ground of the habitual intemperance of the defendant.74

Habitual intemperance, as a ground for divorce under the statute, is the persistent habit of becoming intoxicated from the use of strong drink. The offense is the habit, and frequent drunkenness proves the habit.75 Proof of the habitual but moderate use of intoxicants is not sufficient to establish this ground of divorce.76

The drug habit is not a ground of divorce in this state.77 § 230.-Grounds for Relief-Adultery.-A divorce may be granted under the Florida statutes where the defendant has been guilty of adultery. However, if it appears to the court that the adultery complained of was occasioned by collusion of the parties, and done with the intent to procure a divorce, or that both parties have been guilty of adultery, no divorce will be decreed.78 

Where a wife, after obtaining a divorce decree, but pending an appeal therefrom, marries and cohabits with another man, she is not, because the divorce decree is thereafter declared void, guilty of such adultery as will preclude her from obtaining a new decree on other grounds.79 Mere indiscreet or imprudent conduct between a married woman and young men, all embraced under the general term flirting, is not a cause for divorce.80 

§ 231.—Other Grounds for Relief.—In addition to the grounds of divorce already discussed, the Florida statutes authorize the granting of divorces where the parties to the marriage are within the degrees of relationship prohibited by law, where the defendant is naturally impotent, where the defendant has obtained a divorce from the plaintiff in any other state or country, or where either party has a husband or wife living at the time of the marriage sought to be annulled.81

A divorce a mensa et thoro is a divorce within the meaning of the statutory provision for granting a divorce where the defendant has obtained a divorce from the plaintiff in any other state or country.82

The facts and circumstances upon which a plaintiff bases his claim are matters peculiarly within his own knowledge, and he will be presumed to have stated them as strongly and favorably to himself as he could, exercising the privilege of selecting his own language in which to couch them.86 

A fundamental requirement of a sufficient bill for divorce is an allegation that the plaintiff has resided in the state of Florida for at least ninety days prior to the filing of the bill of complaint. Such ninety days' residence of the plaintiff in this state is jurisdictional, and it must be both alleged in the bill of complaint and established by proof before the court is authorized to grant a divorce. Where no such allegation appears in the bill, the plaintiff is not entitled to maintain his suit and the bill may properly be dismissed at the final hearing.87 Ordinarily, it is sufficient to allege the residence of the plaintiff substantially in the language of the statute.88

A bill for divorce must also, of course, as a necessary predicate to the relief sought, allege a marriage between the parties.90 

In stating the ground for divorce, it is not, as a general rule, sufficient to make the allegation in the words of the statute. In addition to the general charge, the plaintiff must specify leading facts, or at least some facts, upon which the charge is based. These facts must be alleged with sufficient definiteness and clarity to enable the defendant to properly prepare his defense, as well as to enable the court to judge whether, if the facts are proved, they will support the general charge.91 Allegations of mere conclusions not warranted by the facts alleged are not admitted by a motion to dismiss and do not state a cause of action.92 

In a bill for divorce upon the ground of desertion, it is sufficient to allege the ground for divorce in the statutory language, coupled with a charge that the husband without cause left the wife penniless, and continued away from her for the statutory period without in any way contributing to her support.93 It is essential that a bill founded on desertion show that the desertion is willful and obstinate, and has continued for the statutory period.94 

An allegation that the defendant deserted the plaintiff by driving him away is insufficient where there are no allegations showing how, in what manner, and to what extent the defendant drove the plaintiff away.95 But, allegations that defendant's gambling, stealing, and forging checks caused his wife such mental anguish that she was forced to seek security with her parents, and that defendant failed to keep his promise to mend his ways and provide a home for her, are sufficient to show defendant's desertion of plaintiff.96

A bill for divorce, custody of children, alimony, attorney's fees, and confirmation of the plaintiff's title to real estate held in the name of her husband is not multifarious since it affects only the parties thereto and property rights claimed by both.113 Likewise, a bill filed by a wife for divorce, alimony, the imposition of a trust on real estate to the extent of the wife's contribution to the purchase price, and for an injunction to prevent the defendant from conveying the real estate, is not multifarious.114 However, if a conveyance of the real estate has already been made, the bill probably is multifarious in view of the grantee's acquisition of rights therein.115 A bill stating a cause of action against a husband for maintenance, suit money, and attorney's fees, and a cause of action against the husband's son to enjoin the unlawful possession and retention of plaintiff's property, is multifarious. The plaintiff has an adequate remedy at law against the son for withholding her property which she may maintain without joining her husband.116 

§ 233.—Defenses.-Condonation is a valid defense to a proceed ing for a divorce.

It is an affirmative defense which must be spe- cially pleaded.117 But, even though condonation is not specially pleaded, the court may, in its discretion, refuse a divorce where the evidence shows that the injured party actually forgave the other after knowledge of all the facts, and that the injury has not been revived by subsequent misconduct. And where there is reason to believe that condonation exists the court may, in order to guard against fraud and collusion, direct an inquiry into the matter at any time before final decree. Likewise, where condonation is not specially pleaded, the defendant will generally be permitted to amend his answer so as to set up the defense.117A

In the law of divorce, condonation is the forgiveness of an antecedent matrimonial offense on condition that it shall not be repeated and that the offender shall thereafter treat the forgiving party with conjugal kindness. Mere cohabitation in the hope of better treatment or of a better understanding does not constitute

It is well settled that condonation of past matrimonial offenses is conditioned upon the future good behavior of the offending spouse, and it follows that if, after condonation, the offenses are repeated the right to make the condoned offense a ground of divorce revives. To constitute a revival of the condoned offense, the offending spouse need not be guilty of the same character of offense as that condoned. Any misconduct which indicates that the condonation was not accepted in good faith, and upon the reasonable conditions implied, is sufficient. 120 

The innocent party to a marriage need not separate from the other spouse on hearing mere reports of the latter spouse's infidelity in order to avoid a condonation thereof. Condonation is established only by a definite continuation of cohabitation after evidence legally sufficient to establish the offense comes to the knowledge of the condoning party. 121 The occupation of the matrimonial domicile by the wife during the pendency of divorce proceedings brought by the husband, but without cohabitation, is not a condonation. 122 Renewing the relation of living together as man and wife, with respect to condonation, includes the renewal of sexual relations. And sexual intercourse, even without forgiveness, engaged in after knowledge and means of proving adultery, is a condonation of that offense.122A

A suit for divorce may also be barred on the ground of collusion. 

If at any time before the court's jurisdiction of a divorce case has terminated, the fraudulent collusion of the parties is brought to the attention of the court, it becomes the duty of the court to investigate. If the investigation reveals collusion, it is within the power, and it clearly is the duty of the court, to deny the divorce. applied for or to set aside a decree if one has been entered. The court has the power to institute such an investigation and take such action on the motion of either party or of its own motion at any time before it has lost jurisdiction of the cause.125 In the case of adultery, it is specifically provided by statute that, if it shall appear to the court that the adultery complained of was occasioned by the collusion of the parties, and done with the intent to procure a divorce, or that both parties are guilty of adultery, no divorce shall be decreed. 126

Connivance is a special defense applicable to suits for divorce on the ground of adultery. If a husband forces his wife to commit adultery, or conduces or aids her in the commission of the offense, he will be denied a divorce on that ground. Passive permission is not connivance if the one spouse does nothing to encourage the other to commit the offense and does not directly or indirectly place opportunities therefor in the other's way. And connivance will not be implied from negligence, folly, dullness of apprehension, or indifference to the other spouse, nor, as a rule, from desertion. 

But neglect of a husband to support his wife or in any manner to concern himself about her may constitute misconduct conducing to her adultery.127

Proof of a marriage between the parties is, of course, a prerequisite to the entry of a decree of divorce. But presumptive as distinguished from direct evidence is prima facie sufficient, as where a man and woman have lived together, spoken to and of each other as husband and wife, and of the time and circumstances of their marriage, and the like.144 To prove adultery for purposes of divorce, specific acts need not be attested by eyewitnesses. It is sufficient if the circumstances proved are such as convince the guarded discretion of a reasonable and just man of the guilt of the participants.145 Habitual intemperance as a ground of divorce is proved by frequently recurring drunkenness.146 

A divorce should not be granted where the plaintiff's testimony is the only evidence tending to prove the truth of the grounds of divorce alleged in the bill. The plaintiff's testimony is not, however, required to be corroborated in every particular. It is enough if corroborated by the testimony of third persons as to the cause of action alleged.147 And the taking of testimony before a master in ex parte divorce proceedings by the asking of leading questions is improper. Where testimony is adduced by this method, the chancellor should return it to the master with directions to take testimony in accordance with the rules which require the witness to testify and counsel to ask questions without indicating the answer desired.148

§ 237. Decree-As to Custody of Children.-The Florida stat utes provide that, "in any suit for divorce or alimony, the court shall have power at any stage of the cause to make such orders touching the care, custody and maintenance of the children of the marriage, and what, if any, security to be given for the same, as from the circumstances of the parties and the nature of the case may be fit, equitable and just, and such order touching their custody as their best spiritual as well as other interests may require."159 

This statute is in effect a confirmation of the general powers and jurisdiction inherent in courts of equity to control and protect infants and their property. Thus, under the statute, as well as under its inherent power, a court of equity may refuse to dismiss without prejudice a divorce suit involving the custody of children. 

It may retain jurisdiction of the case in order to adjudicate their custody.160 Likewise, where a Florida court has jurisdiction to enter a decree of divorce, it also has statutory jurisdiction to award the custody of a child regardless of a prior decree as to such custody rendered by a foreign court.161

Subject to appellate review, the chancellor, in awarding the custody of children in divorce cases, exercises a wide discretion. He must, however, take into consideration all of the circumstances of the particular case, and he should dispose of the children in the manner which will preserve, as far as practicable, both the rights of the parents and the welfare of the child. 162 

The welfare of the child must, of course, be regarded as the chief consideration.163 But, since the duty remains upon the father to maintain, protect, and educate his children, it is well settled that he is generally entitled to their custody where he is a fit person to have it. Of course, the father's right to custody is not unlimited and, when abused, the court will interfere and remove such custody

Consequently, where the circumstances warrant it, and the interests of the child will not be prejudiced thereby, its custody may be divided between the two parents for appropriate periods.165 

Ordinarily, the fact that a child would have better prospects or advantages in the custody of one parent than in that of the other, and that one is able to do much more for the child than the other, is not considered as a controlling factor in determining custody if all of the child's needs will be supplied in either situation.166 But, where the mother has no means but alimony for her own support, and the children prefer to remain with the father, who is in a position to give them a comfortable home and support, and it appears to be in the children's interest, the better course is to leave them with the father.167 And where a husband obtains a divorce on the ground of his wife's violent and ungovernable temper, it has been held an unreasonable limitation on his rights to allow him custody of his child only two afternoons a month.168 

It is not illegal for parents who have separated to enter into a contract or stipulation with each other for the custody and maintenance of their child, but such an agreement is always subject to the approval of the court, which should not recognize it unless it insures the proper care and maintenance of the child. 169 

The primary duty of supporting and maintaining his children, which rests upon a father, is not affected by a divorce decree awarding their custody to the mother. 170 Consequently, where a divorced wife is awarded the custody of minor children, she is entitled to a reasonable allowance from the income of the husband for their care and support. The provisions of a divorce decree respecting the custody of minor children may be altered or modified from time to time as the exigencies of the case or altered circumstances may seem to require.173

It is the usual practice for the court to expressly reserve this power in its final decree, although it could undoubtedly be exercised regardless of such a reservation. 174 However, the provisions of a divorce decree respecting the custody of a child may not be materially changed thereafter except for the child's welfare, and then only because of conditions arising after the decree or because of material facts existing at the time of the decree but then unknown to the court.175 The custody of a child originally awarded to the father should not be changed to the mother merely as a penalty upon the father for failure to comply with other provisions of the divorce decree.176 

Where a divorce decree awards custody of a child to the wife until the further order of the court, proper provision for the support of the child may be subsequently made in appropriate proceedings.177

But there is no authority in law for requiring the husband to pay the wife's attorney's fees for a separate proceeding concerning the support or custody of minor children brought after the decree of divorce has become final.178

As respects property rights, when the bonds of matrimony are dissolved, the parties should be placed by the decree in as nearly as possible the situation they occupied before the marriage. Thus, a husband's interest in the separate statutory property of his wife being extinguished by a divorce, a decree should be entered that all such property in the possession of the husband be surrendered to the wife. The husband cannot, however, be compelled to account to the wife for the rents and profits of her separate property received by him during coverture.180 

The granting of a divorce to a wife on the grounds of extreme cruelty does not work a forfeiture of property purchased by the husband with his own funds but title to which was taken in the name of the wife. 181 Likewise, where a wife has contributed substantially in funds and industry to the acquisition of property held by the husband, over and above her ordinary duty to him, she has a special equity in such property, and even though the husband obtains a divorce on the ground of her adultery, ungovernable temper, or for some other cause, the wife is entitled to an allowance from such property for her interest therein. Such an allowance is not alimony and is not within the statute prohibiting the granting of alimony to an adulterous wife.182

Where the court places the husband in the possession of a business built up through the joint efforts of the husband and wife and fixes the amount which the wife is to receive as monthly income therefrom, a finding of the exact percentage of the interest of each in the property is not essential to the validity of the decree. 183 

The vendors of property in which both husband and wife claim an interest are not necessary or proper parties to a divorce proceeding in which it is sought to have the respective interests of the husband and wife adjudicated. The vendors have no interest in the equities of ownership between the husband and wife.184

DIVORCE § 239.—Impeachment of Decree.-As a general rule, courts of chancery have the same power to declare divorce decrees to be invalid as they have decrees in other cases. 185 Thus a divorce decree based upon false proof of residence, 186 or a false affidavit for constructive service, 187 will be vacated. However, where it is sought to impeach a final decree of divorce for fraud in its procurement, the fraud complained of must be both alleged and proved,188 and the decree will be vacated only when the proof is clear and convincing. 189

Divorce decrees which have become final can, as in other cases, only be set aside by due compliance with the established and recognized remedial processes of equity.190 If the trial court has not lost jurisdiction of the cause, an unauthorized decree may be set aside on motion to vacate.191 The usual method by which to attack a divorce decree which has been obtained by fraud is by an original bill in the nature of a bill of review.192 But a motion to vacate a final decree of divorce may be considered as a bill in the nature of a bill of review.192A A decree of divorce will not be vacated unless both parties thereto are before the court,193 and an order entered on the court's own motion, after it has lost jurisdiction of the cause, vacating a prior divorce decree on the ground of fraud on the court, without a rule to show cause or other proceedings, is invalid as a denial of due process of law.194 

The fact that divorce, as distinguished from some other subject of equitable cognizance, is involved raises no equity to maintain a bill attacking a final decree of divorce as against defenses sufficient to bar such proceedings generally, and it is well settled that

§ 240.—Appeals.-All of the rules governing appeals in other chancery cases198 apply equally to appeals in suits for divorce. 

In accordance with the general rule, the appellate court may of its own motion notice jurisdictional defects in divorce proceedings in the lower court. If the bill of complaint fails to contain the allegations as to the plaintiff's residence necessary to give the court jurisdiction, the appellate court will notice the defect and reverse the decree.199 And, where the bill is fundamentally defective in not stating all the essential elements of one of the statutory grounds for divorce, the insufficiency will be noticed by the appellate court and the decree reversed even though the defect was not pointed out by a motion to dismiss in the trial court.200 

But, where the court has jurisdiction of the subject matter and the parties, and the evidence establishes the truth of the allegations of the bill of complaint, a decree of divorce will be affirmed.201 

And, as in other proceedings, where the testimony is conflicting, but there is ample evidence to support the findings of the chancellor, the decree entered by him will not be disturbed.202 It must be

A decree adjudicating the custody of a minor child, which expressly retains jurisdiction of the cause for further orders in that connection, is an interlocutory order, and the granting of a supersedeas on an appeal therefrom is within the judicial discretion of the chancellor or of a justice of the Supreme Court.213 While the chancellor's discretion in this respect is not unlimited, a supersedeas will not be granted by the appellate court on such an appeal unless it appears from the record that the custody adjudicated by the chancellor is clearly not for the best interests of the child, or that, for other special reasons, the custody awarded should not be made effective pending the appeal.214 § 241.-Permanent Alimony.-Alimony arises from the marriage relation and is based upon the common law obligation of the husband to support his wife. It literally signifies nourishment or sustenance and it is the allowance which a husband may be compelled to pay to a wife for her maintenance while she is living apart from him or after she has been divorced.215 

Alimony is classified as temporary or permanent. Temporary alimony is an allowance made to a wife for her support during the pendency of a suit for divorce or separate maintenance.216 Permanent alimony is a continuous allotment of sums payable at regular periods for the permanent support of the wife.217 The award of a lump sum as permanent alimony is erroneous.218

In regard to the allowance of permanent alimony upon a decree of divorce, a Florida statute provides: "In every decree of divorce in a suit by the wife, the court shall make such orders touching the maintenance, alimony and suit money of the wife, or any allowance to be made to her, and if any, the security to be given for the same, as from the circumstances of the parties and nature of the case may be fit, equitable and just; but no alimony shall be granted to an adulterous wife."219

It has been said that, unless the granting of alimony is shown to be in satisfaction of an established claim to equitable or other rights in jointly accumulated property, it must find support in statutory provisions therefor.220 However, the better view, which has been expressly approved in this state, is that the right to decree alimony is incidental to the power to grant divorces, and that, even if the statutes which confer upon chancery courts jurisdiction over divorce had totally failed to make any provision for the granting of alimony, still, being clearly incident to that jurisdiction, the right and duty to grant alimony in proper cases would have existed, subject only to express statutory restrictions.221 The soundness of this view is apparent. Even if the legislature had made no provision for the granting of alimony, it should not be considered as having intended that a wife who divorced an adulterous, brutal, or intemperate husband should thereafter be deprived of the support which she was entitled to under a contract faithfully performed by her and which was perhaps her only means of existence. 

While the statute expressly prohibits the granting of alimony to an adulterous wife, and while no permanent alimony will be granted to a wife where the marriage is annulled on the ground that she had living an undivorced husband,222 the statute permits the chancellor to make appropriate provisions for permanent alimony in all cases where the suit for divorce is by the wife. The amount of alimony to be awarded is not regulated by any fixed rule. It is a matter of discretion with the court to be exercised upon an equitable view of all the circumstances of the particular case.223 A much larger allowance will be made for permanent alimony than for alimony pending suit. And where the delinquency of the husband has been established, and the wife is the injured party and separated from the comfort of matrimonial society by her husband's misconduct, she will be liberally supported.224 

The actual income and earning capacity of the husband appears from the cases to be the controlling factor.225 But, in addition to this, the independent means of the wife, and any other elements

The husband's financial inability or the wife's wealth may not be alone ground for modifying the award, but the whole question is in the discretion of the court. Under the statute, the granting or withholding of temporary alimony and suit money in divorce proceedings is discretionary with the court to which the application is made. The discretion is not an arbitrary but a judicial one, to be exercised in accordance with well established principles of law wisely adapted to the facts of each particular case. When the discretion is abused, the appellate court will grant relief.254 The term "suit money," as used in the statute, is broad enough to cover attorney's fees and all costs of the proceeding pendente lite.255

On an application for temporary alimony and suit money, the parties are before the court as husband and wife and the application is founded on the husband's duty to his wife under the marriage contract. Consequently, the fact of marriage between the parties must be made to appear at least prima facie by proof or admission before the court is justified in making an allowance for temporary alimony and suit money, or in referring the matter to a master for the taking of testimony and the making of recommendations on the question.256 Thus a wife who seeks a divorce from her husband on the ground of adultery because he has obtained a divorce in another state and remarried should be denied temporary alimony and suit money until the court can determine whether the foreign divorce is valid.257 Likewise, where a divorce is granted because the wife had an undivorced husband by

In addition to proof of a marriage, a plaintiff wife must show a prima facie case for a divorce before she can be allowed temporary alimony and suit money. Thus, no such relief can be granted where her bill of complaint, on its face, fails to state a case warranting the entry of a decree of divorce.259 Likewise, if it clearly appears from the pleadings in a husband's divorce suit that the wife has no defense thereto, alimony and suit money will be denied.260 And where it appears, in a suit brought by either the husband or the wife, that the wife has abandoned her husband without cause, she is not entitled to alimony or suit money.261 However, if the husband is not entirely free from fault, temporary alimony and suit money may be granted notwithstanding the wife's delinquency.262

After a marriage and cause for divorce are at least prima facie established, two facts must concur and be made to appear before a court is justified in making an allowance for temporary alimony and suit money. First, a necessity on the part of the wife for such an allowance must be shown. This necessity may be predicated upon either a want of means or a want of sufficient means to maintain herself during the litigation and to employ counsel. Second, it must be made to appear that the husband has the means to meet this necessity.263 If the wife has ample means or property of her own, out of which she can maintain herself and employ counsel, the necessity of an allowance for that purpose is lacking and it should be denied.264 And, no matter how clearly the necessities of the wife are shown, it is error to grant temporary alimony and suit money unless the means of the husband are also shown.265

Where an application for temporary alimony and suit money is made, the safer and more commendable practice is to either refer the matter to a master to take testimony as to the necessities of the wife and the faculties of the husband, or to take such testimony before the court.267 Where the necessities of the wife and the faculties of the husband are established by the pleadings, it is not error to make an order for temporary alimony and suit money without reference to a master,268 but the practice of entering such an order on the affidavits of the parties has been disapproved.269 

The husband must be given due notice of all proceedings on an application for alimony and suit money.270

An order awarding attorney's fees to the wife should not direct their payment directly to her solicitor. In such cases the award should be made to the wife to reimburse her for her expenditures in that behalf, or the allowance should be ordered paid into the registry of the court for the use of the solicitor representing the wife.271

An order allowing temporary alimony and suit money is interlocutory in character, and like any other interlocutory order made during the progress of a cause, it remains within the control of the court until the entry of the final decree, in the absence of intervening and effective appellate jurisdiction.272

§ 243.-Alimony Unconnected with Divorce.-Chancery courts of 

Florida are authorized to grant temporary and permanent alimony to a wife justifiably living apart from her husband without at the same time granting a decree of divorce. There are two statutes on this matter. The first authorizes the granting of alimony to a wife, without a divorce, if any of the statutory grounds of divorce exist in her favor. The second authorizes the granting of alimony or separate maintenance to a wife regardless of whether a cause of divorce exists in her favor. 

The first of these statutes provides specifically that, "if any of the causes of divorce *** shall exist in favor of the wife, and she be living apart from her husband, she may obtain alimony without seeking a divorce upon bill filed and suit prosecuted as in other chancery causes; and the court shall have power to grant such temporary and permanent alimony and suit money as the circumstances of the parties may render just; but no alimony shall be granted to an adulterous wife."285

The first is grounded on the fact that there never was a marriage, while the second concedes that a valid marriage exists but proceeds to dissolve it.312 

Marriages which are either void or voidable may be annulled. 

Where a marriage is void, as where one of the parties has living an undivorced spouse by a prior marriage, a judicial decree of annulment is not necessary to avoid the marriage, though it may be advisable.313 Marriages which are voidable, as where they have been induced by fraud or duress practiced by one of the parties, are valid until annulled by judicial decree.314 Invalid marriages may be ratified by the injured party continuing cohabitation after knowledge of the fraud or duress or, in the case of void marriages, after knowledge that the disability of the other party has been removed.315

§ 246.-What Constitutes Fraudulent Conveyance.-A fraudulent conveyance of property is any sale, transfer, or conveyance thereof made for the purpose or with the intention of hindering, delaying, or defrauding creditors of their just and lawful debts and demands.' 

To constitute a fraudulent conveyance there must be a creditor to be defrauded, a debtor intending fraud, and a conveyance of property which is applicable by law to the payment of the debt due. The fraud consists of the intention of the debtor to prevent his creditors. from recovering their just debts by withdrawing his property from their reach. As the fraud rests upon the debtor's intent, it must exist at the time of the transfer.2

However, it matters not whether the actual intention of the parties to a conveyance is to hinder and delay creditors. If the con-

merely nominal is considered voluntary as against attacking creditors.

The mere fact that a person may be indebted to another does not render a conveyance of his property a fraud in law upon his creditors. The owner of property, whether real or personal, possesses the absolute right to dispose of all or any part of it as he sees fit. 

The only restriction imposed by law is that no transfer shall be made which will interfere with the existing rights of other persons. 

If the right of disposition is exercised to the injury or prejudice of other persons, the courts will then interfere and the question arises. whether the circumstances constituted ipso facto a fraud or raise a presumption of fraud.7

It is provided by statute that the question of whether a conveyance is fraudulent depends upon its being made "upon good consideration and bona fide." Both requisites must concur. Even though a conveyance is upon a valuable consideration, it is not valid in point of law from that circumstance alone, for if it is made with the intent to delay or defeat creditors it is void. The term "good consideration" used in the statute has been held to include motives of generosity, affection, or natural duty, as well as those founded. upon money, marriage, or the like. Hence, family settlements and advancements to children are, under some circumstances, good consideration as against creditors where the grantor is not indebted at the time. But, as against existing creditors, it is very doubtful if, in any case, a consideration which is not in law deemed valuable will be allowed to prevail.10

It is likewise an admitted rule that a debtor may give preference to one creditor over another where there is no fraud on the part of the favored creditor.14 And a person who receives property from an insolvent debtor in payment of an antecedent debt occupies a more favored position than a purchaser for a present consideration. 

A preferential transfer of property cannot be declared fraudulent as to other creditors, although the debtor in making it intended to defeat their claims, and the creditor had knowledge of such intention, if the preferred creditor did not actually participate in the debtor's fraudulent purpose. If the only purpose of the creditor is to secure his debt, and the property is not worth materially more than the debt, the transaction is not fraudulent. This is so although the creditor knows that the debtor is insolvent. And he is protected in such cases even though he knows that the debtor is actuated solely by the desire to defraud his creditors, that the transfer is of all of the debtor's property, that there are other creditors, and that the effect of the debtor's action will be to defeat them. But the creditor must act in good faith, for if he takes the conveyance for the purpose of aiding in the fraud, it is void.15

In order that a pre-existing debt may be a good and sufficient consideration for a transfer of property by a debtor, it must be an obligation for which the debtor is legally liable and which he could be compelled to pay by action. And the conveyance will be considered voluntary unless the transfer operates by agreement of the parties to extinguish the debt.16

§ 247.-Who May Attack Conveyance.-A conveyance made for the purpose or with the intention of delaying, hindering, or defrauding creditors is declared by statute to be utterly void and of no effect.19 Notwithstanding the statute, however, such conveyances are not void but only voidable as to creditors.20 It is well established that a fraudulent conveyance is perfectly good and binding as between the parties and their representatives, and as against all persons except creditors.21 Deeds of conveyance and bills of sale entered into for the purpose of defrauding creditors vest title absolutely in the grantees, subject to impeachment only by the persons defrauded by such transactions. A fraudulent transfer cannot be set aside at the instance of the legal representative of the grantor. Only creditors of the decedent have the right to question the fraudulent transactions of their debtor.23

However, where the rights of the grantee under a fraudulent conveyance are incomplete, and require the aid of legal proceedings for their full enjoyment, the court will not assist him in the enforcement of his claim. Thus, where a man makes a deed of gift of personal property and dies, the donee cannot enforce the gift and the property is assets in the hands of the personal representative.24 

Likewise, where the fraudulent transfer is in the form of a mortgage, the mortgagee, being a party to the fraud, will not be permitted to enforce it.25

The statute26 declaring fraudulent conveyances to be void as against creditors is to be liberally construed in favor of the class. of persons designed to be protected.27 A creditor, within the meaning and intent of the statute, is not necessarily one who has a demand for money which is due, or running to maturity, or who has an existing cause of action. Whoever has a legal claim or demand of a contractual nature in existence at the time an alleged fraudulent conveyance is made is a creditor within the meaning of the statute.28 The holder of a contingent claim is as fully protected by the statute as the holder of one that is absolute and, in cases of contingent liability, the liability whenever happening relates back to the date when it was originally incurred.29 Where one surety agrees to save his co-surety harmless, the latter is a creditor of the former within the meaning of the statute and he

The fact that a creditor holds a mortgage upon particular property of his debtor does not exclude him or his assignee from the terms of protection of the statute against fraudulent conveyances, or from obtaining equitable relief against fraudulent dispositions of other property of the debtor.31 However, in order to secure the benefit of the statute, the mortgagee must show that, notwithstanding the mortgage, he also relied upon the general credit of the mortgagor. To make this showing, the mortgagee must establish that, at the time of the mortgage, the property pledged was inadequate to secure the debt. If, at the time of the alleged fraudulent transfer, the security was ample, the imputation of fraud from a voluntary conveyance by the debtor of other property does not obtain.32

A conveyance may be cancelled for fraud whether existing or subsequent creditors were in mind in its making.33 The question of the validity of a voluntary conveyance as against subsequent creditors depends upon whether it was made in contemplation of future debts, or for the purpose of placing the hazards of a business in which the grantor was about to engage upon others instead of honestly holding the property subject to the risk of adverse results.34 If the fraud is directed specifically against subsequent creditors, which may be inferred from the fact of debts having been contracted immediately after the voluntary conveyance, there is no doubt that the transfer may be avoided by them.

There is another sort of fraud which may be taken advantage of by subsequent creditors. Where a conveyance is made with the actual intent to defraud existing creditors, it may be avoided by subsequent creditors. § 248.-Property Which May Be Reached. The property which may be reached by a creditor upon a bill to set aside a fraudulent conveyance thereof is defined by statute as any lands, tenements, hereditaments, or goods and chattels, or any lease, rent, use, common, or other profit, benefit, or charge arising out of lands, tenements, hereditaments, or goods and chattels, or any bond, note, contract, suit, judgment, or execution which has been made for the purpose of hindering, delaying, or defrauding creditors.39 It will be noted that the statute wholly omits equitable assets or interests.40 However, such property may be reached by a creditor's bill.41 Of course, under the statute, only the interest of the debtor in the property fraudulently conveyed can be subjected to the payment of his debt.42

Under the provisions of the Florida Constitution, an attempted transfer of the legal title to a homestead by a husband to his wife does not and cannot give to any creditor of the husband any other, greater, or further right to the satisfaction of his debt out of the homestead property than he had before the attempted transfer. 

If the property continues in good faith to be the homestead of the husband and his family, then his creditors have no lien upon or interest therein which will give them any right to question the validity of the attempted transfer. As to homestead property, there are no creditors within the meaning of the statute against fraudulent conveyances.43

It should also be noted that there is a difference between the rights of creditors in those cases where the husband takes title to land which has been purchased with the separate funds of the wife, and which he afterward, though indebted, conveys to his wife, and those cases where a husband conveys to his wife property of which he has always been the legal and beneficial owner. In the latter case, it has been seen, fraud is presumed and, unless there is an adequate consideration for the transfer, it will be held to be in fraud of creditors. But, in the former case, fraud will not be presumed, and a creditor is not entitled to subject the property to execution unless he shows that the credit upon which his claim is based was extended to the husband while the record title was in his name and on the belief that he was the owner of the property. 

Here the right of the creditor to reach the property does not depend upon any fraud perpetrated by the husband in conveying the property to his wife, but it rests upon the rule that the wife, having allowed the husband to obtain credit by reason of his apparent ownership of the property, is estopped from setting up her rights against anyone so misled. However, if the creditor, at the time of extending the credit, had notice of the fact that the husband only held title in trust for his wife, then the wife will not be estopped from holding title as against the creditor.44

Choice of Remedies.-The recognized rule is that, where property is transferred by a debtor for the purpose of placing it beyond the reach of his creditors, a defrauded creditor may pursue any one of three available remedies. First, he may place his demand in judgment, levy upon the property alleged to have been fraudulently conveyed and cause the same to be sold under execution, leaving the purchaser at the sale to contest the validity of the title. Second, since equity will not compel a creditor to sell a doubtful title, he may bring a suit in equity against the grantor and grantee to remove the fraudulent conveyance as an obstruction to the full enforcement of his judgment lien and await the result of the suit before selling the property. Third, he may bring an action in the nature of a creditor's bill to have the conveyance adjudged fraudulent and void as to his judgment and to have the property sold and the proceeds applied to the satisfaction of his claim. In short, the choice before the creditor is to have the property sold, or to have the conveyance set aside, or to adopt a combination of the two methods.47

While a judgment creditor has the right to treat a transfer of property to which his debtor had legal title as a nullity, and to sell the property so conveyed under execution, as though no transfer by connivance had been made, the existence of this remedy at law does not preclude resort to a court of equity for the purpose of vacating the fraudulent conveyance as an obstacle to the full enforcement of the judgment, since fraud is one of the recognized and most ancient subjects of equity jurisdiction.48

The original equity rule was that a bill to set aside a fraudulent conveyance could not be maintained merely by showing the pendency of an action at law between the parties which might result in a judgment in favor of the creditor.56 In 1903, however, a statute was enacted providing that a creditor's bill could be maintained in the courts of this state before the plaintiff's claim had been reduced to judgment, provided the creditor had first instituted a suit at law for that purpose, and provided, further, that no final decree could be entered on the creditor's bill until the plaintiff's claim had been reduced to judgment.57

Whether a bill to set aside a fraudulent conveyance is a creditor's bill within the meaning of this statute has not been definitely decided. In one decision, rendered long after the enactment of the statute, the Supreme Court of Florida stated that the statute did not define or change the purpose and scope of a creditor's bill and indicated that such a bill, to come within the meaning of the statute, must be one to reach equitable assets as distinguished from a bill to set aside fraudulent conveyances of property to which the debtor had legal title.58 However, in other and later decisions, it has been indicated that a bill to set aside a fraudulent conveyance of a legal title may be maintained upon the filing of an action at law to enforce payment of the plaintiff's claim.59 The later decisions appear to be based on the sounder reasoning. As to what constitutes a sufficient allegation of fraud, the rule generally followed is that the one seeking relief against a fraudulent conveyance must allege that it was made with the intent to hinder, delay, and defraud creditors. This is especially true when by statute the question of fraudulent intent is made a question of fact. It need not be alleged that the conveyance was made with the intent to defraud the plaintiff personally if it is alleged that the intent was to hinder, delay and defraud creditors generally. 

The intent to hinder, delay, and defraud creditors is an ultimate fact and not a conclusion of law. Consequently, it may be pleaded in so many words without stating the specific facts or evidence which go to make up the charge. But a statement of the substantive facts from which the inference of fraudulent intent may be drawn is not improper, and when this is done it is not necessary to allege the conclusion of fraudulent intent from the facts pleaded.76

Thus a bill by a trustee in bankruptcy against certain parties to whom the bankrupt transferred accounts receivable within four months prior to the filing of the petition in bankruptcy, alleging that the transfer operated to give a preference to some creditors over others, and was made to hinder, delay, and defraud creditors, which fact was known to the transferee, sufficiently shows a right to equitable relief.77 Likewise, a bill alleging that a transfer from the judgment debtor to a third person, and a transfer from the third person to the judgment debtor and his wife, were made without consideration and for the purpose of hindering and delaying creditors, is not dismissible as alleging a conclusion of law without stating the facts upon which the conclusion is based.78

Where the allegations of a bill attacking a fraudulent conveyance are sufficient to show fraud, all of the facts evidencing the fraud need not be pleaded.79

As to subsequent creditors, a bill to set aside a fraudulent conveyance should show an intent to contract debts and to avoid their payment by the conveyance. Facts which would justify holding a conveyance fraudulent as to subsequent creditors include proof of prior debts, insolvency of the debtor at the time of making the conveyance, insolvency created by the conveyance, or the intent to hinder, delay, and defraud those to whom the grantor is about to become indebted.80

It is also necessary for a bill seeking to set aside a fraudulent conveyance to show that the fraudulent disposition embarrasses the plaintiff in the collection of his claim and is an obstacle to the full enforcement of his judgment, for, if the debtor has other property sufficient to satisfy the debt, there is no necessity for resort to a court of equity.81

Where a creditor whose claim was secured by a mortgage upon part of his debtor's property seeks to set aside his debtor's fraudulent conveyance of other property, the bill must show that, at the time the debt was incurred, the mortgagee relied upon the general credit of the debtor's property and a confidence that he would not diminish it to the mortgagee's prejudice. To this end, the bill must allege that the mortgaged property, at the time it was pledged, was inadequate to secure the debt.82. However, this rule would seem to be open to serious objections. A mortgagee may take adequate security at the time his claim is incurred, and at the same time rely upon the general credit of the mortgagor to protect him in case of a decline in the value of the mortgaged property. The mere fact that the property originally pledged was adequate security for the debt is not conclusive proof that the general credit of the mortgagor was not relied upon. Therefore, the presumptions of fraud attaching to voluntary conveyances by a mortgagor should apply in favor of the mortgagee as well as in favor of unsecured

A bill to set aside fraudulent conveyances is not multifarious because several grantees, each claiming different portions of the property of the fraudulent grantor, are made defendants with the fraudulent grantor. As against the creditor, the deeds to the property, whether one or many, or whether there is one grantee or many, are void. The entire property is treated as the property of the debtor. As the object of the suit is single, it is permissible to join the several matters, and all parties thereto, in one bill.83 But, when the plaintiff in such a bill also seeks to remove a cloud upon title to land owned by him resulting from one of the debtor's fraudulent conveyances, the objection of multifariousness may be well taken. The rights sought to be asserted are of different natures. Since one is the right of a creditor to have payment of his debt, and the other is that of the owner of real estate to have a cloud removed from his title, it has been held that they cannot be joined in one bill.84 A contrary result might be reached under the 1931 Chancery Act, however, if both causes of action arose out of the same transaction and the parties thereto were the same. § 253.-Answer and Defenses.-A mere denial in an answer of a fraudulent intent in conveying property beyond the reach of creditors, while admitting all the facts which in law and equity constitute the fraud, is insufficient to place the burden of proving fraud on the plaintiff. The denial must be of the facts charged, and not of the conclusions flowing from the facts.85 It is not a good answer to a bill to set aside a fraudulent conveyance that the liability of one defendant as a special partner was limited by the partnership agreement. Such a defense should be made, if at all, in the original suit on the debt.86

The judgment obtained by the attacking creditor against the debtor is not conclusive against the fraudulent grantee. A judgment may be fraudulent as well as a deed. Consequently, the grantee under the deed may show that the judgment was obtained by fraud and collusion.89

The right to set aside a fraudulent conveyance may also be lost by waiver or estoppel. Thus, where a creditor, after acquiring knowledge of a fraudulent transfer, takes no steps to impeach it, but on the contrary goes into partnership with the fraudulent grantee for the purpose of carrying on a business in the stock of goods transferred, thereby inducing the grantee to purchase new goods from time to time to replace the goods transferred, is estopped from thereafter questioning the validity of the sale as against the grantee even though he was not a party to the original fraud.90

However, the statute declaring conveyances made for the purpose or with the intention of hindering, delaying, and defrauding creditors to be void refers to a legal, and not to a moral intent, and, when the legal effect of a conveyance is to hinder, delay, or defraud creditors, the intent will be presumed regardless of the actual motives of the parties.93 Consequently, the rule is well settled that a voluntary conveyance by a debtor, while not fraudulent per se, is prima facie or presumptive evidence of fraud. The presumption may be rebutted or explained, but the burden of proving that the deed was not fraudulent falls upon those claiming under it.94 The conveyance attacked must be shown to be voluntary before the presumption of fraud attaches to it under the foregoing rule,95 although it is not necessary for the creditor to show that the debtor was insolvent at the time of the conveyance.96 

Thus, in a suit to set aside as fraudulent a conveyance made by a husband to his wife, brought by a creditor whose claim existed at the date of the conveyance, the burden of proving that the consideration for the conveyance was bona fide and proportionate to the value of the land conveyed is upon the wife, and clearer and fuller proof is required than if the transaction had been between strangers.97 The husband's declarations, made subsequent to the conveyance to his wife, that the land was purchased with money or

In this connection, it should be noted that the court will not presume that a conveyance by a husband to his wife is voluntary when the husband is not shown to be insolvent or in failing circumstances, when the fact is specifically denied by the husband and wife in their answer, and when no evidence of the voluntary nature of the transfer is made to appear from the instrument of conveyance or otherwise. A wide latitude is permitted in the proof of fraud in those cases where the question becomes one of fact.103 Proof of circumstances reasonably connected with the fraudulent act charged, from which fraud may be inferred or presumed, is admissible. 104 Statements made by the debtor to persons other than the purchaser that he needed money and that they could have his property at their own price are admissible as bearing upon a fraudulent purpose in the disposition of property.105 As a fraudulent intent must usually be shown by circumstantial evidence, circumstances altogether inconclusive, if separately considered, may, by their number and joint consideration, be sufficient to constitute conclusive proof.106

§ 256.-Nature of Remedy.-Injunctions are of two kinds, prohibitory and mandatory. A prohibitory, sometimes called a preventive, injunction is one that operates to restrain the commission or continuance of an act and to prevent a threatened injury. A mandatory injunction is one which goes beyond a mere restraint and commands an act to be done or undone.' The object and purpose of a prohibitory injunction is to preserve and maintain an existing condi- 

1. Zetrouer v. Zetrouer, 89 Fla. 253, 103 So. 625.

[Ch. 26 

tion or state, and to restrain an act which, if done, would be contrary to equity and good conscience. It interposes between the plaintiff and the injury he fears or seeks to avoid. It is the appropriate relief when the remedy at law is subsequent to the injury and does not afford adequate compensation therefor.2 

The writ of injunction is not an ordinary writ, but is drastic and extraordinary, and it should never be granted lightly, but sparingly and cautiously. While an injunction is a beneficial writ, great care should be exercised in awarding it lest it be turned into an instrument of oppression and injury. An injunction is also a discretionary writ.4 § 257.-Right to Relief-In General.-As in the case of all other equitable relief, an injunction will not be granted where the remedy at law is adequate. It is only where the remedy at law is not full, complete, and adequate, or where complete relief is doubtful, and a more ample and appropriate remedy is thereby afforded, that equity will take cognizance and give relief by way of injunction in accordance with recognized principles of chancery jurisprudence.

Another special ground of equity jurisdiction for which the remedy by injunction is freely used is the prevention of a multiplicity of actions at law. However, before a court of chancery will interfere on this ground, there must be several persons controverting the same right, and each standing upon his own pretension of right.

It is fundamental that a prohibitory injunction will never be granted where it appears that the acts complained of have already

§ 258.-Right to Relief-Against Proceedings at Law.-The power to stay proceedings at law for the purpose of exercising equitable control over the parties and proceedings, to the end that justice may be promoted, though exercised sparingly, 14A is inherent in courts of general equity jurisdiction.15 Thus, it is well settled. that equity will enjoin an action at law, at the suit of the defendant therein, where it can afford full relief and grant a more complete remedy than the law court. Likewise, when the bringing in of new parties is necessary in order to do complete justice, and this cannot be done at law, equity will assume jurisdiction of the case and enjoin proceedings at law. The foregoing principles are illustrated by numerous decisions in which they have been applied. Thus, where the administrator of a deceased partner sues the surviving partner in an action at law upon an instrument originally obtained through fraud, and the surviving partner brings a bill to adjust the partnership accounts, and the ascertainment of the true character of the instrument is essential to the adjustment of the accounts between the parties, a court of equity will enjoin the proceeding at law. 17 And where a deed absolute in form is given to secure the payment of a debt, and is in effect, therefore, a mortgage, equity will restrain an action for possession by the grantee prior to foreclosure. 18 

When a court of equity, with all the parties in interest before it, exercises jurisdiction for the purpose of re-establishing a lost deed, and the only question is the amount and description of the land in the deed, and the issue is found against the grantor therein, it will, upon proper prayer, retain jurisdiction of the case and make a final decree enjoining the grantor from further prosecuting a suit in ejectment against a party in possession claiming under the grantee in the deed.19 Similarly, equity having jurisdiction to correct an erroneous description of land in a deed, will enjoin a suit in ejectment against a party who has entered under the deed where the deed, as corrected, constitutes a valid defense to the ejectment suit.20

Where an action at law is brought upon a note given for the purchase price of land, and the purchaser claims that the note was obtained through fraud and seeks a rescission and cancellation of the contract to purchase, equity will, upon a bill setting up those facts, enjoin the action at law since it can grant more complete relief than the law court.21 And a court of equity may, on equitable grounds at the suit of a tenant, enjoin a landlord from prosecuting pending or threatened dispossessory proceedings in order to thereby render available any proper equitable defenses the tenant may have against the landlord.22 In interpleader proceedings, equity may enjoin an action at law in order to draw the entire controversy into one suit.23

However, where a defendant to an action at law applies by bill in equity for relief against matters involved in that action, and for an injunction to restrain the further prosecution of the action, and it appears that under his pleadings in the common law action he can obtain therein the same relief to which the allegations of his bill entitle him, an injunction to restrain the action at law is properly refused. In no case will equity enjoin legal proceedings where the law court is competent to adjudicate, upon proper pleas, the matters presented as a ground for an injunction.24 Thus, where one claiming possession of real estate institutes a possessory action at law against another person who is in possession under an agreement between them, which agreement, if set up in the action at law, is a good defense thereto, equity will not enjoin the proceedings but will leave the party to make his defense at law.25

§ 259.-Right to Relief-Against Judgments and Decrees.-Courts of equity will grant relief from judgments of courts of law and decrees of equity courts in a variety of cases. Where a defense could not at the time or under the circumstances be made available, and the party is free from laches, in cases of surprise where reasonable diligence could not avail, and where the facts constituting the surprise are tantamount to a fraud, the enforcement of a judgment or decree will be enjoined.29

Thus, where a defendant interposes no defense, relying upon the written assurance of the plaintiff's attorney that he will not take judgment against him or hold him responsible in any way, and the plaintiff, contrary to this assurance, does take a judgment, a court of equity will enjoin its execution.30 And where a decree for the foreclosure of a mortgage is alleged to be fraudulent and to have been made for the purpose of defrauding the creditors of the defendant therein, in that no money was ever loaned as pretended by the papers which were the basis for the decree, equity will, upon a bill filed by a creditor to subject the property covered by the decree to the payment of his debt, enjoin its enforcement.31

The enforcement of a judgment may also be enjoined where such action is warranted by some strong equity existing in the plaintiff's favor. Thus, where a judgment has been entered against the plaintiff in favor of an insolvent defendant, and the plaintiff has a claim of set-off which he could not assert in the original action, equity will enjoin enforcement of the defendant's judgment until the plaintiff's set-off can be properly established.35 And where a ward has obtained a judgment against the sureties on his guardian's bond, and an equity for an accounting exists between the guardian and ward, enforcement of the judgment against the sureties will be restrained until the entry of an appropriate decree in the accounting suit.36

But where the record shows that the judgment sought to be enjoined is that of a court of competent jurisdiction, and that the court had jurisdiction of the subject matter and of the parties, and no fraud is charged, and the plaintiff had every opportunity to defend the action, equity will not intervene.37 The existence of a clear and adequate remedy at law of which the plaintiff neglected to avail himself, either by reason of a misapprehension of the rules of practice or of anticipated obstacles which might be met, precludes resort to equity to obtain relief.38 Negligence, inattention, and laches in the defense of a suit afford no basis for equitable relief from an adverse judgment rendered therein.39

In cases where a judgment has been obtained on the basis of an appearance entered by an attorney without authority, and a new action would be barred by the statute of limitations, equity will not relieve against the judgment unless fraud or a meritorious defense can be shown.44 

§ 260.-Right to Relief-Against Executions.-It is competent for a court of equity to enjoin the sale of property under an execution upon the showing of an unquestionable or reasonably clear equity and a clear right in the plaintiff.45

It is well settled, however, that a court of equity will never restrain the sale of personal property under an execution unless the property is of such peculiar and intrinsic value to the owner that adequate compensation for its loss cannot be made in damages. 

The ordinary remedy in such cases is at law by an action of trespass, and the rule rests upon the principle that equity will not act where there is a full, adequate, and complete remedy at law.46 

And in cases where the sale of a unique chattel, not the property of the judgment debtor, is threatened, it would seem that the owner should first be required to exhaust his statutory remedy at law.47

With respect to the mortgagee of chattels, an independent bill in equity will not lie for the sole purpose of restraining the sale of the mortgaged property under execution unless such relief is necessary to prevent the conversion or destruction of the property or the impairment of the mortgagee's security, or unless equity is the only forum with power to determine the mortgagee's rights and afford him full, adequate, and complete relief in the circumstances. Where the attaching creditor is not insolvent, and the purchaser is charged with notice of the recorded mortgage lien and is required to post a bond to have the property forthcoming to answer a decree of foreclosure, the necessity for restraining a sale does not appear.4 48 Likewise, where a writ of attachment is levied upon goods, and afterwards an execution is levied upon the same goods, and the sheriff, before judgment in the attachment suit, advertises the goods for sale under the execution, a court of equity will not enjoin the sale. The law court has ample power to control the process and its officer, and the sheriff acts at his peril in selling the property under a junior levy.49

In the case of real property, it is well settled that, where the land of one person is levied upon to satisfy the debt of another, equity will enjoin the sale on the ground that it casts a cloud upon the title of the true owner. 50 Under the original rule, the right of a court of equity to enjoin execution sales on this ground was restricted to cases where the judgment and execution were against some person who previously had some interest in or title to the property.51 But these rules have been changed by statute and it is now clear that an attempt to sell land as the property of a person other than the true owner may be restrained by the latter even though the other person never had any interest in or title to the land and regardless of the apparent validity of the execution.52 Even where real property is held by a wife on secret trust for her husband, equity will enjoin its sale under an execution issued against the husband because it is in no event subject to sale under an execution upon a judgment against him.53

Under proper circumstances, the true owner of real estate may enjoin its sale under an execution issued upon a judgment against him. Thus, the levy upon land which is exempt by law from levy and sale, and advertising the same for sale, constitute such an attempt to cast a cloud upon title as to give a court of equity jurisdiction to enjoin the sale.54 Originally, a sale of land under an execution void on its face would not be enjoined,55 but this rule appears to have been changed by later decisions.56 

Equity will not, at the suit of the defendant in execution, enjoin a sale of real estate where the legality of the execution has been adjudicated in a statutory proceeding at law brought by him, and where no independent equity appears.57 

Whether a suit to enjoin a sale of real estate under an execution is brought by the defendant in execution, or by a third person claiming to be the owner of the property, an injunction cannot be granted unless the person seeking such relief is in possession of the land about to be sold. If the plaintiff in equity is not in possession, he has an adequate remedy at law.58 

Injunction will not lie to stay the eviction process in an ejectment suit, either because it is sought to be enforced against land not involved in the judgment, 59 or pending betterment proceedings for the recovery of the value of improvements." Full relief may be had through statutory proceedings at law and resort to a court of chancery is unnecessary unless independent equities appear. 60

Nor will equity restrain a trespass upon real estate merely because it is a trespass. As a general rule, two things must concur to give a court of equity jurisdiction to grant an injunction against a trespass upon real property; first, the plaintiff's title must be admitted or legally established; and second, the trespass must be of such a nature as to cause irreparable damage not susceptible of complete pecuniary compensation. The inadequacy of the legal remedy is the foundation and indispensable prerequisite for the intervention of a court of chancery in such cases for the reason that a legal remedy has been devised to redress such wrongs and, if this remedy is adequate, equity has no right to interfere. The practice of granting injunctions in cases of trespass to real estate is now more liberal than it formerly was, but a clear case of the inadequacy of the legal remedy must still be shown in order to justify the action of equity in such cases.64 

In a suit to enjoin a trespass upon land, the plaintiff must have title and, as a general rule, be in possession in order to successfully invoke the aid of the court by injunction. If the plaintiff's title is disputed, equity will not interfere, or, if a temporary injunction has been granted, it will not be made permanent until the title has been successfully established at law. The only exception to this rule is where the aid of equity is necessary to preserve the property from serious and irreparable injury pending an action at law already instituted to try the legal title.65

In cases of repeated trespasses, where it becomes necessary to quiet an admitted or established possession, chancery has often interposed to prevent a multiplicity of suits even though there may be a remedy at law. Equity will not, however, grant an injunction against one person merely because he is guilty of repeated trespasses where the legal remedy affords adequate and complete relief in damages. The rule well sustained by authority is that, before a court of chancery will enjoin a trespass to real property in order to prevent a multiplicity of suits, there must be several persons controverting the same right, and each standing upon his own claim or pretension.68

The power of equity courts to enjoin trespasses to land has been exercised in a wide variety of cases. § 262.-Right to Relief-Against Waste.-Waste is an abuse or destruction of property by one in rightful possession. It is to be distinguished from trespass, which is an injury to or use of the property of one person by another who has no right whatever to the property.79 waste.81

Injunction is available as a remedy to stop waste.80 At the suit of a landlord against his tenant, an injunction is available to stop waste regardless of the irreparability of the injury or the insolvency of the tenant or licensee charged with the commission of The holder of a mortgage upon real or personal property may enjoin the mortgagor from damaging or destroying the property covered by his lien, but in such cases it seems clear that the mortgagee must show that the acts complained of will impair the value of the property as security for the debt and imperil its ultimate payment.82

Ordinarily, equity will interfere only to stay future waste, but under some circumstances it will give satisfaction for waste already done.83

Unless this can be shown, the party is left to his remedy at law.84 

And an injunction will be denied, even where a nuisance is clearly established, where substantial redress can be afforded by the payment of money.85

Anything which annoys or disturbs one in the free use, possession, or enjoyment of his property, or which renders its ordinary use or occupation physically uncomfortable, is a nuisance and may be restrained.86 Thus the erection of a building in the center of a street, to be used as a meat and fish market and a place for confining swine and other animals, is a nuisance and may be enjoined by an owner of residence or business property in front of which the building is to be erected.87 The operation of a dance hall in a residential section during the night may constitute a nuisance which may be enjoined.88 

A distinction is drawn between things which are prima facie a nuisance, and things which may or may not become a nuisance according to the manner of their use. In the former case, equity will enjoin in the first instance, but, in the latter, it withholds interference until final hearing or a trial at law. Nor will equity interfere where the thing complained of is not in existence, but may be called into existence by the threatened acts of the defendant, and it is uncertain whether it will operate injuriously. Thus the operation of a livery stable next to an hotel or dwelling house in a city is not prima facie a nuisance and will not be enjoined unless, in its use, it is injurious to the health, comfort, or convenience of the neighboring residents. 89

On the other hand, where a corporation, or an officer, or a body of individuals, is vested with the power to levy a tax for a specific purpose, a court of equity will not inquire into the regularity of the exercise of the power. It will leave the parties to their remedy at law unless the taxing power has been exercised in such a manner as to amount in law to a fraud.96 And, while equity will give relief against arbitrary action and unjust discrimination in imposing taxes, it will not afford immunity from taxation merely because there may be some inequality in assessments. The duty to bear a just share of taxation, justice to other taxpayers, and the requirements of government make it inequitable to give relief from all taxation merely because there may be some inequality in the assessment roll which might have been remedied by pursuing administrative or other process at the proper time.97 

Nor will equity enjoin an officer from collecting a tax merely because he might adopt a method which would be fairer and more equitable. Thus, a tax may be collected by a sale of the real estate on which it was levied regardless of the fact that the property had been recently sold under a judicial decree directing that the tax be paid out of the proceeds of the sale. It is only when a tax is illegal, or is being illegally collected, that an injunction will be granted.98

§ 266.-Right to Relief-In Matters Relating to Homestead Exemp tion. Jurisdiction is conferred upon Florida equity courts by statute to enjoin the sale of any property, real or personal, that is exempt from forced sale, and to enjoin the sheriff or other officer from setting apart as exempt any property, real or personal, which is not exempt.140 It has been held that the statutes in question give courts of equity full and complete jurisdiction over the matter of homesteads and exemptions. Equity may control and direct the setting apart of such exempt property, restrain any interference therewith by any inhibited process of law, and pass upon and adjudicate the propriety of any exemption set apart by any officer, and rectify it if it is improper.141 

§ 267.-Right to Relief-In Contract Matters.-In some cases, where the remedy at law is inadequate, equity will interfere by injunction to preserve and protect contract rights. An injunction restraining the breach of a contract is a negative specific enforcement of that contract. The jurisdiction of equity to grant such an injunction is substantially coincident with its jurisdiction to compel a specific performance. Both are governed by the same doctrines and rules, and it may be stated as a general proposition that, if the contract is one of a class which will be specifically enforced, a court of equity will restrain its breach if that is the only practical mode of enforcement which its terms permit. 141A 

Thus, equity will enjoin the violation of restrictive covenants contained in deeds to real estate. This will be done at the suit of the one for whose benefit the restriction was established, irrespective of whether there is a privity of estate or contract between the parties, or whether an action at law is maintainable. Where, for example, a covenant in a deed prohibits certain uses of the property conveyed, which may be offensive to others in the neighborhood, those suffering from a breach of the covenant will be afforded relief in equity, though not parties to the deed, upon a showing that the covenant was for their benefit. But, ordinarily, the right
