One type of contract which equity is reluctant to enforce by injunction is that whereby an individual restricts his right to earn a living at his chosen calling.152 In such cases the remedy at law does not appear to be adequate in fact, but equity will not interfere. Thus, it has been uniformly held that, where an employee agrees not to enter into a competing business in the same locality for a specified period after terminating his employment, his employer cannot enjoin him from doing so. The ground for such decisions has been stated to be that the remedy at law is adequate and that equity will not enforce such a contract against the employee when it cannot be enforced against the employer. But the real foundation for the decisions appears to be the reluctance of equity to restrict the right of employees of no peculiar skill or capacity to earn a living.153

In proper cases, equity will enjoin the interference and intermeddling of third persons with contract rights. Where, owing to special features, a contract involves peculiar covenants or advantage, and where the loss occasioned by its breach would be a matter of uncertainty, and the breach cause irreparable injury, the malicious interference of a third person for the purpose of inducing one of the parties to break the contract may be enjoined by the party whose rights are thus endangered. This rule is not restricted to contracts for personal services and it is not necessary to join all the tort-feasors as parties defendant.154

A party to a contract is not entitled to enjoin a breach thereof by the other party unless he himself has performed all that the contract requires of him, so far as that is possible. If the plaintiff is in default, or given cause for non-performance by the defendant, he has no standing in equity.' 155

§ 268.-Right to Relief-Miscellaneous Cases.-Courts of equity will protect by injunction the use of trade names and trade marks.156 

The fraudulent and deceptive imitation of a trade name which the general public, in the exercise of reasonable care, might think is the name of the one first appropriating it, is enjoinable. 157 The right to use a personal name in one's business is also within this rule. No one will be permitted to use even his own name with the fraudulent intention of appropriating the good will of a business established. and built up by another person of the same name. Of course, the use of one's own name cannot be absolutely enjoined, but nevertheless the manner of using it may be regulated by injunction. 158 However, where the only confusion which results from the use of similar names is that which results from carelessness and inattention on the part of the public, and no fraudulent or deceptive purpose appears, equity will not interfere. 159

Equity will protect franchises by injunction. Where a person is properly licensed to operate a ferry, he is entitled to restrain another not so licensed from operating a ferry so near his as to constitute an infringement upon his ferry rights. 160 And where a person is by statute given the right to grow sponges in tidal waters, he is entitled to have his sponge plants and other property in tidal waters protected by injunction.161

Transfers of property by a debtor which are fraudulent as to his creditors may be enjoined in equity.162 And, by statute, courts of equity are authorized, at the suit of a surety on the bond of an executor, administrator, guardian, or trustee, to enjoin the transfer or encumbrance of the property of the principal to the extent necessary to protect the surety.163 Equity courts are also authorized by statute, upon the application of a mortgagee of personal property, to enjoin the removal of such property from the state even though the debt is not due at the time of the application. 164

Suits to enjoin public nuisances cannot be maintained by an individual unless he sustains some special injury to himself or his property. Since private individuals as such have no standing to sue in equity solely for the protection of the general public, a court of equity will not enjoin the collection of taxes or tax sales on the application of one or more individual plaintiffs as to property of non-complaining owners who are not parties to the suit. It is not necessary to join all tort-feasors as parties defendant to a suit to restrain them, as third persons, from maliciously interfering with contract rights.183 § 270.-Bill of Complaint.-As a general rule, no writ of injunction may be granted until a bill of complaint seeking such relief has been filed.184

It is incumbent upon a plaintiff seeking an injunction to allege in his bill of complaint every fact, clearly and definitely, that is necessary to entitle him to relief, and if he omits essential facts therefrom, or states facts which show that he is not entitled to relief in a court of equity, he must suffer the consequences of his so doing. This principle applies to all bills in equity, but it is especially applicable to bills seeking an injunction. The allegations of such a bill must be clear, direct, and positive, and they must state facts and not conclusions of law or the opinions of the pleader. 185 The allegations of the bill should not be upon information and belief, unsupported by other evidence. An exception to this rule is that a preliminary injunction is sometimes allowed upon allegations founded on information and belief until, under an order to show cause, a hearing can be had and better evidence adduced.186

A party seeking an injunction must show, not only a clear legal or equitable right, but also a well grounded apprehension of immediate injury to that right. Where no necessity is shown for the protection of the right by an injunction, it will not be granted.187 

The right, title, or interest of the plaintiff, the violation of which is threatened, should be set forth, not by vague allegations of opinions or conclusions, but by a definite statement of facts, posi-

Where an injunction is prayed on the ground of irreparable injury, the bill of complaint must allege facts which will enable the court to determine whether the injury will be irreparable. A mere general allegation that the injury will be irreparable is not sufficient. 

The court will not act upon the opinion or fears of the plaintiff.

Likewise, where a temporary injunction without notice is sought, an allegation in the bill asserting simply the legal conclusion that notice to the defendant of the application for injunction will accelerate the injury apprehended is not a sufficient excuse and furnishes no reason for dispensing with notice. Where a bill filed to enjoin an execution sale as a cloud upon title to land fails to show that the defendant in execution ever had an interest in the land, it is fatally defective.194 And such a bill brought by one claiming the legal title to land must contain an averment that the plaintiff is in possession or it is subject to dismissal.195 A bill seeking to enjoin an execution, which does not specifically identify the judgment and execution, and which does not limit the prayer for injunction to any particular judgment and execution, is insufficient. 196 Since the purchaser of mortgaged personal property at an execution sale under an inferior claim must give a bond to protect the mortgagee, a bill by the latter to enjoin such a sale must show a diligent but fruitless attempt to pursue , the statutory remedy.197 Where a wife seeks to enjoin the sale of her property under an execution upon a judgment against her husband, her bill of complaint must allege that the property is either her equitable separate estate or her legal separate estate. 198 

A suit to enjoin a trespass must, under some circumstances, be filed in the county where the land lies. Where a single cause of action is presented, in which a present and continuing trespass upon real estate is the sole basis of the suit, and the question of the ownership of the property is actually or potentially involved, and the gravamen of the action is injury to the freehold, the action is local and must be brought in the county where the real estate is situated.199

A bill to enjoin a trespass to land must show that the plaintiff has title to the land and is in possession.200 A failure to show title in the plaintiff, 201 or a disclosure of title in the defendant,202 will render the bill insufficient. § 271.—Answer.-Upon a bill filed and notice of application for an injunction, the defendant may at once file his answer.229 If the answer is verified, it has the effect of an affidavit upon the hearing of the application for a temporary injunction.230

An evasive answer is insufficient.234 So also is an answer stating that the acts complained of have been enjoined in another suit to which the plaintiff is not a party. If the plaintiff is entitled to injunctive relief, he is entitled to a decree in his own name.235

INJUNCTION § 272.-Notice of Application for Temporary Injunction.-In re gard to notice of an application for a temporary injunction, the 

1931 Chancery Act provides: 

"In all cases of applications for injunction, the judge to whom presented, before granting the same, shall be satisfied that sufficient notice of the application has been given to the party sought to be enjoined and of the time and place when the motion is to be made, and no order for such injunction shall be granted without such notice, unless it is manifest to such judge, from the sworn allegations in the bill or the affidavit of the complainant or other competent person, that the injury apprehended will be done if an immediate remedy is not afforded, when he may grant instanter an order restraining the party complained of until the hearing or the further order of the court, which restraining order shall have all the force of an injunction until rescinded or modified by the court."236

The foregoing statute is an enactment of the pre-existing law on this subject, and notice of an application for a temporary injunction should always be given unless the provisions for dispensing with notice have been strictly followed.237

When the issuance of a temporary injunction or restraining order without notice to the defendant is sought, the bill must allege facts showing how and why the injury apprehended will be accelerated if notice is given.238 And, when such an application is made, the allegations of the entire bill should be even more carefully scanned and considered than when the defendant has been served with notice and has an opportunity to resist the application.239 

Before granting a temporary injunction or restraining order without notice, the court should be satisfied that a clear case is made by the bill for such relief, and that it is a case of urgent necessity and one in which irreparable mischief will be produced if the aid of the court is denied.240 The necessity is to be determined by the chancellor in

To the granting of every temporary injunction, there are two prerequisites. The bill must allege facts which appear sufficient to constitute a cause of action or ground for injunction, and, on the full showing made by both sides, it must appear that the injunction is necessary to protect the rights of the plaintiff pending the litigation.253

On the application, the chancellor may consider the merits of the bill of complaint. This must necessarily be the prevailing rule, as an examination of the bill on its merits is the primary means available to the court to determine whether a ground for injunction is stated.254 And relief cannot be granted for matters not charged in the bill. Subject to the foregoing limitations, the granting or denying of a temporary injunction is largely within the discretion of the chancellor, guided by the established principles of equity jurisprudence.259 Thus, while a second application for an injunction, based upon the same evidence as the first application, or on evidence which should have been submitted at the first application, will generally be denied, a court will not, since the matter is within its discretion, be held in error for granting a second application if a clear case is presented.260 But if an abuse of discretion is shown, it is the duty of the appellate court to interfere.261 Accordingly, if the allegations of a bill of complaint are sufficient, and the evidence in support of them is ample to warrant the granting of a temporary injunction, and no sufficient defense is made, an order denying an injunction will be reversed.262 

Since the object of a temporary injunction is to preserve the status quo, it should not be issued where its effect is to change that status. Therefore, where the plaintiff seeks to enjoin the defendant from interfering with acts which the plaintiff is about to do, a preliminary injunction restraining such interference would be erroneous since its effect would be to change the status quo and permit affirmative acts by the plaintiff in advance of a final determination of his right to do them.263

It is well settled that a mandatory injunction will rarely be granted before final hearing, or before the parties have had a full opportunity to present all the facts in the case in such a manner as will enable the court to see and judge what the truth may be. Awarding a mandatory injunction before final hearing would be like awarding an execution before trial and judgment.266

A mandatory injunction is granted at final hearing only to execute the decree of the court.267 Thus, for example, mandatory injunctions have been awarded at that time to require a trespasser to restore to its former condition land which has been trespassed upon by him,268 and to require a railroad company to change an embankment which obstructed the flow of water and caused a constant and recurrent flooding of plaintiff's land.269 

Instances are not wanting, however, where a mandatory injunction commanding the defendant to do some positive act has been issued before final hearing. To warrant such relief there must be a showing of a right that is clear and free from reasonable doubt, coupled with a case of urgent necessity or extreme hardship.270

By clear inference, the statute requires the plaintiff obtaining an injunction to give bond to indemnify the defendant for all costs and damages which he may incur by reason of the issuance of the injunction except in those cases where the conditions of the statute are met. Accordingly, it has been uniformly held that no temporary injunction or restraining order may be awarded without requiring the filing of an indemnity bond unless the statutory exception exists, and that, in order to have the benefit of the statutory exceptions, the plaintiff must prove both the truth of the statements of the bill and the truth of his affidavit that he is unable to give the required security.276 It has also been held that the granting of a restraining order and allowing time in which to file a bond,277

However, the general equity rule on this subject has been to some extent modified in Florida by a statute 302 providing that, upon a motion to dissolve an injunction, either party has the right to introduce evidence, and the chancellor must dissolve or continue the injunction according to the weight of the evidence. 

Accordingly, under this statute, either party may introduce evidence in corroboration or denial of the bill, answer, and affidavits, and the chancellor must then be governed by the weight of the evidence. The same rule applies if the hearing is only on bill, answer, and affidavits, and, since the granting and dissolution of injunctions is largely within the discretion of the chancellor, his ruling on a motion to dissolve will not be disturbed on appeal unless it is clearly against the weight of the evidence, or unless an abuse of discretion is shown.303 

On a motion to dissolve an injunction, the burden of proof is on the defendant.304

An application to dissolve an injunction brings up the question of whether the equities of the bill are sufficient to justify an injunction in the first instance.305 If it is plainly apparent that the bill is without equity, and that an injunction should not have been granted in the first instance, the injunction should be dissolved by the court at the first opportunity and the bill dismissed.306 Likewise, whenever it appears that, for any reason, an injunction should not have been granted in the first instance, it should be dissolved at the earliest opportunity.307 But the chancellor should not, on a mere motion to dissolve an injunction, before the time for taking testimony has expired, dismiss the bill unless it is not a proper one for equitable relief.

And if, after the answer comes in, there remains a reasonable doubt as to whether the equities of the bill are sufficiently negatived, the court may continue the injunction to the hearing.310 

Particularly where the defendants are charged with fraud, the injunction, if right in the first instance, should be retained until the hearing unless the answers are full and satisfactory.311 

A motion to dissolve an injunction which has been issued on an unverified bill of complaint should be granted.312 But the filing of an amended bill does not operate to dissolve a temporary injunction issued on the original bill and affidavits where the injunction by its terms was to continue in effect until the further order of the court.313 And an injunction should not necessarily be dissolved by reason of an inadvertent omission to give bond. In such cases, where equity seems to imperatively require the continuance of the injunction, the court may direct that security be given within a brief period and, on failure to give the security, dissolve the injunction.314 

The right to dissolve an injunction may be lost by delay.

The sheriff is entitled to the property by virtue of his levy.323

§ 281.-In General.-The Constitution of Florida' requires the legislature to provide for giving to mechanics and laborers an adequate lien upon the subject matter of their labor. A lien is a charge upon property for the payment of a debt.2 

The entire subject of mechanics' and laborers' liens was revised in Florida by the enactment of the Uniform Mechanics' Lien Act in 1935. This Act provides for mechanics' and laborers' liens upon real property. It has no application to personal property. 

The prior laws relating to liens upon such property were not affected by the 1935 Act.

A mechanic's or laborer's lien is statutory, and not contractual. 

While a contract is essential as the basis for the lien,4 the right to a lien is not created by the contract between the parties, but by the operation of the statute upon the relationship into which the parties have brought themselves.5 And, a mechanic's lien being entirely statutory, before any person may have such a lien the statutory provisions in regard thereto must be strictly complied with.

Every step prescribed by the statute must be shown to have been substantially followed, or the lien does not exist." 

A mechanic's lien does not confer a substantive right upon the laborer, and it forms no part of the contract of employment. The right of a laborer to be paid for his services is not given by the mechanics' lien laws. Such laws merely provide a remedy by which the right may be enforced. And a mechanic's lien can be acquired only by the performance of a contract and not by its breach. 

A lien does not arise because a laborer was prevented by the other contracting party from performing services for which he would have had a lien if the services were completed.Ⓡ 

§ 282.-Right to Lien.-A contractor, subcontractor, material man, or laborer has a lien on the real property improved by him for any money owing to him for labor or services performed or materials furnished in accordance with his contract and with the direct contract. Any person who performs services as architect, landscape architect, or engineer has a lien on the real property improved for any money that is owing to him for his services in connection with improving the real property, or for his services in supervising any portion of the work of improving the real property, rendered in accordance with his contract and the direct con- But the aggregate amount of all liens allowed for performing labor or services or furnishing materials covered by any direct contract may not exceed the contract price as fixed by the direct contract and as diminished by any money properly paid by the owner under such contract.9 tract.

The Uniform Mechanics' Lien Act provides that when the contract for improving real property is made with a husband or wife who is not separated and living apart from his or her spouse and the property is owned by the other or by both, the husband or wife who contracts shall be deemed to be the agent of the other to the extent of subjecting the right, title, or interest of the other in said property to liens under the Act, unless such other shall, within ten days after learning of the contract, give the contractor and file with the clerk of the circuit court of the county in which the property is situated written notice of his or her objection thereto.18 This provision clearly gives to either a husband or wife a prima facie agency to enter into contracts for and on behalf of the other for the improvement of real estate owned by them as tenants by the entirety, subject, of course, to the restrictions stated in the statute.

The terms of the foregoing statute are also broad enough to confer upon a husband a prima facie agency to enter into contracts for and on behalf of his wife for the improvement of her separate statutory property. This is undoubtedly the effect of the statute, although it is clear that such a contract could not bind the wife personally.19 The statute does not expressly authorize a married woman to make such contracts on her own behalf, but, in authorizing the husband to make them as her agent, it would seem, by clear and necessary implication, to authorize the wife to make contracts of this nature in person. If the foregoing provisions of the Uniform Mechanics' Lien Act are given this effect, they would thereby supersede the prior statutes20 on this subject. And it would seem clear that such a construction of the Act would not conflict with the provisions of the Florida Constitution in regard to married women's separate property but would provide a definite method for the application of the organic law in such cases.21

A lien created by the Uniform Mechanics' Lien Act continues only for a period of one year after the claim of lien has been filed unless, within that time, an action to enforce the lien is commenced in a court of competent jurisdiction and a notice of the pendency of the action is filed with the clerk of the circuit court of the county in which the claim of lien is filed. However, the failure to file a notice of the pendency of the action does not abate the action as to any person liable to the payment of the debt specified in the claim of lien.23 

§ 283.-Priority of Liens.-The Uniform Mechanics' Lien Act provides that all liens arising thereunder have priority over any conveyance, mortgage, building loan contract, attachment, judgment, or other encumbrance or demand against the real property which was not recorded at the time of the visible commencement of operations.24

A number of decisions rendered under analogous provisions of the prior mechanics' lien statutes are no doubt applicable to the foregoing provision of the new Act. Therefore, it may be considered as settled that a person who takes a mortgage from the owner of real property upon which the construction of a building is in progress takes with notice of any liens for labor or materials furnished in the construction of the building, whether a claim of lien has been recorded or not, and without regard to the expiration of the three months' period allowed for the recording of the claim 

22. C. G. L. Per. Supp. 5396(14). 

23. C. G. L. Per. Supp. 5396(20).

of lien after the final performance of the labor or final furnishing of the materials by the lienor.25 Whether the mortgagee, or other purchaser or creditor, had actual notice of the construction or repair is immaterial. The progress of the work is legal notice to him even where there is no actual notice.26 The assignee of a mortgage given under such circumstances has no greater rights than the original mortgagor.27 

Under the prior statutes it was held that a lien for labor or materials did not relate back to the commencement of construction regardless of who began the work. In other words, a lien was acquired separately and individually by each laborer and materialman and it accrued when the first labor was performed or the first materials were furnished by the individual lienor.28 But the 

Uniform Mechanics' Lien Act apparently places no such restriction. upon the lien claimant. Its language is broad enough to charge a purchaser or creditor with notice of all liens which accrue during the progress of the work whether before or after the recording of his conveyance or mortgage. 

While a purchase money mortgage, made simultaneously with the conveyance to the mortgagor, takes precedence over prior and existing liens arising through the mortgagor, yet it is the duty of the purchase money mortgagee, as of any other mortgagee, to promptly record his mortgage if he would preserve his priority over the rights of innocent creditors arising subsequently to the execution of the mortgage. Consequently, when such a purchase money mortgagee withholds his mortgage from record and permits laborers and materialmen to acquire liens upon the property in ignorance of his unrecorded mortgage, the same rules apply to a purchase money mortgagee as to any other mortgagee.25

While the Uniform Mechanics' Lien Act makes no reference to the effect of actual notice of an unrecorded deed or mortgage upon the holder of a mechanic's lien it seems clear that, in accordance with the decisions under the prior statutes, actual notice would be the equivalent of record notice.30 And, where a mortgage securing a building loan was executed and recorded prior to the accrual of a mechanic's lien, the mortgagee is entitled to priority over the lienor even though some installments of the loan are not made until after the accrual of the mechanic's lien.31 

The Uniform Mechanics' Lien Act provides that a claim of lien may be filed during the progress of the work or thereafter, but not later than three months after the performance of the labor or the furnishing of the materials by the lienor.32 While the Act is not clear on the question, it would seem that, if a claim of lien is not recorded until after the completion of the work, the lienor assumes the risk of being subordinated to the claims of those who deal with the property, in ignorance of his lien, between the completion of the work and the date of recording the lien claim. Under the prior statutes it was held that a purchaser or mortgagee whose claim accrued after the work was completed and before the lien was recorded took precedence over the lien.33 This rule is sound and there is no reason why it should not be followed under the present Act. However, the rule has no application where the claim of the purchaser or mortgagee arose before the completion of the work even though the deed or mortgage was recorded between the completion of the work and the record of the lien claim. 

The rule applies only when the purchaser or mortgagee has changed his position after the completion of the work, before the lien was recorded, and in ignorance of the lien claim. 

As between holders of mechanics' liens, the Uniform Mechanics' Lien Act provides that liens of laborers shall be prior to all others.

§ 284.-Enforcement of Lien.-There are several methods pro vided by statute for the enforcement of mechanics' liens. One of them is by bill in equity.35 The existence of other methods of enforcing a mechanic's lien does not preclude the remedy in equity.36 Nor does the remedy in equity violate the constitutional guaranty of a trial by jury. A mechanic's lien was unknown to the common law and hence was not triable by a jury when the constitutional guaranty was adopted.37 It has been held that the 

Uniform Mechanics' Lien Act, providing for the acquisition and perfection of such liens, did not repeal prior statutes relating to their enforcement which were in no way inconsistent with the subsequent statute.38

The Uniform Mechanics' Lien Act provides that no lien arising thereunder shall continue for a longer period than one year after the claim of lien has been filed unless, within that time, an action to enforce the lien is commenced in a court of competent jurisdiction and a notice of the pendency of the action is filed with the clerk of the circuit court of the county in which the claim of lien is filed.39 It would seem to be the meaning and intent of the 

Uniform Mechanics' Lien Act to require liens arising thereunder to be perfected by recording a notice of lien within three months after the completion of the labor or the furnishing of the materials for which the lien is claimed.40

Under the present Act, as under similar provisions in the prior statute, it is clear that, where no suit to enforce a mechanic's lien is brought within one year after the claim of lien has been filed, the lien expires by limitation and no proceeding can be maintained to enforce it. Since the right and the remedy are created by the same statute, the limitation upon the remedy is also a limitation upon the right, and the failure to bring suit within the one year period results, not only in a loss of the right to enforce the lien, but also in the loss of the lien itself.42 

A chancery suit is commenced, within the meaning of the foregoing statute, when the bill of complaint is filed with the clerk of the circuit court. If the bill is filed within one year after the claim of lien is filed, the requirements of the statute are met 43 However, it is imperative that the owner of the property be named as a party defendant within the one year period. Making him a party thereafter is unavailing and amounts to a new suit brought against him at that time.44 It is not necessary that all inferior lien claimants be named as parties defendant within the one year period. 

The only question between the plaintiff lienor and inferior lien claimants is that of priority, and into that question the right of the plaintiff to enforce his lien does not necessarily enter. Consequently, an inferior lienor may be made a party after the one year period, or a new suit to foreclose against him may be filed after that time.45

§ 285.-Parties.-Mechanics' liens are expressly made assign able by statute.49 Consequently, a suit in equity for the foreclosure of such a lien may be maintained by an assignee thereof,50 or by the trustee in bankruptcy of the lienor.51 An assignee may foreclose in one suit as many liens against the same property as he may have.52

And the statutory provisions for the enforcement of mechanics' liens are broad enough to permit all persons having liens upon the same property and arising out of the same improvement to join together in one suit for their enforcement.53

§ 286.-Bill of Complaint.-A mechanic's lien being strictly stat utory, no person may have such a lien unless the statutory provisions are strictly complied with, and before such a lien can be enforced the claimant must allege and prove a strict compliance with every requirement of the statute. No act necessary to the acquisition of a lien can be presumed to have been performed in the absence of an allegation and proof that it was performed.58 

Since the acquisition of a lien under the Uniform Mechanics' Lien Act is apparently dependent upon the filing of a claim of lien within three months after the final performance of the labor or the final furnishing of the materials,59 a bill of complaint seeking to enforce such a lien must show that a claim of lien was filed within that period, and that all statutory requirements applicable thereto have been substantially complied with.61 And, since proceedings

The extent to which a direct contractor's abandonment of his contract defeats a subcontractor's right to a lien depends upon the circumstances of each case. A right to enforce a mechanic's lien, based upon a contract under which the contractor was to be paid his actual expenses plus a specified percentage thereof for his services, will be lost where it is shown that the contractor padded his labor and material accounts.76 

Such a right may also be lost where it appears that the original bid submitted by the contractor was raised as the result of collusion between the contractor and the owner's agent.77 

Where it does not appear that the status quo can be restored, and there is no intimation of fraud, undue influence, or bad faith, the right to foreclose a mechanic's lien is not defeated by showing that the owner was of unsound mind at the date of the contract.78 Nor, where the foreclosure suit is revived against the administrator and heirs within the time for presenting claims against the estate of a deceased owner, is it barred by the failure to present a claim within that time.79 However, the failure to file a claim bars the right to enforce any personal liability.80 

The right of a direct contractor to enforce a mechanic's lien may be defeated by his failure to furnish the owner with a list of the subcontractors holding such liens. The Uniform Mechanics' Lien 

Act provides that, when final payment becomes due the contractor from the owner, the contractor shall give to the owner a statement under oath that all lienors contracting directly with or directly employed by him have been paid in full, or showing the name of each lienor who has not been paid in full, the amount due or to become due such lienors, and describing in a general way the labor performed or materials furnished by each. The Act further provides that the contractor shall have no lien or right of action against the owner under his contract while in default in giving the owner this statement under oath.81 A lienor may also lose his lien by a failure to furnish the owner with a statement of his account when the owner demands and is entitled to such a statement under the pro visions of the Uniform Mechanics' Lien Act.82

Under the statutes in force prior to the enactment of the Uniform Mechanics' Lien Act, where the owner procured the release of his land from the lien by substituting a bond therefor, the rule was that the lienor might nevertheless maintain his suit in equity and obtain a decree in personam against the owner, but that he was, at least where the sureties denied the validity of the bond, compelled to resort to an action at law for relief against them. 312. Appeals. § 290.-In General.-Under the original common law doctrine, a mortgage conveyed the legal estate and right of possession to the mortgagee. The mortgagee's estate was defeasible by performance of the condition subsequent, that is, payment of the debt secured, but, if the mortgagor failed to pay the debt at the time specified, the legal estate became vested absolutely in the mortgagee. 

Courts of equity, however, gradually came to look with disfavor upon the harshness of the common law rule of absolute forfeiture of the mortgagor's estate upon non-payment of the debt. Regarding the land as security for the debt, they came to the relief of the mortgagor and permitted him to redeem the land, even after breach of

§ 291] 

653 

MORTGAGE FORECLOSURES 

As equity gave the condition, by paying the amount of the debt. this relief, the right to it was called the equity of redemption. 

Equity also gave the mortgagee a remedy by foreclosure, through which a time limit to the right of redemption might be fixed by judicial decree, and, if redemption was not made within the time specified, the mortgagor's rights were extinguished and legal title became absolute in the mortgagee. This was called strict foreclosure.¹

The common law doctrine of mortgages was, however, definitely abrogated in Florida by a statute enacted in 1853 providing that a mortgage should be held to be a specific lien on the property mortgaged, and not a conveyance of the legal title or right of possession.2 

It is further provided by statute that all mortgages shall be foreclosed in chancery. Consequently, since a mortgage is a mere lien, the legal title to, and the right to possession of, mortgaged property can only be acquired by the mortgagee or a third person by his becoming the highest bidder and purchaser of the property under a decree of foreclosure and sale.4 The primary purpose of a bill in equity to foreclose a mortgage is to subject the mortgaged property to the payment of the debt secured. If the proceeds received from a sale of the property are insufficient for that purpose, an action at law may be maintained for the balance due, or a deficiency decree may be rendered in the foreclosure suit. But, since it is primarily directed against the mortgaged property, a suit to foreclose a mortgage is a suit quasi in rem. It must, therefore, be brought in the county where the land lies even though other relief, such as a deficiency decree, may be prayed for and granted. If the mortgaged land is situated in two or more counties, foreclosure may be had in any one of the counties.7

The validity of reasonable provisions in a trust deed limiting the right of foreclosure by bondholders, and placing the right solely in the trustee, except upon stated conditions, is generally acknowledged. Thus, where a trust deed confers the sole right to foreclose upon the trustee unless, upon request of a certain percentage of the bondholders, he refuses to institute such proceedings, a bondholder is bound thereby even though the trustee unjustly neglects to take appropriate action, or occupies a hostile position to a minority of the bondholders, or conspires to defeat the rights of some of the bondholders. Such actions may give rise to independent equities, but they do not confer a right to foreclose in violation of the restriction contained in the trust deed.26 

Where there are two trustees under a trust deed securing a bond issue, and the deed provides that, upon the death or resignation of either of them, the remaining trustee shall, without any instrument of transfer or other formality, succeed to the rights of both, a foreclosure suit may be filed by one trustee alone upon the resignation of the other.27 And, where a trustee under a trust deed submits himself to the jurisdiction of the court in a foreclosure suit, the court may, upon the trustee's petition, discharge him and appoint a successor to prosecute the suit.28 The statutory liquidator of an insolvent trust company may foreclose a trust deed under which the company was trustee even though the deed provides another exclusive method of selecting a successor trustee. The liq- uidator is not a successor trustee but a statutory instrumentality for carrying out the trust.29

In 1892, the statutes respecting real estate of a decedent were changed, and it was provided that title to real estate should pass to the heir or devisee and remain in his possession unless the personal representative should take possession of or sell it under a court order for the payment of debts. Under this statute, it was held that the decedent's heirs or devisees were necessary parties to the foreclosure of a real estate mortgage executed by him.45 

However, the 1933 Florida Probate Act reverted at least in part to the earlier rule.46 It provides that the personal representative shall take possession of all of the real estate of a decedent, except homestead, and that it shall be assets in his hands for the payment of expenses, debts, legacies, and taxes.47 By analogy to the 1828 statute, it seems clear that the personal representative is again a necessary party to the foreclosure of a mortgage upon property of a decedent's estate. That the heirs or devisees are also necessary parties under the present law seems reasonably clear. They were not necessary parties under the 1828 statute, but that statute contains several provisions upon which the rule was based that are not contained in the 1933 Probate Act.48 Furthermore, the 1933 

Probate Act specifically provides that "in all actions or suits involving the title to real property, against an estate for the possession or recovery of real property or for the purpose of quieting title thereto, the personal representative and the heirs or devisees of such property shall be made parties."49 The applicability of this provision to a mortgage foreclosure is not entirely clear, but in any event it is the better, if not the necessary practice, to join the heirs or devisees as parties defendant.

And, without special features of an equitable nature to authorize such action, one claiming adversely to both mortgagor and mortgagee by paramount title cannot be joined as a defendant to the suit. Thus, since a tax title is one in fee, extinguishing all prior interests and liens, the holder thereof cannot be joined in a foreclosure suit for the purpose of adjudicating the validity of his claim. The advantage of joining claimants of an adverse title is obvious. It enables the mortgagee in one suit to remove all obstacles to the enforcement of his debt and to sell the property free from the cloud of an adverse claim of title. But, to the adverse claimant, the practice is objectionable because it entangles him in a contest between the mortgagor and mortgagee with which he has no concern and, when he is in adverse possession of the premises, it deprives him of his right to a trial by jury. The objections to this practice have been uniformly held to outweigh its advantages.61 

There is an exception to the foregoing rule, however, where a charge is made of fraud or collusion between the mortgagor and the purchaser at the tax sale, or where good faith requires that the purchase of the tax title be treated as a payment of the taxes. In such a case, the holder of the tax title may be joined as a party defendant.62 And, in any event, an adverse title holder may waive his right to be omitted from the suit by failing to raise the objection.63

Where a person is allowed to intervene in a foreclosure suit, and it then appears that he has parted with his entire interest in the property, the bill should be dismissed as to him and he should be required to pay all costs occasioned by his action.76 § 294.-Accrual of Right to Foreclose.-The accrual of a right to foreclose a mortgage depends, of course, upon the conditions and covenants of the mortgage.

In the absence of a provision in the mortgage to the contrary, the mortgagee cannot foreclose until there has been a default in the payment of the principal debt secured.77 Thus, where mortgage and note merely contain an agreement to pay interest, but not in specified installments, there can be no foreclosure prior to the maturity of the principal debt.78 And, where by the terms of a note and mortgage, the latter is not subject to foreclosure until there has been a default in the payment of an annual installment of principal and interest, a foreclosure suit filed prior to such a default is premature and will be dismissed.79 But, where the mortgage contains a covenant to pay interest in specified installments, a default in the payment of a single installment will entitle the mortgagee to foreclose even though the time for the payment of the principal has not yet arrived. And subsequent foreclosures may be maintained for the failure to pay succeeding installments of interest. This rule applies even where the mortgage contains an acceleration clause if the option to accelerate is not exercised.80

There are two possible rules in regard to the effect of delay upon the part of the mortgagee in exercising his option to accelerate. One rule is that if the option to accelerate is not exercised within a reasonable time it will be deemed to have been waived. The other rule is that the right to exercise the option exists as long as the default continues and is not waived unless the delay operates to the benefit of the holder of the mortgage or to the detriment or loss of the mortgagor.8 The Supreme Court of Florida has not definitely committed itself to either rule. It has stated that the former rule is supported by the weight of authority, but it has also indicated that in Florida the right to exercise an option to accelerate is affected only where delay results in advantage to the mortgagee or detriment to the mortgagor.91 

However, any apparent approval of the latter rule appears to be definitely qualified by a decision that, where an option to accelerate is not exercised within a reasonable time, equity may require that the mortgagors be given notice and an opportunity to pay all past due installments before a bill to foreclose may be maintained.⁹2 

Where a mortgage contains an acceleration clause, but the number of days after default when the option to accelerate may be exercised is, through inadvertence or otherwise, not specified in the mortgage, the mortgage may be accelerated at any time after a default.93 Where mortgage notes represent both principal and interest to maturity, an acceleration clause will not be enforced except upon cancellation of the unearned interest.94 The failure to present a mortgage note for payment at the time and place specified therefor will defeat the right to accelerate where the note would have been paid if presented.95

As previously stated, a suit to foreclose a mortgage cannot be maintained prior to the maturity date of the principal debt unless such a procedure is authorized by the provisions of the mortgage. 

Thus the foreclosure of a mortgage prior to the due date of the debt is not authorized merely by the breach of a covenant to keep the mortgaged property in repair and to pay the taxes thereon.96 

But, where a mortgage contains a covenant to pay taxes, and a further provision that, upon a default in the payment of taxes, the mortgagee may pay the same without waiving his right to foreclose by reason of the default, the latter provision indicates a right to foreclose upon default in the payment of taxes and, where the mortgagee has paid such taxes, he may maintain foreclosure prior to the due date of the principal debt.97 And, upon a default in the payment of taxes, foreclosure may be maintained for the entire debt where the mortgage authorizes the mortgagee, upon such a default, to declare all sums thereby secured to be immediately due and payable and, in such a case, the mortgagee need not pay the taxes as a prerequisite to exercising his option.98 

Where a mortgage contains a covenant that the mortgagor will pay all expenses of collecting the debt, including a reasonable attorney's fee, and that all of said sums shall be secured by the mortgage, and the mortgagee obtains a judgment at law for the amount of the debt, but the mortgagor refuses to pay attorney's fees, foreclosure may be maintained for such fees and costs.99 

A plaintiff, who, in foreclosing his mortgage, omits as parties defendant to the suit any persons claiming an interest in the mortgaged property inferior to his own, may maintain another bill in the same court to foreclose against the parties omitted from the first suit. 100 The benefit of this rule also accrues to purchasers at the sale under the first suit.101 A mortgagee who settles a foreclosure suit by accepting a deed from the mortgagor may renew his suit

§ 295.-Bill of Complaint.-The allegations of a bill of complaint to foreclose a mortgage must be sufficient to support a decree of foreclosure or the decree will be reversed.105 In general, a foreclosure bill should allege the execution of the note and mortgage, with a full description of both instruments, the plaintiff's ownership of them, the covenants of the mortgage, the breach thereof on which the right to foreclose is predicated, and the amount claimed to be due the plaintiff.106 

In regard to the execution of the mortgage, where a bill exhibits a mortgage signed by the president and under the seal of a corporation, it makes out such a prima facie case of right in the plaintiff as to require an answer to raise an issue as to the validity of the mortgage.107 Where a mortgage is signed by the mortgagors as trustees, this is sufficient to put the mortgagee on inquiry as to their powers.

Before a bill can be maintained to foreclose such a mortgage, the authority of the trustee to execute it must be alleged and proved. And, if it is claimed that the beneficiaries ratified the mortgage, the facts imparting such validity should be set up in the bill.108 An allegation that land was conveyed to secure a

It is provided by statute that no suit in equity shall operate as a lis pendens as to any property involved therein until there has been filed in the office of the clerk of the circuit court of the county where the property is situated, and recorded in a book to be kept for that purpose, a notice of the institution of such suit, containing the names of the parties, the time of the institution of the suit, the name of the court in which it is pending, a description of the property involved, and a statement of the relief sought as to such property.¹ 150 A lis pendens is literally a pending suit. It has been defined as the jurisdiction, power, or control which courts acquire over property involved in a suit pending continuance of the action and until final decree.151 Accordingly, when a notice of lis pendens is filed and recorded in accordance with the statute, every transferee or assignee of the property who acquires his interest after the institution of the foreclosure suit and after the lis pendens has been filed takes subject to the result of the suit just as if he were a party thereto.152 It is absolutely essential, however, that the notice of lis pendens be filed and recorded in order to be effective for this purpose. 153

Constructive service is valid in a suit to foreclose a mortgage even as against non-residents of the state of Florida. Such defendants are under a duty to be attentive to judicial proceedings that affect their rights in land and to take measures that will insure their receipt of reasonable notice that a suit has been brought involving their property. This is especially true when their rights are subject to contract, statutory, or other encumbrances. The Florida constructive service statutes have been held to give reasonable notice. and to comply with the requirements of due process of law in this respect. Consequently, proper constructive service is a sufficient predicate for a valid decree of foreclosure and sale against an interest in real estate of any defendant so served.156 

Of course, a deficiency decree cannot be entered on constructive service. 

In a mortgage foreclosure suit, notice given to the mortgagor by the name which appears in the record of the mortgage is sufficient. 157

An answer tendering payment of all amounts due under the mortgage will defeat a foreclosure suit.170 If the defense is based upon a tender prior to suit it need only show a tender of the amounts then due, but if the tender is made after the institution of suit it would seem necessary to include all sums required for redemption, including costs, expenses, and attorney's fees. An answer setting up a tender of payment in money as a defense to a foreclosure suit must, in order to be sufficient, show a production of the money to be paid and an offer of it to the person to whom it should be paid. It must further show that the debtor has ever since been ready to pay and be accompanied by a payment of the money into court.171 A tender of a sum less than is due on the mortgage is no bar to foreclosure.172

§ 301.-Taking of Testimony.-Testimony is taken in a suit to foreclose a mortgage in accordance with the same rules which apply to the taking of testimony in all chancery cases, 227 but it is within the province of the trial court to regulate the order of the introduction of evidence and its rulings in such matters will not be interfered with by the appellate court except where an abuse of discretion is shown.228

Where the evidence of the debt alleged to exist is a note, bond, or mortgage, the party seeking a final decree thereon should produce the note, bond, or mortgage.229 In a suit to enforce a mortgage, however, where the mortgagor calls for proof, it is not enough that the bond or note be physically before the master. The Constitution of Florida provides that mortgages which have been proved for record and recorded according to law shall be taken. as prima facie evidence in the courts of this State without requiring proof of execution. The Constitution further provides that a certified copy of the record of any mortgage that has been recorded according to law shall be admitted as prima facie evidence thereof, and of its due execution, with like effect as the original mortgage duly proved, provided it is made to appear that the original is not within the custody or control of the party offering the copy.236 

Prima facie evidence, within the meaning of the constitutional provision, is such as in the judgment of the law is sufficient to establish a fact and, if unrebutted, remains sufficient for that purpose. 

Where its conditions are complied with, the foregoing provisions. of the Constitution are applicable even where the execution of a mortgage is denied in the answer. 237

In a suit to foreclose a mortgage, the plaintiff, of course, has the burden of proving every material allegation of the bill contested by the answer.246 Thus, an answer setting up a want or failure of consideration casts the burden of proving a consideration upon the plaintiff.247 The defendant has the burden of proving an affirmative defense. Payment is an affirmative defense, and the burden is on the defendant of proving it by a clear preponderance of the evidence.248 Possession of the mortgage note by the party liable on it is strong presumptive evidence of payment.249 And the burden is on the plaintiff in a mortgage foreclosure to negative the presumption of payment arising from his agent's delivery of a satisfaction of mortgage to the owner of the property.250

A mortgagee claiming superiority over mortgages admittedly prior in point of time as to execution and recordation has the burden of proving equitable circumstances entitling him to such priority.253 

The defense of usury must be established by the defendant by clear and satisfactory evidence.254

A provision in a mortgage for the payment of reasonable attorney's fees in case of foreclosure being intended as indemnity to protect the mortgagee's interest, the burden is on the plaintiff, in case of suit, to prove his right to such recovery and to establish the basis for determining the amount thereof.255 It is essential that the plaintiff's right to an attorney's fee be established by testimony and, where an attorney's fee is allowed in the absence of such testimony, the decree will be reversed.256 Proof that the plaintiff has paid or agreed to pay an attorney's fee,257 and that such fee is reasonable, 258 is required. Where liability for an attorney's fee rests upon an implied contract, the testimony should show that the mortgage was given to an attorney to foreclose, the services performed, and what fee would be reasonable.259 While the plaintiff's solicitor is an improper witness as to the reasonableness of his fee in foreclosure proceedings, and it is not good practice to award a fee solely on the basis of his testimony, he may testify as to his agreement with the plaintiff for the payment of a fee.260 Testimony as to the reasonableness of an attorney's fee may be taken after the time for taking other testimony in the cause has expired. 

The statute limiting the time for taking testimony applies only to testimony on the issues made by the pleadings.261

The decree must be regarded as a final one to that extent.263 But the decree does not terminate the suit. It gives the mortgagee no right to the possession of the land, and he can acquire no such right unless he obtains a deed under the foreclosure sale.264 The determination of the amount due on the mortgage debt is not a personal judgment against the parties liable therefor,265 and the mortgagee cannot have execution thereon for the sale of any property.266 Therefore, the decree is not final to the extent that jurisdiction of the cause is retained for the supervision of its enforcement and for the further adjustment of the accounts between the parties. It is, however, referred to and considered as a final decree of foreclosure and sale. 

A final decree of foreclosure and sale should be clear and definite in its terms.267 It should clearly show from whom the mortgage debt is due, that the master is to sell certain definitely described property for cash, and that the notice of sale is to be published in a prescribed manner.268 Where the language of a foreclosure decree is open to more than one interpretation, it should be interpreted so as to make it correct and proper with reference to the pleadings and proceedings in the case. 269

270 A defendant in a mortgage foreclosure proceeding should not, in order to save his property from foreclosure sale, be required to pay any amount in excess of what the plaintiff is entitled to recover.2 

This amount includes, of course, the principal of the mortgage debt with interest thereon to the date of the final decree. Unless the note or mortgage provides for interest upon past due interest, or for compound interest, it is not permissible to compute interest on either basis in determining the amount of the final decree.271 In this connection, the rule is that the debt bears interest at the contract rate to the date of the final decree, after which date the total amount found to be due for principal, interest, attorney's fees, costs, and the like bears interest at the rate provided by statute for money judgments.272 It is erroneous to include in a final decree interest on the principal debt to a time beyond the date of the decree, 273

The amount which a defendant should be required to pay in order to save his property from a foreclosure sale should not include any taxes against the mortgaged land which have not been paid or advanced by the plaintiff.274 But, while a mortgagee is under no duty to pay taxes on the mortgaged property, he is entitled, as against both the mortgagor and junior encumbrancers, to reimbursement for any taxes which he does pay and such amounts should be allowed him in the final decree.275 Even where there is no provision in the mortgage to that effect, such an allowance is authorized by statute.276 And, where a second mortgagee pays taxes upon the mortgaged property, he is, in a foreclosure of the first mortgage, entitled to priority over the first mortgage to the extent of his payment. 277

The rules as to the sufficiency of the description of property are the same whether the deed is to be made by a party in his own right or by an officer of the court.293 If the description contained in the mortgage is such that the land cannot be identified, the court may, in default of a showing and prayer for reformation, properly refuse to order a sale, even as between the parties to the instrument, since to do so would simply cause confusion in the public records and cast suspicions and doubts upon the title to property supposed to be adjacent to or in the vicinity of that intended to be mortgaged.294

§ 304.-Vacating Final Decree.-Jurisdiction and authority are conferred upon the circuit courts by statute to rescind, vacate, and set aside any decree for the foreclosure of a mortgage upon property at any time before the sale thereof has been actually made pursuant to the terms of the decree, and to dismiss the foreclosure proceeding upon the payment of all court costs. Whenever a decree of foreclosure has been so vacated and set aside, and the foreclosure proceedings dismissed, the mortgage together with its lien and the debt thereby secured are, both in law and equity, completely relieved of all effects resulting from the foreclosure proceeding and decree. They thereafter have the same force and effect as they had prior to the institution of the foreclosure suit and the entry of the final decree therein.324 § 305.-Redemption.-The right to redeem is an incident to every mortgage, and it belongs to the mortgagor and those claiming under him. This right can be extinguished only by due process of law.325 Consequently, a final decree of foreclosure specifically permits redemption by the parties entitled thereto within a specified time after its entry upon payment to the plaintiff of the amounts found to be due him.326

Anyone who has an interest in the mortgaged land which would be lost by foreclosure is entitled to redeem.327 Thus, the mortgagor or his grantee is entitled to redeem.328 A wife who has joined in the execution of a mortgage for the purpose of relinquishing her dower is also entitled to redeem.329 A lessee claiming under the mortgagor may redeem.330 A second mortgagee may redeem and, if he has not been made a party to the foreclosure of the first mortgage, he may redeem without paying the costs and

In the absence of a statute, a court of equity has no power to extend the period of redemption in mortgage foreclosure proceedings beyond a reasonable time after the entry of the final decree merely because of unusual conditions or periods of extreme economic depression. The time for payment of the mortgage debt is definitely fixed by the contract of the parties, and the mortgagee is entitled to the prompt enforcement of his contract regardless of changes in the circumstances of the mortgagor or of conditions generally.333 § 306.-Sale and Confirmation.-Upon default in the payment of the debt found to be due the plaintiff by a final decree of foreclosure, the decree is enforced, as therein provided, by a sale of the mortgaged property to satisfy the debt. 

The final decree usually directs that the sale be made by a master whom the court therein appoints for that purpose. However, the court is not restricted to any particular designation of official title for the person it appoints to execute a foreclosure decree. 

Such a person is usually called a master, but if he is given any other appropriate title, and the duties and powers usually conferred upon masters in making foreclosure sales, his appointment is not invalid and his acts should be confirmed.334 Where a master appointed by a final decree dies before making the sale, it is not improper to appoint a second master without notice to the defendant.335 

There being no statute in Florida prescribing the method of giving notice of foreclosure sales, the master appointed to make the sale should give notice in the manner prescribed by the final decree under which he is acting.336 Publication of the notice of sale may proceed during the period allowed by the final decree for redemption, but a publication of notice after the signing but before

The general rule is that a master, in making a foreclosure sale, is bound to accept all bids and to sell the property to the highest bidder. However, the master may reject the highest bid for substantial reasons. Thus, where the highest bidder is unable to give security when lawfully requested to do so, or where he is without means of paying the purchase money and is apparently bidding in the idle hope of being able to pay, the master may accept the next highest bid.338 But a bona fide bidder who is able to comply with his bid is entitled to appropriate redress if his bid is arbitrarily rejected. He may not be entitled to have the property even though his bid is the highest, but he may object to the confirmation of the sale and compel a resale to be started at the point of his bid and, in case no higher bid is then made, he is entitled to have the property sold to him.339

Whether a trustee who has foreclosed a mortgage for the benefit of various bondholders may bid at the foreclosure sale depends in the first instance upon the provisions of the trust instrument under which he is acting. If that instrument authorizes him to bid in the property, and use the bonds deposited with him in payment of the purchase price, he may, of course, do so. If the provisions of the trust instrument are not clear as to his authority in this respect, the trustee may by motion apply to the court for a ruling on the question. Where the trust instrument contains no provision on the matter, the authorities are not entirely clear as to whether the trustee may bid, but the better view appears to be that he may do so.340 The receiver of an insolvent corporation. may be authorized to bid in property at a foreclosure sale in order to be in a position to make a more advantageous disposition of it at a private sale.341

A court of equity has power, upon a rule to show cause or other appropriate procedure, to make and enforce an order requiring the purchaser of property at a mortgage foreclosure sale to pay the amount of his bid. However, before such an order may be made, the sale must be confirmed.345 Payment for property bid in at a foreclosure sale need not always be in cash. Where the plaintiff is the successful bidder, the amount due him under the final decree may be applied on his bid over and above the sums required for the costs and expenses of the suit. Where the sale securing an issue is made under a decree foreclosing a trust deed of bonds, any purchaser may use his bonds in payment of the purchase price, but in such a case the value of the bonds used by the purchaser as the equivalent of cash is determined by that proportion of the net proceeds of the sale which his bonds bear to the total indebtedness due. The balance of the bid must be paid in cash.346

Where a sale in a foreclosure proceeding has been made by a master duly appointed for that purpose, upon proper notice, in compliance with the terms of the final decree, and for an adequate price, the action of the court in confirming the sale is not only a proper exercise of its discretion but is the performance of a judicial duty.349 The court has a reasonable discretion in confirming a foreclosure sale not made pursuant to the terms of its final decree.350

Since the amount bid at a foreclosure sale is conclusive as between the parties in further proceedings for the collection of the mortgage debt, the court should not confirm a sale where the amount bid is inequitably less than the real value of the property. 

In such a case a resale of the property should be ordered.351 But the fact that the property did not sell for enough to satisfy the amounts found due by the final decree is no ground for denying confirmation of a sale in the absence of a showing that the amount realized was a grossly inadequate price.352 The failure to record the final decree of foreclosure is sufficient to defeat confirmation of the sale, although not to render the sale void on collateral attack.353 

The death of the defendant after the entry of the final decree will not preclude confirmation of a sale thereunder.354 

An order confirming a sale under a decree of foreclosure is equivalent to an adjudication that the sale was a proper one and creates a presumption of the regularity of the proceedings under which it was made.355 It cures all irregularities, misconduct, and unfairness in the making of the sale, departures from the provisions of the final decree, and errors in the decree and proceedings under it. § 307.-Distribution of Proceeds of Sale.-The proceeds arising from the sale of property under a final decree of foreclosure should be distributed by the master in accordance with the provisions of the final decree. The decree usually provides that the master shall first pay all costs and expenses of the suit, including attorney's fees, and shall then pay to the plaintiff the amounts therein found to be due him on account of principal and interest on the mortgage debt.

A Florida statute imposes upon any master in chancery making a sale of property under order of the court the duty of paying, from the proceeds of the sale, and after the payment of costs, expenses, and attorney's fees, all taxes upon the property which may be due and unpaid.357 The duty imposed 

The duty imposed by this statute is not, however, unqualified. Notwithstanding the statute, a master has no authority to pay taxes unless the final decree contains a provision directing him to do so.358 Furthermore, it is error for the court to enter a decree directing the master to pay taxes unless the amounts thereof have been put in issue and adjudicated in the final decree.359

Where the final decree determines the amount of unpaid taxes and directs the master to pay them, but the proceeds of the sale are insufficient for that purpose, the master should so report to the court and obtain directions from the court as to which taxes are to be paid.360

Where the proceeds arising from a mortgage foreclosure sale are more than sufficient to pay all sums directed to be paid by the final decree, the surplus should be paid by the master into the registry of the court, and the court has full and complete jurisdiction to determine the rights and priorities of claimants to this fund.361 The surplus money stands in the place of the land itself in respect to liens and vested rights therein, and it is well settled

If the mortgagor has any defense to the second mortgage, it can be set up in an answer to the petition.365 § 308.-Deficiency Decrees.-A deficiency decree is one for the balance of the debt found by the final decree to be due the plaintiff after applying thereon the proceeds of the sale of the mortgaged property.366 A deficiency decree is a personal judgment for the payment of money upon which execution may issue.367 

In the absence of a statute or a court rule made in compliance with law, a court of equity has no authority to enter a decree for a deficiency remaining after the sale of mortgaged property, unless the debt, without the mortgage, was one which a court of chancery had jurisdiction to enforce. Without such a statute or court rule, or circumstances giving equitable jurisdiction over the debt, the only remedy for a deficiency is by an action at law on the note.368

In 1927, a new statute specifically authorizing the entry of deficiency decrees was enacted. This statute provides that, in all suits for the foreclosure of mortgages, the entry of a decree for any portion of the deficiency, should one exist, shall be within the sound judicial discretion of the court, but that the plaintiff shall also have the right to sue at common law to recover such deficiency.373 In 1929, this statute was amended by adding thereto a proviso that no suit at law to recover a deficiency may be maintained against the original mortgagor in cases where the mortgage was for the purchase price of the property involved and where the original mortgagee became the purchaser at the foreclosure sale and was also granted a deficiency decree against the mortgagor.374 .374 These statutes are still in effect.

The purpose of the statute is to relieve the parties from the expense and vexation of two suits, one equitable and one legal, when the whole controversy can be adjusted in one suit.375 

The right to a deficiency decree is not absolute.376 Where the mortgaged property does not sell for a sufficient sum to pay the amount of the final decree, the mortgagee does not have an absolute and unequivocal right to demand that a deficiency decree be rendered in his favor. His right to a deficiency decree depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case, and the power exercised by the court in granting such a decree is, as provided by the statute, a discretionary one, that may be exercised or not, as the court deems best after a consideration of all the facts and circumstances.377 

The exercise of the chancellor's discretion in granting a deficiency decree involves two main considerations. The first is whether the equity court will, under the facts and circumstances of the case, enter upon the legal inquiry at all. The second is how far the court will, in the equity suit, allow the legal claim by way of a personal decree against the defendant. The latter phase involves the question of whether an equity court may conscientiously, upon all the facts of the case, allow a judgment for the entire deficiency, or permit judgment to be taken for only a part of it, or deny a judgment entirely.378

the discretion contemplated by the statute is not an absolute and unbridled discretion, but is a sound judgment supported by established equitable principles as applied to the facts of the case. 

No inflexible rule for its exercise can be formulated, but the chancellor may consider principles other than those which would control the strict legal rights of the parties in an action at law.379 A deficiency decree entered upon the theory that it was a matter of absolute legal right in the plaintiff, and that only a strictly maintainable legal defense would avoid it, is erroneous and will be reversed. The defendant is entitled to the exercise of the chancellor's discretion as to whether a deficiency decree should be entered and as to its amount.380 

Under the 1927 statute, a deficiency decree may be entered against the original mortgagor or a grantee of mortgaged property who has assumed and agreed to pay the mortgage.381

Where neither the final decree nor the order confirming sale contains an express reservation of jurisdiction of the cause for the purpose of determining the plaintiff's right to a deficiency decree, the court has no jurisdiction to enter such a decree after the final decree and the order confirming sale have become absolute.395 

Any defense to the entry of a deficiency decree should be presented in due course during the foreclosure proceeding.396 

Facts showing that the plaintiff is not entitled to a deficiency decree, or that such a decree should be granted for a less amount than the plaintiff demands, may be set up in the answer even though they do not constitute a defense to the foreclosure.397 

Such facts may also be set up at the time a motion for a deficiency decree is filed. 

Since the foreclosure decree fixes the amount of the mortgage debt and is a final adjudication thereof, no objections to the amount of the final decree will be considered on the application for the deficiency decree except such as go to the discharge of the debt and have arisen since the confirmation of the sale.398 And failure to seek a deficiency decree against a grantee of the mortgaged premises who has assumed the mortgage does not preclude the entry of a deficiency decree against the original mortgagor where the mortgagee has done nothing to prejudice the rights of the mortgagor against the grantee.399 But, for example, where the mortgagee, though requested by the mortgagor to do so, has failed to enforce the mortgage against the grantee promptly upon a default, and during the delay the mortgaged property has greatly depreciated in value, he will be precluded from obtaining a deficiency decree against the original mortgagor.400

On an application for a deficiency decree, the defendant against whom it is sought may show that the price at which the property sold was so low that the sale should not have been confirmed.401 

Likewise, the chancellor may take into consideration the fact that the mortgage was a purchase money mortgage and that the mortgagee became the purchaser at the foreclosure sale, although other equitable considerations must be coupled with these facts in order to warrant the denial of a deficiency decree.402 

Since, as between the parties to the suit, the sum for which the mortgaged property sold at the foreclosure sale is the conclusive test of its value,403 it is frequently desirable for the mortgagee to sue at law for any deficiency. He can thus avoid having his claim determined upon equitable instead of legal grounds. In order to preserve his right to sue at law, however, it is better practice for the mortgagor to avoid entirely the submission of his claim to a deficiency judgment to the equity court. 

Prior to 1929, the rule was well established that the entry of a deficiency decree in a mortgage foreclosure for part or all of the balance due, or the denial of a deficiency decree on the merits, was res judicata in a subsequent action at law on the mortgage notes. 

A mortgagee was not compelled to submit his legal demand to a court of equity for adjudication but, if he did so, he was bound by the equity court's decision, subject only to his right of appeal where the chancellor's judgment was wrong or his discretion. abused.404

Since the office of a proviso is to restrain the enacting clause, and to except something which would otherwise be within it, the effect of adding the 1929 proviso to the 1927 statute, assuming the proviso to be valid, is to place a legislative construction upon the entire statute under which its provisions are broad enough to permit an action at law for a deficiency even after a decree there for has been entered in the foreclosure suit, or has been denied in that suit on its merits, except, of course, in cases which are fairly within the letter and spirit of the proviso.412

It is the duty of the court to exercise its powers in this respect whenever necessary in order to protect parties from fraud, unfairness, or imposition in the execution of a decree.414 

A foreclosure sale may be set aside on an original bill filed for that purpose, or on a petition or motion.415 While no rigid rule has been laid down prescribing the time within which proceedings to vacate a sale must be taken, reasonable diligence is imperatively required. The purchaser at a foreclosure sale, immediately upon receiving a deed and the confirmation of the sale, is entitled to possession of the mortgaged property as against the parties to the suit. His right to possession may be enforced by a writ of assistance.425

A writ of assistance is a form of process issued by courts of equity to transfer possession of land, the title to and right to possession of which has been previously adjudicated.426 The issuance of a writ of assistance is largely discretionary with the court, but it should be granted only when the right of the person in whose favor it is sought to be issued is clear. Where the right is doubtful, the writ should be denied.427

A writ of assistance may be granted to the purchaser at the foreclosure sale even though he is a stranger to the final decree. 

A writ may be granted in favor of an assignee of the purchaser's bid or a grantee of the purchaser.428 And a purchaser at the foreclosure sale who has sold the land may also obtain a writ of assistance since he has an interest in seeing that possession is transferred to the holder of legal title.429

A writ of assistance will be granted against any party defendant to the foreclosure suit. Persons not parties to the suit may also be brought in on a proceeding for a writ of assistance.
