§ 311.-Correction of Mistakes in Proceedings. Where a mort gage erroneously describes other land than that intended to be mortgaged, and the mistake has been carried through the foreclosure proceedings and into the master's deed, the purchaser at the foreclosure sale cannot maintain a bill to correct the description in the mortgage and the foreclosure proceedings. The mortgage must first be reformed and a new foreclosure suit must then be brought. The reason for this rule is that, if the land intended to be mortgaged had been correctly described, other and greater bids might have been received at the foreclosure sale. The original mortgagee may have thought he was bidding on the property intended to be mortgaged, but third persons would be under no such misunderstanding.443 The rule on this subject is otherwise, however, where the mistake is sought to be corrected prior to the execution and delivery of the master's deed.444

Where a mortgage correctly describes the land intended to be encumbered, but an erroneous description has been carried through the foreclosure proceedings and the master's deed, a correction of the description cannot be had without a resale of the property.445 § 312.-Appeals.-The rules and principles applicable to all chancery appeals apply equally to appeals in mortgage foreclosure suits. 

Thus, the chancellor's findings on conflicting evidence will not be disturbed unless they are clearly wrong.446 And a decree of foreclosure, rendered after a full hearing on the merits, will not be reversed on appeal for merely technical, formal, and unimportant irregularities in the proceedings. The real effect of an appeal with supersedeas in a mortgage foreclosure is to suspend the power of the court of original jurisdiction to make any order tending toward the execution or enforcement of the decree appealed from, but it does not interfere with the power of that court to make any orders necessary for the preservation of the property involved in the litigation when such orders do not tend toward an execution or enforcement of the superseded decree or to place the property beyond the reach of the judgment of the appellate court.466 Likewise, where an appeal with supersedeas is taken from an interlocutory decree in a mortgage foreclosure, the court is not thereby precluded from otherwise proceeding with the litigation when this can be done without having to depend upon the decree appealed from. § 313.-In General.-While the jurisdiction of equity courts over suits for partition is, independent of statute, of ancient origin and well established, the Florida practice in dealing with partition suits is mainly statutory.' The statutes provide that suits for a partition of real estate shall in all cases be by bill in chancery, and all proceedings, except where otherwise specifically provided, shall be as in other cases in chancery.2

Partition is authorized only among joint tenants, tenants in common, or coparceners who have title to the lands involved. A bill for partition may be maintained against all co-tenants or coparceners or others interested in the lands to be divided.4 

A suit for partition cannot be used as a substitute for the action of ejectment, nor for the sole purpose of testing the legal title to land. However, when the bona fide object of a suit is the partition of land between the common owners thereof, one or more of whom are plaintiffs and the others defendants, and they or some of them are in possession, then all controversies between them as to the

The statutes provide that all the provisions of law applicable to the partition of real estate and the proceedings therefor shall be applicable to the partition of personal property and the proceedings therefor, as far as the nature of the property will permit. A partition of both real and personal property may be had in one suit.7 § 314.-Venue.-Suits for partition must be brought in the county where the lands which are the subject matter of the suit lie. If the lands lie in more than one county, the suit may be brought in any county in which a part of the lands lie. In such a case the decrees of the court must be recorded in every county in which any part of the lands lie.Ⓡ § 315.-Parties Plaintiff.-The Florida statutes provide that a suit for partition may be brought by any one or more of several joint tenants, tenants in common, or coparceners.9 

The joint tenants, tenants in common, and coparceners contemplated by the statute are those who are in some way the owners of a beneficial estate in the land or whose status and duties are of such a nature as to require the exercise of the right to compel partition by judicial proceedings. Unknown owners or claimants of an interest in the lands sought to be partitioned may be made parties defendant to a partition suit.35

The statute authorizing joint tenants, tenants in common, and coparceners to maintain suits for partition against their cotenants and coparceners has also been held to be broad enough to authorize a decree of partition against unborn contingent remaindermen where their interests are otherwise represented in the proceeding.36 § 317.-Process.-Service of process in partition suits is made in the same manner as in other suits in equity.37 

Where unknown owners or claimants of an interest in the lands sought to be partitioned are made parties defendant to a partition suit, service of process upon them is governed by special statutory provisions. If the heirs, devisees, grantees, or other claimants under a deceased person are made parties defendant to the bill, the order of publication should describe such unknown defendants as "all parties claiming interests under (the deceased person) or otherwise," in the property, which must be briefly but definitely described in the order. If any known person and the heirs, devisees, grantees or other claimants under such known person are made parties defendant, such defendants should be described in the order of publication as "name of known party, if living, and, if dead, all parties claiming interests under (name of known party), deceased or otherwise," in the property, which must be briefly but definitely described in the order. All of the defendants may be embraced in one order of publication.38 Proof

Publication of the order is made in the same manner as is required by law for all other orders to appear in chancery cases.39 of publication must be made by the affidavit of the owner, publisher, proprietor, editor, business manager, or foreman of the newspaper in which the order has been published. The affidavit must specifically set forth the date of each publication of the order, and have

In any suit for partition in which a non-resident infant has such an interest as to make him a proper party, service of process may be perfected upon him in the same manner provided by law for perfecting service upon other non-resident defendants to such suits. 

Upon proof of such service, the court may appoint a guardian ad litem for the non-resident infant in the same manner provided by law in cases where there has been personal service.42 § 318.-Bill of Complaint.-It is provided by statute that a bill for the partition of real estate must be sworn to by one or more of the plaintiffs, must set forth a description of the lands of which partition is prayed by metes and bounds or other sufficient description, and must state, according to the best of the knowledge and belief of the plaintiff, the names and places of residence of the several owners, joint tenants, tenants in common, coparceners, or other persons interested in the lands, and the quantity or proportionate share held by each. The bill should also state such other matters, if any, as may be necessary to enable the court to adjudicate fully upon the rights and interests of the parties.43 

In case the names, residence, quantity of interest or proportionate share of any of the owners or claimants of the lands sought to be partitioned are unknown to the plaintiff, then it shall be so stated in the bill, and the suit may proceed in the same manner as though such unknown defendants were named in the bill.44 If the unknown persons are known or believed to be the heirs, devisees, grantees, or other claimants under a person deceased whose name is known to the plaintiff, the name of such person must be stated in the bill, although the failure to do so does not invalidate any decree obtained

A bill for partition must, of course, first show that legal title to an undivided interest in the lands involved is held by the plaintiff, and that title to the remaining interest is held by the defendants as joint tenants, tenants in common, or coparceners with the plaintiff.45 The statute authorizes partition only among those who have legal title to the lands in controversy.46 A common possession must also be shown, but this is always implied from a common title until the contrary is shown.47 

It follows from the foregoing principles that, where the plaintiff has only an equitable interest in the land, he cannot maintain a bill for partition even though his equitable interest may be enforced in a proper proceeding.48 For the same reason, a bill for partition cannot be maintained while the premises are held adversely by other parties. The legal title must first be established.49 

However, while a suit for partition may not be used as a substitute for the action of ejectment to try the title to lands, or for the purpose of establishing rights or titles, yet, where the bona fide object of a suit is a partition of lands between the common owners thereof, some of whom are plaintiffs and the others defendants, and some of the parties to the suit are in actual or constructive possession of the lands, then, under the broad provisions of the statute, all controversies between the parties as to the legal title and right of possession may and should be settled by the court in the one suit even though some of the joint owners claim adversely

As required by the statute, a bill for partition must disclose the respective interests of the parties in the land sought to be partitioned.51 But, even though the bill does not in terms specifically allege the quantity and proportionate share held by each person in the lands involved in the suit, yet it will nevertheless be held sufficient if the allegations are sufficiently clear to enable the court to adjudicate fully the rights and interests of the parties and the quantity and proportionate share held by each.52 

As a general rule, a co-tenant cannot enforce a partition of a part only of the common lands, leaving the rest undivided. The entire property should be included in the proceedings for partition.53 

However, this rule in all probability applies only where the suit involves a single connected tract of land as distinguished from separate and distinct tracts.54 A plaintiff may maintain a suit for partition only as to his undivided interest without segregating the portions of the several defendants.55 After the death of the head of a family, a suit may be maintained for the partition of homestead property among those entitled thereto just as in the case of other property.5

A bill for partition is not necessarily mutifarious because there may be united in it several causes of action. If all the different causes of action grew out of the same transaction, the bill may be maintained. Where the subject matter of the controversy is encumbered with many conflicting claims, equity will entertain a suit for determining and adjusting all of these interests at once.57 Thus a bill is not multifarious because it seeks in a proper case to procure both partition and an accounting. A suit for partition and to quiet title may be joined where the parties and subject matter are the same.59 But a suit for partition cannot be joined with one for the foreclosure of a mortgage since the manner of proceeding in each suit is entirely different.60 

A bill for partition is required by the statute to be sworn to by one or more of the plaintiffs. Consequently, no one but a party plaintiff is authorized to make an affidavit as to the truth of the bill. And a bill for partition sworn to by the solicitor for the plaintiff is insufficient either as the basis for constructive service or a final decree in the cause. However, while a decree rendered on such a bill is subject to reversal, it is not void to the extent that it may be collaterally attacked even by defendants who were made parties to the suit by constructive service.61 § 319.-Defenses. As previously stated, a suit for partition cannot be maintained unless the plaintiff shows that he has legal title to an undivided interest in the property in controversy.62 But, even prior to the enactment of the Florida statutes governing partition suits, a bare denial of the plaintiff's legal title was not sufficient to send the plaintiff to law to establish it. It was necessary for the defendant, if he claimed adversely to the plaintiff, to set out his own title in his answer, or, if he denied the plaintiff's title, to show wherein it was defective. If, upon the showing made, there appeared no valid legal objection to the plaintiff's title, the court of equity could proceed with the partition. It was only when the plaintiff's legal title was shown to be disputed or doubtful that he was remitted to his action at law. 

The defect in the law as it then stood was that in all cases where one joint owner had ousted another, or claimed adversely under a doubtful legal title, or showed the plaintiff's title to be doubtful, the plaintiff was required to maintain two actions before he could obtain a partition, one at law to establish his title or right to possession, and the other in equity for partition. If the court of equity

While this was the state of the law, the Florida statutes 63 governing partition suits were enacted. These statutes divest the law courts of power to partition property, vest that power exclusively in courts of equity, and direct them to ascertain and adjudicate the rights and interests of the parties and to decree partition if the parties are entitled to it. These statutes can, therefore, bear no other reasonable interpretation than that they were intended to remedy the defect in the law existing at the time of their enactment. 

Consequently, whenever the case is one whose bona fide object is the partition of land among the common owners thereof, one or more of whom are plaintiffs and the others defendants, and some of the parties to the suit are in actual or constructive possession of the lands, then all controversies between them as to the legal title may and should be settled by the chancellor under the statute.64 

This construction of the partition statutes does not render them unconstitutional as infringing upon the constitutional guaranty of a trial by jury. The statutes were enacted in 1844, while the first 

Constitution of the state of Florida did not become effective until 1845. The Constitution of 1845, as well as the subsequent Constitutions of 1865, 1868, and 1885, all guarantee the right of trial by jury, but they have all been construed as securing the right only in those cases in which it was enjoyed when the Constitution became effective. As the statutes of 1844 had invested equity courts with the power to try legal titles in partition suits before the Constitution of 1845 became effective, the constitutional provisions cannot be construed so as to take away that power. Consequently, the statutes are valid. 65

Where an answer to a bill for partition sets up by way of defense that the bill has omitted a portion of the tract of land held by the parties under the same co-tenancy as that alleged in the bill, the plaintiff will be required to amend his bill to include the additional land. In default of amendment, his bill will be dismissed.73 § 320. Counterclaim.-As a general rule, a cross-bill or counterclaim in a partition suit is neither necessary nor proper in order to bring before the court additional lands which a defendant has a right to have partitioned.74 If any defendant has the right to have additional lands brought before the court for partition in the same action, he should take the proper steps to require the plaintiff to amend his bill so as to embrace such additional lands.75 

The right of the defendant to have additional lands embraced in the partition suit exists only where the plaintiff seeks the partition of part of a single tract of land. Where the bill covers all of a single tract, it is doubtful if the defendant can bring in an entirely different and disconnected tract even though it is owned by the same parties as co-tenants. In any event, the question would probably depend upon the circumstances of each case.76 

An owner of a mortgage upon the entire interest in a part of the lands sought to be partitioned may maintain a counterclaim in the partition suit for the foreclosure of his mortgage.77 § 321-Decree of Partition. Having this The plain meaning of the statute seems to be that all proper issues made in a suit for the partition of lands should be tried and determined by the court in which the proceeding is commenced and whatever investigation is necessary to enable the court to adjudicate the rights and interests of the parties may be conducted. power, the court should exercise it. The power of the court to adjudicate the rights and interests of the parties cannot be delegated to commissioners, and a decree appointing commissioners and directing them to ascertain the several interests of the parties and make a partition of the land accordingly is erroneous.80 

If the plaintiff in a partition suit fails to establish his title, it becomes unnecessary for the court to consider any of the other questions presented. Where the suit is properly brought, however, the quantity and proportionate interests of the parties is not determined by what they claim, but by what the testimony proves they are legally entitled to. The interests of the parties must be adjudicated by the court, and a mistake on the part of a party as to what his interest is does not preclude his being decreed what he is entitled to even if he remains passive and abstains from making an answer. 82

The court may decree a partition as to the portion of the land to which the plaintiff is entitled without apportioning the remainder among the several defendants. 

The statute authorizes partition to be made to some of the parties jointly, leaving for future adjustment by further proceedings in the same cause, the rights, shares, and interests of the others.83

In making a partition, the commissioners may assign to the parties respectively such parts of the estate as will best accommodate them and be of the most value to them with regard to their respective situations in relation to the property before partition.86 The fact that a co-tenant has located upon a particular portion of the land and has enhanced its value by making improvements, or by reducing it from a wild state to one fit for profitable cultivation, is a circumstance always worthy of consideration. The law declines to compel one tenant to pay for improvements made without his authorization, but it will not, if it can avoid so inequitable a result, enable a co-tenant to take advantage of improvements for which he has contributed nothing. When the common lands come to be divided, an opportunity should always be offered to a co-tenant who has enhanced the value of part of the premises to take that parcel, or so much thereof as represents his share of the whole tract. This rule is subject only to the qualification that the improvements must have been made in good faith, and with no purpose to embarrass the other joint owners.87

In making partition, it is also proper for the commissioners to assign the share containing the homestead to a surviving son who has occupied it, rather than to grandchildren. When testimony is taken for the purpose of ascertaining the value of the property to be divided, the parties should have notice so that they may be present, and the commissioners should return the testimony to the court so that the court may determine as to the correctness of their report. Final decrees entered against unknown parties in a partition suit are conclusive on them and persons claiming under them, from the date of rendition, unless a rehearing is applied for within one year. 

However, if the plaintiff, within six months after the entry of such a decree, serves a copy of it on any person who becomes known to him, a rehearing as to such person must be applied for within six months from the date of service.97 And if any unknown defendant, at any time before the expiration of the time allowed for a rehearing, appears and petitions the court for a rehearing, and gives a proper bond, he may defend the bill as if he had been personally served with process. The court may, pending such defense, stay all proceedings upon the original decree. If the decree has been executed, the court may decree restitution. But title to property

The right of tenants in common to have a partition and enjoy its incidents is paramount to the rights of lien creditors of one of the co-tenants. Consequently, a mortgage lien upon the undivided interest of one co-tenant shifts, upon a partition, to the entire interest in that part of the land allotted to that co-tenant in severalty. This rule is, however, subject to some modification in cases of fraud or an unfair division between co-tenants resulting from an agreement between them, or where the lien creditor is not given an opportunity to be heard.99 

§ 324.-Sale of Non-Divisible Real Estate.-If the commissioners report to the court that the lands, tenements, and hereditaments of which partition has been directed are so situated that a partition thereof cannot be made without great prejudice to the owners of the property, and if the court is satisfied that this report is true and correct, the court may, upon the application of any party and notice to the others before the court, if the others are within the state, order the premises so situated to be sold at public auction, by and under the direction of the commissioners, to the highest bidder. 

The proceeds of the sale must be paid into court and divided among the respective parties in proportion to their shares or interests. 100 

For good cause shown, the court may order a partition sale to be made upon reasonable credit for part or all of the purchase price, although at least one-third of the purchase price must be paid in cash unless all parties consent to a greater credit. Any part of the purchase price not paid in cash must be secured by a mortgage upon the property and such other security as the court may direct.101

The confirmation of a sale in partition proceedings is a matter which rests within the sound judicial discretion of the chancellor.102 

And an order confirming sale cures all irregularities in the sale and errors in the proceedings in which it was made, and, if the court had jurisdiction and the officer authority to sell, the sale is valid against collateral attack even though it was previously voidable.103

337. Reopening Final Decree. § 327. Jurisdiction of Equity.-Courts of equity have inherent jurisdiction of suits to quiet title to real estate,' but, in Florida, such jurisdiction has also been conferred upon them by statute. 

There are two sets of Florida statutes granting jurisdiction to equity courts in suits to quiet title. The first set of statutes was designed to broaden and amplify the inherent equity jurisdiction.2 

The second set of statutes, enacted in 1925, was designed, not only to further broaden the scope of suits to quiet title, but to expedite them by authorizing a number of material changes in procedure.³ 

The 1925 statute, however, specifically provides that it does not repeal any laws existing at the time of its enactment, but is intended to provide merely a cumulative and additional remedy to those already existing.4 Consequently, it is important to note that a suit to quiet title may now be brought under either the 1925 statute or those previously existing, and that the procedure to be followed depends, in many material respects, upon which set of statutes is invoked.

Both statutes provide that courts of equity shall entertain suits by any person or corporation claiming to own any land, or by any two or more persons or corporations claiming to own the same land

The basis for such relief in equity is the want or inadequacy of a legal remedy in cases where a deed or other instrument exists which may be vexatiously or injuriously used against a party after the evidence to impeach or invalidate it has been lost, or which may cast a cloud or suspicion upon his title. The plaintiff is entitled to relief in equity because, if he is in possession, he is not in a position to sue in ejectment at law. The defendant, who can bring ejectment, may forbear to do so, and there is thus no remedy by which the plaintiff can have the title settled except in equity. Therefore, in order that the plaintiff may be quieted in his title and possession, and relieved from the fear of annoyance from the adverse claim in the future, equity will take jurisdiction and remove the cloud from his title.7

Courts of equity have laid down two requirements which must be met in order to invoke their inherent jurisdiction to quiet title or to remove a cloud from title. The first requirement is that the plaintiff must show title in himself. It is well settled that he who comes into equity to get rid of a legal title as a cloud upon his own must show clearly the validity of his own title and the invalidity of his opponent's. Equity will not act in such cases in the event of a doubtful title. And a party, to be relieved and to succeed in contests of this character, must do so on the strength of his own title, and not on the weakness of his adversary's.9 

The second requirement for the maintenance of a bill to quiet title is, in the absence of a statute providing a different rule, that the plaintiff be in actual possession of the land. This is necessary because, if the defendant is in possession, the plaintiff has an adequate remedy at law by ejectment, and the defendant, being in possession, cannot, by proceedings in equity to quiet title, be de-

While the foregoing requirements have been imposed by courts of equity upon the exercise of their jurisdiction to quiet real estate titles, it is always competent for the legislative power to remove those restrictions. 12 No change has been made in the first requirement in Florida, but, in regard to the second requirement, both the 1925 and prior statutes provide that a suit to quiet title may be maintained in equity whether or not the plaintiff is in actual possession of the lands involved.13 However, these statutes cannot constitutionally authorize a suit in equity to quiet title against a defendant who is in actual possession. Suits to quiet title to personalty are infrequently brought, but a court of equity will give relief in respect to personalty and quiet the title thereto when, owing to exceptional circumstances, there is no adequate remedy at law.17 § 328.-Grounds of Remedy.-The original equity rule was that, whenever the instrument or proceeding alleged to constitute a cloud upon title was absolutely void upon its face, so that no extrinsic evidence was necessary to show its invalidity, or, where a deed or other instrument was not thus void on its face, but the party claiming under it would be required, in order to recover upon it, to offer evidence that would inevitably show its invalidity and destroy its effect, then there was no cloud upon title and a suit in equity could not be maintained.18 Thus, for example, it was held that an execution sale under a judgment against one who never had any title to or interest in the land did not create a cloud upon title.19

The grounds for a suit to quiet title were, however, substantially broadened by the statute enacted in 1925. This statute provides merely an additional and cumulative remedy for clearing and removing clouds from the title to land, and it therefore leaves unaffected the grounds upon which a suit to quiet title could previously be maintained. But, in addition, it provides a remedy by which relief may be had in equity in the following three general situations: (1) Where a person or corporation, not the rightful owner of designated real estate, has any conveyance or other evidence of title thereto, or asserts any claim, or pretends to have any right or title thereto, which may cast a cloud, doubt, or suspicion upon the title of the true owner. Under this provision of the statute, the rightful owner may bring into court any person who is not the rightful owner, but who nevertheless asserts some claim

Under this provision of the statute, one whose title would be good but for the defective execution or acknowledgment of a deed or mortgage under which he claims, and which was intended to convey or mortgage the entire title, may have his title established, quieted, and confirmed against the defective execution or acknowledgment and against those who may claim or appear to have some title or interest in the land by reason of the defect. This procedure is analogous to the equitable remedy for the reformation of an instrument. This provision affords a means by which an existing record title may be extinguished as a cloud upon the title of one who has acquired a good title by adverse possession. 

In any of these three situations, the statute provides that the real owner may have the cloud, doubt, or suspicion removed from his title whether he is in possession or not (unless the defendant is in actual possession), whether he is threatened to be disturbed in his possession or not, whether the defendant is a resident of Florida or not, whether the title has been litigated in a court of law or not, whether the adverse claim or interest is void upon its face or not, or whether, if not void upon its face, it may require evidence extrinsic of itself to establish its validity.20

Among those instruments which equity may remove as a cloud upon title are contracts to sell real estate. A distinction should be noted, however, between a suit to remove as a cloud upon title a real estate sales contract upon which the purchaser has defaulted, and which has expired in accordance with its own terms and provisions, and a suit to rescind and cancel such a contract because of fraud, mistake, undue influence, or some other matter of equitable cognizance rendering it voidable at the option of the vendor. In the former case, the vendor need not, as a condition precedent to obtaining relief, return to the purchaser any amounts he has paid on account of the purchase price, but in the latter case such restoration must be made before relief will be granted.22 These rules also apply where the vendor seeking relief is a married woman.23 And where a married woman is a purchaser under such a contract, but has performed no part of it, the vendor may have the record of the contract cancelled as a cloud upon his title.24

Building restrictions may be cancelled as clouds upon title where they have become unenforceable by reason of a radical change in the character of the neighborhood or because they have been mutually disregarded. And equity has this jurisdiction even though the grounds upon which a cancellation is sought would constitute a complete defense to their enforcement.25

A personal representative may bring and maintain a suit for the purpose of quieting title to real estate owned by the decedent. And heirs or devisees of a decedent may themselves or jointly with the personal representative maintain suits to quiet the title to such real estate against anyone except the personal representative.35 

Where two or more persons are interested in removing a cloud from or quieting title to one or more parcels of real estate as against the same clouds or adverse claims, it is permissible for them to unite as plaintiffs in a single bill for that purpose, and to obtain a single decree removing such clouds and quieting the titles, even though their interests relate to separate portions of the land.36 

A suit to quiet title does not abate or become defective by the death or transfer of interest of one or more of the plaintiffs, provided other plaintiffs survive whose interests continue, and the decree rendered, whether for or against the plaintiffs, binds the successors in interest, pendente lite, of each original plaintiff without the necessity of making a suggestion of his death or the transfer of his interest, or of making his successors parties to the suit.37 § 331.-Parties Defendant.-Since no person is bound by a final decree in a suit to quiet title who has not been made a party to the suit, the plaintiff should join as parties defendant to his bill any and all persons having title to or otherwise interested in the land involved or any portion thereof.38 And, where the proceedings seek the cancellation of certain warranty deeds as clouds upon title, all the warrantors whose deeds are sought to be cancelled are necessary parties defendant.39 But the rule is otherwise where the deeds sought to be cancelled are without covenants of warranty.40

Where a conveyance is sought to be removed as a cloud upon title on the ground that it is fraudulent, the grantors against whom the fraud is charged are indispensable parties defendant.41

In all suits against an estate for the purpose of quieting title to real property, the personal representative and the heirs or devisees of the property should be made parties.42 

Unknown persons may be made defendants to a suit to quiet title.43 But, while a suit to quiet title may be maintained against known defendants having claims of a known or unknown nature, or against unknown defendants having claims of a known nature, such a suit cannot be maintained against unknown defendants, the nature and existence of whose claims are also unknown to the plaintiff. Such a bill would neither advise the unknown defendants of the nature of the case they are called upon to defend, nor the court of what decree it should render if the bill is true.44 § 332.-Process.-As in other suits in chancery, personal service should be made upon all defendants to a suit to quiet title where such service is possible.45 it It is not essential, however, that the court have jurisdiction of the person of the defendant. A state may regulate the manner in which, and the conditions upon which, real property located within its territory may be acquired, enjoyed, and transferred, and the title thereto quieted and determined. While the state cannot bring the person of a non-resident owner or claimant within its limits, may nevertheless determine the extent of his title to real estate within its limits, and, for the purpose of such a determination, the state may provide any reasonable method of imparting notice. It is the duty of a non-resident owner of real estate to take measures which will insure his being represented when proceedings are taken which involve his interest in such property. If he fails to do this, and fails to get notice by the ordinary publications which have usually been required in such cases, it is his misfortune, and he must abide the consequences. Therefore, where the state has provided a reasonable method of giving notice to non-resident owners and claimants, such a procedure meets the requirements of due process of law.46

There are also two sets of Florida statutes providing for constructive service in suits to quiet title.47 Proceedings may be taken under either set of statutes, since the subsequent statutes, enacted in 1925, provide that they do not repeal any existing laws, but merely provide an additional and cumulative method of quieting titles.48 There is, however, no substantial difference between the two statutes, and it is probable that a combination of both of them can be used where the nature of the case justifies such a procedure. 

In either case, the notice to appear must be predicated upon proper allegations in the bill of complaint.49 two. 

The subsequent statute, enacted in 1925, is the broader of the It provides for constructive service binding upon all defendants who cannot be personally served with process, whether they are known or unknown, residents or non-residents, or their residence unknown, or whether they are infants, adults, or persons non compos mentis.50 If the names and addresses of the defendants are known, they must be stated in the notice to appear. If there are parties interested in the land who are unknown to the plaintiff, and he has made diligent search and inquiry for their names and cannot obtain them, they may be made defendants by a notice addressed: "To all persons having or claiming any interest in the following described lands (then describing lands involved)." If the plaintiff does not know and has not been able to ascertain by diligent search and inquiry whether any defendant is dead or alive, the notice may be addressed to such person, "if alive, and if dead, to his unknown heirs, devisees, legatees, or grantees."51 Under this statute, the notice must also state the nature of the suit.52 

Where the proceeding is not taken under the 1925 statute, but under those previously existing, the general statutes providing for constructive service in all chancery cases may be used against known defendants.53 As to unknown defendants, the provisions of the prior statutes are somewhat different from those of the 1925 statute, but not materially so. The prior statutes provide that, if the heirs, devisees, grantees, or other claimants under a deceased per-

§ 333.-Bill of Complaint.-A bill of complaint in a suit to quiet title must show that the plaintiff has title to the lands in controversy.60 

Where the suit is not brought under the 1925 statute, an allegation that the plaintiff is the owner in fee of the lands in question is sufficient for this purpose without setting out in detail the facts showing such ownership. Ownership is the ultimate fact and the others are mere evidentiary facts. If, however, in addition to an allegation of ownership in fee, the facts which constitute the title, of whatever nature they may be, are also set out, and such facts show title not to be in the plaintiff, the bill is subject to a motion to dismiss.62

The original rule in suits to quiet title was that the plaintiff must not only allege that he was the owner of the lands in controversy, but also that he was in actual possession of them when the bill was filed, or that the lands were wild, unimproved, and unoccupied. As previously stated, however, this rule was changed by both the 1925 and prior statutes, and a suit to quiet title may now be maintained by the owner of real property upon the constructive possession which follows his legal title, provided the defendant is not in actual possession.67 Where the plaintiff is in actual possession of the real estate, an allegation to that effect is sufficient, 68 but, in any event, his bill should negative actual possession in the defendant.69 Possession by a duly authorized agent of the plaintiff is sufficient to maintain a suit predicated upon actual possession.70

355. Appeals. § 338.-Appointment-In General.-The power to appoint a receiver is one which is inherent in a court of equity.' As a general rule, however, the appointment of a receiver is discretionary and not a matter of right. But the action of the court in this respect must be governed by a sound and judicial discretion, exercised for the purpose of promoting the ends of justice and protecting the rights of all parties interested in the controversy and subject matter, and based upon the fact that there is no other adequate remedy or means of accomplishing the same result. Furthermore, this discretion is to be exercised with great caution, and only after full 

1. Armour Fertilizer Works v. First 362; Bayview Homes v. Sanders, 102 

National Bank, 87 Fla. 436, 100 So. Fla. 516, 136 So. 234.

The appellate consideration of the facts of the particular case.2 court will not interfere unless a clear abuse of discretion is shown.3 

While the appointment of a receiver is to a large extent within the discretion of the court, to be exercised or not according to the circumstances and exigencies of each particular case, yet there are certain well established rules that should be observed by the court in exercising its discretion. These are: 

1. The power to appoint a receiver is a delicate one, to be exercised with great circumspection. 

2. It must appear that the claimant has either a clear legal right to the property in controversy, or some lien upon or property right in it, or that it constitutes a special fund out of which he is entitled to payment, and the court must be satisfied that a receiver is necessary to preserve the property. 

3. A receiver will never be appointed merely because such action can do no harm. 

4. It must be established to the satisfaction of the court that the appointment is necessary either to prevent fraud, or to save the property from injury, loss, or destruction. 

5. Unless the necessity is of the most urgent character, a receiver will not be appointed unless the defendant is first heard in response to the application.4

Furthermore, while the appointment of a receiver does not involve the determination of any right, or affect the title of either party in any manner whatsoever, such relief should be granted only where there is strong reason to believe that the party asking for a receiver will recover.5 And, except in rare and unusual instances, the appointment of a receiver is an ancillary remedy and cannot be obtained in a suit instituted solely for that purpose.

§ 340] 761 RECEIVERS It is axiomatic that the consent of the parties to the litigation cannot confer power or authority on a court to appoint a receiver in a case where the pleadings do not state a case for such relief.7 § 339.-Appointment For Partnerships.-A court of equity has no authority to appoint a receiver with a view to permanently carrying on the partnership business, but there is no impropriety in appointing a receiver to superintend the business during the pendency of legal proceedings instituted for the purpose of dissolving the partnership. Accordingly, whenever the intervention of a court of equity becomes necessary, because of dissensions or disagreements between partners, to effect a settlement and closing of the partnership affairs, upon a bill filed by one partner, showing either a breach of duty or a violation of the partnership agreement by any of the other partners, a receiver will be appointed as a matter of course. Thus, where a bill is filed to settle and close a partnership, and it appears that the principal item of partnership property is a vessel about to be taken by one of the parties out upon the high seas, a receiver will be appointed in order that the jurisdiction of the court may not be defeated, either by inadvertence or design, by the removal of the vessel beyond its territorial limits. § 340.-Appointment-For Corporations.-A corporation is a creature of the state and its life depends upon the action of the state or of its stockholders as a whole. As a general rule, therefore, and in the absence of a statute, a court of equity has no authority, at the instance of a stockholder, to appoint a receiver for the sole purpose of dissolving a corporation and winding up its affairs. 10 

In extreme cases, however, and where milder methods are clearly of no avail, a court of equity will appoint a receiver for a corporation upon the application of minority stockholders.11 But this power is a discretionary one, to be exercised with great circumspection and only in cases where there is fraud, spoilation, or imminent

The right of a creditor to have a receiver appointed for a corporation is governed by the principles applicable to the appointment of receivers generally. 14 While the Florida statutes authorize an equitable execution against a corporation, by the appointment of a receiver, 15 they do not authorize the appointment of a receiver for an insolvent corporation, at the suit of a creditor, merely for the purpose of winding up its affairs. the rents and profits to the mortgagee's claim, even though, prior to that time, there was no lien upon them.33 

It will be noted that the constructive equitable lien on rents and profits which courts of equity have thus created is only recognized where the mortgagor in default is insolvent and the security afforded by the real property is inadequate. However, the modern mortgage frequently contains an express provision pledging the rents and profits to the payment of the mortgage debt and consenting to the appointment of a receiver upon default. Such provisions do not give the mortgagee an absolute right to the appointment of a receiver upon a default by the mortgagor, since such a construction of them would result in a violation of the statute denying the power of a mortgagor to convey his right of possession prior to foreclosure and sale. But, while these provisions are not controlling upon the court, they are accorded due weight, and in many cases they will authorize the appointment of a receiver where without them the application would be denied. 

Thus, for example, where the rents and profits are expressly made a part of the security, and the mortgagor is receiving them but refusing to apply them to the mortgage debt, which is in default, a court of equity will appoint a receiver unless the mortgagor makes it clear that the real property covered by the mortgage will sell for enough to pay the debt and charges due the mortgagee. Having voluntarily pledged the rents and profits as part of the security, a mortgagor in default who is misapplying them should not be heard to object to their being impounded by the court pending foreclosure proceedings, regardless of his solvency, unless he satisfies the court that the remaining real estate security is entirely adequate and that there is no need to disturb the possession accorded him by the statute, or unless he gives security to account for the rents and profits. 

As to the question of insolvency, he should not be heard to say that, while he has specifically pledged the rents and profits, a receiver should not be appointed because he is solvent and has other property upon which the mortgagee can levy an execution. Having expressly given a lien upon the rents and profits of the mortgaged property, he has no right to require the mortgagee to look to other

He has estopped himself from so doing by his written contract, and he will not be heard to object to a receivership unless he first assumes and bears the burden of satisfying the court that the corpus of the estate is ample in value to protect the rights of the mortgagee, or gives security approved by the court to properly account for the rents and profits.34

As a predicate for the appointment of a receiver under mortgage provisions specifically pledging the rents and profits, and consenting to the appointment of a receiver, it must, however, be definitely shown that the mortgagor is receiving such rents and profits but is failing and refusing to apply them to the payment of the mortgage debt or to the payment of taxes and insurance on the mortgaged property, and is thus dissipating the mortgagee's security. If it is made to appear that, although in default, the mortgagor is exercising reasonably good care and management of the property, and is applying the receipts from rentals to the payment of taxes and interest on the mortgage as far as they will go, no equitable ground exists for interfering with his right of possession. A receiver could do no more.35 Likewise, where it appears that no rentals will be collected during the pendency of the foreclosure suit, because they have been paid for a long period in advance, a receiver will not be appointed.36 In case the mortgaged property is the homestead of the mortgagor, and is being used for that purpose and not as rental property at the time of the foreclosure, it is the policy of the law to allow the mortgagor to continue to occupy it until after a decree of foreclosure and a sale and confirmation thereunder notwithstanding provisions in the mortgage pledging the rents and profits and consenting to the appointment of a receiver.37

A receiver is entitled to the immediate possession of all property specified in the order appointing him. Where a receiver is appointed for an insolvent corporation, the court may require the officers of the corporation to turn over to him all papers, books, and accounts in their possession belonging to the corporation.77 In the case of a receiver appointed in a mortgage foreclosure for the purpose of subjecting rents and profits to the payment of the mortgage debt, he is entitled to all unpaid rents accruing prior to his appointment and after the default, as well as to those accruing after his appointment.78

The appointment of a receiver to protect and preserve property pending litigation does not ipso facto affect the status of liens existing against the property. But, where a receiver is appointed at the instance and for the benefit of lien creditors, all proper charges, expenses, and liabilities incurred as incident to duly conferred receivership powers and duties will be a charge upon the earnings and corpus of the property superior to the liens of creditors who take part in or expressly or impliedly consent to the receivership proceedings.79

It has been seen that a real estate mortgagee may, under special circumstances, be entitled to the appointment of a receiver to subject the rents and profits of the mortgaged property to the payment of his claim.80 But this equitable right of a mortgagee is not prior to the right of a creditor obtaining an express lien upon the rents and profits by chattel mortgage, execution, or otherwise.

The appointment of a receiver for a corporation pending a suit against it does not abate or bar the prosecution of the action to judgment. The receiver may, at his request, be made a defendant to the action, but the plaintiff need not bring him in.82 

The appointment of a receiver for specified property does not preclude such property from being assessed for taxes or sold for non-payment of taxes with like force and effect as if no receivership had ever existed. Any other rule would result in subjecting the state's sovereign power of taxation to private contract rights.83 

As a general rule, a receiver appointed in a prior suit should not be displaced by the appointment of another receiver of the same subject matter by the same court in a subsequent suit. The receivership in the first suit should be extended to the second, subject to the legal and equitable claims of all parties, and the rights of the parties in each suit are substantially the same as if different persons had been appointed at the several times when such receiverships were granted. If, however, a different receiver is appointed by the same court in the subsequent suit, then the receiver in the first suit must deliver the subject matter to the receiver appointed in the second.84

Where the court has jurisdiction of the subject matter and the parties, an order appointing a receiver cannot be collaterally attacked for any purpose no matter how erroneous it may be.85

Consequently, a receiver is not in general personally liable on bona fide contracts made by him as receiver within the scope of his authority when there is no express or reasonably implied assumption or promise, and no fraud or deceit, on his part. 92 A receiver is not required to give notice to the parties in interest of any payments he may make within the scope of his authority. He may make such payments, and any objections to them which the parties may wish to make may be raised when his accounts come up for approval.9 93 The circuit court appointing a receiver has exclusive jurisdiction over the management and administration of all property included in the receivership estate even though it may be situated in more than one judicial circuit.94 Any attempt by another circuit court to interfere with this jurisdiction is irregular and without authority.95 § 351.-Suits By and Against Receivers.-A receiver may maintain any suits or actions necessary to effectuate the purposes for which he was appointed.96 Where he succeeds to rights in any action pending at the time of his appointment, he may also, on the verified petition or motion of himself or the plaintiff in the action, and after notice to the parties affected, be substituted as the plaintiff in the cause.97

A receiver appointed by the courts of a sister state may maintain suit in the courts of Florida to reduce the assets of the receivership estate to possession provided the suit works no hardship on local creditors and does not interfere in any manner with the enforcement of their claims.100

Suits against a receiver cannot be maintained without leave of the court which appointed him. 101 Of course, this rule applies only to an independent suit against the receiver and not to an application by an interested party to the receivership court for directions to its own receiver as to the administration of the property in his hands.102 A receiver of an insolvent corporation cannot be sued for a tort committed by the corporation prior to his appointment. 103 § 352.-Disposition of Property.-As a corporate receivership is for the benefit of both creditors and stockholders, the court in which the receivership was obtained must make a distribution of the funds in the hands of its receiver to all persons having just claims against the property. The court must also determine the validity of each claim, the amount justly due thereon, and the pro rata distribution to which each claimant is entitled. Consequently, a person submitting a claim to a receiver invokes the judgment of the court upon its validity and amount and the part he shall take in the distribution of the funds in the receiver's hands. If the claimant is aggrieved by the court's judgment on his claim, he may appeal. The receiver also has the right of appeal where the judgment is detrimental to the remaining creditors and stockholders.104

A creditor who has received any of the debtor's assets as collateral security for his claim must deduct from the amount of his claim the value of the security or any cash realized from its sale. Unless the claim is for the net amount due and unpaid at the time it is filed, it should not be approved by the receiver. 105

In the case of railroad and other public service corporations, the operation of which has been continued by the court, through its receiver, for the public good, all liabilities incurred in its maintenance and operation may be made a first lien upon the property superior even to prior contract liens. In such cases the creditors take their liens subject to the rules of law making property of this character first liable for the continuance of the service to which it is devoted.106 And, where judgment creditors secure the appointment of a receiver to operate a railroad company for their benefit and protection, the court may give wage claims which accrued in the operation of the railroad during a short period prior to the receivership priority over the claims of the judgment creditors.107 

Where the business of a private corporation is continued after it has been placed in the hands of a receiver, prior mortgage lienholders have priority over subsequent creditors in the operation of the property unless the prior lienholders consented to such operation. But prior lienholders do not have priority over the proper expenses of a receiver in collecting and preserving the property.108 

In any receivership under the laws of Florida, a public accountant has a preferred claim for his fees for services rendered the person or corporation in receivership during a period of ninety days prior to the appointment of the receiver.109

A court of chancery appointing a receiver to take charge of an estate and make a sale of the property under its direction is charged with the solemn duty of carefully scrutinizing the terms of any proposed sale in order to insure the most advantageous returns for the estate. And, where it is brought to the attention of the court by the report of its receivers or otherwise that a proposed sale is for less than the property should reasonably be expected to bring, the court should refuse to authorize or confirm the sale.110 

In a suit to foreclose a mortgage, where a receiver has been appointed to manage the property and collect the rents and profits, such rents and profits become a part of the mortgage security and are the property of the mortgagor, impounded in the hands of the court's receiver, but subject to the equitable rights of the parties.

If a final decree of foreclosure is entered, any funds in the receiver's hands, after deducting therefrom any amounts reasonably necessary to preserve the property or meet current expenses between the entry of the decree and the sale, should ordinarily be applied by the decree on the amount found to be due under the mortgage, or they should be made available to the mortgagor for that purpose, so that he will have that much less money to raise to redeem the property from sale.'11 It is not necessarily error, however, for the court to fail to include such provisions in its final decree, especially in the absence of an application by an interested party that the matter be dealt with in that way.112 

Where an order appointing a receiver is reversed on appeal, the trial court must order the receiver to turn over the funds or property in his hands to the rightful owner, although there may be charged against such funds any expenses paid by the receiver for the benefit of the receivership estate. 113 A receiver will not be heard in proceedings to vacate the receivership and restore the property to its owner." 114 § 353.-Compensation of Receiver.-There is no definite rule by which compensation for the services of a receiver may be fixed. 

Each case must be controlled by its own circumstances. Among the factors to be considered in fixing such compensation are the value of the assets coming into the receiver's hands, the time occupied by the receiver in the performance of his duties, the difficulty of conserving and administering the receivership estate, and the ability and efficiency of the receiver as reflected by the results obtained. 

The fixing of the receiver's compensation lies largely within the court's discretion, which should be judicially exercised with due regard to the claims of those interested in the estate but bearing in mind that officers of the court occupying positions of trust and confidence are entitled to just compensation.115

§ 356.-Jurisdiction.-The power of a court of equity to enforce the rescission and cancellation of a contract, though well recognized in character and application, is very exceptional. Its purpose is to supplement the powers of courts of law when there exists an equity of a settled and well recognized kind. In compelling rescission, equity will not interfere with freedom of contract, or substitute itself for legal remedies, even though a bad and improvident bargain has been made. The grounds upon which equity interferes for rescission and cancellation are distinctly marked, and every case proper for this branch of its jurisdiction may be classified under a particular ground.

These grounds are primarily fraud, mistake, duress, undue influence, and circumstances entitling to relief on the principle of quia timet. Generally, they do not include inadequacy of consideration, improvidence, surprise, or mere hardship. Promises honestly made, which the promisor cannot fulfill, do not furnish sufficient grounds for vacating a contract based thereon, but mutual mistake, or false

§ 356] 783 

representations as to material facts which constitute an inducement to the contract, and upon which the other party had a right to rely, will give equity jurisdiction. Relief by way of rescission and cancellation lies within the sound discretion of the court, to be exercised according to what is reasonable and proper under the circumstances of each particular case. And the court will, in granting relief, emphatically apply the maxim that he who seeks equity must do equity and impose such terms on the party seeking relief as justice may require.¹ 

Where an application for rescission presents no independent equity, and the only relief sought, or which can appropriately be granted, is one for which the law provides an adequate and complete remedy, resort to a court of equity is unnecessary and improper.2 The particular instances in which a remedy by way of rescission is most often given are in connection with instruments concerning land and negotiable paper before maturity, the legal remedies in these cases being, as a general rule, inadequate. The remedy is also frequently given in case of bonds, policies of insurance, settlements and compromises, awards, and judgments." There has been some question as to whether equity ought to exercise its jurisdiction to order instruments absolutely void at law, and not merely voidable, to be delivered up and cancelled, since, under such circumstances, the legal remedy is adequate and com plete. But it is now well settled that jurisdiction will be exercised in such cases, except where the invalidity of the instrument is apparent on its face.4 Equity may also decree the rescission of a contract entered into in disregard of the statute of frauds, since such contracts are generally held to be voidable and not void.5 A judgment or decree entered by consent may be cancelled when one of the usual grounds for rescission and cancellation is made to appear.

§ 357.-Grounds for Relief-Fraud and Misrepresentation.-Courts of equity have jurisdiction to grant relief by way of rescission and cancellation against contracts procured by false representations, fraudulent concealment, or fraud in any of its other forms. The jurisdiction of equity in such cases is in one sense concurrent with that of courts of law, for fraud is a tort for which compensation in damages may be given at law. But this does not exclude the wider jurisdiction of equity, under which a fraudulent transaction may be completely undone and the parties restored to their former position. If the remedy which the law affords is adequate to the case, equity may properly refuse to interfere. But if the injury which would be caused by allowing the contract to stand cannot be adequately compensated for in damages, and complete justice can be done only by rescinding the fraudulent transaction, then the jurisdiction of equity is clear.7

In order to constitute a ground for the rescission of a contract, a false representation must be of some material fact or thing, unknown to the plaintiff, either from his not having examined, or from want of an opportunity to be informed, or from entire confidence reposed in the defendant, and such confidence must be a right growing out of relations of a fiduciary character existing between the parties. The misrepresentation must be made with the intention that it shall be acted upon by the party to whom it was made. It must also appear that the complaining party acted in reliance upon the false representation, and that he would not have entered into the contract, or changed his position, if it had not been made. 

Finally, the party relying and acting upon the false representation must be prejudiced by its falsity. He must suffer some pecuniary

loss or injury as the natural consequence of the conduct induced by the misrepresentation. Fraud without resulting pecuniary damage is not a ground for the exercise of remedial jurisdiction, legal or equitable. But, if any pecuniary loss is shown to have resulted, the court will not inquire into the extent of the injury. It is sufficient if the party misled has been very slightly prejudiced, if the amount is at all appreciable.10

The foregoing rule is, however, subject to the qualification that the person to whom the false representation is made must not only believe it is true, but he must be so situated with respect to what is represented that he has, at the time, the right to rely upon the truth of the representation as made." For while it is true that one cannot by false representations induce carelessness upon another's part and then profit by such negligence, yet the policy of the law is that he who will not reasonably guard his own interests when he has an opportunity to do so, and when there is no circumstance calculated to deter him from that opportunity, must take the consequences. 

Where there is inattention amounting to gross carelessness on the one side, and misstatement on the other, and but for the former the latter would not be effective, and loss occurs to the inexcusably negligent party, he is remediless. This is not because the wrongdoer can plead his own wrongdoing as an excuse for not making reparation, but because the consequences are attributable to the inexcusable negligence of the injured party, and because the court will not protect those who, with a full opportunity to do so, do not protect themselves.12 And, of course, where a party institutes an inquiry for himself and learns the real facts, he cannot claim to have relied upon the misrepresentation.13 

While the foregoing principles apply primarily to false representations knowingly made, they are not restricted in their application to such cases. It is now well settled that a misrepresentation of material facts, though innocently made, will, if acted upon by the

The real inquiry is not whether the party making the misrepresentation knew it to be false, but whether the other party believed it to be true and was misled by it in making the contract. Whether the misrepresentation is made innocently or knowingly, the effect is the same. An innocent misrepresentation is as conclusive a ground of relief in equity as a willful and false assertion, for it operates as an imposition upon the other party, and the party making it should be held to his representation.14 

In order to warrant the rescission of a contract, a misrepresentation must be of an existing fact. The non-performance of a mere promise, even where it was made for the purpose of inducing another person to enter into a contract, will not be sufficient to authorize its rescission.15 Thus, promises by a vendor to make future improvements upon land, though made for the purpose of selling the land and subsequently broken, will not warrant a rescission of the contract to purchase.16 However, while the mere failure to carry out a promise does not justify the rescission of a contract, yet a promise or promissory representation as to a material matter, made without any intention of performing it, or with the positive intention not to perform it, is a sufficient basis for the rescission of a contract where it was made to induce the other party to enter into the contract and he acted in reliance upon it.17 

It is also a general rule that, where no fiduciary relation exists between two contracting parties, mere statements of opinion or belief, even though untrue and resting upon no information, are not such false representations as constitute fraud and justify the rescission of their contract.18 But it has been held that, when one of the

The concealment of a material fact by a party having a duty to disclose it may be the predicate for the rescission of a contract in exactly the same manner as a false representation.20 As a general rule, a purchaser having information as to the value of land is under no duty to disclose his information to the owner, but if he undertakes to answer inquiries, or discloses any facts, he must disclose the whole truth without doing anything calculated to prevent an investigation by the vendor. And very little is necessary to invoke the application of this principle. Statements ordinarily regarded as mere expressions of opinion may be sufficient when calculated to mislead and prevent an examination of the property by the vendor.21 

§ 358.-Grounds for Relief-Mistake.-Courts of equity have a well recognized jurisdiction to decree the rescission and cancellation of a contract where either or both of the parties labored under a mistake of fact at the time of its execution. The reason for granting relief in such cases is that there was no mutual assent to all of the terms of the contract. In order to warrant rescission and cancellation on this ground, the mistake must be material to and affect the substance of the transaction.22

Thus, for instance, in a sale of real estate, if one party believes he is buying a particular piece of property, while the other party thinks he is selling another piece, there is a lack of the mutual assent necessary to constitute a valid contract. If the purchaser, desiring to inspect the property before completing the sale, has a particular lot pointed out to him which is satisfactory and which he believes he

However, where a vendor sells real estate simply by the description contained on the face of the title papers, he is not accountable for a mistake of fact as to location or boundaries resting wholly in the mind of the other party.23 

As a general rule, in a sale of land in gross, that is, where a specific lot, section, or parcel of land is sold as a whole without regard to quantity, the purchaser is not entitled, in the absence of a gross mistake, to a rescission or abatement of the purchase price for a deficiency in the quantity of land contained in the tract which the parties estimated at the time of the sale. Where it is clear that the parties intended a contract of hazard, equity will not interfere. But the rule is otherwise, of course, where the vendor gave a guaranty as to the quantity of the land.24

In the case of a unilateral mistake of fact, it has been held that equity will decree a rescission and cancellation even where the mistake is negligent unless the negligence amounts to the breach of a legal duty.25 However, the later rule, and that supported by the weight of authority, is that rescission will not be decreed where the mistake results from a want of that degree of care and diligence which should be exercised by persons of reasonable prudence under the same circumstances.26

Rescission of a contract will not be decreed for mistake where reformation will furnish an adequate remedy.27 In other words, where there has been actual assent by both parties to the terms of a contract, but the written evidence of the contract does not express what was really intended by the parties, equity will reform the instrument so as to make it express their true intention.28 Furthermore, in the case of a unilateral mistake, the court will sometimes

§ 359.-Grounds for Relief-Duress.-Equity will rescind a contract obtained by duress.30 Legal duress implies that one party has been unlawfully constrained by another to perform an act under circumstances which prevent the exercise of free will.31 Thus where a married woman, who was sick and nervous and had no opportunity for consideration and consultation with disinterested advisers, made a deed to her separate property under threats of the prosecution of her husband for embezzlement, and to save him from such prosecution, equity will rescind and cancel the conveyance.32 

In order to constitute a ground for rescission, the duress must have been participated in by the opposite party to the contract. 

Where a husband coerces his wife into executing a mortgage to a third person for a valuable consideration, the wife cannot rescind. the transaction unless the third person had knowledge of or participated in the coercion.33 

§ 360.-Grounds for Relief-Disability.-Mere mental weakness does not authorize a court of equity to rescind a contract if such weakness does not amount to an inability to comprehend the effect and nature of the transaction and is not accompanied by evidence of imposition or undue influence. The presumption is always in favor of the validity of the contract and the capacity of the parties, and the contract will under no circumstances be rescinded unless it is proved by a preponderance of the evidence that the mind of one of the parties was so affected as to render him incapable of understanding the transaction.34 Thus, a contract entered into by a person who is so intoxicated that he is incapable of transacting business intelligently is voidable by him.35 And mental incapacity or imbecil-

§ 361.-Grounds for Relief-Undue Influence.-Equity will rescind a contract obtained by one person through the exercise of undue influence over another. Undue influence is not susceptible of precise definition, but in order to warrant rescission the undue influence relied upon must be of such a character as to overcome the will of the opposite party, to deprive him of free agency, and to substitute the will of another for his own.37 The character of the transaction, the mental condition of the person whose act is in question, and the relationship between the parties concerned are all elements that may be taken into consideration in applying the rule.38 

Undue influence is frequently predicated upon a confidential relationship between the parties. A confidential relation will be held to exist in every case in which confidence is reposed on one side and there is a resulting superiority and influence on the other. The relation and duties involved need not be legal, but may be moral, social, domestic, or merely personal. Whenever such a relation exists and the influence resulting from it is exerted by the party in whom the trust or confidence is imposed to obtain an advantage at the expense of the confiding party, the person so availing himself of his position will not be permitted to retain the advantage even though the transaction could not have been impeached if no such confidential relation had existed.39 In some cases of confidential and fiduciary relationship, such as that of trustee and beneficiary or client and attorney, the rule is absolute that the person in whom the trust is imposed shall derive no benefit from the contracts or bounty of the former. In such cases the burden is on the trustee or attorney to show that the transaction was fair and that no undue influence was used.40

There must be combined with it some other inequitable circumstance, such as mistake, fraudulent advantage, mental weakness, or undue influence, before rescission can be obtained.42 A sale for an inadequate consideration will not be set aside merely because it is made reluctantly and when the vendor is greatly in need of money, the sale not being unusual or oppressive, and there being no fraud, duress, or other inequitable circumstances.43 And a county is not entitled to rescind a sale of land for an inadequate price because it did not know that certain improvements on the lands were its property, the means of knowledge being available equally to the county and the purchaser.44 

§ 363.-Grounds for Relief-Failure of Consideration. It is a well settled rule that, if a contract is entire and remains executory either in whole or in part, and one party fails to perform his part of the contract, the other party may treat this as an offer to rescind and, if he is not in default, maintain a suit in equity for rescission and cancellation.45 Thus, where the purchaser under an executory contract for the sale of land is not in default and has paid all or a part of the purchase money, and the vendor fails to comply with the contract on his part, either by not tendering a deed, or by tendering a defective title,46 or by failing to make improvements called for by the contract,47 the purchaser is entitled to disaffirm the contract and maintain a suit in equity for its rescission and the return of the purchase money.48 And, if necessary, the purchaser is also entitled to the adjudication of an equitable lien against the property described in the contract for the amount of the payments which he has made thereunder.49

In order to entitle one party to the rescission of a contract because of non-performance by the other party, the party seeking rescission must himself be free from default. But this does not necessarily mean that the party seeking rescission must completely perform the contract on his part before he may sue to rescind, since such a rule would entitle the other party to the benefit of the contract without requiring performance of his own obligations. In such cases the rights of the parties depend upon whether the covenants of their contract are dependent or independent and, if the covenants of the rescinding party are dependent, he need not complete performance as a prerequisite to maintaining suit. 

In this connection, the question of whether covenants are dependent or independent rests upon the intention of the parties and is to be determined from the sense of the entire contract rather than from any particular form of expression. The order of time in which the intent of the contract requires performance is usually considered as controlling. And the general rule is that the covenants of a contract will be construed as dependent unless a contrary intention appears.

Thus, for example, in contracts for the sale of land, where the purchaser agrees to make his payments in specified installments, and the vendor agrees to make certain improvements upon the property, the undertakings of the parties will, unless a contrary intention clearly appears, be construed as dependent. Consequently, the purchaser may cease to make his payments and sue for rescission whenever it appears that the vendor cannot or will not perform the acts which are to be concurrently done by him. In cases where the purchaser covenants to pay for land in installments, and the only covenant of the vendor is to convey a good title when the last installment is paid, all of the purchaser's covenants, except the last one, are independent, but the purchaser's covenant to pay the last installment and the vendor's covenant to make title are dependent and, upon the vendor's default in making a good title, the purchaser may sue to rescind without paying the last installment.50

The primary object of rescission and cancellation is to undo the original transaction and restore the status quo. Therefore, in accordance with the principle that he who seeks equity must do equity, a party seeking to rescind a contract, whether on the ground of fraud, mistake, or otherwise, must offer to restore to the opposite party any property or other consideration which he has received under the contract, and actual restoration must be made a condition precedent to the granting of the relief sought.53 This rule applies, not only to persons who are sui juris, but also to married women who have received part or all of the consideration under a contract which is unenforceable against them because of coverture.54 As a general rule, equity will not grant relief by way of rescission and cancellation, even on the ground of fraud or misrepresentation, where it is impossible to restore the parties to their original positions with their original rights.55

[Ch. 32 § 366.-Bill of Complaint.-A bill of complaint to rescind a contract should set out the agreement, the parties thereto, and the time, place and circumstances of its execution.
