A plaintiff may allege as many different grounds for the rescission and cancellation of a contract as he may desire. Furthermore, the bill of complaint must show that the plaintiff is able to make restoration of the property, or allege facts from which that ability may fairly be inferred.77

§ 367.-Defenses.-Ratification is a complete defense to a suit for rescission. Where a party, with knowledge of the facts entitling him to rescind, afterwards ratifies the contract, he has no claim to relief. An express ratification is not required in order to defeat his remedy. Any acts which recognize the contract as still existing, or any conduct inconsistent with an intention of avoiding it, have the effect of an election to affirm. This rule rests upon a principle of public policy that all that justice or equity requires is that a person having a right to rescind a contract should have one fair opportunity, after full knowledge of the facts, to affirm the contract and accept its benefits or to disaffirm it and demand the consequent redress. And, since the remedy of rescission and cancellation is not favored by the courts, even slight circumstances which indicate a purpose or intention on the part of the one seeking rescission to waive that right will preclude the granting of relief.⁰⁰ 

Thus, any unreasonable or unnecessary delay in asserting a right of rescission and in taking steps to make it effective will amount to a waiver of the right. Where a party desires to rescind a contract on the ground of fraud, mistake, or for other cause, he must, upon discovery of the facts, promptly announce his intention to rescind, adhere to it, and be guilty of no undue delay or vacillation in moving to have his rights made effective by a decree of rescission.

§ 368.-Testimony.-The burden of proving fraud as a ground for the rescission and cancellation of a contract is upon the party seeking to avoid the contract.93 While a wide latitude is permitted in seeking evidence of the fraud alleged,94 evidence of other acts of fraud than those alleged in the bill cannot avail the plaintiff.95

Where a contract is executed by one enfeebled in mind and body for an inadequate consideration, a presumption of fraud arises, but the burden of proving these conditions is upon the party seeking rescission.97

§ 371.-Reformation-Jurisdiction. The reformation of written. 

instruments is a well established branch of equity jurisdiction.107 

Such relief cannot be obtained in an action at law, either on an equitable plea or otherwise.108 

A court of equity does not, however, rectify the contract itself, but only the instrument purporting to but not in fact evidencing the terms of the contract.109 The court cannot make a new agreement between the parties. It can only re-establish in written form the evidence of an existing contract which has been validly made but defectively evidenced in writing.110 And the right to the reformation of an instrument is not absolute, but depends upon an equitable showing.111

Causing the true description to be read into a deed neither makes a new conveyance nor changes an old one. It simply makes the conveyance effective by applying to it the property intended to be included.116 

It is likewise well settled that, when a policy of insurance as issued does not, because of mutual mistake or fraud, conform to the contract which it purports to evidence, and the insured accepts the policy in the belief that it does conform to his contract, a court of equity will reform the instrument. And after a loss has occurred, the reformation of the policy and a judgment for the loss may be had in the same suit.117

A contract may be reformed for a mistake of law as well as for a mistake of fact. If a written instrument fails to express the intention which the parties had in making the contract which it purports to evidence, equity will grant relief even though the failure may have resulted from a mistake as to the legal meaning and operation of terms or language employed in the writing.118 Thus, where the parties to a deed understand that a restrictive covenant contained therein does not prohibit the use of the property for the purpose intended by the grantee, but it subsequently develops that the covenant does apply to such use, equity will reform the deed to conform to their original intention and understanding.119 

In order to warrant reformation, however, the mistake must be mutual. It must be shown that the reform sought is according to the agreement of both parties at the time the instrument was written and the mistake made. If the misunderstanding exists in the mind of only one of the parties, there is no mutual assent to all of the terms of the contract, and consequently there is no prior contract to which the writing may be made to conform. A reformation cannot make a new instrument which the parties never agreed to make. Thus, while a mistake on one side may be a ground for rescinding a contract, it cannot be a ground for altering its terms. 120

As a general rule, equity will not undertake to reform a conveyance or other instrument which is voluntary and not based upon a consideration. In other words, equity will not reform a voluntary conveyance without the consent of all parties. If there is a mistake or a defect, it is a mere failure in a bounty which the grantor was not bound to make and is therefore not bound to perfect. But a meritorious consideration, such as a conveyance to charity, or a deed for the support of a wife or child, may be sufficient to support a reformation.121 

Since a right to the reformation of an instrument depends upon an equitable showing, relief will not be granted to correct immaterial mistakes. Unless an instrument, if reformed as prayed, will

§ 373.-Reformation-Procedure.-Proceedings to reform written instruments are subject to the general rule in chancery that all persons interested in the subject matter of the litigation, whether their interest is legal or equitable, should be made parties defendant to the suit so that the court may settle all rights at once and thus eliminate the necessity of a multiplicity of suits. Accordingly, in a suit brought by the insured to reform a fire insurance policy containing a standard mortgage clause, the mortgagee is a necessary party defendant. 124 And where it is sought to reform a lease of real estate containing covenants of warranty, the lessors must be made parties to the suit even though they subsequently conveyed the fee to others. 125 But, where a mortgage recites that it is second to one executed to a third person on a prior date, this recital is binding on the second mortgagee, and a mutual mistake in the description of the property in the first mortgage may be corrected without making him a party to the suit.126

Ordinarily, an action at law upon a contract as written is an affirmance of the contract and will preclude a subsequent suit for its reformation. When a court of equity has assumed jurisdiction for the purpose of reforming a written contract, it may, in order that full and complete justice may be administered, retain jurisdiction and proceed to enforce the contract after its reformation.140 Thus, where it is sought to reform an insurance policy after a loss, the court may reform the policy and enter a judgment for the loss in the same suit. 141

The court may also, in a suit for reformation, enjoin actions at law where that is necessary to protect the rights of the parties. 

Thus, where the court has jurisdiction to correct the description of land contained in a deed, it will enjoin a suit in ejectment against a party who has entered under the deed, if the deed, as corrected, will constitute a defense to the ejectment suit.142 Likewise, where a suit is brought in equity to reform a promissory note, an action at law upon the note may be enjoined.143

§ 374. Jurisdiction.-The specific performance of a contract is not a matter of right, like the enforcement of a lien or the recovery of a judgment at law. The granting or denial of such relief rests. in the sound discretion of the court. This does not mean an arbitrary discretion, but a sound and reasonable discretion controlled by established principles of equity as applied to the facts of each case. It is fundamental, however, that equity will not grant specific performance where the remedy at law for damages affords complete and adequate relief. But where the injury is peculiar in its nature, so that a jury cannot estimate with any degree of certainty the damages sustained, and the contract is fair and

It is a general rule that courts of equity will not entertain jurisdiction for the specific performance of contracts relating to chattels and other things of a personal nature. But the exercise of equity jurisdiction for specific performance does not depend upon any distinction between real and personal property. It depends upon whether damages at law afford a complete remedy in the particular case.4 Thus, where the chattel involved in a contract to sell is of peculiar value and character, and the loss of it cannot be fully compensated in damages, equity will grant full relief by requiring specific delivery.5

There are numerous other exceptions to the rule that equity will not entertain jurisdiction for the specific performance of contracts relating to personal property and other things of a personal nature.

In the case of an executory agreement for the sale of land, it must, in order to be enforceable in equity, describe or otherwise identify the land and name the purchase price and time of pay- The description of the land to be conveyed is one of the most essential parts of an agreement to sell. Specific performance will not be decreed unless the agreement describes the lands to be conveyed, either in terms or by reference, or unless the agreement furnishes the means by which the land can be identified with reasonable certainty and without resort to parol evidence. However, where the description shows that a particular tract, as distinguished from other lands, is meant, then parol evidence can be resorted to for the purpose of applying the description, or locating the land, even though the description is somewhat general. In other words, parol evidence is inadmissible to supply a description, but it is admissible for the purpose of showing that the description contained in the contract refers to a particular tract or parcel of land. This is not adding anything to the terms of the contract.21

The rule that specific performance will only be decreed in cases where the terms of the contract have been expressed or agreed upon with reasonable certainty applies with equal force to a contract to make a lease,24 and to a contract to insure, whether such contracts are written or oral. In the case of a contract to make a lease, however, an agreement providing for the execution of an instrument in the form customarily used in the community has been held enforceable.25 In the case of a contract to insure, the agreement must be certain as to the subject matter, the risk insured against, the amount of insurance, the rate of premium, and the identity of the parties. But the terms of the agreement may be determined from the relationship of the parties, their previous dealings, and the facts and circumstances attending the transaction.26

Since the basis for specific performance is a valid and binding contract, such relief will not be granted unless the contract sought to be enforced complies with the Statute of Frauds in any case where it is applicable. Therefore, where it is sought to specifically enforce a contract for the sale of land, the contract must be signed by the party sought to be charged therewith or by his duly authorized agent.27

Notwithstanding this rule, however, it is well settled that, where there has been such part performance of an oral contract to sell land as to take the case out of the operation of the Statute of Frauds, a decree for specific performance may be entered. Payment of the purchase price, no other act being done by either party, is not enough to take the case out of the statute.28

The more modern rule, and the rule which has been definitely adopted in Florida, is that only a mutuality of remedy at the time of filing the bill is required. If, at the time the bill in equity is filed, the defendant could not have the remedy of specific performance against the plaintiff, then the contract will not be enforced against the defendant, but the plaintiff will be left to his remedy at law. In other words, equity will refuse specific performance only where it finds that, in granting relief to the plaintiff, the defendant, without fault on his part, will be left to his remedy at law.35 

In accordance with the latter and modern rule, it has been held that an executory contract containing mutual covenants which cannot be enforced against one of the parties because of infancy, coverture, or other disability cannot be enforced against the other. Thus, where a married woman has contracted to purchase land, she is not ordinarily entitled to specific performance because the contract cannot be specifically enforced against her. The court is without power to enter a personal decree against her for the purchase money, or to make the purchase money a charge against her separate statutory property. It will, therefore, refuse to enter a decree against the vendor for a conveyance when it cannot at the same time compel the purchaser to pay the purchase price. 36 Of course, where a contract containing mutual covenants was originally unenforceable against one of the parties by reason of some disability, yet that party performs all of the obligations required of him under the contract, the objection of want of mutuality does not lie.37 Likewise, where the party under disability has, at the time suit is filed, placed himself in a situation where he can be compelled to specifically perform his part of the contract, want

A Florida statute provides that a married woman's contract to convey her separate statutory real property may be specifically enforced against her if it is acknowledged in the form prescribed for conveyances of such property by her.41 Accordingly, where, as vendor, she properly acknowledges a contract to sell real estate, there is a mutuality of remedy and the contract is specifically enforceable by and against her. But where her contract to sell is not properly acknowledged, a married woman is not subject to a decree of specific performance at the suit of the purchaser.42 It would seem, however, that she could obtain a decree of specific performance against the purchaser under her unacknowledged contract to sell by tendering into court a properly executed and acknowledged deed to the property.

§ 377.-Prerequisites to Relief-Performance by Plaintiff.-It is incumbent upon a party who seeks the aid of a court of chancery to compel the specific performance of a contract to show that he has performed, or has been ready, able and willing to perform, all of the essential terms of the contract on his part. This rule is based upon the principle that he who seeks equity must do equity, and it requires the plaintiff to do everything within his power to fulfill his part of the contract which he is seeking to enforce.45 

Accordingly, in a suit for specific performance by the vendor under a real estate sales contract, where payment of the last installment of the purchase money and the conveyance of title are concurrent and dependent acts, the vendor, before he can maintain his bill, must tender to the purchaser such a conveyance of title as is required by the contract. The tender need not, however, be unconditional. From its very nature it must be conditional and to be performed only in case the purchaser concurrently performs his part of the agreement by paying the balance of the purchase price.4 46 Under some circumstances, a tender by the vendor may be excused. One is not required to do useless or unnecessary acts to obtain relief to which he is otherwise entitled. Consequently, where the purchaser repudiates the contract, and announces his determination to refuse further performance, the tender of a deed is unnecessary as a prerequisite to a suit for specific performance by the vendor.47

The well established rule is that, unless the contract specifically requires a perfect record title, the purchaser cannot avoid specific performance of his contract to purchase on the ground that the vendor's title rests wholly or partially upon parol proof of adverse possession for the statutory period. Under a contract calling only for a perfect title, or a good and sufficient warranty deed, the vendor may tender a title based on adverse possession where the proof of such possession is so clear as to be free from doubt.48 Nor will immaterial defects in title defeat the validity of the vendor's tender where they are so partial and immaterial that the substance of the contract and its essential terms can nevertheless be carried into effect.49 

Where a suit for specific performance is brought by the purchaser under a land sales contract, and payment of the last installment of the purchase money and the conveyance of title are concurrent and dependent acts, the purchaser must, before he can maintain his bill, pay or tender to the vendor the unpaid balance of the purchase money in full. As in the case of the vendor, the purchaser's tender need not be unconditional, but must necessarily be conditional and dependent upon a concurrent conveyance of title by the vendor.50 

In this connection, the requirement of a tender of the purchase money does not mean a tender strictly valid at law. A present readiness, willingness, and ability in good faith to perform the acts required, provided the other party will concurrently do the things which he is required by the contract to do, and notice by the former to the latter of such readiness, willingness, and ability to perform, is sufficient.51

But, even where time is expressly made of the essence of a contract, a failure to perform within the time limited will not in every case defeat the right to specific performance. This is particularly true in cases where performance is subsequently rendered without unreasonable delay and no circumstances have intervened which would render it inequitable or unjust to give relief. The discretion which a court of equity has to grant or refuse specific performance, and which is always exercised with reference to the particular case before it, may and of necessity must often be controlled by the conduct of the party who bases his refusal to perform the contract upon the failure of the other party to strictly comply with its conditions.53 § 378.-Prerequisites to Relief-Diligence of Plaintiff.-A party seeking the aid of a court of equity to specifically enforce a contract for the sale of land must show that he has acted with promptness and diligence. While equity does not regard time as of the essence of the contract, unless it is expressly so stipulated, yet it will require that one who seeks specific performance shall not be guilty of unreasonable delay and shall bring his suit with reasonable promptness. 

Any unreasonable delay not satisfactorily accounted for will be considered in equity as an acquiescence in the refusal of the other party to perform and as an abandonment of the plaintiff's own equitable rights.54 And a claim to specific performance may be lost by delay even though it is otherwise meritorious.55 

In determining the amount of delay which will preclude relief by way of specific performance, no general rule, applicable to all cases, can be formulated. The question is whether the plaintiff has been guilty of laches, and this depends, not merely upon the lapse of time, but also upon the nature of the rights involved and whether

One of the principal considerations in determining whether delay will preclude the right to specific performance is any change in the value of the property between the accrual of the right and the attempt to enforce it. A court of equity will not allow either party to take advantage of a turn in the market and have the contract performed only in case it is to his advantage.57 

Another consideration of primary importance is whether the defendant has in any way changed his position in reliance upon the plaintiff's apparent abandonment of his equitable rights. It is well settled that a delay in seeking specific performance raises a presumption that the dilatory party has abandoned the contract. In other words, the defendant's default is equivalent to an offer to rescind, and the plaintiff's delay is considered as a consent to the rescission.58 If, in reliance upon this apparent condition, a vendor, for example, materially changes his position, as by making improvements upon the property,59 or making conveyances thereof, even to third persons with notice, so the purchaser will not be granted specific performance.

Delay in seeking specific performance will not, however, preclude relief on behalf of a purchaser in possession. Where a right to specific performance has once accrued in favor of one of the parties to a land sales contract, the other party to the contract may eliminate further uncertainty as to whether the contract is to be enforced against him by a proper notice and tender of performance on his part. In other words, while time may not be of the essence of the original contract, it may be subsequently made so by an express notice given by a party not in default, or whose default has been waived and who tenders performance, requiring the other party to perform the contract within a reasonable time fixed in the notice. The notice may be written or oral, and what constitutes a reasonable time depends upon the circumstances of the case. If performance is not rendered in accordance with the notice, the contract may be treated as abandoned and specific performance cannot thereafter be enforced by the party on whom it was served.64 It would seem that this procedure could also be followed by a party inexcusably in default where he is then ready, able, and willing to perform and wishes to compel the other party to either enforce or abandon the contract. 

§ 379.-Venue. A suit for the specific performance of a contract to sell land is purely in personam. When a court of chancery has acquired jurisdiction over the person of a party, it may, by virtue of its power to coerce obedience to its decrees, compel him to execute a conveyance or pay the purchase price of land regardless of where it may be situated.65 Consequently, a suit for specific performance of such a contract need not be brought in the county where the land lies.66

Such a suit cannot be maintained by the husband alone.71 

Where one of the parties to a land sales contract dies, both his heirs and personal representative should join as plaintiffs in a suit for its specific performance. If the decedent was the vendor, title to the land is in his heirs but payment must be made to the personal representative. If the decedent was the purchaser, the heirs are entitled to the land, subject to the personal representative's right to possession, but the purchase price must be paid by the personal representative. In either event, therefore, both the heirs and personal representative are necessary parties plaintiff.72 

All parties claiming an interest in land from a vendor subsequent to his contract to sell are necessary parties defendant to a suit to specifically enforce the contract.73 If such persons take with notice of the contract, it may be enforced against them. § 381.-Process and Procedure Against Unknown Defendants.-The 

Florida statutes provide that if the plaintiff, or his agent or attorney, in a suit in chancery for the specific performance of a contract to convey or exchange real estate shall state in a sworn bill that he believes there is a person, or are persons, interested in the property involved in the suit whose name or names are unknown to him, and shall pray for relief against them in the bill, he shall be entitled to process by publication to bring in such persons as parties defendant to the suit. 

If the unknown persons are known or believed to be the heirs, devisees, grantees, or other claimants under a person deceased whose name is known to the plaintiff, the plaintiff must state the name of such person in the bill, although the failure to do so does not invalidate any decree obtained by the plaintiff in the suit. If the plaintiff states in his sworn bill that he does not know and has not been able to ascertain whether any person believed by him to be interested in the property or, if dead, to have been interested therein, is dead or alive, he may make such person a defendant by name, and he may also make the heirs, devisees, grantees, or other claimants under such person parties defendant to the bill. Any final decree rendered on such a bill of complaint after service by publication has been had as prescribed by law is conclusive upon the known person, if alive, and upon the heirs, devisees, grantees, or other claimants under the known person, if dead. The bill of complaint may be instituted and maintained wholly against unknown persons.82 

If the heirs, devisees, grantees, or other claimants under a deceased person are made parties defendant to the bill, the order of publication should describe such unknown defendants as "all parties claiming interests under (the deceased person) or otherwise," in the property, which must be briefly but definitely described in the order. 

If any known person and the heirs, devisees, grantees, or other claimants under such known person are made parties defendant, such defendants should be described in the order of publication as "name of known party, if living, and, if dead, all parties claiming

82. C. G. L. 4897.

interests under (name of known party), deceased, or otherwise," in the property, which must be briefly but definitely described in the order. All of the defendants may be embraced in one order of publication.83

Publication of the order is made in the same manner as is required by law for all other orders to appear in chancery cases.84 

Proof of publication must be made by the affidavit of the owner, publisher, proprietor, editor, business manager, or foreman of the paper in which the order has been published.85 

After service by publication, decrees pro confesso may be entered against absent unknown defendants as in other cases of service by publication in chancery. Upon the entry of such a decree, a guardian ad litem must be appointed for the absent unknown defendants and the cause then proceeds accordingly.86 

Final decrees rendered against unknown parties in interest are conclusive upon them, and persons deriving through them, from the date of rendition, unless a rehearing is applied for within one year thereafter. But, if the plaintiff, within six months after the entry of the decree, serves a copy thereof upon any person interested who has become known to him, a rehearing will not be granted unless applied for within six months from the date of service.87 If any defendant against whom such a decree has been rendered applies for a rehearing within the time allowed, and gives bond with the conditions fixed by the court, he will be permitted to defend the bill as if he had been personally served with process. The court may stay proceedings upon the original decree pending such defense or, if the decree has been executed, order restitution at the final hearing.88

Where a copy of the contract sought to be enforced is attached to and made a part of a bill for specific performance, the contract may be read in connection with the allegations of the bill in order to determine the existence of any grounds for relief.94 Thus, a bill for specific performance will not be dismissed for an alleged variance between the description of the property contained in the bill and that contained in the contract where the contract is made a part of the bill.95

A bill for the specific performance of a contract to sell land need not allege that the contract is in writing.96 Where the bill sets out the contract in general terms, the presumption of law is that the contract is valid, in writing, and signed by the party to be charged.97 That the contract may be in conflict with the Statute of Frauds is defensive matter which must be set up by answer.98 

However, where the power to contract, as distinguished from the validity of the contract, depends upon compliance with statutory requirements, such compliance must be alleged in the bill. Thus, a bill to enforce a married woman's contract to sell land must allege that the contract was executed and acknowledged by her as required by statute.99 A bill based upon a contract to sell a homestead must also allege compliance with applicable statutory requirements.100 And a bill to compel a conveyance of land by public officials must allege compliance with all statutory conditions necessary to authorize them to make the conveyance sought.101 

Where the contract sought to be enforced was executed by an agent of the defendant, it is sufficient for the bill to allege that the contract was made by the defendant by and through his agent thereunto lawfully authorized.102 And, where it is sought to enforce a contract to sell against a grantee of the original vendor, the bill should contain clear allegations as to his notice of the contract. 103

In addition to complete allegations in regard to the contract sued upon, a bill for specific performance must allege that the plaintiff has performed the agreement on his part or, if the covenants of the contract are dependent, that he has tendered performance and the defendant has refused to perform.104 If time is of the essence of the contract, it must be alleged that the tender was made before the date agreed upon, or, if time was not of the essence, within a reasonable time thereafter. 105 However, since that which is not required to be done is not required to be alleged, a plaintiff seeking specific performance need not allege a tender where his bill shows that the defendant definitely repudiated the contract and notified the plaintiff that he would not perform.106 A bill for specific performance should also allege that the plaintiff is ready, able, and willing to perform at the time of filing suit.107 

When the wife of a vendor under a contract to sell land does not join in the execution of the contract, the purchaser seeking performance should allege in his bill that, at the time he entered into the contract, he either did or did not know of the wife's inchoate dower interest, as the fact may be, and he should frame the prayer of his bill for a conveyance of what the husband can give without abatement of the purchase price or not, as the case may be.108

Whenever a bill for specific performance filed by the purchaser under a land sales contract shows that the vendor cannot convey a good title, and the purchaser does not ask to have a decree for such title as the vendor has, but only for a good title, specific performance is not in the power of the vendor and consequently the court will not decree it. 109 A vendor's bill for specific performance may properly include a prayer for execution against the purchaser for any balance due upon the purchase price.110

Con- § 384.-Defenses.-Since the granting or withholding of relief by way of specific performance is largely within the discretion of the chancellor, the maxim that "he who comes into equity must come with clean hands" applies with peculiar force to such cases. sequently, a court of equity will not decree the specific performance of a contract unless it is strictly equitable and free from deception and unfair advantage on the part of the party seeking relief. And, in order to establish that the plaintiff is not entitled to equitable relief because he does not come into equity with clean hands, it is not essential that the fraud or deceit be sufficient as a defense to an action at law, or to warrant a court of equity in cancelling the contract. It need only appear that the plaintiff has been guilty of taking undue advantage of his position, or of unscrupulous practices, or overreaching, or of concealing important facts.113 

Specific performance may, under some circumstances, be defeated by showing a want of title or defective title in the vendor. Thus, a bill for specific performance brought by the purchaser under a contract to sell land cannot be maintained when it appears that the vendor has no title, legal or equitable.114 But the fact that the vendor had no title when the contract was made is no defense to specific performance if he subsequently acquires such title.115

Where a court of equity acquires jurisdiction for the specific enforcement of a contract, it will proceed to administer complete justice by adjudicating all matters properly presented and involved in the case.

In a suit for specific performance against a vendor whose title proves to be defective, the court has three possible courses of action. 

First, if the vendor is in a position to remove the defects in title, by an application of the purchase money or otherwise, the court will retain the bill, will require the vendor to perform the acts necessary to clear his title, and will decree specific performance. 141 

Second, where the vendor is not in a position to correct the defects in his title, the court may nevertheless, if the purchaser requests such relief, retain the bill and enter a decree for specific performance with compensation to the purchaser for the defects.142 

Specific performance with compensation has been decreed in cases where the vendor's title was defective, 143 where there was a deficiency in the quantity of land agreed to be sold, 144 and where the vendor failed to make improvements upon the property in accordance with his contract.145 It has also been applied in cases where the vendor was a married man and his wife did not join in the execution of the contract to sell.146

In order to warrant a decree of specific performance with compensation, however, it must appear that, at the time the contract was made, the purchaser had no notice of the defect in the vendor's title. 147 Thus, where the purchaser enters into a contract not knowing that the vendor was a married man and believing that he could convey an unencumbered title, he is entitled to a decree of specific performance with an abatement of the purchase price to the extent of the present worth of the wife's inchoate dower right. 

But, if the purchaser knew that the vendor was a married man at the time the contract was made, he can only obtain specific perform-

§ 387.—Appeals.—An application for the specific performance of a contract to sell land is addressed to the sound judicial discretion of the chancellor, such discretion to be controlled by the principles of law and equity as applied to the facts and circumstances of the particular case. Consequently, when the chancellor's discretion is thus controlled, his decision in refusing a decree of specific performance will not be disturbed on appeal unless it is shown to be clearly erroneous. 154 But, if it appears on appeal that the principles of equity justify specific performance, and no provision of law would be violated by granting such relief, a decree refusing specific performance may be reversed.155

The rule that the discretion of the chancellor in refusing specific performance will not be disturbed on appeal unless clearly erroneous applies only to a final decree on the merits. The chancellor does not exercise discretion in granting or denying a motion to dismiss the bill of complaint. In such matters he applies settled rules and principles of law and equity, and his orders must be rendered in accordance therewith.156

§ 388.-Bills of Discovery.-While any bill in equity may seek discovery in connection with other relief, the species of bill usually known as a bill of discovery is usually brought to obtain the disclosure of facts within the defendant's knowledge, or of deeds or writings or other things in his custody, and seeking no relief in consequence of the discovery. It is most commonly used in aid of the prosecution or defense of an action at law, and it may pray for a stay of the proceedings at law until the discovery is made.' 

As a general rule, if the sole object of a suit is to obtain discovery, there is no proceeding beyond an answer by which the discovery is made. The cause is never brought to a hearing, and there is no decree upon the matters set forth in the bill. However, where the necessary discovery cannot be given by merely answering the bill, the court may, within the exercise of its judicial discretion, cause appropriate proceedings to be taken in order to obtain such discovery. Thus, where it is necessary to ascertain the existence or non-existence of merchantable phosphate upon designated land, the court may appoint a master or receiver to make the inspection and tests necessary for the discovery sought.2 

In addition, where a court of equity has once obtained jurisdiction of a cause for purposes of discovery, it will, in proper cases, retain jurisdiction and finally dispose of the cause even though the remedy at law is full and adequate. Thus, where jurisdiction is taken to compel the discovery of the names of the real owners

As a general rule, it is necessary, in order to maintain a bill of discovery, that there be an action pending in another court to which the bill of discovery is auxiliary. It is also usually necessary that the bill have for its purpose the discovery of facts material to the plaintiff's cause of action or defense in the other suit. But there are exceptions to this rule, as where the object of the discovery is to ascertain the name of the proper party against whom the other suit should be brought.5

The general requirements of a bill of discovery are well settled. 

The bill must show that the disclosure of facts which it seeks is necessary to enable the plaintiff to maintain his cause of action or defense in a suit pending or about to be brought in another court, and that the cause of action or defense is legally sufficient. Discovery cannot be had of facts material only to the cause of action or defense of the adverse party, nor where the facts, if disclosed, would not support a cause of action or defense at law. A bill of discovery must also show a present interest of both the plaintiff and defendant in the subject matter, for such a bill cannot be maintained by a stranger or against a witness. The particular matters as to which discovery is sought must, of course, be set out clearly and definitely. A bill for discovery need not be sworn to.7 

While it is true, as a general rule, that a person who has no interest in the subject matter of a suit or is a mere witness, cannot be made a party defendant to a bill for discovery, there is an exception to this rule in the case of a proceeding against a corporation. It is a well established rule that, in order to enable a plaintiff to obtain full knowledge of all facts material to his action or defense, he is permitted to make the officers of a corpora-

Accordingly, it has been held that the provisions of the 1931 Chancery Act in regard to interrogatories did not abolish bills of discovery.10 § 389.-Interpleader.-A bill of interpleader is a remedy available to a plaintiff who has a fund in his hands in which he neither. has or claims to have any interest, and to which the defendants set up conflicting claims. The plaintiff may bring the fund into court and pray that the defendants litigate their claims between themselves. The remedy is based upon the theory that the stakeholder, being willing to bring the fund into court, should be protected against the conflicting claims of those interested in it. 

The purpose of the remedy is to protect the plaintiff against conflicting claims and double vexation in regard to one liability." 

Thus an attorney who has collected money for a client, which is claimed by two creditors of the client, and in which the client has disclaimed any interest, may maintain a bill to compel the creditors to interplead and contest their claims between themselves. 12 Likewise, an insurer may maintain a bill of interpleader where the proceeds of a life insurance policy are claimed by a receiver of the V. In order to maintain a bill of interpleader the plaintiff must show that he has no interest in the litigation, but seeks only to be relieved of the danger of being molested by the conflicting rights of others. He must stand indifferent between the claimants and be in the position of a mere innocent stakeholder. When the plaintiff stands in the relation of a wrongdoer with respect to either party to the suit, he cannot have relief by interpleader. Nor can the plaintiff in an interpleader suit adjust his own claims against the fund in controversy and interplead as to the remainder.15 

Another prerequisite to relief by interpleader is that the plaintiff be free from any contractual relation with one of the adverse claimants in regard to the subject matter of the suit. A plaintiff cannot have an order that two adverse claimants interplead when one question to be tried in determining the defendants' title to the subject matter is whether the plaintiff, by reason of his own act, is under an independent contractual liability to one of the defendants with reference to the subject matter. Any such independent contractual relation cannot be determined in litigation solely .between the conflicting claimants. It must be litigated between the parties to the contract.16 Thus, a depository in escrow cannot, by a bill of interpleader, cast upon the parties to the escrow agreement the burden of determining whether it is obligated to make delivery to one of them who has complied with the terms of the escrow agreement.17

In accordance with these requirements, it is well settled that a bill of interpleader must allege that the plaintiff is indifferent to the conflicting claims, that the same fund is claimed by the defendants against whom relief is sought, that the plaintiff claims no interest in the subject matter, and that one adverse claim is derived from the other or from a common source.19 The bill should also show that the plaintiff cannot determine, without hazard to himself, which of the defendants is entitled to the fund, and it should offer to bring the money into court. There should also be attached to the bill an affidavit that there is no collusion between the parties.20

An interpleader suit consists of two major phases. It should first be determined whether the bill will lie. That phase of the matter may be determined by the appropriate method for testing the sufficiency of any bill in chancery if the objectionable matter appears on the face of the bill. If there are any facts not appearing on the face of the bill which constitute a valid defense to the suit, they may be set up by answer, and the answer must, of course, be supported by proof. If it is found that the bill will not lie, a dismissal follows. If it is found that the bill will lie, then the court so decrees and, upon bringing into court the property in dispute, the plaintiff is discharged from further liability, with his costs.21

The second phase of the matter is then taken up. 

If the case is ready for decision between the defendants, as well as between them and the plaintiff, the court may forthwith settle the conflicting claims of the parties and enter a final decree as to all matters at the one hearing. If, however, the cause is not then ready for decision as between the conflicting claimants, the court should order

In regard to the framing of issues between the claimants in an interpleader suit, there is no rigid rule to be followed. § 390.-Bills to Charge Separate Property of Married Women.- 

The Constitution of Florida provides that a married woman's separate real or personal property may be charged in equity and sold, or the uses, rents and profits thereof sequestrated (a) for the purchase money thereof, or (b) for money or thing due upon any agreement made by her in writing for the benefit of her separate property, or (c) for the purchase price of any property purchased by her, or (d) for labor and material used with her knowledge or assent in the construction of buildings, or repairs, or improvements upon her property, or (e) for agricultural or other labor bestowed thereon, with her knowledge and consent.27 

This constitutional provision is self-executing and is the organic and paramount law on the subject of charging married women's separate property in equity for the payment of obligations contracted by them with reference thereto.28 The effect of the provision is to remove from a married woman the common law disability of coverture in the cases therein enumerated and to enable her, in such cases, to assume obligations that can be enforced out of her separate property.29 But the constitutional provision does not under any circumstances give a married woman capacity to make a contract which will be personally binding upon her.30 

The test of jurisdiction of a court of equity over a bill to enforce a claim against the separate property of a married woman is whether the bill shows the existence of an obligation which the Constitution authorizes a court of equity to deal with and enforce. 

The jurisdiction of equity over such obligations must be confined to the cases specifically enumerated in the Constitution.31 

The first class of obligations which may be charged against the separate property of a married woman are those contracted for the purchase price of such property. In accordance with the express provisions of the Constitution these obligations are enforceable whether they are incurred in the purchase of real or personal

The authority given by the Constitution to charge a married woman's separate property "for the purchase money thereof" is intended to apply only where the property purchased by the married woman remains hers in kind, and is not commingled with her other separate property.34 And a married woman's separate property may not be charged for the purchase money thereof if a mortgage has been given to secure the amount due. In such a case it is considered that the vendor has chosen his security and that the Constitution did not intend to confer upon him an additional remedy for enforcing payment of the purchase price.35 However, if the mortgage is unenforceable because defectively executed, the constitutional remedy remains.36 

The second class of obligations which may be charged against the separate property of a married woman are those arising from an agreement in writing made by her for the benefit of her separate property. In order to come within the purview of this provision of the Constitution the written agreement must be contemporaneous with or antedate the furnishing of money or materials.37 It must also appear that the agreement inured to the enhancement, increase, or benefit of the separate property, and not merely contemplated such a benefit.38 Thus, an agreement in writing between a married woman and a real estate broker that the latter would, in case of forfeiture, be entitled to one-half of the purchaser's deposit under the former's contract to sell her real estate is enforceable because the married woman's separate estate is enriched to the extent of the sum forfeited.39 But, whether a married woman's separate property can be charged with the payment of attorney's fees in accordance with her written agreement

It can have no effect except as evidence of the value of the services in a proceeding to charge the property for labor performed thereon with the married woman's knowledge and assent.42

The third class of obligations which the Constitution authorizes to be charged against a married woman's separate property are those contracted for the purchase price of any property purchased by her. Thus, where a married woman carries on a mercantile business in her own name, and purchases goods upon her sole credit, her separate property may be subjected to the payment of the purchase price.43 A written agreement is not necessary in order to proceed under this provision.44

However, the authority given to charge a married woman's estate for the price of any property purchased by her applies only where the real or personal property actually purchased has been disposed of, lost, or consumed, or, if personal property, so commingled with other property that its identity has been lost. If the property actually purchased is still retained and owned by the married woman, the creditor must proceed under the first classification. specified in the Constitution to charge that property with the payment of its purchase price. And only the specific property purchased may be charged with the debt.45

This rule produces unequal results where the property in question declines in value after its purchase by the married woman. If the property is still owned by her when the proceeding to collect the purchase price is brought, the creditor is restricted in his recovery to the depreciated value of that property. But, if the property has been disposed of or commingled by the married woman, the creditor may recover its full value from her other separate property. 

The fourth class of obligations chargeable against a married woman's property are those incurred for labor and materials used in the construction of buildings upon, or the making of improvements or repairs to, her separate property with her knowledge or assent. The fifth class of obligations includes charges for agricultural or other labor bestowed upon a married woman's property with her knowledge or assent. Obligations of these two classes may be based upon agreements made directly with the married woman, or through her husband as her agent, provided her knowledge and assent to the transaction can be shown.46 A proceeding to charge the separate property of a married woman under the Constitution is a distinct and separate remedy from that afforded by the mechanics' lien laws, and the requirements of the latter need not be met in order to maintain the former.47

The constitutional provisions which provide for charging a married woman's property with the payment of the obligations therein specified do not create a lien upon the property to secure the demands named. Until proceedings are brought to charge the property, no lien arises, and the married woman may dispose of her property in accordance with the statutes permitting her to do so.48

A bill to charge the separate property of a married woman with the payment of an obligation incurred by her must clearly show that the obligation sought to be enforced comes within one of the classifications enumerated in the Constitution. While either of these forms of relief are authorized, the appointment of a receiver and the sequestration of the rents and profits should be decreed in preference to a sale where such a procedure will afford adequate relief to the plaintiff.54 § 391.-Ne Exeat.-The writ of ne exeat is a writ in common use in equity. It is a personal writ intended to enable the court to retain jurisdiction over the defendant, and it is primarily based upon the inherent power of a court of equity to prevent a person from leaving the jurisdiction until he gives security for his appearance or for the performance of a decree. But, being contrary to the right of free locomotion, the writ of ne exeat is sparingly used and it will not be granted without regard to the relative disadvantages which its refusal or allowance would bring upon the respective parties. 55

One of the most common instances in which a writ of ne exeat is used is in the enforcement of decrees for alimony in suits for divorce or separate maintenance. In such cases, the writ may be issued even before the entry of a decree fixing the amount of alimony to be paid.56

A writ of ne exeat can only be issued upon a sworn bill praying for such relief, except in the special cases and for the special causes in which such writs are authorized by the courts of the United States exercising equity jurisdiction. The writ may also issue in any case where courts of equity have concurrent jurisdiction with courts of law and where its issuance seems just.57 It is not necessary that a summons in chancery be served on the defendant before or simultaneously with the writ. On being arrested on a writ of ne exeat, the defendant may immediately enter his appearance and demand copy of the bill without waiting for service of the summons.58 

In granting the writ of ne exeat, the chancellor must fix the conditions of the bond to be required of the plaintiff. The bond must have two good and sufficient sureties, and the writ cannot issue until the bond is given.59 However, a writ issued without such a bond is not void but only erroneous.60

A defendant may be released from arrest under a writ of ne exeat by executing a proper bond to insure his appearance or performance as required by the court. But unreasonable security should not be required and, if it is required, a reduction or modification should be made upon appropriate motion. Likewise, if the writ itself is improvidently or unnecessarily issued, it should be promptly discharged upon application to the court which issued it. But all questions relating to the amount of security to be required of the defendant, and to the continuance, modification, or discharge of such writs, are primarily within the province of the chancellor whose writ it is.1

A trustee may sue or be sued and any appropriate action at law or suit in equity may be brought by or against him. A cestui que trust may also maintain any appropriate proceeding at law or in equity against the trustee. 

But in all of these cases the fundamental rules of pleading and practice are the same as in such actions or suits generally. 

Since a trust is a creature of equity, a court of equity is the appropriate forum for the enforcement of all rights and obligations growing out of the trust relationship. Thus, a cestui que trust may maintain a suit in equity for an accounting by the trustee as to his administration of the trust.64 And a trustee may come into a court of equity and obtain a judicial settlement and approval of his accounts and the allowance of compensation for his services.65 

Where the situs of a trust is in Florida, jurisdiction of non-resident beneficiaries in a suit for instructions or for the adjudication of rights in the trust estate may be obtained by publication.66 § 393.-Vendors' Liens.-A vendor's lien is a right which the law by implication accords to a grantor of land who has conveyed title to the purchaser but who has reserved no lien and taken no security for the purchase money other than the personal obligation of the grantee. By virtue of this lien, the vendor may, in equity, subject the land to the payment of the purchase money if the rights of others are not thereby injured, and if the circumstances and relations of the parties, with reference to the land conveyed, make it equitable to do so. 

A vendor's lien is not the result of any agreement between the parties but is simply an equity raised by the courts for the benefit of the vendor. It is wholly independent of possession and may be implied even where the vendor remains in possession. But the con-

A vendor's lien is implied in law for the benefit of the vendor and it may be waived. Such a waiver may be expressly made, or it may be implied from the facts and circumstances. Any conduct on the part of the vendor tending to show that he does not rely solely upon the legal implication in his favor will operate as a waiver of the lien.72.

The lien of a vendor upon land for the purchase money is lost in all cases where any security is taken on the land or otherwise for the whole or any part of the purchase money, unless there is an express agreement to the contrary. That the additional security proves unavailing does not affect the question. The lien is waived. by the taking of the security because it shows the intention of the vendor not to rely upon his implied equitable lien.73 Thus, the vendor's lien is lost by the taking of a purchase money mortgage,74 by requiring an endorser on the purchase money notes, 74A or where the vendor accepts a mortgage upon other property in payment of the purchase price.75 But a purchaser's promise to pay a debt of the vendor to a third person as part of the purchase price is not a waiver of the vendor's lien because the purchaser's undertaking is merely a personal obligation.76 

Ordinarily, the right to a vendor's lien is restricted to the vendor and it does not arise in favor of third persons not parties to the transaction. A vendor's lien may be enforced against a subsequent purchaser who takes a conveyance from the original purchaser with notice of the lien, although it may not be enforced against a purchaser for value without notice.81

Form No. 1 BILL AGAINST PARTNER FOR ACCOUNTING, RECEIVER, IN- JUNCTION, AND DISSOLUTION OF PARTNERSHIP 

In the Circuit Court in and for Leon County, Florida. In Chancery. 

VS. 

Bill of Complaint 

William Smith,

Defendant 

John Doe, a resident of Tallahassee, in Leon County, Florida, brings this bill of complaint against William Smith, a resident of Tallahassee, in Leon County, Florida, and alleges:

FORMS 

871 

1. On the first day of January, 1930, the plaintiff, John Doe, and the defendant, William Smith, formed a co-partnership, to be carried on under the firm name of Doe & Smith, for the purpose of manufacturing and selling lumber. A copy of the articles of partnership is hereto attached, marked Exhibit "A," and made a part of this bill of complaint. 

2. The property of the partnership at the time of its inception consisted of a saw mill located upon lands owned by the partnership in Wakulla County, Florida, a lumber yard located in Tallahassee, in Leon County, Florida, four tracts of land located in Wakulla and Leon Counties, Florida, and various articles of personal property necessary to the operation of the partnership business. A complete and detailed description of all of the said partnership property, both real and personal, is contained in the copy of the articles of partnership hereto attached as Exhibit "A." Said property was purchased by the plaintiff and defendant for their partnership business at a cost of ten thousand dollars ($10,000.00) cash. Both plaintiff and defendant contributed five thousand dollars ($5,000.00) each to the cost of said property. 3. By the express terms of the articles of partnership, each partner was required to devote his whole time and attention to the business of the partnership, and they were to share equally in the profits of the partnership business. The plaintiff was to have charge of and operate the said saw mill, and the defendant was to have charge of the said lumber yard and sell the lumber manufactured by the partnership. 

4. The business of the partnership was carried on from the first day of January, 1930, to the first day of June, 1934. During said period plaintiff furnished to the defendant a total of two million three hundred thousand (2,300,000) feet of lumber of all grades and of an aggregate value of one hundred and seventy thousand dollars ($170,- 000.00). A more detailed statement of the lumber furnished by the plaintiff to the defendant according to grades and values is hereto attached, marked Exhibit "B," and made a part of this bill of complaint. 

5. The defendant has failed to keep a proper account in the partnership records of the lumber received and disposed of by him, and the defendant has, at various times, sold said lumber and collected large sums of money therefor. No entries appear on the books of the

partnership for the moneys so collected by the defendant, but the defendant has applied the said moneys to his own individual use. In addition, the defendant has used large quantities of the lumber, amounting to twenty thousand dollars ($20,000.00) in value, in the construction of houses for himself which he has sold and appropriated the proceeds of the sale to his own use. 

6. On or about the first day of January, 1931, and in every subsequent January thereafter up to the present time, the plaintiff has endeavored to induce the defendant to render an accounting of their partnership affairs, but each time the plaintiff has been induced by the defendant, for one reason or another, to forego his rights, believing that the defendant would finally do him justice. On the first day of 

June, 1934, the plaintiff finally insisted on a settlement with the defendant and the defendant then stated that there was nothing due to the plaintiff on account of the partnership business. 

7. During the said period from the first day of January, 1930, to the first day of June, 1934, the business of the partnership has been operated at a substantial profit, but the plaintiff has received nothing from the said partnership during that period except the sum of one hundred dollars ($100.00) per month. The defendant has received an equivalent sum per month and in addition has appropriated to his own. use the entire balance of the profits of the partnership business in a very substantial amount. 

8. There are a large number of debts due to the said partnership which are now in the course of collection and, by reason of the facts above alleged, the plaintiff believes that the defendant will possess himself of the money so collected, or portions of it, and will appropriate the said moneys to his own use without accounting to the plaintiff for it.

WHEREFORE, the plaintiff prays (a) that a receiver be appointed to take charge of the partnership books and accounts, and its goods and effects, and to collect the debts due the firm, and to preserve and dispose of the same under the direction of this court, (b) that the defendant be enjoined from selling any lumber which he may now have on hand, from collecting or receiving the partnership debts, and from intermeddling in any way with the business of the partnership, and that a temporary injunction be issued as above prayed, (c) that a special master be appointed to take an account of all the partnership

FORMS 

873 transactions from the commencement thereof, and that, upon said accounting, the defendant be decreed to pay to the plaintiff whatever may be found to be due him, and (d) that the partnership be dissolved and that the partnership property be sold forthwith and the proceeds of the sale disposed of as equity may require. 

Solicitor for Plaintiff Note. The foregoing form is based upon a bill of complaint stated in Nims v. Nims, 23 Fla. 69, 1 So. 527. Since the bill includes a prayer for a temporary injunction and a prayer for a receiver, it must be verified. Chapter XXVI, Section 270, supra; Chapter XXXI, Section 345, supra. See Forms Nos. 7 and 

11, Appendix B, for form of affidavit. For a form of bill of complaint for accounting against a co-tenant, see Form No. 14, Appendix B. 

Form No. 2 CREDITOR'S BILL TO REACH EQUITABLE ASSET OF DEBTOR 

VS. 

William Smith and 

Elizabeth Smith, Defendants

Bill of Complaint 

John Doe, a resident of Jacksonville, in Duval County, Florida, brings this bill of complaint against William Smith and Elizabeth Smith, both of whom are residents of Jacksonville, in Duval County, Florida, and alleges: 

1. On the 15th day of August, 1937, a judgment at law was rendered by this court in favor of the plaintiff against the defendant 

William Smith for the recovery of ten thousand dollars ($10,000.00), with interest and costs. Said judgment is recorded in Minute Book 

12, at page 100, of the records of this court. Plaintiff caused an execution to be issued upon said judgment and placed in the hands of the sheriff of this county, but there has been a return of nulla bona on said execution. No part of said judgment has been paid and the plaintiff is now the sole owner and holder thereof. Said judgment was rendered uppp a promissory note in the sum of ten thousand dollars ($10,000.00) executed by the defendant William Smith, dated 

January 1st, 1932, and payable to the plaintiff five years after its date.

2. The defendant William Smith is now and since the 4th day of 

December, 1932, has been the owner of certain real estate situated and being in Duval County, Florida, more particularly described as Lots 

1 and 2, Block 3, of Wayne's Addition to the City of Jacksonville, according to a plat thereof recorded in Plat Book 25, page 50, of the public records of said county. 

3. On the 4th day of December, 1932, by deed executed and recorded on that day in Deed Book 200, page 350, of the public records of Duval County, Florida, the said property was conveyed by James Jones to the defendant Elizabeth Smith, a niece of the defendant William Smith. Said conveyance was made under an agreement theretofore made between the defendant William Smith and James Jones under date of June 1st, 1932. The consideration for the said conveyance was paid by the defendant William Smith, and the said conveyance was made for his use and benefit, although the deed was made to the defendant Elizabeth Smith and title to the said property has remained in her name from the 4th day of December, 1932, up to and including the present time. During the said period from December 4, 1932, up to and including the present time, the defendant William Smith has been the real owner of the said property and has received and enjoyed and now receives and enjoys the rents and profits therefrom. The said property was taken in the name of the defendant Elizabeth Smith and held by her by the procurement of the defendant William Smith and under an agreement with him for the purpose of defrauding the creditors of the said William Smith and preventing the collection of the debts due by him to various and sundry creditors, including the plaintiff. 

4. The defendant William Smith has no property other than the real estate above described, and said real estate, being an equitable and not a legal interest, is not subject to an execution at law. 

WHEREFORE, the plaintiff prays that the said lands hereinabove described may be decreed by this court to be held by the defendant Elizabeth Smith in trust for the defendant William Smith, and that the said lands be subjected to the payment of the plaintiff's judgment hereinabove described. Solicitor for Plaintiff

FORMS 

875 Note. The foregoing form is based upon a bill of complaint stated in Robinson v. Tischler, 69 Fla. 77, 67 So. 565. A creditor's bill to enforce the statutory liability of stockholders is set out in full in Knight v. Tampa Sand Co., 55 

Fla. 728, 46 So. 285. The substance of a creditor's bill to reach an equitable asset of a non-resident debtor is stated in First State Bank v. Fitch, 105 Fla. 

435, 141 So. 299.

Mary Doe, a resident of Sanford, in Seminole County, Florida, brings this bill of complaint against John Doe, a resident of Sanford, in

1. Plaintiff, Mary Doe, and the defendant, John Doe, were married in Volusia County, Florida, on the 21st day of February, 1936. The plaintiff and defendant lived together as man and wife at Sanford, Florida, from the date of their said marriage until the 25th day of 

May, 1937. 

2. On the 25th day of May, 1937, the defendant, without just cause, deserted the plaintiff at Sanford, Florida, leaving her without any money and without any means of support. The defendant, since said date, has not resided with the plaintiff and has not in any way contributed to her support. The said desertion of the plaintiff by the defendant has continued since the said 25th day of May, 1937, and has been willful, obstinate, and continued for a period of more than one year prior to the filing of this bill of complaint. 

3. The defendant deserted the plaintiff without just cause and the plaintiff has always demeaned herself in a proper manner and performed all of her duties toward the said defendant as his wife prior to the said desertion. Since the said desertion, the plaintiff has been compelled to support herself by her own efforts, without any aid or assistance from the defendant.

4. There were no children born of the marriage between the plaintiff and the defendant. There is no property, either real or personal, to be divided by decree of this court. The plaintiff's maiden name was 

Mary Smith. 

5. Plaintiff is an actual bona fide resident of Seminole County, in the State of Florida, and has been a bona fide resident of said county and state for more than ninety days next previous to the filing of this suit for divorce.

WHEREFORE, the plaintiff prays that a decree be entered herein absolutely dissolving the marriage existing between her and the defendant and forever freeing the plaintiff from the bonds of matrimony existing between them, and plaintiff further prays that she be authorized by said decree to assume her maiden name of Mary Smith and to use the same in all respects as if said marriage had not intervened. Solicitor for Plaintiff Note. A bill of complaint containing substantially the same allegations as those of the foregoing form was held sufficient in Fielding v. Fielding, 67 Fla.

Form No. 4 BILL FOR DIVORCE ON GROUND OF EXTREME CRUELTY AND FOR SUIT MONEY, ALIMONY, AND CUSTODY AND MAINTENANCE OF CHILDREN 

In the Circuit Court in and for Orange County, Florida. In Chancery. 

Mary Doe, Plaintiff

VS. 

Bill of Complaint 

John Doe, Defendant 

Mary Doe, a resident of Orlando, in Orange County, Florida, brings this bill of complaint against John Doe, a resident of Orlando, in Orange County, Florida, and alleges: 

1. Plaintiff is now and has been for more than ninety days next previous to the filing of this bill of complaint an actual bona fide resident of Orlando, in Orange County, Florida.

FORMS 

877 2. During the month of January, 1925, the plaintiff and defendant were married to each other in Orlando, Orange County, Florida, and they have resided there as husband and wife ever since their said marriage. There have been two children born of said marriage, to wit, William, a boy of the age of ten years, and Jane, a girl of the age of five years. 

3. During her entire married life to the defendant, the plaintiff has been a true, dutiful, affectionate, and industrious wife, and has, in every way that lay within her power, contributed to the defendant's happiness and contentment and has made his home a cheerful and pleasant abiding place. Plaintiff has never in any manner given the defendant any cause to be dissatisfied with her or to be unhappy in his married life, and plaintiff has been industrious and frugal and done everything in her power to contribute to the defendant's material welfare in life. 

4. Notwithstanding these facts, the defendant, in about the month of June, 1931, commenced to exhibit toward the plaintiff a coldness of manner, an utter disregard of her welfare, and an indifference to her happiness. This coldness, disregard, and indifference has been carried by the defendant to the extent of treating the plaintiff as an inferior being and as a mere convenience to perform household duties and to entertain guests and business associates of the defendant. In this respect, in the month of June, 1933, for the purpose of humiliating and torturing the plaintiff, the defendant told her that he did not love her and that he had lost all love for her six months previously. In furtherance of a deliberate plan to inflict on the plaintiff intense mental pain and humiliation, the defendant abused her mother and father, and continually denounced her father as a mere money maker, without any charitable thought or thought on any subject save and except the acquisition of money. Defendant further stated to plaintiff that her mother was insane and should be committed to an asylum. Plaintiff entertains the usual affection existing between child and parents, and such abuse of her parents by the defendant has been a matter of continual occurrence from the date of their said marriage, the defendant even insisting that, as a consideration for the further recognition on his part of the marital relation, plaintiff should cease all communication with her parents.

5. At a reception at the home of a Mrs. Richard Roe, on May 20, 1933, the defendant, in the hearing of many other guests, and without cause or justification, called plaintiff "a g- d- fool," and said in a loud and insulting manner that he could not bear the sight of her, that he never wanted to see her again, and that he was absolutely through, repeating the latter statement several times. Again on June 1, 1933, the defendant called the plaintiff, in a vicious and insulting manner, "a g— d— fool," and frequently thereafter applied the same insulting epithet to her. 

6. On the 24th day of February, 1934, the defendant suggested, without cause or provocation, that a divorce be obtained and that plaintiff procure the same, and the defendant informed plaintiff that he would be satisfied with nothing but an absolute divorce from her. Continually thereafter the defendant recurred to the question of plaintiff procuring a divorce and repeatedly solicited plaintiff for suggestions as to how the same might or could be effected. Again, as a part of his plan of studied insults, and for the purpose of inflicting mental torture on plaintiff, the defendant, on May 14, 1933, at the Atlantic Country Club's dance, used insulting language to the plaintiff, and to her great humiliation, in the presence of others, refused to dance with her. 

7. On December 21, 1934, the defendant in a fit of rage, referred to plaintiff's mother as "a g- d- mother-in-law," and cursed and gd swore at the plaintiff and all of her ancestors. At that time, not content with driving the plaintiff from the room by his profanity and abuse, the defendant pursued the plaintiff from room to room of their apartment until, after the lapse of several hours, he became exhausted and desisted. 

8. On December 23, 1934, the defendant attempted to extort from the father of the plaintiff the sum of $100,000.00, and insinuated that he should be paid that amount for living with the plaintiff. Knowledge of this attempt did not come to the plaintiff until some months after its occurrence, but it caused plaintiff excruciating mental pain, suffering, and anguish. 

9. On April 1, 1935, the defendant, in a fit of rage, threatened to strike plaintiff with a milk bottle. On another occasion during the same month, the defendant told a mutual acquaintance that he was through with the plaintiff, that he would not live with her again for fear that there might be another child born to them, thereby increasing

FORMS 

879 the plaintiff's hold upon him, and the defendant boasted that, at about that time, he had affairs with other women. The defendant knew all of this would be communicated to the plaintiff, and in fact it was communicated to her shortly thereafter and caused her great mental pain, suffering, and embarrassment. 

10. During the spring of 1935, while preparing to attend a benefit dance, the defendant, for the sole purpose of humiliating and torturing plaintiff, and in the presence of others, bemeaned and abused her, and to further exhibit his disregard and contempt for her, commenced a flirtation over the telephone with a young lady telephone operator, proposing and attempting to date the said operator for some future party. 

11. The defendant, from and after the year 1931, refused to provide the plaintiff with clothing, food, and the other necessities of life, or to provide a home for her, or clothes or food or shelter for the minor children above mentioned, although during all of said period the defendant was earning at his profession as a physician more than $10,- 000.00 per year. In an effort to make her marriage happy and successful, the plaintiff secured funds from her father, and by this means provided clothing and shelter for herself and her children. During a portion of this time the plaintiff was forced to wash and iron the clothes of defendant. The defendant was well able to employ others to do said work, but at all times he treated plaintiff as a menial and inferior being and as a mere possession, without any rights or will of her own. 

12. During all of the period from 1931 up to the time of filing this suit, the defendant, by studied neglect, abuse, insults, abuse of plaintiff's parents, failure and refusal to support, and by other ways and means, has planned to and has inflicted mental torture and extreme cruelty upon the plaintiff, so that she, having been raised in a home of refinement, mutual respect, and love, lived in a state of mental torture and distress, all of which seriously impaired her health, drove her to the verge of a nervous breakdown, and rendered the discharge of her marital duties impracticable. As a result thereof, plaintiff ceased to cohabit with the defendant on the first day of June, 1935. 

13. The defendant has refused to provide for the plaintiff and her children, although he is well able to do so, having an annual income from his profession in excess of $10,000.00 per year and real and per-

sonal property of a minimum value of $25,000.00. Notwithstanding his financial condition, the defendant has forced the plaintiff and her children upon the charity of the world and her relatives for support. 

Plaintiff has no means of her own with which to support herself and her children and, in her weakened condition, she is unable to earn a living for herself and her children. Plaintiff is also without means with which to prosecute this suit. 

WHEREFORE, the plaintiff prays (a) for a decree of this court forever annulling the bonds of matrimony existing between her and the defendant and granting to her an absolute divorce of and from the said defendant, (b) that this court grant to plaintiff the entire care, custody, and control of the children of said marriage, to wit: William 

Doe and Jane Doe, and that the defendant be denied the care, custody, and control of said children and each of them, (c) that the defendant be required to pay to plaintiff such temporary alimony as may be found necessary to support her during the pendency of this suit, to furnish maintenance for the said children pending this suit, and to furnish plaintiff with sufficient money to prosecute this suit and to employ counsel for that purpose, and (d) that, in the final decree of this court, the defendant be required to pay to the plaintiff, as permanent alimony, as long as both the plaintiff and defendant shall live, such sums of money in such installments as to this court may seem right and proper, and that, in said final decree, the defendant be required to furnish the plaintiff such amounts as shall be necessary and proper for the maintenance, support, and education of the said children as long as they or either of them are under the age of twenty-one years. 

Solicitor for Plaintiff Note. The allegations of the foregoing bill of complaint as to the cause of action were held sufficient in Gratz v. Gratz, 127 Fla. 605, 173 So. 442. The remaining allegations and the prayer are predicated upon a bill of complaint set out in full and held sufficient in Wetherington v. Wetherington, 57 Fla. 

551, 49 So. 549. Another bill for divorce on the ground of extreme cruelty which was held sufficient is set out in Dowdy v. Dowdy, 181 So. (Fla.) 901.
