CHAPTER XV HEARING ON COMPLAINT AND ANSWER 

§ 131. Before Cause at Issue. Cited in Nystrom v. Nystrom, 105 

So.2d 605 (Fla. App. 2nd Dist. 1958), noting the distinction between the action taken on a motion for final hearing on complaint and answer, the time for taking of testimony having elapsed, and a motion for decree on the pleadings under Rule 1.11(c), 1954 Fla. R.C.P., which is contemplated as a pre-trial step, whereas the former is a final hearing on the merits. 

§ 131-A. Motion for Decree on the Pleadings.— 

(3rd paragraph, page 98, 1958 Supp.)

Paradise Pools v. Genauer, 104 So.2d 860 (Fla. App. 3rd Dist. 1958), outlining the rule of law to be applied upon a motion for judgment on the pleadings. 

Rule 1.11 (c), 1954 Fla. R.C.P., contemplates the motion for decree on the pleadings as a pre-trial step, as distinguished from a motion for final hearing on complaint and answer, the time for taking of testimony having elapsed, which is on the merits. Nystrom v. Nystrom, 105 So.2d 605 (Fla. App. 2nd Dist. 1958).

A motion for judgment or decree on the pleading is not available to either party until after the pleadings are closed. Pleadings in a civil action are not closed until after the complaint and counterclaim have been answered by the opposing party. Davis v. Davis, 123 So.2d 

377 (Fla.App. 1st Dist. 1960).

Allegations of complaint must be considered as true for purposes of defendant's motion for decree on the pleadings. May v. State ex rel. 

Ervin, 120 So.2d 792 (Fla. App. 2nd Dist. 1960).

Allegations of answer are deemed denied and do not establish such as facts for purpose of defendant's motion for decree on the pleadings. 

May v. State ex rel. Ervin, 120 So.2d 792 (Fla. App. 2nd Dist. 1960).

Suit by former wife to establish and enforce in Florida an Illinois divorce against remarried husband. Order granting wife's motion for decree on pleadings and final decree entered thereon was reversed because the divorced wife could not obtain a determination of amount of arrearage of child support payments by such motion, in the face of denials in the answer which put in issue the exact amount remaining unpaid. Morris v. Truax, 152 So.2d 515 (Fla. App. 2nd Dist. 1963).

§ 131-B. Motion for Summary Final Decree.-The allegations of a sworn complaint will be considered as against a motion for summary decree with supporting affidavits only if the allegations of the sworn complaint meet the requirements of Rule 1.36(e), 1954 Fla. R.C.P. 

Central Bank and Trust Company v. Davis, 102 So.2d 600 (Fla. 1958).

A summary decree may be entered even though motion to strike answer and portions thereof had not been ruled on. Froelich v. Rowley, 102 So.2d 720 (Fla. 1958). 

Note that Olin's, Inc. v. Avis Rental Car System of Florida, 102 

So.2d 159 (Fla. App. 3rd Dist. 1958), was quashed in 104 So.2d 508 (Fla. 1958), on ground that admissions made in motions to dismiss. and to transfer case were improperly considered in entering summary decree.

Where an affidavit contains incompetent and inadmissible matter, the whole affidavit should not be disregarded, but the court should disregard the incompetent and inadmissible matter and give consideration to the competent and admissible portions. Humphrys v. 

Jarrell, 104 So.2d 404 (Fla. App. 2nd Dist. 1958), restating the general principles regarding motions for summary judgment; and reversing summary final decree for specific performance where parties' affidavits, along with other portions of record, established a genuine issue of material fact, and even if vendors' affidavit was insufficient to create an issue on the marketability of the title or otherwise, purchasers' affidavits were also so deficient that they precluded entry of summary decree.

Plaintiff's motion for summary decree before the defendant has answered should not be granted unless it is clear that an issue of material fact can not be presented. Olin's v. Avis Rental Car System of Florida, 105 So.2d 497 (Fla. App. 3rd Dist. 1958), holding that record disclosed genuine and material issues of fact as to whether there had been a breach of contract for which it could be cancelled, precluding summary decree.

In action for adjudication of propriety of increases in salary of corporation's officers, there was a material question of fact as to the reasonableness of the increases precluding a summary decree. Sarasota Tile & T. Corp. v. De Soto Terrazzo Corp., 105 So.2d 811 (Fla. 

App. 2nd Dist. 1958).

Where married woman, by joining with her husband in bringing suit for specific performance of contract for sale of her property signed only by him, ratified his acts and thus adopted the contract as her own, the defendant's denial of such agency was not a genuine issue which would preclude a summary decree. Williams v. Noel, 105 

So.2d 901 (Fla. App. 3rd Dist. 1958).

While it may be better practice to have motions for summary decree supported by proof in the form of affidavits, there is no compulsion to do so if the interested parties elect to submit it orally and the trial court so permits. Hall v. Davis, 106 So.2d 599 (Fla. App. 1st Dist. 1958).

SUPPLEMENT 

37 Where wife's affidavit claimed husband consented for removal of children from Wisconsin to Florida, and husband's affidavit denied such consent, this raised a genuine issue of a material fact that should not have been resolved by a summary decree. Shulman v. Miller, 107 

So.2d 274 (Fla. App. 3rd Dist. 1959).

Where the effect of admissions in an answer is that defendant concedes liability as to certain items in an accounting, it is error not to grant plaintiff's motion for summary decree for liability for such sums. Brooker v. Smith, 108 So.2d 790 (Fla. App. 2nd Dist. 1959).

It being a question of fact as well as law whether vel non a zoning act as applied to specific property is invalid, it is error to make such determination on a summary procedure. City of Punta Gorda v. 

Morningstar, 110 So.2d 449 (Fla. App. 2nd Dist. 1959).

Summary decree was properly entered for defendants in suit to void sale of sovereignty lands by Trustees of Internal Improvement Fund where depositions, affidavits and exhibits failed to show existence of grounds for suit. Anderson v. Collins, 111 So.2d 44 (Fla. App. 2nd 

Dist. 1959).

See Comment, Recent Developments in the Law of Summary Judg ment in Florida, 13 U. of Mia. L. Rev. 457 (Summer, 1959).

Genuine issues of material facts with respect to substantial economic dependency of community's general welfare upon business of tourism which would be damaged if not destroyed in event aesthetic beauty of area is threatened by indiscriminate display of outdoor signs advertising rates for accommodations precluded summary decree that ordinance against same was unconstitutional. City of Daytona Beach v. 

Abdo, 112 So.2d 398 (Fla. App. 1st Dist. 1959).

See deposition as to way of necessity which precluded summary decree for defendant, in Bradshaw v. Prasek, 114 So.2d 821 (Fla. App. 

2nd Dist. 1959).

Pleadings, affidavits and exhibits held to present a triable issue of fact as to whether mortgagor had been misled as to length of grace period, precluding entry of summary decree for foreclosure of mortgage under acceleration clause. Groner-Youngerman, Inc. v. Denison, 117 So.2d 210 (Fla. App. 2nd Dist. 1959), restating applicable rules.

Deposition, opposing evidentiary effect of return of service, showing that parties were not in the county and that house was occupied by others when service was purportedly made there, precluded summary decree for defendants in suit to set aside foreclosure decree and sale. 

Rumpf v. Freedman, 118 So.2d 237 (Fla. App. 3rd Dist. 1960), noting that the need to satisfy a higher quantum of proof does not change the rule that where there is a genuine issue to be resolved as to any material fact, a summary decree should not be entered. 

Where validity of contract was the issue raised by counterclaim in suit for foreclosure, and motion to dismiss counterclaim had not been passed upon, it was error to award plaintiffs a "final" summary decree prior to adjudication of counterclaim. Mannion v. Owen, 121 So.2d 

816 (Fla. App. 1st Dist. 1960).

In the absence of proof of material allegation of complaint, a summary final decree must be set aside, even though opposing party does not file counteraffidavits or other proof. Langley v. New Deal Cab 

Co., 138 So.2d 789 (Fla. App. 1st Dist. 1962).

CHAPTER XVIII TAKING TESTIMONY  

See Evidence, Fourth Survey of Florida Law, Part One, 14 U. of Mia.

§ 143. Time for Taking.— 

(7th paragraph, page 115, 1958 Supp.)

A cause is not at issue within the meaning of Rule 3.13, 1954 Fla. 

R.C.P., so long as there remains an undisposed of motion for decree pro confesso. A litigant can only benefit from the rule when issues have been created by a complaint and an answer thereto, or a decree pro confesso has been duly entered. Cellucci v. King-Universal Corp., 106 So.2d 629 (Fla. App. 3rd Dist. 1958). 

Defendant's motions for leave to amend answer and to rescind order appointing special master, neither of which was granted, did not have the effect of postponing the time for taking testimony. Nystrom v. 

Nystrom, 105 So.2d 605 (Fla. App. 2nd Dist. 1958). 

In suit to set aside conveyance and assignment made to defraud minor judgment debtor, affidavits that expense of treating minor for injuries so depleted funds that timely prosecution of suit had been impossible justified extension of time to take testimony. Tornwall v. 

Carter, 106 So.2d 96 (Fla. App. 2nd Dist. 1958). 

Ch. 59-64, Laws of Florida, amended § 65.20, F.S.A., relating to delay in divorce cases. 

Where, upon remand after reversal of final decree, the cause is pending for the submission of any available additional testimony before the 

Chancellor, the time limitation prescribed by Rule 3.13, 1954 Fla.

R.C.P., 31 F.S.A., can not in any event come into play; and when the 

Chancellor sets the matter for the further taking of testimony pursuant to the mandate he acts in complete accord with the provisions of the rule. Smith v. Smith, 118 So.2d 204 (Fla. 1960).

Footnote 5.-Hevia v. Palm Terrace Fruit Co., 119 So.2d 795 (Fla. 

App. 2nd Dist. 1960), where defendants having filed answer and proceeded to taking of testimony without having secured ruling on motions to dismiss, strike, and for more definite statement were held not to be in position to complain that cause was not at issue at time testimony was taken.

Footnote 8.-Tornwall v. Carter, 106 So.2d 96 (Fla. App. 2nd Dist. 

1958); Bollet v. Di Filippo, 113 So.2d 432 (Fla. App. 2nd Dist. 1959),

affirming two-month continuance as to plaintiff's case in rebuttal of defendant's counterclaim. 

§ 144. How Taken.- Footnote 45.—The provisions of § 54.09, F.S.A., relative to the right of a plaintiff to take a non-suit before the jury retires, have been applied generally in law actions. Assuming they could apply to a chancery suit in which a jury trial was authorized, the plaintiff does not come within the provisions thereof by requesting a voluntary non-suit before the impaneling of a jury for the reason that the cause is not "on trial." Welgoss v. End, 112 So.2d 390 (Fla. App. 3rd Dist. 1959).

Evidence relating to procedures employed by comptroller with respect to hearings afforded under F.S.A. § 212.15 (4) was relevant and should have been admitted in action for injunction against executing collection of delinquent sales taxes. Green v. Hood, 120 So.2d 223 (Fla. App. 2nd Dist. 1960), which also see as to proffer of excluded evidence, and admissibility of carbon copy of letter.

§ 149-A. Depositions Under Common Law Rules.-A careful read ing of Rule 1.22, 1954 Fla. R.C.P., reveals that the requirement for verification is contained in the portion of the rule providing for depositions before action, subsection "a". The reference is to a petition. 

On the other hand, in subsection "b", where the reference is to a motion there is no requirement for verification. Such a distinction has sense because in the first situation the verified petition sets the court's machinery for preservation of testimony in operation, and in the second situation the motion is for an order which should be granted as a matter of course, unless the trial judge, who is already familiar with the case, finds that there is some reason that the preservation of testimony is not proper. Chaachou v. Chaachou, 102 So.2d 820 (Fla. 

App. 3rd Dist, 1958).

Denial of a motion to compel the attendance of defendants at a deposition is proper when the case is pending on an interlocutory appeal from an order denying a temporary injunction. Buck Plumbing v. Bel-Aire, Inc., 103 So.2d 670 (Fla. App. 3rd Dist. 1958). 

The reason for taking the deposition is not one of the elements of notice required of depositions pending action. 1954 Fla. R.C.P. Rules 

1.21 and 1.24, 30 F.S.A. Depositions of a party may be used by the adverse party for any purpose. 1954 Fla. R.C.P. Rule 1.21(d)(2), 30

F.S.A. Refusal to admit same in evidence is not reversible error where the deponent is available, testifies and is extensively cross-examined at the trial. Vecsey v. Vecsey, 115 So.2d 719, (Fla. App. 3rd Dist. 1959). 

See Spector v. Altere, 138 So.2d 517 (Fla. App. 3rd Dist. 1962), where it was held that the court, by quashing notice to take deposition of defendants' attorney, improperly prevented discovery of information in areas not privileged. 

Union brought an action against an employer to enforce an arbitration award requiring the employer to pay sums into a welfare fund.

The dismissal of the action was not an abuse of discretion where the union, after court had entered summary judgment for it but reserved jurisdiction to determine issue of amount due, refused to comply with notice for taking of deposition on ground that testimony and records sought were privileged. Local 415 Miami Joint Council of the 

International Ladies Garment Workers' Union v. Weitz, 141 So.2d 

18 (Fla. App. 3rd Dist. 1962). 

§ 150. Production of Records and Documents.-Rules 1.28 and 

1.34, 1954 Fla. R.C.P., are in pari materia; and, as a consequence, a party must make the showing of good cause required by Rule 1.28 before another party will be required to produce documents under the subpoena duces tecum provided for in Rule 1.34(d). Brooker v. Smith, 108 So.2d 790 (Fla. App. 2nd Dist. 1959). 

Motion for production of documents filed after issues have been determined will be denied. Rule 1.28, 1954 Fla. R.C.P., 30 F.S.A.; Mack v. Mack, 115 So.2d 447 (Fla. App. 2nd Dist. 1959).

A party, who is required to defend against a complaint or counterclaim which charges that his actions have resulted in a loss of business to his opponent over a period of time, is entitled to discovery inspection of his adversary's books and records reflecting the business which allegedly sustained such loss. Cooper v. Fulton, 117 So.2d 33 (Fla. App. 

Where records of a business are to be examined for discovery, ordinarily they should not be required to be delivered to the adversary, but to be made available for inspection, etc., at the owner's place of business during reasonable business hours, unless the parties mutually agree to some other place and time. Cooper v. Fulton, 117 So.2d 33 

(Fla. App. 3rd Dist. 1960).

Cravero Constructors, Inc., 117 So.2d 764 (Fla. App.

§ 167. Right to Appeal.- 

Fla. App. Rules 2.1f(2), and 3.10, amended Oct. 8, 1958, effective 

November 1, 1958. 105 So.2d 209.

Supreme Court will decline to take jurisdiction of direct appeal under Fla. App. Rule 2.1a (5) (a), which for all intents and purposes is identical with Art. V, Sec. 4(2), Fla. Const., where the decree did not undertake to construe a controlling provision of the Federal Constitution, but will transfer same to District Court of Appeal. International Hod Carriers, Etc., v. Heftler Const. Co., 112 So.2d 848 (Fla. 

1959), stating four procedural prerequisites to be established to invoke jurisdiction, viz: 

1. The constitutional question must have been raised at the first opportunity, 2. The constitutional provision claimed to have been violated must have been designated specifically either by explicit reference to the article and section or by quotation of the provision, 3. The facts showing the violation must have been stated, and 

4. The constitutional question must have been preserved throughout for review. This requirement contemplates adequate coverage of the constitutional question in the appellate briefs. 

See Davies v. Davies, 113 So.2d 250 (Fla. App. 3rd Dist. 1959), for illustration of proper certified question under Fla. App. Rule 4.6. 

The general rule is that mere construction of a statute, whether right or wrong, does not present a constitutional question vesting the appellate court with jurisdiction to review the judgment. A challenge to a statute that invests the appellate court with jurisdiction

on the ground that a constitutional question is raised must be grounded on the fact that the statute is inherently invalid or uncon stitutional. Fla. Const. Art. 5, Sec. 4(2). Borden Co. v. Odham, 121 

So.2d 625 (Fla. 1960). See also, In Re Kionka's Estate, 121 So.2d 644 (Fla. 1960), specially concurring opinion.

The Supreme Court does not have jurisdiction of a direct appeal from a decree which merely holds a statute unconstitutional as applied to plaintiffs under the facts of the particular case without determining the validity of the statute per se. Snedeker v. Vernmar, Ltd., 139 

So.2d 682 (Fla. 1962). 

Footnote 1.-In Re Rasey's Estate, 105 So.2d 904 (Fla. App. 2nd 

Dist. 1958); In Re Juen's Estate, 105 So.2d 908, 911 (Fla. App. 2nd 

Dist. 1958).

Footnote 2.-Under Fla. Const. Art. 5, § 4(b), as amended in 1956, direct appeal does not lie to the Supreme Court from a decree in a proceeding under F.S.A. § 104.27 (2) and (9) where contentions of unconstitutionality of statute constituted abstract issues not related to the particular facts of the case, and did not require disposition, so that an adverse ruling thereon could not be said to be inherent in the decision. Evans v. Carroll, 104 So.2d 375 (Fla. 1958), transferring appeal to the District Court of Appeal under Fla. App. Rule 2.1 subd. a (5) (d).

Decree, based on finding that property owners did not have property right that was being invaded by construction of dam, is not appealable directly to the Supreme Court. Carmazi v. Board of County 

Com'rs of Dade County, 104 So.2d 727 (Fla. 1958).

District Court of Appeal rather than Supreme Court has jurisdiction of appeal from final decree applying constitution in upholding validity of municipal ordinance. Armstrong v. City of Tampa, 106 So.2d 407 (Fla. 1958).

Supreme Court will entertain interlocutory appeal from order to show cause issued on petition for enforcement of final decree it had affirmed before July 1, 1957. South Dade Farms, Inc. v. Peters, 107 

So.2d 30 (Fla. 1958).

Supreme Court has jurisdiction of appeal from decision of Circuit Court holding statute constitutional. Standard Newspapers, Inc. v. 

Woods, 110 So.2d 397 (Fla. 1959).

Supreme Court has jurisdiction for direct review of decree "directly passing upon the validity of a state statute," where a decision on the validity of an act was necessary to a determination of the cause as was inherent in the decree. Harrell's Candy Kitchen v. Sarasota-Manatee

Air. A., 111 So.2d 439 (Fla. 1959); Fla. Const. Art. 5, Sec. 4. 

Supreme Court had no jurisdiction of appeal from decree declaring a statute unconstitutional, where appellant by its briefs and points raised did not assert its right to a review of that aspect of the decree, or rely on the same as a point on appeal, but merely raised and argued points that the trial court lacked jurisdiction to determine the constitutionality of the statute, and that the appellees were estopped to raise the question. City of Miami v. Steckloff, 111 So.2d 446 (Fla. 1959).

Post final decree order is subject to review by appeal under Fla.

SUPPLEMENT 

71 A judgment of affirmance by an equally divided court is a bar to any subsequent action for the same cause, but possesses no dignity as a judicial precedent. Rainsford v. McArthur Dairies, 114 So.2d 617 (Fla. 1959).

Dismissal of appeal for failure of appellant to file assignments of error does not have the effect of directly affirming the trial court's order, but it has that practical effect, as between the parties. Bailey v. 

Bailey, 114 So.2d 804 (Fla. App. 1st Dist. 1959).

Where appellate court determined that adoption should have been denied, and custody of child returned to mother, and reversed the decree and remanded the cause "for further proceedings not inconsistent with this opinion," the Chancellor was not authorized to further try the issue of custody and could only vacate the decree of adoption and direct transfer of custody to mother. In Re Chakmakis' Adoption, 116 

So.2d 256 (Fla. App. 3rd Dist. 1959). 

Where Supreme Court, on stipulation pending appeal, remanded the cause to the Circuit Court "for a hearing and specific rulings as to the constitutional issues raised," it was the understanding of the Supreme Court that by the use of the words "issues raised" they were to comprehend issues previously presented and considered by the trial judge but not specifically passed upon in his final decree. It was certainly never intended to restore the cause to the docket of the trial court in order to enable the parties to generate new issues and thereby belatedly establish a jurisdictional foundation for direct appeal to the Supreme Court. When the trial judge announced that "the matter of constitutional issues was never before presented in this court," such finding fully complied with the mandate, and in effect eliminated any jurisdictional basis for the Supreme Court's consideration of the matter on direct appeal, so it was transferred to the District Court of appeal. Amendola v. Amendola, 118 So.2d 13 (Fla. 1960).

When a given cause has received consideration on appeal, its merits determined, and the cause remanded with specific directions, the court to which such mandate is directed has no power to do anything but obey the mandate. Petition of Vermeulen, 122 So.2d 318 (Fla. App. 

1st Dist. 1960).

The respondent in a rule to show cause based on non-payment of alimony or child support provided for in a previously entered divorce decree need not be served with process, but may be served by mail or by such other method as the court may direct which is reasonably calculated to convey to him notice of the proceeding and thus to afford him an opportunity to respond thereto and to be heard. Service on the attorney who represented the defendant in the divorce suit ordinarily will not be adequate or proper service or notice to the defendant after final decree, where it does not result in his receiving notice of the proceeding and when the attorney disclaims continued representation of the defendant. This rule is different where the cause is pending or not yet concluded. Ginsberg v. Ginsberg, 122 So.2d 30 (Fla. App. 3rd 

Dist. 1960).

So.2d 557 (1962).

§ 268. Right to Relief-Miscellaneous Cases.-Where record did not disclose violence sufficient to give state jurisdiction to enjoin picketing on that ground, Florida courts were without jurisdiction to enjoin organizational picketing of resort hotels engaged in interstate commerce, even though National Labor Relations Board refused to take

jurisdiction. Hotel Employees Union, Local No. 255 v. Sax Enterprises, 79 S. Ct. 273, 358 U. S. 270, 3 L. Ed. 2d 289 (U. S. Fla. 1959).

App. 3rd Dist. 1959). 

State court has no jurisdiction to enjoin peaceful and non-mass picketing designed to require the employer to recognize union as bargaining representative, where employer is engaged in interstate commerce. Amalgamated Cloth. Wkrs. v. Donald S. La Vigne, Inc., 111 So.2d 462 (Fla. App. 3rd Dist. 1959).

Estate Commission, 113 So.2d 714 (Fla. App. 2nd Dist. 1959). 

Where testimony failed to disclose any acts of violence in connection. with the picketing, a temporary injunction against picketing will be reversed, but affirmed insofar as it enjoins union from molesting, interfering, coercing or directing any violence toward employer's prop erty or employees. International Ladies Garment W. U. v. Sherry Mfg. 

Co., 115 So.2d 27 (Fla. App. 3rd Dist. 1959).

State court has jurisdiction as to restaurant not engaged on interstate commerce, to enjoin union from picketing and interfering with right of ingress and egress. Hotel & Restaurant Emp., Etc. v. Creighton's R. Corp., 115 So.2d 30 (Fla. App. 2nd Dist. 1959).

If unfair labor practice (secondary boycott) has an effect on interstate commerce, state court will deny injunction as National Labor 

Relations Board has exclusive jurisdiction. International Hod Car riers', Etc. v. Heftler Const. Co., 116 So.2d 30 (Fla. App. 3rd Dist. 

1959), also declining to transfer claim for damages to law side of court.

Generic Terms or mere descriptive words are not ordinarily susceptible of exclusive appropriation by an individual as a trademark or trade name. They are deemed to be the common property of the public, available for use by anyone offering goods or performing services which they describe. However, they may, by usage, acquire a secondary, special or trade meaning as indicating or identifying the goods, business or services of the user, as distinguished from its common or general meaning. In such cases the user is entitled to protection against subsequent unfair or piratical use by another. The subsequent user is under a duty to take precautions to distinguish or identify his goods or business and thus avoid confusion of customers or patrons. The fraudulent use of such terms or words to entice patrons or customers in the belief that the goods or services are those of the prior user is unlawful. Williamson v. CHAPTER XXIX PARTITION 

§ 313. In General.-Where wife complied with condition of divorce decree granting her a tenancy in common in premises, previously owned as estate by the entireties, with sole use and possession for as long as she used same for a home and remained unmarried, such use and possession could not be disturbed by partition by children of husband who devised his interest to them. Radford v. Radford, 117 So.2d 522 (Fla. App. 1st Dist. 1960).

In action for partition it was held that plaintiffs who allegedly owned the entire fee excepting an undivided one-half interest in oil, gas and other minerals owned by defendants were entitled to partition of mineral rights but not of entire fee. Rudman v. Baine, 133 So.2d 

760 (Fla. App. 1st Dist. 1961). 

Upon acquiring jurisdiction to partition, the court may proceed to ascertain and adjudicate the rights and interests of the parties as authorized by statute. As an incident to the main relief, the court may determine questions of right arising out of relation existing between parties at the time of the occurrence of the incident giving rise to differences between them. Leonard v. Browne, 134 So.2d 872 (Fla. App. 

1st Dist. 1961). 

$319. Defenses.- 

Footnote 71.-Vaughn v. Vaughn, 119 So.2d 391 (Fla. App. 1st Dist.

Allen v. Wilhelm, 113 So.2d 857 (Fla.

App. 2nd Dist. 1959). 

A tenant in common is not liable to his co-tenant for the rental value for exclusive enjoyment of occupancy without objection, and should be required to account only for rent received from third party. Taylor v. Taylor, 119 So.2d 811 (Fla. App. 2nd Dist. 1960), also holding finding as to value of land erroneous, in absence of evidence to support it.

§ 384. Defenses.- 

Specific performance is not a remedy of absolute right but one that rests within the sound judicial discretion of the Chancellor. Because of this, reasonable latitude should be allowed the defensive pleader to assert matters which have a bearing upon the discretion of the Chancellor and yet may not be strictly in bar of the action. Mills v. Beims, 132 So.2d 228 (Fla. App. 2d Dist. 1961).

Where the case is a close one and the evidence conflicting, the finding of an implied trust by the chancellor will not be affirmed if the appellate court can find evidence to support the chancellor's findings. 

The evidence in such case must be of clear and convincing character.

2nd Dist. 1959).

APPENDIX E IN THE SUPREME COURT OF FLORIDA JANUARY TERM, A.D. 1962 In Re: Florida Rules of Civil Procedure 1962 Revision Opinion filed June 20, 1962 PER CURIAM. 

Appended to this order is a complete compilation of the Florida Rules of Civil Procedure and all amendments, revisions or additions which have been made since July 1, 1957, adopted pursuant to the power vested in this Court by Article V of the Florida Constitution. This compilation and revision shall govern all proceedings within the scope of these rules after midnight September 30, 1962. 

This compilation and revision shall supersede all conflicting rules and statutes. 

All statutes not superseded hereby or in conflict herewith shall remain in effect as rules promulgated by the Supreme Court. 

Adopted and approved by the Court en banc June 18th, 1962. 

It is so ordered.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF FLORIDA JANUARY TERM, A.D. 1962 

In Re: Florida Appellate Rules 1962 Revision Opinion filed June 20, 1962 PER CURIAM. 

Appended to this order is a complete compilation of the Florida Appellate Rules and all amendments, revisions or additions which have been made since July 1, 1957, adopted pursuant to the power vested in this Court by Article V of the Florida Constitution. This compilation and revision shall govern all appellate proceedings in the Supreme Court, district courts of appeal and circuit courts after midnight, September 30, 1962. This compilation and revision shall supersede all conflicting rules and statutes. All statutes not superseded hereby or in conflict herewith shall remain in effect as rules promulgated by the Supreme Court. 

Rule 2.2 relating to district courts of appeal is included in this compilation and revision for the convenience of the Bench and Bar and contains, according to information furnished this Court by the district courts of appeal, all amendments, revisions or additions from July 1, 1957. Such portions of Rule 2.2 as are within the jurisdiction of this Court to enact or approve are hereby approved and promulgated.

Adopted and approved by the Court en banc June 18th, 1962. 

It is so ordered.
